Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
- Published
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published8 October
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."
Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the biggest general strike in French history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.
Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.
"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.
Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.
France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.
Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.
Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.
The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.
"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".
"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."
I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."
"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day.
Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.”
Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon. “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” he added.
The alternative, he argued, would be tantamount “to a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership … I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.”
Rama, who won a historic fourth term last year, has vowed to get what was once the continent’s most isolated Stalinist state into the 27-member bloc by 2030.
The unrest – in contrast to the largely peaceful protests of recent months – marks the veteran leader’s biggest challenge yet.
On Thursday, after a night of running street battles between demonstrators and riot police, residents awoke to see the facades of shops smashed and traffic signals destroyed, with government buildings and banks burned and ransacked. An estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured.
The renewed violence has created an atmosphere of unpredictability amid predictions that public patience may finally be running out for the socialist government after 13 years in power.
“Young Albanians are tired of all the corruption, tired of all the arrogance. They want to live in a better country and they are not afraid to use violence,” said Afrim Krasniqi, the director of the Albanian Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. “There is no prognosis. Nobody can say what will come next.”
But Rama, who emerged from the protest movement himself – becoming the face of state violence when he dared to criticise Albania’s first-post-communist government 30 years ago – also doubled down.
“Students are the future. They are the ones who look ahead, who want to go further and faster,” he said as he visited the fire-damaged premises of Tirana’s College of Europe on Thursday. “Today, this is the ruin left by hands that are not, and can never be, the hands of students. These are the hands that try to push Albania down every time Albania tries to rise.”
While he was willing to talk with the younger generation about the rising costs of education – a central complaint that has also spurred the unrest – vandalism would not be tolerated, he said.
For nearly five months, demonstrators have gathered daily outside Rama’s office, prompted by plans for a controversial tourism complex championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The venture foresees construction along pristine coastline deemed a conservation zone of unique natural beauty, including the uninhabited island of Sazan.
Labelled the “flamingo revolution” because of the risk posed by the development to wildlife and delicate ecosystems, the rallies have attracted crowds big and small. They, too, have demanded the prime minister resign.
Despite the opposition, Rama has steadfastly refused to back down, defending the project as a “gift” that will boost the economy and provide badly needed jobs by transforming Albania into a high-end tourist destination.
But Krasniqi said he believed the protest movement was at an inflection point – even if the demonstrations had also been inspired by similar student unrest sweeping Europe, particularly France.
“I think this week we reached a turning point,” he said. “The government had more than four months to talk to people, who every day have been out on the street. It chose to belittle and dismiss them instead. And now students have joined in, and they appear to have the upper hand.”
For the first time, Krasniqi said, he had heard young people saying they were prepared to be hurt or go to jail if that was the price “for ensuring democracy”.
“Their demands are very different to the [flamingo] protesters. They want better education, better university buildings, a society that offers them hope. They also don’t believe Albania should be for sale.”
At €4bn (€3.37bn), the Trump family-backed resort would be the biggest investment the nation has seen.
Last week, addressing the controversy triggered by the project, Kushner admitted he and his investment firm, Affinity Partners, were “betting on a country that has never had a project of this scale”.
“There are no guarantees,” he said. “We are taking that risk because we believe in Albania and we believe in Albanians. If successful, the project would represent approximately €4bn of investment and create significant jobs, economic activity and international visibility for Albania.”
This week environmentalists, who first led the charge against the development, begged to differ. Months after the protests began, people still felt as exercised about a venture many believed would only benefit the elite, said Aleksandër Trajçe, who heads the country’s leading conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania.
“Anger over the [Kushner] project has prepared the ground for the violence we are seeing, because day after day protesters have been faced with the arrogance of a government that has refused to listen to them, or give an inch.”

B2B ecommerce unicorn Udaan’s operating revenue grew 12.6% to ₹5,134 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 (FY26) from ₹4,561 Cr in FY25. The startup’s net loss narrowed 19.4% to ₹851.5 Cr from ₹1,055.4 Cr in the previous fiscal, according to its financial statements. The recovery follows an uneven revenue trajectory — a 40% decline in FY23, marginal growth of 1.7% in FY24, and a 20% fall in FY25. During this period, Udaan also closed a $114 Mn Series G funding round in June 2025 at a 59% valuation dip. In a LinkedIn post, Udaan’s senior vice president Vishnu Menon attributed the improvement to the startup’s focus on profitable growth, operational efficiency, and tighter execution across its markets. Over the 10 quarters from Q4 CY23 to Q1 CY26, the company’s revenue grew at a CAGR of around 25%, while its contribution margin improved by nearly 500 basis points and EBITDA burn declined by around 70%, Menon said. Menon attributed this progress to its cluster-led operating model, which focuses on accountability for performance at the city and category levels, deeper operations in existing markets, and tighter cost controls. However, Udaan’s financial statements flagged material uncertainty that could cast significant doubt on the group’s ability to continue as a going concern. At the end of FY26, the group’s current liabilities exceeded its current assets by ₹1,391 Cr, while its total liabilities exceeded its total assets by ₹790.9 Cr. The startup said it received additional funding after the financial year ended and expects revenue growth and cost-cutting measures to improve operating cash flows. Founded in 2016 by former Flipkart executives Amod Malviya, Sujeet Kumar, and Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan operates a B2B digital marketplace connecting manufacturers, brands, wholesalers, and retailers, including kirana stores, chemists, and general merchants, through a mobile app. Udaan’s Bumpy FY27 Despite the improvement in its FY26 financial performance, Udaan faced fresh challenges in the ongoing fiscal, with creditors initiating insolvency proceedings against its offshore parent over a bond default. Creditors, including Tor Investment Management, Samena Capital, and Arena Investors, initiated proceedings in the Singapore High Court after Udaan’s offshore holding entity, Trustroot Internet Pvt Ltd, defaulted on $170 Mn worth of compulsorily convertible notes due on June 30. Confirming the development at the time, Udaan told Inc42 that the proceedings concerned its offshore holding company and would not have any material impact on its operations in India. Later in July, Udaan announced a proposed $160 Mn financing transaction, comprising fresh equity, new debt, and conversion of existing debt into equity. Last month, Udaan announced an agreement to acquire Swiggy’s retail distribution business, LYNK, in an all-share transaction valuing the business at ₹500 Cr. Swiggy also announced plans to invest another ₹75 Cr in Udaan’s parent entity. Udaan expects the acquisition to expand its retail distribution capabilities and market reach, while improving efficiency across the combined network. Udaan Bets On Private Labels, Institutional Sales Udaan is also looking to improve its revenue mix and margins through private labels and its institutional procurement business, horeca360. According to Menon, private labels now account for 15-25% of staples sales across Udaan’s operating cities. He expects the segment to improve margins and capture a larger share of customers’ spending using its existing sourcing and distribution infrastructure. Meanwhile, horeca360, which caters to hotels, restaurants, caterers, and institutional buyers, expanded into Hyderabad and Chennai during FY26. The business aims to deepen customer relationships and improve utilisation of Udaan’s supply chain network. Menon said it would continue to focus on improving revenue quality, strengthening execution at the city level, and increasing operating efficiency as it works towards sustained profitability and a public listing.

Valve is introducing a major new feature for Steam achievements called “achievement sets” that lets developers list different groups of achievements for a base game and DLCs.
Steam can now show game achievements in separate ‘sets’
Developers with games on Steam can split achievements from a base game and its DLC into sets with their own progress bars.
“In games that support sets, you still unlock achievements by playing the game as usual,” Valve says. “But when you browse what you have unlocked afterward, Steam will break the long list of game achievements into the developer-created sets, making it easier to see what you have completed and to find other related achievements you can unlock next.” Achievement sets have their own progress bars, and if you finish a set, you’ll get a “set complete” trophy that’s visible on your profile.
Steam will support seasonal achievement sets that developers can archive, too. “We think there are a lot of fun ways games can take advantage of the temporary nature this can add, such as adding achievements to season-based games or enabling time-limited holiday achievements,” Valve says.
A handful of games already support achievement sets, per Valve:

The new achievements features are available in the latest Steam client beta, Valve says.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila
BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell
Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan appear on vintage game shows in the retro music video for the “Expectations” remix, featuring appearances from musician David Byrne and producer Dan Nigro.
The clip, directed by Bardia Zeinali, shows Rodrigo and Roan (in her first-ever feature) appearing on sets clearly inspired by “Family Feud” and “Hollywood Squares.” Byrne appears as Johnny Johnson, host of the “Big Expectations” show, where he asks three Rodrigos in different outfits “a little bit how you got here.”
What follows is a trip to the different sets and a new “Expectations” verse from Roan, who shows up on the set of “Sister Squabble” to contend with Rodrigo in a “Family Feud” face-off. “I took her to a concert front row thought it’d be fun,” she sings. “Her hand moving up my skirt, no piercing on her tongue / She said she’d call me later, that was three weeks ago / Classic L.A. behavior, she could’ve just said no.”
Popular on Variety
Nigro, who produced “Expectations” along with Roan and Rodrigo’s albums, pops up at the end clutching a giant brick of a phone straight out of the 1990s. His appearance makes sense, as he produced the track and its parent album “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love.”
Speaking to Apple Music’s Zane Lowe on Thursday afternoon, Roan and Rodrigo explained why they teamed for the remix. “This is obviously my first feature,” said Roan. “I’ve never done this before, so it feels perfect to me. I don’t know. I feel like it represents a generation of songwriters that are just really thinking about their lyrics. I felt like with this song, I was like, ‘Wow, it’s so cool that she is putting a pretty difficult concept within the pop song,’ which is my favorite pop songs ever.”
Rodrigo explained that she had asked Byrne to appear in the video but was a “bit sheepish” about making the request. “I always feel shy asking people for favors, but he was so down,” she said. “He showed up the entire day. He had a character that he had built out and he made this Johnny Johnson character. There’s so many outtakes we have of him just improvising and riffing and he was so into it. And I was like, ‘Gosh, David, maybe he should be an actor too one of these days.” He’s very multi-talented.”
Beyond sharing Nigro as a producer, Rodrigo and Roan go back some years, as the latter supported the former on both her “Sour” and “Guts” tours. Roan recently performed at Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival in late August as part of an all-female lineup that featured Doechii, Rachel Chinouriri, Garbage, the Breeders and more.

A large swathe of Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west has been locked down by police as they search for a man reportedly carrying a shotgun who allegedly set alight a stolen car in the area before fleeing on foot.
A police helicopter and armed tactical police focused their search for the man on an area around Williams Parade and Constitution Road.
Police were called to a car park on Williams Parade at about 10.20am on Friday in response to reports of a stolen vehicle. Officers were told a man carrying a longarm weapon was sitting inside the vehicle. It is alleged the man then set the car alight before fleeing on foot.
Speaking to reporters, police Supt Despa Fitzgerald said: “Do not approach this person – we understand he’s armed with a shotgun.”
She said there was no indication shots had been fired.
Police described the man as being of Caucasian appearance, aged in his 20s, about 160cm tall and of thin build, with shaggy hair. He was last seen on Union Street wearing a blue T-shirt and long black pants.
No injuries have been reported. Police have been doorknocking, telling residents to stay inside.
Light rail services in the area have been suspended and nearby businesses and cafes have been put into lockdown, along with neighbouring primary schools.
People outside the police exclusion zone are being advised to avoid the area.

Crawley signs Kent extension after losing England deal
- Published
England batter Zak Crawley has signed a one-year contract extension with Kent to keep him at the county next summer.
The 28-year-old has agreed the new deal three days after his central contract was not renewed when the England and Wales Cricket Board released its updated list.
Crawley has not featured in a Test since the final game of last winter's Ashes tour in Sydney and last appeared for England in a one-day international in Sri Lanka in January.
He played in 12 County Championship matches for Kent this season as they won promotion back to Division One, making 608 runs with a top score of 89 among four half-centuries.
"It's an exciting time as we head back into Division One of the County Championship and I'm looking forward to the challenge of competing for Kent this coming summer," said Crawley.
"It's great to see so many young players coming through the system here, similar to my journey into first-team cricket, and I'm excited to help them settle into the first team and further their development for the long term."
The opener has made more than 180 appearances in all competitions for his home county since his debut in 2017.

Modern medicine has never been more capable than it is today. Tests detect illness earlier, scans reveal invisible abnormalities, medicines prevent and treat diseases, and interventions and procedures can save lives within minutes. Yet, the same system that can do more is increasingly tempted to overtreat and overmedicate.
Also read |Lifestyle, not medicine, is key to good health
Overtreatment and overmedication are not simply the use of an unnecessary medicine but often a chain: a test detects an incidental abnormality, which leads to another test, a diagnosis and then a prescription that may become permanent. What begins as prevention can end in long-term medication or surgery. Then, in India, overtreatment coexists with undertreatment: unnecessary interventions are offered to some, while many others still lack essential primary care, affordable medicines and timely treatment.
Health packages and tests
The rise of overtreatment is the result of a convergence of several factors. The first driver of overtreatment is unnecessary and excessive testing — both screening and diagnostic — which creates a cascade of care. A review article in the prestigious National Medical Journal of India in 2016 found that routine health-check packages often include unwarranted tests that can lead to false-positive results, anxiety, further investigations, overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The truth is that the ability to test has expanded faster than our ability to decide who actually needs testing.
The second driver is the fragmentation of health and medical care. Its most visible manifestation in India is an excessive focus on specialist and super specialist care. A person with a common health problem often goes directly to a specialist or superspecialist. A person with chronic conditions may consult several specialists, each optimising one part of care without necessarily paying attention to the person’s other health problems. The patient is treated in parts, while the human body does not live in specialties.
This matters particularly in older adults. A systematic review and meta-analysis of Indian studies, published in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2021, reported polypharmacy in about 49% of older adults. Another study, published in Scientific Reports in 2025, found that roughly one-third of older adults were taking five or more prescribed medicines (polypharmacy), with potentially inappropriate medicines identified in 28.8% of cases.
These figures do not mean that everyone taking several medicines is being overtreated. They do, however, show why medication reviews and deprescribing must become routine.
A third force is the transformation of health care into a marketplace. Laboratory tests, radiological investigations, procedures, supplements and monitoring devices have become products to be sold — sometimes products in search of potential customers. As a result, the boundaries between those who genuinely need these interventions and those who do not can become blurred. A linked aspect is that much of health care and medical care in India operates on a fee-for-service model, which can reward activity rather than restraint. Many patients consider a medical consultation complete only when several medicines and investigations have been prescribed.
Health insurance is a proven solution for financial protection from health-related expenses, as the cost is borne by the insurer. However, it can create both ‘ex-ante’ and ‘ex-post’ moral hazards, discouraging preventive care and encouraging hospitals and patients to favour costlier interventions. What is forgotten is that while someone else may bear the financial cost, it is the patient’s body that undergoes the intervention. Paying insurance premiums for years does not mean that one must ‘recover’ the money by undergoing a relatively unnecessary procedure or surgery.
Fourth, patient beliefs and expectations arising from advances in medical care where people want certainty when they are worried and may feel that something tangible should follow a consultation. Reassurance can look like inaction; observation can feel inferior to a scan; lifestyle advice can appear less serious than medication. Doctors may respond to these expectations, particularly in crowded clinics where explanation requires time.
The fifth driver is the rise of ‘defensive medicine’, in which clinicians, fearing that they might miss a rare diagnosis, may consider ordering another test as the safer option. What is often forgotten, however, is that every test carries potential risks, both from the test itself and from the discovery of abnormalities that may never have caused harm.
Choosing wisely
India is not alone in facing this problem. Overtreatment first became widely recognised in high-income countries and is now increasingly visible across many middle-income nations. This gave rise to the global Choosing Wisely movement, which encourages people to choose health-care interventions more carefully. It is against this backdrop, between 2012 and 2023, that nearly 80 specialty societies worldwide published close to 700 recommendations identifying hundreds of tests and treatments that clinicians and patients should question. The message is that medicine requires stronger mechanisms for self-correction. The solutions are about practising better medicine. Halting and reversing overmedicalisation requires the engagement of all stakeholders, including individuals, communities, professional societies and health policymakers.
First, India needs to rebuild stronger and functional primary care and restore the family physician as the first point of contact for most non-emergency health needs. A general physician can decide which problems require specialist expertise, reconcile multiple prescriptions and recognise when treatment can safely be reduced. Initiation of care by a general physician, followed by continuity through the referral pathway, protects patients against overmedication and excess surgeries.
Second, every medical prescription should carry a review date and, where appropriate, a possible stop date. Medicines should not become lifelong simply because nobody asks whether they are still needed. Older adults and people taking five or more medicines should periodically undergo a structured medication review assessing indication, benefit, duplication, interactions and opportunities for deprescribing.
Develop India-specific lists
Third, professional medical societies and the Indian Council of Medical Research should develop Indian lists of low-value tests, treatments and procedures — similar to Choosing Wisely — and embed these principles in medical training, accreditation and quality-improvement programmes. Hospitals should measure not only whether recommended care was provided, but also whether unnecessary care was avoided.
Fourth, before starting any test or treatment, patients should note that these four questions matter: Why do I need this? What happens if I wait? What are the possible benefits and risks? What are the alternatives? These questions can substantially improve clinical conversations and outcomes.
Fifth, payment systems and health insurance must reward outcomes, clinical reasoning and continuity of care rather than volume alone. A health-care system should not make it financially easier to order a scan than to explain thoughtfully why that scan may be unnecessary.
Medical advances will continue — and they should. However, the next stage of medical progress will come not only from discovering more tests, medicines and procedures, but also from learning when not to use them. Good medicine requires action when action helps. In an age of medical abundance, it increasingly requires something more difficult — restraint.
Dr. Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician and the author of ‘Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed’ (2026)

Rocket Lab announced Wednesday that its Neutron launch vehicle won’t fly until 2027, citing an issue discovered during manufacturing of the rocket’s carbon composite structures.
The announcement was public confirmation of what nearly everyone inside Rocket Lab and the wider space industry already knew. The most recent official update from Rocket Lab in August suggested the company still held hope of delivering the first Neutron rocket to its launch pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, before the end of this year, a schedule that would have almost certainly pushed the first flight into 2027.
But Rocket Lab’s statement Wednesday about Neutron’s schedule suggests the company is still struggling with manufacturing the rocket’s large booster stage. Neutron’s reusable first stage is made of carbon composite structures, which offer low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance. But carbon composites in aerospace are generally harder to manufacture than metallic structures.
Peter Beck, Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO, identified a manufacturing defect as the reason for Neutron’s latest schedule slip. The problem lies in the dome sections at the ends of the rocket’s first stage propellant tanks.
“Recently, we identified an issue with the manufacturing process for the propellant domes specifically, and this caused us to delay production and investigate further,” Beck said in a video released by Rocket Lab.
Scaling up
Engineers discovered voids, or air pockets, between layers of carbon fiber that make up the domes’ composite structure. Carbon composite manufacturing involves laying down carbon fiber layers in a mold, then curing, or heating, the material to bind the fibers together. But this is a tricky process, especially for large structures that won’t fit into an autoclave, a high-pressure thermal curing chamber common in modern aerospace factories.
The Neutron rocket’s first stage is the “largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite,” Beck said. “Because of its scale, we’ve had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes to build Neutron, and this includes custom cure cycles for the very large pieces, like the forward and aft domes for the propellant tanks on Stage One.”
Inspections revealed voids in a newly cured forward dome, defects that could affect the structure’s strength, durability, and reliability, Beck said. “They don’t necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight, but our practice is to proceed only when we believe the system has the appropriate margins.”
Engineers traced the voids to a recent design change intended to strengthen the rocket’s structure. Rocket Lab introduced the design change after a Neutron propellant tank unexpectedly ruptured during a hydrostatic pressure test in January, a failure blamed on a manufacturing defect at a “critical join” in the tank.
Officials said the failed carbon composite tank was manufactured by a “third-party contractor using a manual hand-lay process,” a decision made to allow tank testing to move forward while Rocket Lab brought online an automated fiber placement machine, which is now operational. Rocket Lab also deleted joints in the first stage tank structure and increased the thickness of some sections of the carbon composite.
“Those thicker sections are where the voids formed,” Beck said.
Propellant domes inside Rocket Lab’s Neutron factory.

Propellant domes inside Rocket Lab’s Neutron factory.

Curing the void
Rocket Lab said the problem appears to be solved after modifying the manufacturing process again. An aft propellant dome made with the updated procedure passed inspection.
“We’ve solved the problem,” Beck said. “That gives us complete confidence to move forward with the new forward dome. That process to make a new forward dome, combining with all the time that it took to investigate, identify, and resolve the issue, has pushed Neutron’s first launch date to next year.”
The Neutron rocket is significantly larger than Rocket Lab’s Electron launch vehicle, also made of carbon fiber. The light-class Electron rocket is 3.9 feet (1.2 meters) in diameter, while the medium-lift Neutron measures 23 feet (7 meters) across at its widest.
Rocket Lab completed qualification testing on Neutron’s expendable second stage and payload fairing last year. The rocket’s design is unique: The upper stage and payload rest inside the first stage’s nose cone during the initial phases of launch. A few minutes after liftoff, Neutron’s booster stage will open its clamshell-like nose cone to release the upper stage and payload to continue accelerating into orbit. Then the first stage will close its payload fairing and return to landing on an offshore platform for reuse.
Neutron’s first stage methane and liquid oxygen tanks are the largest elements of the rocket, and they must withstand internal pressure and the rigors of launch and reentry.
Rocket Lab’s checklist for the first Neutron flight is long. Final qualification of the first stage is still pending, as is qualification of the rocket’s methane-fueled Archimedes engine, nine of which will power the Neutron booster. Rocket Lab reported in August that it was heading into the “final stretch” of engine qualification testing.
Once that is complete, teams will begin the launch campaign on Virginia’s Eastern Shore. Launch campaigns for new rockets often take months before a first flight, involving multiple integrated fueling tests, countdown rehearsals, and a static fire.
Engineers often discover new problems during integrated testing, requiring repeat tests and tweaks to procedures and hardware on the launch pad and the rocket. That is the purpose of such testing.
Rocket Lab announced the Neutron rocket in 2021, aiming for a first flight in 2024. The Neutron development timeline has now doubled.
Beck said Wednesday that Neutron’s development remains “on an ambitious timeline.” In previous statements, Beck has emphasized Rocket Lab’s focus on quality and its unwillingness to launch an “unproven product.”
“Our aim is to make orbit on the first try,” Beck said last year. “You won’t see us using some qualifier about us just clearing the pad, and claiming success and whatnot, and that means that we don’t want to learn something during Neutron’s first flight that could be learned on the ground during the testing phase.”
Rocket Lab has achieved great success with its Electron rocket, with a capacity of deploying up to 660 pounds (300 kilograms) of payload into a low-altitude orbit. Electron has made 97 flights to date, with 56 consecutive successes.
With Neutron, Rocket Lab seeks to compete for a wider range of launch contracts, eyeing opportunities to sell launches to the US military and operators of satellite megaconstellations. Its lift capability to low-Earth orbit is nearly 29,000 pounds (13,000 kilograms).
“We’re building the program’s long-term infrastructure at the same time as we build our first rocket, so that we can scale quickly, unlock global launch crunches, and commercial customers, governments, and our own future satellite services are also counting on it,” Beck said Wednesday. “But I’ve also said that we won’t rush to the pad with unnecessary risk, and that development programs like Neutron have their challenges.”
Neutron’s latest challenge popped up just as the rocket’s prospective customers clamor for more launch capacity. SpaceX, the market leader, is pivoting to the giant Starship rocket and will, in the next few years, retire from commercial service its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, without which many satellite startups would be unable to put their payloads into orbit affordably.
That puts Rocket Lab in the mix to scoop up business from satellite operators whose payloads don’t match up with Starship’s capabilities. But there’s stiff competition. Other rocket companies, such as Relativity Space, Stoke Space, and Firefly Aerospace, are working on medium-lift rockets to address the same market.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Mason Crane 'buzzing' at England recall as Glamorgan leg-spinner credits Richard Dawson with turnaround in fortunes
Mason Crane tells the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast: "I don't want to just be a highlights reel bowler"; watch England's first game of ODI tri-series in Pakistan on Tuesday, against the hosts, live on Sky Sports Cricket from 8.30am (play starts 9am)
Friday 16 October 2026 06:01, UK
Mason Crane said he was "buzzing" to be back in the England fold, adding that his ambitions go beyond being a "highlights reel" leg-spinner as he looks to make the most of his second bite at international cricket.
Crane was capped three times as a 20-year-old, nine years ago, the last of which was his Test debut in the final match of England's 2017/18 Ashes tour in Sydney. He'd take a single wicket as the tourists signed off a 4-0 series drubbing with another defeat.
Speaking to the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Crane admitted that he was "resigned to the fact it may not come again" as a near decade passed without further recognition, until getting the call for England's upcoming ODI tri-series in Pakistan.
"I didn't really expect it, to be honest," Crane said. "It was a bit out of the blue. But it's really cool and I'm buzzing.
"I think there was a period a few years ago where I was sort of resigned to the fact it may not come again, where I maybe put a bit too much pressure on myself and wasn't particularly enjoying it.
"But the last couple of years I feel like I've I sort of got that spark back and the ambition that comes with it."
Following his initial England breakthrough in 2017, injuries ruined Crane's 2018 season and he struggled to nail down a regular spot for his county Hampshire, until a 2024 move to Glamorgan prompted a change in fortunes.
There, he thrived under the coaching of Richard Dawson, who has just left to join England's red-ball staff as assistant to the newly-appointed Stephen Fleming.
"Daws is a brilliant coach. He's been absolutely amazing for us," Crane said. "He has very high standards; he pushes you to become the best version of yourself, and we all sort of thrived off that.
"From a Glamorgan point of view, we'd obviously rather have kept him. But when you have someone like Daws as your coach, if we're if we're being brutally honest, I think you know at some point that he's going to go on to international cricket.
"He's such a brilliant manager of people. He'll be amazing in any role he does.
"It's amazing for England. And like I said, I'm sure one day he will be in a position to take over an international side. He's that kind of calibre of coach."
Crane on batting form - 'My confidence just grew and grew'
Crane's return to the England fold has as much to do with his hugely-improved form with the bat, as much as his performances with the ball.
Crane struck a maiden first-class century, swiftly following with a second, as Glamorgan finished safely in sixth place upon their first County Championship season in Division One since 2005.
"I've always believed I underperformed a bit with the bat," Crane said. "When I moved to Glamorgan and started playing a lot more regularly, I kind of realised I had a few more shots.
"My confidence just grew and grew. And then this year, to get a few big scores has been amazing.
"Ironically, that's helped my bowling because I'm now bowling in matches where I probably wouldn't be playing in to start with."
Crane claimed 34 wickets across 14 County Championship appearances in 2026, and 15 in 10 Vitality Blast outings. He also played three times for London Spirit in The Hundred, taking two wickets.
A couple of his dismissals went viral on social media, particularly those of Yorkshire batters George Hill and James Wharton as part of an eight-wicket match haul back in April, but Crane doesn't want to just be Insta-famous.
"I don't want to just be a highlights reel bowler, every now and then bowl a really good ball and just live off that," he added.
"I pride myself on trying to play to the situations really, trying to work out how I'm going to get the most out of a wicket and get a particular guy out.
"I've also given myself a bit more freedom, I guess, with the ball now. I try and bowl more variations, but I'm also better at bowling them now.
"It's about sort of adding as many strings to your bow. It's really important."

Bournemouth 3-0 Sturm Graz: Cherries win first ever home European game as they make it two from two in Europa League
Match report as Bournemouth win their first-ever home European game, beating Sturm Graz; Evanilson scored at the end of the first half to hand the Cherries the lead; Rayan and an Alvaro Rodriguez penalty added after the break; Bournemouth face AC Milain in the Europa League next Thursday
Thursday 15 October 2026 22:43, UK
Bournemouth's history-making season continued on Thursday as they played - and won - their first-ever home European match, beating Sturm Graz 3-0 in the Europa League.
It makes it two wins from two for the competition debutants and perhaps more importantly, they held on to a lead they took towards the end of the first half - something they have been unable to do in a poor start to the Premier League.
Evanilson will go down as the man who scored the first European goal at the Vitality Stadium and it was a thing of beauty. Adam Smith - captaining a team he joined in England's third tier 16 years ago - found him with a cross, with the Brazilian curling a powerful header past the goalkeeper from 15 yards out.

Sturm Graz came out with intent at the start of the second half and could have equalised just after the hour. Jurgen Heil smashed the woodwork before Djorde Petrovic was needed to keep out Jacob Hodl's follow-up.
But the Cherries rode the wave and doubled their lead through another Brazilian, Rayan. It was a howler from Daniil Khudyakov, whose spilled save from a corner landed to the Bournemouth forward. His low, fizzing shot then sped through the goalkeeper's outstretched hands.
And in second-half added time, Bournemouth were awarded a penalty. Former Huddersfield man Jon Gorenc Stankovic was penalised for a foul on James Hill - also coming in the aftermath of a Bournemouth corner.
Summer signing Alvaro Rodriguez stepped up to chip the spot kick in for his first Bournemouth goal, sealing another three points. It puts the Cherries fifth in the Europa League league phase table ahead of welcoming Ruben Amorim's AC Milan to the Vitality next Thursday.
Key moments from the Vitality Stadium...
12: CHANCE! Smith curls in a wonderful cross for the incoming Tavernier, but he's defended well as his attempt goes wide.
29: NO GOAL! The ball is in the back of the net for Bournemouth - but it's immediately ruled out for a handball against Bafode Diakate.
33: OFF THE POST!! Tavernier's curling effort hits the woodwork.
41: PENALTY?! REFEREE SAYS NO! Sturm Graz have their best attack of the half, with calls for a penalty after Beganovic goes down. He is unfairly booked after, but looked to already be losing his footing as Smith made contact.
43: GOAL! Evanilson gives Bournemouth the lead with an incredible curling header from some distance.
63: OFF THE POST! SAVE! Heil hits the post with a thunderous effort from the right, before Hodl's follow-up is stopped by Djorde Petrovic's legs.
76: GOAL! Rayan's low, hard shot beats Khudyakov after some poor goalkeeping.
90+2: PENALTY SCORED! Stankovic fouls Hill as he strikes inside the box and Bournemouth are awarded a penalty. Rodriguez scores from the spot.
'That was a Bournemouth performance'
Bournemouth captain Adam Smith to TNT Sports: "It's been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we're very happy with the performance.
"It wasn't my best cross [for Evanilson's goal], but I put it into the area and what a finish from him. It's a great header. He's deserved it because he's worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.
"We deserved that bit of luck and from there, we went on to win the game. In the second half, we got a bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great. We look forward to Sunday now."
On if this can be a springboard for Bournemouth: "It was very disappointing at the weekend [against Chelsea]. We let ourselves down as players, we know that. We had a chat with each other and got a reaction today.
"That's a Bournemouth performance right there, but the week is not done. We have a massive game against Sunderland and we need to get three points."
Rose: A deserved win - now we have to be consistent
Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose to TNT Sports when asked if he saw what he wanted from his team: "Yes. Performance wise, clean sheet, attitude, effort. A deserved win and now we have to continue and get consistent in this kind of thing. Sunderland is the next challenge.
"I believe in this team and I know we are always confident, despite being in a difficult situation [in the Premier League]. Even today, we changed some players.
"We could see that the squad is working, that everyone is keen to play, that everyone deserves to play and it's good for us for the next few weeks to have a competitive squad.
"Today, we won 3-0 and it's a really good result after a good performance, but we have to prove it [consistency].
"Alvaro Rodriguez did some steps the last three weeks which began with the national break. He worked really hard individually and you could see every step and I'm quite happy that he scored.
"If we stick together like this, if we have our fans then we are hard to play [against] and then it's hard to beat us. That's what we should take into the next game. It's getting tough one but it helps this kind of game, this result."
'This needs to be a springboard for Bournemouth's season'
Analysis from Sky Sports News' Mark McAdam at the Vitality: "Back-to-back wins in the Europa League!
"Not a classic by any stretch but one that will live long in the memories for Bournemouth fans; their first ever taste of European football at the Vitality - a real moment in history. A game they dominated across the pitch from start to finish.
"This needs to be the springboard for their season and their next match against Sunderland in the Premier League on Sunday. Win that and suddenly their season is off and running..."

Serb player banned to 2050 for tennis match-fixing
- Published
A player from Serbia has been given a 24-year suspension from tennis - one of the most severe punishments imposed by anti-corruption investigators outside of a lifetime ban - for match-fixing.
Stefan Milicevic, who reached a career-high world ranking of 1,338th in 2014, was charged with fixing six matches, including five in which he was competing.
The 29-year-old, who played on the lower rungs of the professional ladder, was also charged with attempting to fix a further six matches between 2022 and 2024.
Along with the match-fixing, the International Tennis Integrity Authority (ITIA) said Milicevic was also charged with recruiting or attempting to recruit multiple professional players "as part of a corrupt network".
Players who were recruited by Milicevic have also been accused by the ITIA of fixing matches.
The severity of Milicevic's sanction is partly down to a lack of co-operation in the investigation.
The ITIA said he "did not engage" in the process despite seven separate attempts from the independent organisation to contact him.
Milicevic, who also received a £53,000 fine, cannot take part in the sport until his ban ends in October 2050, by which time he will be 53 years old.
While suspended, he is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association.
In December, French player Quentin Folliot was banned for 20 years, external after the ITIA discovered he was a central figure in a network of players operating on behalf of a match-fixing syndicate.
Foillot, who reached a career-high of 488 in the rankings in 2022, denied charges relating to 11 matches which took place between 2022 and 2024, including eight which he played in.
However, at a hearing, some 27 of the 30 charges against him, relating to 10 of the 11 matches, were upheld.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman told employees an in-house model was better than a similar offering from OpenAI, one of the software giant's biggest customers and partners.
"We now have a stronger pre-trained base model than the model that currently powers GPT 5.6 Sol," Suleyman said during a town hall meeting with employees on Thursday. "And in fact, we used one-quarter of the compute that OpenAI used to train their model."
Pre-training is the first stage of building an AI model, when it learns patterns from huge amounts of text, images, and other information. This takes massive amounts of expensive computing power, so Microsoft could save money if it's worked out a way to do this more efficiently.
Microsoft announced the model, MAI-Base-2, earlier on Thursday.
Suleyman said Microsoft privately tested this model against OpenAI models, including one nicknamed "Spud" that powers GPT-5.6. He added that Microsoft's model performed better on tests measuring how well AI can understand and predict patterns in information.
The comparisons are based on technical information Microsoft has about OpenAI's models, Suleyman said.
"Privately and confidentially, we've also compared it to the OpenAI models," Suleyman told employees, while suggesting that Microsoft has special access to information on how OpenAI models perform.
It's notable that Suleyman would choose to highlight limitations of OpenAI models, even in private discussions. Microsoft has invested billions of dollars in OpenAI, and owns a stake in the startup that is likely worth more than $100 billion. Any criticism of OpenAI could potentially dent the value of this huge investment.
The two companies also have a major partnership, with Microsoft offering OpenAI models to its Azure cloud customers. Microsoft has used OpenAI models for its own products such as Copilot, too.
But the relationship between the two companies has frayed in the past year or so. Increasingly, Microsoft has tried to branch out from OpenAI, including by working on its own models.
Suleyman also said Microsoft's new AI model used "12 times less computation than was used for DeepSeek, for example, on compute efficiency."
Suleyman didn't specify which DeepSeek model, but a public blog post described the pre-training of MAI-Base-2 being a lot more efficient than a similar offering from the Chinese lab, called DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base.
Microsoft in March created a new combined team for its commercial and consumer Copilot products and reassigned Suleyman to focus on building AI models in the company's superintelligence unit.
Microsoft declined to comment and OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s launch rollout will differ significantly from previous Call of Duty games, as Activision is offering early access to both the campaign and the new DMZ mode. Although Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 releases globally on October 23, 2026, you can start playing the campaign and the DMZ extraction mode around a week before.
So, here’s the complete Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 release schedule, covering early access and the full launch, with countdown timers for each.
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Early Access Times
Activision has confirmed that players who pre-order Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 digitally before its October release will get early access to the campaign on October 16, 2026, at 10 AM PT/1 PM ET and DMZ on October 20 at 10 AM PT/1 PM ET.
This applies to both the digital Standard and the Vault Edition, excluding the physical. So, here are the release times you should follow for Modern Warfare 4’s simultaneous early access global release for campaign and DMZ on all platforms:

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Full Release Times
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s release schedule concludes with the full release on October 23, 2026, which includes access to the campaign, DMZ mode, and multiplayer. Unlike campaign and DMZ early access, Activision has confirmed that the full release will follow a midnight local schedule on PC.

Downloading COD HQ with MW 4 is mandatory, but you can choose whether to install Warzone alongside it. However, you can only launch the new Warzone when Season 1 releases on November 6, 2026. So, selecting Warzone will install the current version of it.
Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Overview
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s Campaign early access begins a week before full release on October 16, giving you ample time to complete it. The campaign takes the series into a new fictional conflict on the Korean Peninsula, with North Korea invading the South. Meanwhile, John Price is on the run after being outlawed for assassinating General Shepherd.
As a rogue agent, Price teams up with the Las Almas cartel, as seen in Modern Warfare 4’s “Traffic” teaser, and hunts down a world-ending weapon while his trusted allies track him down. As a sequel to Modern Warfare 3, the upcoming shooter shares two perspectives: rookie South Korean soldier Private Park Hyun Jun and the outlawed Captain John Price.
The campaign spans various global locations, including New York, Paris, and Mumbai. While familiar faces like Ghost, Gaz, and Makarov return, the biggest surprise of the campaign is its mysterious “The Archer” antagonist, played by Mads Mikkelsen in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
So, with Modern Warfare 4’s release schedule, you can probably beat the main campaign before the game fully releases. However, it depends on how long the campaign actually is.
Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Overview
Starting October 20, you can access Modern Warfare 4’s DMZ mode if you’ve pre-ordered the game. According to Activision’s DMZ deep dive, Players deploy solo or in squads, explore abandoned settlements and military installations, gather valuable loot, complete objectives, and fight AI enemies and rival Operators.
The mode also includes the brand-new Hajin map in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. This map offers a wide range of locations to explore, including Chang-san Air Base, 14th Political Prison, rural farmland, urban districts, industrial facilities, and the Haneul Nuclear Reactor. Each area has its own “Threats”, so players can either avoid combat to gain more loot or go guns blazing.
Story Missions advance narrative objectives, while Dynamic Operations offer rewards such as DMZ Cash, XP, and increasingly valuable Supply Drops. At the same time, Side Operations let players uncover new intel and hunt high-value Lieutenants and Commanders.
Players will have a Forward Operating Base (FOB) to manage their Operators, resources, loadouts, and prepare for the next run. So, DMZ is already shaping up to be an exciting Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game mode that you can access early thanks to the release schedule.
Modern Warfare 4 Multiplayer Overview
Infinity Ward and Activision will officially launch Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on October 23, thus ending the launch rollout. The full release includes the campaign, the DMZ, and the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer.
At launch, Modern Warfare 4’s multiplayer will include five categories and 17 modes. Of course, the developers will add more modes for the game’s post-launch support, but for now, here’s what they confirmed:

Guwahati: In a major boost to international connectivity and diplomatic integration for Northeast India, Assam Chief Minister Dr. Himanta Biswa Sarma on Thursday inaugurated the region’s first dedicated Visa Application Centre in Guwahati. Established by VFS Global at the Inter-State Bus Terminal complex in Khanapara, the new facility marks a significant milestone for the region, eliminating the decades-long need for residents across the eight northeastern states to travel to Delhi or Kolkata for foreign visa applications.
The newly inaugurated centre will immediately process visa applications for Cyprus, Egypt, Ireland, Japan, Malta, Morocco, and the United Kingdom, alongside handling Schengen visa applications covering 29 European nations. Speaking at the inauguration, Chief Minister Dr. Sarma emphasized that the centre brings international travel services directly to the doorstep of the region, fundamentally bridging the geographical distance between the Northeast and the global community while aligning with the Union Government's Act East Policy.
The development coincides with a major aviation milestone for the region. Beginning October 27, Guwahati’s Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport will operate under a new hub-and-spoke international immigration arrangement designated by the Ministry of Civil Aviation. Under this model, international passengers completing immigration formalities in Guwahati will no longer need to repeat the process at secondary Indian transit airports. The airport, which already connects to Dubai, Singapore, and Bhutan, is set to launch new direct flight services to Bangkok on the same day, establishing Guwahati as a strategic international gateway for eastern India.
The infrastructure expansion follows unprecedented growth in the state's travel sector. Official data released during the event revealed that Assam recorded over 6 crore tourist visits—including more than 2.41 lakh foreign nationals—over the last decade spanning FY 2016–17 to FY 2025–26. Bolstering this international engagement, major foreign governments including Australia, Japan, and all 27 European Union member states recently revised their travel advisories for Assam, citing substantial improvements in the state's security environment.
The inaugural ceremony was attended by key dignitaries, including state Transport Minister Charan Boro, Tourism Minister Ajanta Neog, MP Bijuli Kalita Medhi, VFS Global South Asia COO Yummi Talwar, alongside diplomats representing nations such as France, the Czech Republic, Switzerland, and Italy.

Young voters split on gun control despite nearly 80% being fearful of mass shootings
A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry law

Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.
Gun control is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been a recurring part of American life.
Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, at least two students on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at Florida State University. As one of them put it: “This is America.”
Researchers have called today’s young adults the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era, with routine lockdown drills, heightened security in schools and nonstop media coverage of mass violence.
As criminologists who study the impacts of victimization and gun violence among young people, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In a recent study, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.
A debate that repeats after every shooting
Mass shootings account for about 1% of gun deaths in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 survey by the American Psychological Association, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they avoided certain places because of it. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have screening tools to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.
Young adults have also grown up watching the same heated gun debates play out after every tragedy. Gun control advocates call for stricter firearm restrictions to prevent the next mass shooting, whereas gun rights advocates push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase made popular by the National Rifle Association. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses.
Researchers have known for a long time that more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence. A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after decades of mass shootings, federal gun policy has barely budged. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, they’ve faced Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court.
Young people have become some of the loudest voices in this debate, most notably through March for Our Lives – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and other youth-led groups across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among older Americans, many political observers assume stricter gun laws will follow as young people gain voting power.
This fall, voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws, and in a few states they’ll weigh in on gun policy directly. In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to keep or repeal a 2024 law that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons.
In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to change the state constitution to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.
Young adults are split
So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. Our survey asked young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.
In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.
We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high.
In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the largest voting bloc in the country. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.
