But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official.
Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.
Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."
Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.
Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.
The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.
Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
US President Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.
Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.
Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

On Oct. 8, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed (archived) reports that the U.S. military was planning to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, which is currently set for Dec. 3.
A military jury sentenced Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, to death in 2013 after it found him guilty of killing 13 people and injuring 30 more during a shooting rampage at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas in 2009. U.S. President Donald Trump approved (archived) Hasan's death sentence on Oct. 2, clearing the path for his execution.
On Oct. 8, Hegseth shared an X post by CBS News that read:
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3, a Pentagon official said.
Hegseth wrote, "Correct."
One day later, on Oct. 9, the Associated Press reported that Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he reportedly said. About a week after Hegseth's initial confirmation, on Oct. 15, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Hasan's execution would go ahead "but this event will not be streamed."
Following Hegseth's confirmation, discussion abounded online about whether executing Hasan in such a public manner was legal (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the legality of the planned livestream.
The military justice system, which is separate from the civilian justice systems in the U.S., carried out Hasan's trial and sentencing in 2013. On Oct. 5, Hegseth's assistant secretary for public affairs Sean Parnell wrote on X (archived) that the Army's firing squad would execute Hasan, meaning his execution would be governed by Army regulations.
At the time of this writing, the U.S. Army did not have regulations explicitly allowing it to livestream an execution. Rather, Army Regulation 190–55, which covers procedures for military executions, included requirements that would likely hinder the Army's ability to provide a public livestream.
Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 15 that the "immediate families" of Hasan's victims could still view the execution in person in accordance with current Army regulations.
Gary Barthel, a former U.S. Marine Corps officer and managing partner at the Military Law Center, told Snopes on Oct. 9 that if the Army wanted to legally livestream Hasan's execution, officials would have to either seek an exemption to regulation 190-55 from the Office of the Provost Marshal General as laid out in the regulation itself or amend the existing regulation to allow livestreaming. 
We contacted the Department of the Defense to ask if it was planning to do either of these things and await a reply.
Because the legality of livestreaming Hasan's execution was potentially subject to change, we leave this claim unrated.
What Army regulation says
Chapter 2-5 of regulation 190-55 lists who may and may not witness a military execution. According to the chapter, no person younger than 18 years old may witness an execution and the Army must approve the list of witnesses beforehand.
Those two stipulations could make it difficult for the Army to provide a public livestream without violating its own regulations because it would have to vet the audience's age. Hosting a truly public livestream would make it impossible to approve a list of "witnesses" ahead of the execution because people might log in to watch on the day without registering beforehand.
Barthel told Snopes via phone on Oct. 9:
The Army is required to follow its regulations. If the Army wants to stream this execution they need to change the regulations to allow it. And, either way, I would anticipate that there is going to be some efforts to stop it.
Barthel said that Hasan's defense team could still ask a civilian court to stop the execution and live stream by filing a habeas corpus petition. Such a petition allows a detainee to challenge their detention in court.
Would public execution be 'cruel and unusual punishment'?
Daniel Maurer, an associate professor at the Claude W. Pettit College of Law at Ohio Northern University, told Snopes that livestreaming Hasan's execution could raise constitutional concerns that would ultimately play out in court.
Hasan's defense could bring up such constitutional concerns as part of a habeas petition. Maurer said via email on Oct. 9 that Hasan's defense could argue that being executed on livestream amounted to "cruel and unusual punishment," which is banned by the U.S. Constitution's 8th Amendment. Maurer wrote (links ours):
The remaining legal issue is maybe more complicated and would need courts to resolve it: does such a practice violate Hasan's 8th Amendment protection from "cruel and unusual punishments?" - this protection is also stated in the UCMJ, article 55, and Army Regulation 190-47 ("The Army Corrections System") so it applies to prisoners already confined, not just defendants at court-martial sentencing.
In order to establish whether livestreaming Hasan's execution amounted to cruel and unusual punishment, the courts might apply the "Evolving Standard" test, according to Maurer. The test allows courts to consider whether a punishment is cruel and unusual under current societal standards, rather than according to standards at the time the Constitution was written.
Cornell Law School's Legal Information Library wrote that "in the context of capital punishment, the Court has generally viewed the Eighth Amendment to prohibit punishments that 'involve the unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain.'"
Though livestreaming may not inflict "unnecessary and wanton" pain, Maurer said there are other factors at play:
Given that federal law prohibits photographic or other visual or audio recording of an execution of any other civilian federal prisoner, this is strong evidence that our own federal government (of which the DoD is of course a part) would consider it to be "cruel and unusual," and thus would be an 8th Amendment violation.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, called the decision to livestream Hasan's execution "sick-making" when speaking to Snopes on Oct. 9. He previously told DRM News that a habeas petition could postpone Hasan's execution past the end of the Trump administration as it progressed through the civilian court system. That means Hasan's execution and any potential livestream could be halted by an administration without "the same penchant for executions," Fidell reportedly told the Associated Press.
It was unclear whether Hasan would file a habeas petition. The Associated Press reported that Hasan had begun his 2013 trial by firing his lawyers and telling jurors that he was the gunman in the 2009 shooting. The outlet reported that this move "convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence." It remained unclear whether Hasan's goal remained the same in 2026.
The nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center wrote that Hasan's execution would be the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961.
The Washington Post, citing the center, reported that the last high-profile public execution of any type in the U.S. took place in 1936. Another public execution took place the year after.
For further reading, Snopes compiled 17 claims about the death penalty that we've investigated over the years.

- NetEase Games urges players to delete mods that trigger the anti-cheat system and violate the game rules.
- The developer has shared a list of mods that are strictly prohibited.
- They have now warned that players who continue to use gameplay-balance-affecting mods will be severely punished.
NetEase Games released a lengthy statement urging Marvel Rivals players to remove unauthorized mods that give an unfair advantage on the battlefield. After lifting suspensions issued over the past two days for using mods, the dev team warned players that those who continue to use mods that disrupt game balance will face strict disciplinary action.
Marvel Rivals Warns Players Against Mods That Trigger Anti-Cheat Detection
Recently, the Marvel Rivals developers permabanned cheaters and also began cracking down on AFK players, throwers, and early leavers with harsher penalties. During these investigations, the developer team found that several mods used by players involved memory injection and modification behaviors.
Technically, these techniques are very similar to those used by cheat engines, causing them to trigger NetEase Games’ anti-cheat detection system. The developers have now outlined several mod characteristics that violate the game’s anti-cheat rules:
- Modifying Structural Models or Textures: Generating an asymmetrical line-of-sight between players, offering an unfair vision advantage.
- Eliminating Weapon Recoil & VFX: The removal of screen shake, bullet trajectories, and impact visual effects makes it easier to aim and track targets.
- Altering In-game Audio: The modification of footsteps and other sound effects makes it easier to pinpoint the opponent’s positions.
- Enlarging Character Models: Altering enemy character models makes it far easier to spot, identify, and target opponents.
All the modifications listed above are classified as mods that give an unfair competitive advantage and ruin the game balance. So, the developers have warned that gameplay-affecting mods are strictly prohibited and that they will impose severe penalties on violators. In case you didn’t know, Marvel Rivals recently introduced a new independent penalty-tier system.
In addition, the developers have reversed recent player suspensions for mod usage. This wasn’t done to encourage players to use mods. Instead, the developers are giving the suspended players an opportunity to stop using and permanently remove these game-altering mods.
More importantly, NetEase has specifically asked players to delete the violating .asi files, including pystubber.asi and MarvelRivalsUnmountBlocker.asi. According to the developer, these files perform operations that trigger the Anti-Cheat system’s detection.
As always, if you believe your account was wrongfully banned, you can submit an appeal through Marvel Rivals’ official Customer Support channels. The team will review and reverse the ban after verification. Lastly, NetEase Games hasn’t clarified whether mods that only affect in-game cosmetics are allowed in Marvel Rivals Season 10.5.
But the developers have stated that they always aim to strike a balance between player customization and a fair competitive environment. So, we hope they provide further clarification on which types of mods are permitted in the future.

Southgate does not see return to Premier League management
- Published
Former England manager Gareth Southgate says he does not see himself returning to club management in the Premier League.
The 56-year-old has been out of management since resigning as Three Lions boss after guiding them to the final of Euro 2024, where they lost to Spain.
Southgate, who also took England to the Euro 2020 final, has not managed at club level since a three-year spell with Middlesbrough from 2006.
When asked if he would consider a return to managing in the Premier League, he told the The Amol Rajan Connection: "I don't see a scenario where I do that."
He added: "Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying, at the very least for a period, the wins keep you going.
"By the end, I didn't even enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes. So, I've hardly watched football.
"I went to the FA Cup final to see my team, Crystal Palace, win their first trophy. I've not been to a football ground since. So my sort of desire to be involved in football has changed."
Since leaving the England role, Southgate has also spent time working in the media and earlier this year he fronted a BBC documentary where he travelled across the UK to understand challenges facing young men and boys.
He has also spent time as a visiting lecturer at Harvard Business School in Boston.
"I've loved the last 18 months of my life," he added.
"I've had 37 years where my sense of self depended on did I win or lose on Saturday. And actually I've loved having different experiences. I've met politicians, I've met people in the media industry, I have learned about leadership in all sorts of areas, I've travelled around the world learning things.
"I've just enjoyed playing a different film in my life."
'No winners' in Manchester City charges
Last month, Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".
The club have denied any wrongdoing and submitted an appeal on 2 October.
"There'll be the tribal fans' response to punish Manchester City as much as we can, relegate them, fine them, do whatever you can," added Southgate.
"I've been in football boardrooms, I've been in meetings with Uefa, I've been in meetings with Fifa, I have been in all these spaces and I know how complicated all of this is.
"My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners because if you're at the Premier League, for a very brief moment you might feel justified that all the flak you've had for this case taking so long, this is why it's taken so long and there's the verdict, and I'm sure there's an element of justification in that.
"Then there's this realisation of how do we deal with all of this because you know the possibility of all the different legal cases that emerge from this, how long this could still take, what's the right sort of punishment, how do you keep the whole game on track?
"That's unbelievably complex."

I have spent my career studying nurses and why that workforce so often fails the people it is meant to serve. But my understanding of the system changed deeply the day my daughter died.
She was 21 years old. She had intellectual and developmental disabilities and had just moved into a group home in New Jersey. Within 48 hours, she was gone. Her caregivers accidentally gave her too much medicine.
The people responsible for her care were not nurses. They were direct support professionals — workers who often help people with disabilities live in community settings. Yet their work is deeply connected to nursing. They are part of the same health care system that depends on them even as it gives them too little training, pay, and support.
In the years since my daughter died, I have tried to make sense of what happened, not only as a mother, but as a nurse and researcher. I have come to believe that we are asking the wrong questions.
The world knows it has a nursing shortage, and policymakers have been working to create new nurses. Governments track our progress and publish reports projecting how many more nurses will be needed.
And yet, for all this attention, we’re not fixing the shortfall. It’s worsening as baby boomers age, driving an even greater need for health care.
We focus on producing more nurses (expanding enrollment, accelerating training, recruiting across borders) while paying far less attention to whether the system they enter can sustain them.
But the evidence and the lived reality of care suggest otherwise. It’s the workplace we need to fix.
But what you don’t measure, you can’t fix.
Across countries, workforce data is strongest where the questions are easiest to answer: How many nurses exist? Where are they located?
It is weakest where the answers matter most: What happens when nurses enter practice? Are they supported? Do they stay? These are not secondary questions. They determine whether a workforce functions at all. Yet we rarely measure them.
This blind spot extends beyond nursing. Direct support professionals, or those who care for people with disabilities, older adults, and others with complex needs, are among the least visible workers in the system. Nurses cannot compensate for the deficiencies in the rest of the system.
New nurses often enter practice under intense pressure, expected to manage complex patients with few colleagues and limited support. Structured transition programs like mentorship, residency models, and protected learning time are uneven or absent. The difference often determines whether a nurse stays.
Working conditions are the larger problem.
Burnout, chronic understaffing, and high turnover are among the most consistent predictors of workforce loss, yet they are harder to quantify than headcounts and are often overlooked.
For direct support staff, the situation is even more stark: inconsistent training, low wages, and high turnover in roles that involve caring for some of the most vulnerable people in our system.
In New Jersey, my daughter’s death prompted proposed legislation, still pending, requiring a nurse, or a certified medication aide supervised by a nurse, to administer medications in group homes and supervised apartments. The proposal recognizes a difficult reality: We are often asking workers without sufficient clinical training to manage medications that can become dangerous or even lethal if dispensed incorrectly.
When my daughter entered that group home, she encountered a workforce that was not adequately prepared and a system that relied on staffing models without sufficiently investing in clinical support, training, or supervision.
Expanding the pipeline without fixing the workplace is like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in it.
We see this globally. Health systems invest in training, only to lose early-career nurses within a few years. High-income countries recruit from lower-income ones, shifting shortages rather than solving them.
This is not a failure of individuals. It is a failure of design.
Systems solutions, such as improving training, adding sufficient staff, and supporting early-career professionals, are slower to implement.
But they are the only solutions that endure.
We should track whether new nurses get structured transition support, not just whether they graduate. We should measure retention and turnover with the same rigor as supply.
And we must stop treating the rest of the care workforce as invisible.
Direct support professionals, home care workers, and others are central. Without standardized training, sustainable wages, and meaningful integration into workforce planning, no amount of nurse supply will stabilize care delivery.
I wish I had not learned some of these lessons the way I did. But my daughter’s death enabled me to see the problem more clearly.
I no longer believe that we can fix the system only by training more nurses. Instead, we need to build a health care system that supports the people we are asking to care for us.
Lynne S. Moronski is an associate fellow at the Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics at the University of Pennsylvania.

The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.
Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.
“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”
Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.
Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.
The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.
Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.
In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”
Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

For some couples, surrogacy is a miracle: an opportunity to have a child even if they’re unable to conceive one naturally. But it’s also big business. Not only is surrogacy expensive — think six figures — but it’s also largely unregulated. And that last part is becoming a bigger problem.
The problem with the US surrogacy system
Why it’s easier to open a surrogacy agency than a nail salon in most US states.
Just last week, a California couple was arrested on child abuse charges after it was revealed that they had over 20 children from different surrogate mothers living in a large mansion in Arcadia, a city near Los Angeles. Many of the surrogates are currently fighting for custody through the courts of the children they carried.
The Arcadia case, however, is only the most recent example of how surrogacy can go wrong. Every case is different, but every one illuminates how opaque — and often ripe for abuse or legal issues — the American surrogacy industry is.
Emi Nietfeld is a reporter at Washington Sun who writes about surrogacy, IVF, and how we build families. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what’s kept lawmakers from regulating the surrogacy industry, the recent high-profile cases bringing these problems to light, and why more regulation doesn’t necessarily offer a straightforward fix.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
The United States does not regulate the surrogacy industry seemingly at all. What is going on? Why not?
The lack of federal regulation is both political and financial. Politically, this goes all the way back to the start of IVF. Anti-abortion Republicans were not comfortable with the idea of creating and destroying embryos during IVF, and so they fought against efforts to regulate it.
People on the left were worried that limiting what kinds of technology you could access would lead to the government controlling who could have families. You still see these arguments today. People who think that IVF is murder don’t want to have any surrogacy. And people on the left don’t want the government saying who can and cannot have a family.
One of the issues raised by the New Yorker story is that there are surrogacy agencies that connect parents and potential surrogates. And it makes you wonder who gets to do that? Who can own and operate a surrogacy agency in the US today?
Anyone.
Oh. Oh no.
Only one state, New York, requires a special license. And everywhere else it’s easier to open an agency than a hot dog stand or a nail salon. This has resulted in the rise of so-called pop-up agencies where businesses come onto the scene, and nobody really knows who owns them or who’s running them. That has led to many people who aren’t experienced, who sign up with these agencies, then feeling like they weren’t prepared or that they were deceived in entering the agreement.
Have we ever tried in the past to regulate this better? Have there been efforts made?
In the 1980s, there was the case of Baby M. That was called traditional surrogacy where Mary Beth Whitehead was the surrogate, but it was also her egg. So the child she delivered was genetically related to her. After she gave birth, she changed her mind. She kidnapped the child, went on the run for several months, and it was a national crisis where this was all over the news.
Ultimately, a judge in New Jersey ruled that the surrogacy arrangement was unenforceable. Commercial surrogacy arrangements became illegal in New Jersey, and they stayed illegal in New York until 2020.
Part of why regulation looks the way it does is because in 1995, Congress passed a piece of legislation saying that there would be no federal funding for embryo research, which means no federal funding for IVF. That left all of the research, development, innovation up to the free market. And so while that could be seen as an attempt to regulate IVF, it actually meant that those things would no longer be under the government’s purview.
In the US, we’ve seen over the past few years some really high-profile cases that are making lawmakers reckon with the fact that we do not have laws around this. Tell me about some of those cases.
There’s the Mark surrogacy case in California, which is both a really unique case and also illustrates some of the fears around Chinese intended parents coming to the United States to have their kids. This is part of larger geopolitical tensions between the US and China, which are playing out in the surrogacy industry.
There’s the case of Xu Bo, the Chinese video gaming billionaire who is rumored to have more than 100 children via surrogacy in America. His story taps into fears of birth tourism and people from other countries, especially China, coming to the United States to do surrogacy so that their kids are American citizens.
Republican lawmakers are talking a lot about the idea that people could come from enemy countries, have American citizens, and raise them with the intent that they might one day become spies or president of the United States and be double actors.
In Texas, there’s the case of McKenna West, where she learned at 20 weeks’ gestation that the baby was very sick. The intended parents asked her to get an abortion. She refused to do so. McKenna went to Texas and began fighting for custody to keep the baby while the parents objected. They wanted the baby, and she petitioned the Supreme Court, which declined to hear the case.
And finally, there’s the case of Kyla Simpson in Florida, whom I wrote about for New York Magazine, and she gave birth for a single dad in China who wasn’t there for the birth. He hadn’t applied for a visa to come to the United States, and when he did apply, he was rejected. Kyla Simpson tried to adopt the kids and is now fighting for custody in a case that’s still working its way through the Florida courts.
These examples are extraordinary, and they point to just chaos. But how common are they? Are they outliers? Is this going on all the time?
Most of the time things go right. In the academic papers around surrogacy, surrogates are usually happy with their experience. Attorneys and surrogates tell me that it’s absolutely beautiful to hand people the baby that they’ve been working hard for. The issue is that when things do go wrong, there’s often not a lot of recourse or there’s a really big legal mess that parents and surrogates have to go through.
I wonder if there is a case against more regulation. As disastrous as some of these examples are, you said that most of the time, it does go right. And it seems like we could get into tricky territory if we start saying who can and can’t have a kid.
Surrogacy is already really time-consuming. It often takes several years, and it’s expensive, usually costing between $150,000 to $250,000 for a single pregnancy. Regulation tends to make things more expensive and take longer. A lot of people fear that if you introduce more requirements and more burdens, surrogacy will become even more out of reach to people.
There’s also the fear of government overreach. If you ask the government how many kids a gay couple should have, the answer might be zero. And that libertarian streak is driving a lot of opposition to things that most people might consider common sense.
For example, there’s a lot of talk around whether intended parents should go through background checks before they have kids via surrogacy. Right now, no state in America requires intended parents to go through a criminal background check before having a kid. Critics of regulation say heteros don’t need a background check to have sex in the back of a car and make a baby the old-fashioned way, so it’s unfair to require that from people who need to do surrogacy to have a family.
Most people can agree that surrogacy could be better regulated, but like many things in our country, it’s almost impossible right now because of politics.

Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
- Published
Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.
A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.
Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.
Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.
Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.
Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.
"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.
He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.
The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.
A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.
More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.
In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Saimah Chaudhry, cofounder and chief operating officer of Zevo. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Back in 2015, I was working for a SaaS company that I'd founded. It mostly served clients in the restaurant industry, where my parents and grandparents were both entrepreneurs.
One day, I was meeting with an out-of-town client who was staying in Manhattan Beach. He mentioned he'd rented the BMW he was driving from Relay Ride (which later became the car rental app Turo).
That was the first time I heard of car sharing. I was working from home, and my Smartcar was definitely an underutilized asset. On a whim, I listed it for rent. A grad student at UCLA booked it for three months, and I pretty much never saw that car again — after that, it was always rented.
I quickly got 2 more cars to rent
My day-to-day car use was pretty minimal, but I still needed to drive occasionally. I leased another Smartcar because they were very cheap at the time. I listed that one too, and soon acquired a third car.
At the time, I was about 25. I couldn't afford to buy real estate to get into the short-term rental market. But renting cars gave me an accessible way to turn an underutilized asset into a productive asset.
My friends and family thought I was crazy, but I loved the business's efficiency. I began researching what cars were most in demand in greater LA. I bought mid-range luxury cars like Corvettes and BMWs, which were popular with tourists. Before long, I had a fleet of more than 50 cars and was making hundreds of thousands annually.
Maintaining my fleet was challenging
A little more than a year after I started renting, a client offered to buy my SaaS company. It wasn't a hugely profitable sale, but the timing was good because it allowed me to expand my rental business. I also started a YouTube channel teaching other entrepreneurs how to manage their fleets. That was hard to monetize, so rentals accounted for about 90% of my income.
I learned a lot about operations and logistics. At first, I had cars parked all over my neighborhood in free public parking. Eventually, I leased a small lot. There wasn't a ton of storage needs, because the cars were always rented out.
The bigger challenge was vehicle maintenance. They took a lot of wear and tear, and I couldn't always account for when things went wrong.
My company now focuses on renting to gig workers
About five years ago, another owner found me via my YouTube channel. We thought we could do something similar to Turo, but better. We wanted to focus only on electric cars. Not only were they the way of the future, but they also had fewer moving parts and maintenance demands.
We launched Zevo in 2021. Today, our rentals drive about 8 million miles each month.
I love that the business supports entrepreneurs on both sides. The people who own vehicles typically have fleets of five to 250 cars. We work with dealership partners to help them purchase the most in-demand vehicles. On the other side, most of our renters are drivers for the gig economy. They typically take longer-term rentals of about 90 days.
I believe that everyone — even a 25-year-old woman like I was when I started — should be able to play in the asset class. Control of those assets shouldn't be concentrated just with big tech companies.
I paused from renting my own vehicles while we got Zevo off the ground. I just recently purchased a Tesla to list on the platform, and I'm excited to be back in the game.

Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
- Published
Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.
Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.
The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.
"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.
Protesters burned tyres and blocked roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.
The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.
Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.
But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.
When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.
The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.
"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.
While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.
The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.
David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.
Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)
But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.
The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.
The front touchscreen lets you troubleshoot and ready prints. When the printer starts, it’s relatively quiet and odor-free. 3D printing with resin can be stinky, but Formlabs-branded resins are UL GreenGuard–certified, the same standard used to ensure baby products aren’t harmful from skin contact or off-gassing. Lakatos says the idea is that the Studio 1 can be used anywhere without the room being overwhelmed by resin stank.
“We know that some people are going to put it in their bedrooms,” Lakatos says. “I don't sleep with my printers, but you could if you really wanted to.”
After going through the stack of boxes, I set up the Form Studio 1 and the Form Studio Wash+Cure. They’re stylish, with translucent orange cases that conjure old-school iMac aesthetics. The printing process itself is supposedly quick. Lakatos says you can print a casing for a Raspberry Pi setup in around eight minutes.
I’ve only printed a couple of things so far, but have had a good experience with the orders. (Full review coming soon.) I printed a clear cover for the toolbox that comes with the Studio 1. It took about 17 minutes and came out clean and intact. The process was relatively quiet. The resin smell was there, but really only when lifting the hood after the process was done. I’m excited to use it more and see what kind of very detailed unholy abominations I can make.
The SLA printing enables very detailed constructions. In Formlabs’ internal testing, the company says it has had a roughly 2 percent failure rate for its prints. If that holds in the real world, it’ll be a big jump over competitors. That’s if you use its own resins, though.
“You can use any material,” Lakatos says. “If you want to use the toxic resin on Amazon, you can do it. We don't recommend it, but you can do it.”
Formlabs also has an app called Form Mobile that can control prints or send designs to the Form Studio 1. The overall printer experience feels surprisingly straightforward.
“It’s great if you want to mess around with some stuff,” Lakatos says. “For serious, beautiful things and projects that really require better material properties, beautiful resolution, stuff like that—it's hard to compete with it.”

Assam University assistant professor booked for molesting woman researcher in Bengaluru: Police
Assistant professor at Assam University was booked for allegedly molesting a woman researcher during a conference held in Bengaluru
An assistant professor at Assam University in Silchar was booked for allegedly molesting a woman researcher during a conference held in Bengaluru, police said.
The woman researcher lodged a complaint at the Assam University police outpost on October 11, alleging sexual harassment, Cachar senior superintendent of police (SSP) Partha Pratim Das said. “We received a complaint and we are probing it,” Das said.
He added that the matter involves a central university and that, under the Vishaka guidelines, the university’s internal investigation report is important before the police intervene.
Registrar of Assam University, Silchar (AUS), Pradosh Kiran Nath, said that the woman researcher lodged a complaint alleging molestation around October 7, and the matter was referred to the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
“We held a meeting, and the ICC has been asked to complete the investigation as soon as possible and submit its report,” he said, adding that the university has a strict policy on sexual harassment.
The woman researcher told HT on Thursday that the incident occurred during an international academic conference held in Bengaluru in September and that she was subsequently threatened by the assistant professor several times.
“On the night of September 26, after an academic discussion, the supervisor insisted on accompanying me to my allotted room. We were alone at the lift when he made an inappropriate personal proposition and asked me to engage in physical intimacy. When I refused, he said that it could have adverse consequences for my academic progress,” she said.
She said that she later contacted her fiance and sought help from two female faculty members from other universities. “The two faculty members extended their support and stayed with me that night,” she added.
She alleged that the assistant professor from the department of performing arts later began creating obstacles in her academic progress and that she was denied information about two Research Advisory Committee (RAC) meetings.
“He threatened to create difficulties for me and said he would not let me complete my PhD. He also said that my research work would not progress unless I complied with his instructions,” she said.
HT reached out to the assistant professor accused of molestation, but his official contact number remained switched off until the report was filed.
Registrar Nath said that the assistant professor attended an online meeting last week and that the ICC was examining his attendance after the complaint was lodged.
Assam University has witnessed similar incidents in the past as well, and the registrar said that strict action had been taken against the accused in those cases.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

LUCKNOW: The search for absconding model-influencer Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the Shiva Sharma death case, has widened beyond India, with police following leads that place her in Nepal.

The trio was last traced to Mahim Nagar in Nepal, where CCTV cameras recorded them crossing a road and entering a bus station.
Sources said they stayed at the facility overnight and left by bus the next morning, departing before cops could reach the spot. Police have not issued an official confirmation of the identities of the people seen in the footage, and verification of the visuals remains part of the ongoing inquiry.
The reported Nepal trail has added a new dimension to the probe into the death of a 28-year-old businessman and restaurateur.
Sharma died after falling from the fourth floor of an apartment building in Lucknow on Oct 9. His family has alleged foul play and accused Shraddha and others of involvement, allegations she has denied in public statements. 
Police believe the accused may have fled Lucknow soon after the incident.

Police teams have been deployed at multiple locations to trace Shraddha, Rashmi and the third accused, while officials work to reconstruct their movements based on footage, photographs and other inputs.
Lucknow Police have announced a reward of 25,000 for information leading to Shraddha’s arrest.

She alleged Sharma was under heavy financial stress, citing debts of 15 lakh to 20 lakh, and said investigators should examine CCTV footage, mobile data and call detail records.

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.
