Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

Mauritius tightens security and extends curfew after days of unrest
Mauritius is extending a curfew for two more nights and tightening security after unrest sparked by police shooting a woman during protests over water shortages and the cost of living
JOHANNESBURG -- JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Mauritius extended a curfew for two more nights and tightened security after days of unrest sparked by police shooting a woman who was taking part in protests over water shortages and the cost of living.
The protests began last week and intensified Friday after a police officer shot and wounded a 27-year-old woman in Camp Levieux, a densely populated residential neighborhood about 15 kilometers (about 9 miles) south of the capital, Port Louis.
The officer was arrested and taken into custody as police investigate the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The unrest prompted an initial curfew, running from 8:30 p.m. Tuesday to 6 a.m. Wednesday.
The curfew, which was announced after a special Cabinet meeting on Wednesday, restricted movement in designated areas of the Indian Ocean island from 8:30 p.m. until 5 a.m. the following morning on Wednesday and Thursday nights until it ends on Friday morning.
The Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam, cited a police report saying 94 people had been arrested through Tuesday, including 16 minors and one police officer. Police reported 26 arrests during Wednesday night’s operations and said all roads were clear of obstructions Thursday morning.
Police are set to increase deployments, particularly in areas affected by violence, and reinforce roadblocks and vehicle checkpoints, according to the executive.
“Police will step up measures and will act firmly, as appropriate, to contain further escalation of violence,” its statement said.
The Cabinet said those arrested could face charges under the Prevention of Terrorism Act where applicable. Authorities also established a process to fast-track cases after consulting judicial and law enforcement officials.
The protests reflect anger over water shortages and rising costs. On Oct. 8, the government reported that reservoirs were at 57.1% capacity, down from 87.4% a year earlier, with Mare aux Vacoas at 35.7%. Emergency measures announced include drilling boreholes and deploying water tankers.
Statistics Mauritius reported that annual inflation rose to 4.1% in September, up from 3.4% a year earlier, partly due to higher petrol and food prices.
Police were monitoring social media for hate speech and incitement to violence. Citing the involvement of minors in the unrest, the Cabinet said it would consider amending the Children’s Act to lower the age for detention and prosecution from 14 to 12.
The government also restricted fuel sales in portable containers but allowed motorists to fill their vehicles as usual, according to a Commerce Ministry statement reported by L’Express.
The Education Ministry said school classes in Mauritius were canceled for Thursday and Friday because of security concerns. Some primary and secondary school exams scheduled for those days were also postponed in Mauritius and on the nearby islands of Rodrigues and Agaléga, while international exams would go ahead.
The ministry said it would announce when schools could reopen as the situation developed.
Tourism and financial services are central to Mauritius’ economy. The island, one of Africa’s most stable democracies, experienced similar unrest in 1999, when a popular musician’s death in police custody sparked days of rioting.
Britain and Canada urged travelers to avoid demonstrations and warned of possible transport disruptions. Canada said further protests could occur with “little or no warning.” The U.S. Embassy in Port Louis said in a security alert Tuesday that it had canceled scheduled services and told visitors to arrange any visit in advance.

The promise of GLP-1 drugs has always depended on people being able to afford them. These drugs still cost hundreds of dollars per month if you’re paying cash, at which point access becomes a privilege: The higher-income executive who wants to trim a few pounds might be able to afford them either way, but the low-income worker who needs the drug to lose significant weight might not be able to afford them — unless their health insurance covers it.
Why your health insurance is dropping GLP-1 coverage
Coverage for these anti-obesity drugs was finally becoming more common. Not anymore.
For a while, the trend lines for GLP-1 insurance coverage were positive. As of 2026, roughly two-thirds of private employer plans, which insure half of Americans, were covering GLP-1 medications for weight loss to treat obesity. Over the summer, Medicare launched a new $50-per-month prescription program. The US has struggled with an obesity epidemic for decades, but it looked like powerful drugs to treat it were finally starting to be more seamlessly integrated into the health system.
At least that’s how things appeared earlier this year. But now, private plans are pulling back from GLP-1 coverage. People are being left in the lurch, debating whether to try to pay for these drugs on their own or stop taking medicines they feel are making a real difference for their health.
The dilemma reveals one of the structural flaws in American healthcare. For working-age adults, your insurance depends on your job. Unfortunately, because people no longer stay at the same job for decades, there is not a strong financial incentive for employers to make investments that will benefit your health in the long term — but there is a strong incentive to minimize short-term costs as much as possible. It’s the kind of perverse rationale that could compel employer-sponsored health plans to stop covering a drug that, if taken over the full course of a person’s life, could help them not only lose weight but ultimately reduce their risk of heart disease, kidney disease and other chronic health problems, improving their health and saving all of us money as they get older.
“An employer or an insurer making coverage decisions doesn’t necessarily care if they’re saving Medicare money,” said Dan Sacks, a healthcare economist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “That’s a classic problem with the American health insurance system, and it’s certainly salient here.”
This mismatch between what’s good for people’s health and what’s good for the corporate bottom line has long been one of the underlying flaws in the US health system. Now access to GLP-1 drugs is shrinking just as these drugs were starting to make a real dent in the US obesity crisis. The stakes couldn’t be higher.
Why employer-sponsored health plans are suddenly dropping GLP-1 coverage
From the beginning, insurance coverage was the big question hanging over GLP-1s and their potential to revolutionize US healthcare. But recently, it looked like we’d turned a corner.
When I attended the Aspen Ideas: Health festival over the summer, pharmaceutical reps seemed visibly relieved that GLP-1 coverage had been picking up among private insurers. In 2026, about two out of every three employer-sponsored plans were covering some of these drugs for weight management, up from about 20 percent just the year before.
“They’re recognizing that this is an investment in their workforce,” said Laura Steele, who leads the cardiometabolic health unit at Eli Lilly, which manufactures Zepbound and Foundayo. “Yes, there is a budget, and there is a benefit design that every employer has. That’s real. That’s not going away. But they’re also recognizing the overall cost that they’re experiencing by not dealing with this too.”
But as employers and private insurers make coverage decisions for next year, they are suddenly pulling back. At least 10 percent of employer plans that currently cover GLP-1s for weight loss say they are likely to discontinue coverage in 2027, according to one survey by the Business Group on Health — and that number may still increase. A Mercer survey of large employers found that 6 percent had dropped coverage in 2026 and another 5 percent were planning to in 2027 or actively considering it. A separate report from the Health Policy Commission in Massachusetts found that the number of commercially insured people in the state taking a GLP-1 drug had fallen by 50 percent between 2025 and the first quarter of 2026 as private coverage started to drop off.
Some of the biggest brands in the US are reportedly eliminating or reducing their coverage: PepsiCo, Starbucks, and Lowe’s among them. And their reasons are simple: It’s too expensive. The drugs still carry a high net price tag — $600 or more for a 30-day supply — and potential demand is high (two in every five American adults have obesity).
When a lot of people start taking an expensive medication all at once, it’s going to raise costs for employer insurance plans — and they have to figure out how to adapt. Insurers set premiums at the start of each year, based on how many people are on the plan and how much healthcare they are expected to need. But if those estimates are off — say, if more people take an expensive GLP-1 drug than the insurer expected — they have to offset those costs somehow, and raising premiums the following year is a common solution. According to one estimate, premiums are projected to grow by 5 to 13 percent due to GLP-1 costs — and the burden of paying those higher premiums is likely to fall on the workers. The employer can also try to limit GLP-1 use by, for example, asking workers to pay more out of pocket for these drugs; according to Mercer, 27 percent of large US employers instituted some kind of utilization controls for GLP-1 drugs over the past year or plan to next year.
They also have the option to simply stop covering these drugs for weight loss altogether — and that’s the route more and more of them are deciding to take. The abrupt reversal has even caught economists like Sacks off guard.
3 big reasons employer health plans are dropping GLP-1 coverage
- Employers aren’t invested in people’s long-term health: As Americans switch jobs more often, companies want to cut short-term costs.
- GLP-1 prices are still high, upward of $600 per month per person for insurers.
- A lot of people are eligible to take them for weight loss; two in five US adults have obesity.
“I was surprised that anyone would do an about-face because I thought they understood the trade-offs well,” Sacks said. “My guess is that it turned out to be more expensive than they anticipated: Take-up is higher, and possibly more people are sticking with it. That’s one reason that you might not want to continue to offer it.”
For employers, the short-term costs of covering a drug often outweigh the long-term benefits that medication may confer, at least from the employer’s POV. One analysis — notably produced by Blue Cross Blue Shield Kansas — concluded that covering GLP-1s for weight loss increased average employee health costs by $7,000 in the first year and another $4,200 in the second, largely due to the cost of the drugs themselves. And yet at the same time, there were no decreases in obesity-related medical events in that time period. Another study from Sacks and his colleagues at Indiana University and the University of South Carolina found that GLP-1 use did not lead to any cost savings over five years.
So in the short term, these employers are arguably making an economically rational decision — but one that may still come at their employees’ expense. “I’m completely screwed,” said one person on Reddit about Cigna’s plans to drop GLP-1 coverage for their own employees. They’re looking at at least $300 for one month’s supply at cash prices.
They weren’t alone either: “I’m devastated,” said another person, commenting on Starbucks’s decision to stop covering GLP-1 drugs. They said they had an autoimmune condition that had made it difficult to lose weight — until this new class of medicines came along.
Where GLP-1 coverage goes from here
How could we end up here, where it makes good business sense for companies to make a decision that could potentially harm their workers’ health in the long term? It is at least in part a result of the haphazard way the US has ended up insuring people.
When employer-sponsored insurance started to arise in the mid-20th century, eventually becoming the primary way to cover the working-age population, people tended to stay at the same job for a long period of time. In theory, there was a synergy: Companies wanted their workers to stay productive, and so it was worth it for the company to invest in their long-term health via their insurance benefits. And research has found that people who stay with the same company — and the same insurance plan — tend to have better health than those who switch a lot.
But these days, people change jobs all the time or work various gigs to piece together an income. You probably don’t expect to stay at your job for 10 years — and your employer doesn’t expect you to either. Instead, they want to keep their own costs as low as possible in the short term. This leads them to cut GLP-1 coverage, even though doctors do believe that people could benefit tremendously long term from the weight loss these drugs help them achieve and all of its potential health benefits.
“There are very real health benefits of these drugs,” Sacks told me. “The fact that we don’t find offsets or they’re even more expensive than we thought doesn’t necessarily mean that we shouldn’t cover them.”
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy. Sign up here.
In theory, the market is supposed to fix the price problem: Drug companies get a period of exclusivity for the drugs they develop, and then, once that time elapses, cheaper generic versions can come onto the market. But generic semaglutide won’t be available in the US until at least 2031 — and for some versions, the generic competitors aren’t going to debut until the 2040s. Offering GLP-1 coverage could become a competitive advantage for employers, a perk they can offer to entice potential workers as part of their benefits package.
Beyond that, though, the path to more affordable GLP-1s is not immediately obvious right now. A lot of people are already willing to pay cash for these drugs — and that may continue as long as people can afford to do it. But with inflation still steadily rising, these drugs could slip out of reach for more and more Americans.
The government could get involved, but, for now, the federal government’s negotiating authority only covers Medicare, not the private plans that are dropping coverage. Serious healthcare reform is probably off the table until at least 2028, and then only if Democrats win both Congress and the White House and decide to make a healthcare package their legislative priority.
But the lesson of these recent developments is that, at some point, the US may have to look seriously at the underlying problem creating this mess in the first place. A patchwork method of insuring people that privileges short-term cost-cutting over people’s long-term health isn’t a real healthcare system.

With customers in more than 220 countries and territories, global shipping and logistics provider DHL has seen firsthand the trade compliance challenges businesses face when expanding internationally.
Against a backdrop of shifting geopolitical dynamics and macroeconomic uncertainty, businesses must navigate evolving trade regulations, sanctions, export controls and customs requirements, as well as a growing number of free trade agreements (FTAs), said Mr Chee Yaw Chek, vice president (commercial) at DHL Express Singapore.
Despite shifting trade policies and restrictions, global trade remained resilient in 2025, according to the DHL Global Connectedness Tracker. Mr Chee also pointed to opportunities in intra-Asia trade as companies diversify their supply chains and expand into new markets across the region.
Trade AI Advisor helps businesses navigate trade requirements. (Video: Singapore Business Federation)
But entering new markets also brings practical questions around trade requirements. “Many of our customers approach us for guidance when exploring new markets,” he said. “They often have questions about market entry, duties and tariffs, and FTAs. Understanding how these affect international trade is important for managing risk and business continuity.”
Large companies may have dedicated trade and compliance teams to manage complex cross-border requirements. But small- and medium-size enterprises (SMEs) may have to spread the work across finance, operations or procurement teams that are already stretched, noted Mr Wayne Yap, CEO of Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF).
“These documentation bottlenecks can mean more administrative work, delays and costs,” he said. “They can also make it harder for smaller businesses to assess trade opportunities when exploring new export markets. For more complex questions, they may still need to seek specialist advice.”
To help Singapore businesses navigate cross-border trade, the Centre for the Future of Trade and Investment (CFOTI) at Singapore Business Federation (SBF) launched Trade AI Advisor (TAIA) at the Future of Trade Forum 2026 in September.
SCALING ACCESS TO TRADE GUIDANCE
Powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI), TAIA provides practical guidance on trade agreements, tariffs, market access, customs and documentation requirements, rules of origin and manufacturing cost statements. It helps businesses identify the information, rules and supporting documents that may apply, before seeking further specialist advice where needed.
Mr Heng Peng Kwang, executive director of CFOTI, said TAIA aims to make relevant trade information easier to search, understand and apply to specific business questions, reducing the need to consult multiple sources. TAIA is expected to provide 24/7 advisory support to 30,000 companies in Singapore, helping them navigate trade requirements as they expand internationally.
For example, before entering a new regional market, a Singapore manufacturer may need to determine its product’s Harmonised System code, the applicable tariff, the required origin documentation and whether the product qualifies for preferential treatment under an FTA.
TAIA also helps businesses work through more structured requirements, such as preparing a manufacturing cost statement to assess whether a product may meet the relevant origin criteria under an FTA. This helps businesses understand not only what information is needed, but also the steps and supporting inputs involved.
Businesses can enter these questions into TAIA, which provides responses with citations to curated trade data sources from SBF and its partners. These include SMF, an authorised organisation for issuing Ordinary Certificates of Origin.
“This gives businesses greater traceability, so they can understand where the information comes from and refer to the relevant sources when navigating requirements,” said Mr Yap.
COMBINING AI WITH HUMAN EXPERTISE
TAIA combines AI guidance with human expertise, with more complex trade queries escalated to specialists when needed.
“TAIA doesn’t replace professional judgment,” said Mr Heng. “It helps a company frame its question, identify the rules and requirements that may apply and see the sources behind the response.”
For example, a company may be assessing whether a product meets a specific rule of origin when production takes place across several countries and involves multiple manufacturing steps. TAIA can help identify the relevant agreements, rules and supporting information.
If further confirmation is needed, the matter can then be referred to an adviser at CFOTI or the relevant authority.
DHL was among the industry partners that tested TAIA. It drew on real-world questions from customers to assess how the platform addressed common concerns around market entry, duties, tariffs and FTAs, Mr Chee said TAIA could be especially useful for SMEs, which may have limited resources or in-house expertise to keep pace with changes in the global trade landscape.
TAKING TAIA TO THE REGION
TAIA’s reach is not limited to enterprises in Singapore. In July, at the Singapore-Indonesia Leaders’ Retreat, SBF and the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KADIN Indonesia) signed a two-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help SMEs in Indonesia trade more easily across borders. One of the first initiatives under the MOU is TAIA-ID, a version of the platform being localised for Indonesian businesses ahead of its launch later this year.
TAIA-ID is being developed in Bahasa Indonesia and designed for mobile access. It will provide guidance based on Indonesia’s trade agreements in areas such as tariff eligibility, rules of origin, export procedures and market access, with complex queries referred by email to trained trade advisers. Its first phase will focus on export-oriented horticulture enterprises.
The initiative combines the digital platform with support from trained KADIN Indonesia trade advisers, SME outreach and pilot export shipments, extending the programme’s reach while retaining access to human expertise.
“As Singapore assumes the ASEAN Chairmanship in 2027, we see an opportunity to work with ASEAN partners to adapt this approach for their markets, so SMEs across the region can more easily access support to trade and expand regionally,” said Mr Heng.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission and detained thousands of protesters, including three CJP leaders. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some protesters gathered elsewhere. On 12 October, opposition leaders also marched to the Supreme Court against the SIR exercise, but police stopped them (here, here, here, here).
In this context, visuals showing crowds are being shared on social media with the claim that they show gatherings at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and outside Parliament House (here, here, here). Let’s verify these videos.
Claim: Visuals showing anti-CEC protestors gathering outside Parliament and Jantar Mantar.
Fact: These videos are AI-generated, not real visuals. No media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. Hence, the claims made in these posts are FALSE.
Video 1: 
Upon closer examination, we noticed a Gemini logo, associated with Google’s AI tool, in the bottom-right corner of the video, suggesting that it may have been AI-generated. We further analysed a keyframe from the viral video using SynthID, which also detected AI-generated content in the clip.
Video 2:
On performing a relevant keyword search, we found that no media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. We analysed the viral video using Hive’s AI-detection tool, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Furthermore, PIB Fact Check and Delhi Police also clarified that the viral video was fake and had been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
To sum up, these videos are AI-generated and do not show a protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar in Delhi.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
- Published
Eight of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a tanker ablaze off Romania's coast, naval authorities say.
The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire on Thursday morning. Romanian President Nicușor Dan later confirmed it was struck by drones.
The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. A swarm of Russian drones was detected overnight not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.
Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing. It did not name the vessels.
On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.
A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.
The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.
The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.
The tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT).
Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader was hit by two drones.
The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked.
This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.
The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."
Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.
The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.
Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports.
On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports.
Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

A rumor that legendary comedian and satirist George Carlin once performed a comedy bit that involved jokes about televised public executions circulated online in October.
Carlin, who died in 2008, was known for his scathing political takedowns and clever wordplay.
People on social media shared a clip that appears to be from one of Carlin's standup comedy TV specials, in which the comic allegedly waxed poetic about using public executions to help balance the United States' budget.
The clip circulated as the Pentagon announced its plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 during a shooting at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas.
Some users suggested Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's move with his comedy bit from decades earlier.
The video was authentic and clipped from Carlin's 1996 HBO special, "George Carlin: Back in Town," recorded at The Beacon Theater in New York City on March 30 of that year. The special is available to stream for free on Tubi and was also released as an album on Sept. 17, 1996.
The clip in question is part of a segment titled "Capital Punishment," which begins around the 14:30 mark in the full special. The clip was also available to viewon Carlin's official website.
During the special, Carlin joked about performing crucifixions during "Monday Night Football" in a satirical bit about executing white collar criminals facilitating the laundering of drug money.
The joke leads into the moment shown in the viral clip, beginning around the 15:15 mark. Carlin said (emphasis ours):
I don't care about capital punishment one way or another, because I know it doesn't do anything. It doesn't do anything except maybe satisfy a Biblical need for revenge. You know, if you read the Bible, you see that it's full of retribution and revenge. So really, capital punishment is kind of a religious ritual. It's a purification rite. It's a modern sacrament. And as long as that's true, I say, let's liven it up a little!
I honestly believe that if you make the death penalty a little more entertaining, and learn to market it correctly, you just might be able to raise enough money to balance the stupid f***ing budget!
And don't forget, the polls show the American people want capital punishment and they want a balanced budget. And I think even in a fake democracy people ought to get what they want once in a while. Just to feed this illusion that they're really in charge.
Let's use capital punishment the same way we use sports and television in this country, to distract people and take their minds off how bad they're being f***ed by the upper 1 percent. Now, unfortunately, "Monday Night Football" doesn't last long enough. What we really need is year-round capital punishment on TV every night with sponsors! Gotta have sponsors. I'm sure as long as we're killing people, Marlboro cigarettes and Dow Chemical will be proud to participate.
To say Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's planned livestream of an execution was a stretch, but it's accurate to say he joked about televised capital punishment 30 years earlier.
The special also featured Carlin's takes on other hot-button issues that continue to be part of the national discourse in 2026, including abortion and the prison system.
"Back in Town" was Carlin's ninth HBO comedy special, of which he would do 14 before his death in 2008.

Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, blamed Iran for the dramatic escalation in the war with the rebels
The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack on Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government’s interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

How did a P.E.I. cold case fall apart just before it was set to go to trial?
Charlottetown police admit investigators should have been more transparent with Crown about evidence
There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to go to trial.
The provincial Crown Attorney’s Office announced Tuesday that the charges against Todd Joseph Irving in connection with the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr were being withdrawn after it came to light that Charlottetown police had lost "extensive crucial evidence" in the case.
CBC News first learned about that missing evidence — which includes the knife found at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr — at a bail hearing in July. The Crown confirmed that’s when they first learned about it, too. But Charlottetown police later told CBC News they knew physical evidence was missing as far back as 2007 when the case was reopened.
- Charges were dropped in a decades-old murder case. Now, there are calls for an independent review
- Charlottetown police lost the evidence in a P.E.I. cold-case murder. How did it happen?
Interim Charlottetown police Chief Darren MacDougall believes police did tell the Crown at some point that some items were missing, but not the full picture of how much physical evidence or exactly which items were lost.
He acknowledges that information should have been provided to the Crown sooner.
"There was likely not enough transparency with regard to the evidence as it relates to the Crown and the investigators. So there was certainly a breakdown there. I think that the investigators clung to the hope that they would be able to interview some of the people involved in 1989 to determine where they might have put these exhibits," MacDougall said.
"It’s the responsibility of the police, for full disclosure, to move that disclosure to the Crown."
But MacDougall was quick to point out that the DNA evidence collected from the items wasn’t lost — that material was processed and stored appropriately. It was the items themselves, after they’d been processed and sent back to Charlottetown police, that were misplaced.
Michael Arntfield is a professor and criminologist at Western University who heads up the school’s cold case research group. He’s also a former police detective.
"It’s both unusual and unfortunate because this was a great solve using state-of-the art investigative genetic genealogy, IGG, to track down the still alleged or once alleged offender in a very infamous cold case," he said.
"However, it turned out to be sort of an exploding cigar in that once, sort of, the novelty of the solve subsided … the two key pieces of evidence seem to have disappeared, which sort of pulls the rug out from underneath the whole case."
'It contaminates the whole investigation'
Arntfield believes police were hoping the DNA evidence was incontrovertible. And police have said as much.
Todd Joseph Irving walked out of court on Tuesday a free man after the charges against him in connection with the death of Byron Carr were dropped. (CBC)
"With the evidence that we relied upon, and we had significant forensic DNA evidence, we believed the evidence met the threshold to believe that [Irving] committed the offense," MacDougall said in an interview with CBC News after the charges were dropped.
At the July bail hearing, police testified that Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.
His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind, according to police testimony.
The entirety of the missing evidence isn’t clear, but the Crown described it as "the overwhelming majority of the critical physical evidence," going on to say that included "key exhibits central to the prosecution."
- Family of Byron Carr speaks out after murder charges in decades-old cold case withdrawn
- Charges laid in decades-old P.E.I. cold case murder withdrawn after key evidence lost
With that, Arntfield said, the credibility of the Charlottetown Police Services is lost — along with whatever remaining evidence they had.
"It contaminates the whole investigation because a judge or jury or both … would be left wondering, 'OK, if they have slipshod record-keeping and no chain of custody for key exhibits, what else don’t we know? What else was overlooked? What other corners were cut?'" he said.
"This isn’t corruption, this isn’t malicious. What I think it is is they were fixated on solving this, they cut corners and ultimately at the end of the day they were motivated by getting an alleged killer off the streets and ensuring justice for the family decades later."
If police had been forthcoming with the Crown about what physical evidence they did — and didn’t — have in their possession, Arntfield said the outcome could have been much different.
"You would think in a case like this — a high-profile historical homicide using a state-of-the-art and still somewhat controversial technology, IGG — that, even just as a courtesy, some senior officer or the case manager might have notified the Crown that a complex, high-profile case is coming down the pipe, apprise them of the strengths and weaknesses of the case, what witnesses are still alive and locatable and exhibits are still intact," he said.
"There’s other things that could have been done based on what police knew in order to shore up those deficiencies.… I think they would have had probably more evidence to incentivize maybe a quick guilty plea, which is I’m almost certain what police were relying on here. They were expecting a quick guilty plea and none of this suspicious disappearance of evidence would have ever seen the light of day."
Police, Crown look through different lenses: MacDougall
In Ontario, Arntfield said, cold cases get what he calls a "concierge approach," where the Crown is brought in early to weigh in on the strength of the evidence.
MacDougall acknowledges that, in this case, investigators were perhaps weighing the strength of the evidence differently than a prosecutor might.
"Perhaps the Crown, who views this through a different lens — the weight that existed with the missing exhibits measured with the weight of the DNA evidence, the forensic DNA evidence that was very compelling, I would say — [the Crown], again viewing it through a different lens, they came to the conclusion that they were unable to provide the accused with a fair trial."
Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, says he would welcome an independent investigation. (Barry Acton/CBC)
While Arntfield called the outcome of this case a rare and regrettable snafu, he said it shouldn’t erode public confidence in police.
"The investigation was solid, there was a chokepoint along the way where something happened and I wouldn’t even call it a coverup, I would say they strategically omitted that information at the last minute," he said.
"The question will be: who made the determination to suppress this glaring deficiency and suspicious disappearance and proceed at great time and expense?"
There have been calls for an independent review of how the case was handled, which MacDougall said he would welcome.
It’s up to P.E.I.'s justice and public safety minister to call such an investigation. In a statement to CBC News, the department said it was communicating with Charlottetown police about the Byron Carr case, saying "government has various options to consider in terms of a review and scope, so a particular path is not set yet. It's still under discussion."

In mid-October, social media users claimed U.S. President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated video of himself playing with a tiger.
The rumor spread days after a tiger mauled and killed a man at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster, England, on Oct. 10. The clip shows an artificial intelligence tool's depiction of Trump pointing his finger at the tiger before playfully wrestling and hugging it.
One X user who shared the footage wrote (archived), "Trump actually posted this AI video of him with a tiger in the middle of the night."
Trump did indeed post the AI video on his Truth Social account, hours after sharing authentic footage of the moment a tiger attacked a man in the U.K. The AI clip Trump posted shows the president mimicking the hand gesture the British man made as the tiger attacked him in the authentic video. As such, we rate this claim true.
The president posted the AI-generated video (archived) on Truth Social late at night on Oct. 13.
Hours earlier, he posted (warning: the link contains violent and distressing content) authentic footage, meaning not AI-generated or digitally created, of a tiger mauling a man named William Chapman in an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park (archived). Trump's caption reads, "Don't ever mess with nature! President DJT."
(Truth Social user "realDonaldTrump")
Trump also posted (warning: the link contains violent and distressing content) a compilation of clips (archived) of big cats attacking humans on Oct. 13. Snopes has not determined the authenticity of those videos.
Chapman was a former child actor. On Oct. 10, he entered the tiger's enclosure and sustained fatal injuries from the attack. His family criticized Trump for posting the authentic footage of Chapman, who, they said, suffered from mental illness. A family statement reads:

The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.

Student protesters attack government buildings in Tirana
- Published
Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".
"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.
"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

Almost nine years ago, a tanned, relatively well-rested-looking CEO named Elon Musk announced that his electric car company would make a new sports car, the Tesla Roadster 2. It would be “the fastest sports car ever made, period,” Musk said on stage in 2017. “The point of doing this is to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars.” Lights flashed, and the red prototype did a few speedy laps behind him.
Times have changed. Musk is the leading donor to a political party that last year nixed buying incentives for electric vehicles and last month adjusted fuel-economy standards to make it easier for automakers to skip making EVs altogether. Musk has said he’s not even in the business of making cars anymore, instructing investors to think of Tesla as a robotics and autonomy company. On Thursday night, Tesla will host what it has billed as its last unveiling event for a human-driven vehicle. Six years after it was supposed to roll into driveways, the Roadster 2 is finally here. Tesla is slated to start deliveries next year.
“EVs exist today in a massively different environment than when the Roadster was introduced,” says Ed Kim, president of AutoPacific, an automotive research firm. When Tesla announced the car back in 2017, electrics were “toys for early adopters,” he says. By 2020, other automakers saw Tesla’s sky-high valuations and lawmakers’ plans to transition vehicles to batteries and made big electric promises, investing heavily in the shift. China began to dominate EV-making. Now, after the Trump administration reversed the US’s course on the powertrain, EV sales are shrinking, not growing.
Still, lots more options are available now. In 2017, research firm Cox Automotive says, US customers had 15 EVs to choose from; today, that number has jumped to nearly 90. Potential EV buyers are more likely to be normies, and so their needs are more practical. “People are looking for range, performance, charging ability, resale value,” says Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of Industry Insights at Cox.
What success looks like for the Roadster, then, is a bit complicated. It’s a hypercar targeted squarely at, well, non-normies—people who like to show off and go very, very fast. Some of them want that signature gasoline-engine power and roar. That’s why some luxury automakers have taken pains to reproduce the sound of a V-8 without one present. And it’s why others—Porsche and Ferrari among them—have said they’ll keep developing gas engines. Lamborghini said earlier this year it would shelve electrics altogether. Even Bugatti’s CEO, who founded his own electric hypercar company, said he expects loud ICE cars to become a status symbol among the wealthiest car buyers.
“EVs in this space really have to wow the shopper with a lot more than practical things,” says Kim. “Great range, really quiet, charging at home—none of that matters.” In 2017, Tesla said the car would start at $200,000; reservation holders put down $50,000 deposits.
In 2017, Musk promised a then-record-breaking sub-2-second 0-to-60 acceleration time. Now that a handful of other production cars have broken that barrier, Tesla will have to meet a high bar. One option: Musk has suggested several times over the years that the new Roadster will fly, and reports suggest that the automaker will get help from Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. (In 2018, SpaceX used its Falcon Heavy rocket to launch the first Roadster into space.)
Going that fast “is not terribly comfortable," says Shea Burns, a partner in the automotive and industrial practice at AlixPartners. “The laws of physics are catching up with them, outside of the rocket piece.” It would be an interesting way for an EV-maker to exit human driving.

H-1B holders may face tougher scrutiny under proposed US rule | What will change?
The new proposed rule being considered would allow federal immigration officers to disregard previous approvals when reviewing extension requests.
The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has put forward a regulatory proposal that could undermine an important aspect of how temporary work visas are processed, sparking concern throughout the Indian immigrant community.
The new proposed rule being considered would allow federal immigration officers to disregard previous approvals when reviewing extension requests for non-immigrant work visas, such as the widely used H-1B and L-1 programmes. The DHS’ proposal hasn’t been put into action yet. Currently, the department is actively seeking feedback on the “entirety of this proposed rulemaking package.”
Indian nationals make up roughly 70% of all H-1B beneficiaries in FY 2025, based on US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) data.
The proposal put forward by DHS and USCIS seeks to eliminate a specific policy (8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)). This policy currently requires USCIS to show “deference to a prior approval” when reviewing the same circumstances during visa extension or petition renewal requests.
Also Read I US visa waits soar worldwide as consulates lose staff; Indian travelers also face lengthy appointment delays
According to the US department’s explanation, this change would alter how extension requests are handled going forward. “When adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 (Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker) involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, USCIS gives deference to its prior determination of the petitioner’s, applicant’s, or beneficiary’s eligibility.”
This requirement typically comes into play when an employer submits a petition to renew or extend a foreign worker’s permission to work or stay in the United States under the same nonimmigrant worker category that was previously approved.
According to the proposal, the current regulation requires USCIS to generally rely on the earlier eligibility determination for the nonimmigrant worker classification “unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information.”
Employers submit Form I-129 to petition for a nonimmigrant worker to enter the US temporarily for work, labour, or training purposes in categories including H-1B, H-2A, H-2B, H-3, L-1, O-1, O-2, P-1, P-1S, P-2, P-2S, P-3, P-3S, Q-1, or R-1 nonimmigrant classifications.
What will change?
The US is looking to eliminate the deference policy — a system that lets officers grant visa extensions by relying on earlier approvals. The department explains that this shift would touch every benefit request submitted via Form I-129. That said, it wouldn’t stop USCIS officers from taking a prior approval into account when it makes sense to do so. “Rather, it would remove the requirement that officers begin from a position of deference to the prior approval,” the proposal says.
This change would lead to more rigorous examination of visa extension requests. People who previously received visa extensions won’t have any special advantage anymore. Instead, they’ll face the same level of scrutiny as those applying for visas for the first time.
Under this new rule, visa extension applications wouldn’t automatically get expedited approval when an employer submits a qualifying Form I-129 extension request. The DHS believes this adjustment would allow for a comprehensive evaluation of every petition.
Experts expect a rise in requests for additional evidence (RFE), which means petitioners will need to spend more time gathering and submitting extra documentation and supporting materials.
“For workers who need an extension to keep working, the USCIS deference policy proposal could lead to a closer review. Officers could review facts that USCIS already accepted once before,” the Vasquez Law firm stated on its website.
Additional financial burden on petitioners
The firm clarifies that this proposal doesn’t alter the fundamental eligibility criteria for a classification. Rather, it modifies how USCIS would evaluate subsequent filings.
“A worker may feel the practical effects even though the employer is often the petitioner...If USCIS requests more evidence, the employer may need to document the offered role, business operations, compensation, contracts, work location, and the worker’s qualifications again. The worker may also need records showing continued maintenance of nonimmigrant status. Maintaining status means following the rules of the worker’s temporary immigration category,” the firm added.
According to the US government, this rule would also create financial burdens for petitioners by extending the time needed for decisions and adding uncertainty about job continuity. The Department of Homeland Security projects that the rule would generate roughly $133,987 (aprox ₹1.2 cr) in new yearly expenses for petitioners, primarily from a rise in Requests for Evidence.
“In addition, the rule would impose costs on USCIS by increasing the adjudicative workload and operational costs, as officers would spend more time reassessing eligibility issues previously reviewed and may issue an increased number of RFEs, thereby increasing overall resource demands,” the proposal says.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.
