Acceleration shock
NASA’s planetary science budget remains under pressure. The Trump administration has twice proposed deep cuts in planetary science. Congress restored most of the funding for fiscal year 2026 and is expected to do the same in the 2027 budget.
Ending support for Europe’s Envision mission and canceling Mars Sample Return freed up enough funding for NASA to move forward with DAVINCI and VERITAS, and in some cases, buy back some of their past delays. DAVINCI is now targeting a launch in December 2030, a year earlier than the previous plan.
“Thanks to encouragement in early ’26 from our leaders at NASA Headquarters and the Planetary Science Division,” said Garvin, who leads the DAVINCI science team. “This is our new scenario for the most cost-effective and science-effective launch to Venus … What we’ve done now is accelerated launch by 54 weeks to a case where we have a very low delta-V trajectory that gets off the ground in late December 2030.”
Low delta-V is an important qualifier. This means the trajectory for DAVINCI will require relatively little energy, at least as far as interplanetary missions go. A flyby with Venus in early 2032 will set up DAVINCI to release its atmospheric entry probe for descent to the planet’s surface on October 3, 2032. The mission’s carrier spacecraft will continue zooming through the inner Solar System, and the revised trajectory should allow it to hold enough fuel in reserve to enter orbit around Venus when it comes back around again, something that wasn’t always assured, Garvin said.
The comeback of VERITAS is even more striking.
“VERITAS is now funded with a launch date of November 2032, so this is great news for us,” said Dan Nunes, the mission’s deputy project scientist at JPL. “We’re staffing up. We’re accelerating, not to the point of Jim’s acceleration [on DAVINCI], but we’re moving.”
VERITAS is targeted to launch the month after DAVINCI arrives at Venus. “It keeps building on momentum for Venus science, which is great,” Nunes said. “We’re going to arrive at Venus close to the middle of 2033, and we’re going to have a phase of aerobraking” before beginning routine science observations.
In recent months, engineers working on the DAVINCI mission completed experiments showing how the Venus probe’s cameras and instruments will capture data during its one-shot descent through the atmosphere. It will take about an hour for DAVINCI’s battery-powered titanium descent craft to travel from space to the surface of Venus, and all of its imagery and data must be relayed to Earth through a radio link with DAVINCI’s carrier spacecraft before it goes over the horizon.
“We have to optimize everything in the final eight to 10 minutes of descent as we come into the supercritical atmosphere to get this data back for all of us to work with,” Garvin said.
The DAVINCI team also recently subjected a prototype of the entry probe to the extreme temperatures it will see at Venus. The insulated sphere kept its internal components below 86° Fahrenheit (30° Celsius), meeting requirements. DAVINCI’s managers at Goddard reported results from these two tests to NASA Headquarters and Administrator Jared Isaacman, and to the White House, Garvin said.
The news is similarly positive for VERITAS, according to Nunes, who credited scientific advocacy groups for the mission’s survival.
“VERITAS is going,” Nunes said. “We would like to thank all the support from the community, from VEXAG, the Planetary Society, all those people that went out there and made the case for Venus exploration for keeping VERITAS alive and getting us a launch date, so we’re very thankful for that.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, despite the true prevalence of the condition likely being a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA.
The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will lead to a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations for military members. Those evaluations could result in inappropriate testing, inaccurate results and diagnoses, and overtreatment that could cause harm, including infertility. Medical experts, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association (AUA), have recommended against blanket screenings for these reasons. Still, the Pentagon has moved forward with the plans, releasing clinical guidance in September.
The JAMA study highlights the reasons why testosterone levels are not measured in men without symptoms—and also offers a glimpse of how many Army members could become ensnared in the clinically dubious screenings.
Researchers at the Pennington Biomedical Research Center in Louisiana and the US Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine in Massachusetts conducted the study. The researchers drew data from a large military health survey, which included members at five US Army installations. The survey data included morning blood draws from fasting military members. The samples were collected between August 2024 and January 2026.
Estimating impact
From those samples, total testosterone levels were measured from 479 male, active-duty Army service members. (Those receiving testosterone treatment were excluded from the study—three men were excluded for this reason.) With some statistical weighting, the 479 included members were representative of the active-duty US Army personnel; the weighted mean age was about 30 years old, and the weighted mean body mass index (BMI) was 28.4, which falls in the “overweight” category.

GuliKit TT Max review: The granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers
This is the Switch 2 gamepad for big hands.
The TT Max from GuliKit is the heftiest Switch 2 controller in town. Wider, thicker and heavier than Nintendo's Pro Controller or 8BitDo's Ultimate 2, the TT Max feels like it was designed to make PC, Xbox and PlayStation fans feel at home on Switch 2. With aligned and adjustable TMR thumbsticks, four removable back paddles, a customizable floating D-pad, multiplatform support and other quality features, the TT Max is a versatile gamepad for serious play on the Switch 2 and beyond.
In the world of controllers generally, the TT Max is a standard size and fairly lightweight, but compared with Switch 2 gamepads, it's a beast. In my admittedly small hands, it sits more like an Xbox pad than a Nintendo Pro Controller, though it has aligned joysticks like a DualSense. (Dr. Frankenstein would be proud.) The metal rear paddles, which are attached out of the box, are raised above the grips like slim butterfly wings and they press in with a satisfying click. They make the controller feel even bigger than its chassis, for better or worse.
The entire gamepad hits fidget-toy-levels of fulfillment: Its triggers flare upward and are roughly textured at the tips, and there's a switch to swap between an ultra-smooth Hall effect pull and a digital click. The controller's face is matte plastic while its rear grips are heavily textured like the triggers, and the bumpers are nice and wide. The floating circular D-pad can be set to a 4-way or 8-way mode, and the TMR thumbsticks are super precise, with a slick glide and adjustable stepless tension. The TT Max comes with an extra D-pad and a stick kit providing two additional heights, each featuring silicone caps with low-profile edges.
The TT Max looks like a multiplatform controller because it is, supporting PC, Android and iOS play, as well as Switch and Switch 2. Its face buttons are shiny with a hard-rubber feel, they press in with a stiff click, and the box includes a spare set of PC-style keycaps. Plus, you're able to swap between Nintendo and PC layouts on demand.
Something about the way the TT Max powers on is super cute. Press the small home button, and the controller shakes while the RGB rings light up around the left joystick, the right joystick, and then the central logo. The default mode leaves rainbow circles flowing around the sticks, but there are four light modes altogether: constant on, stick tracing, trigger tracing and rainbow. The lights also serve as quick-look indicators for your thumbstick sensitivity settings, with pink for 50 percent, blue for 100 percent and green for 150 percent.
The TT Max has gyro controls for supported games and adjustable haptics with three modes: rotary motor, maglev haptics and HD vibration. When paired with the Switch 2, the controller's default mode is HD vibration. While this offers pinpoint haptics and a lovely all-over rumble, it tends to make a grinding noise that's noticeable even over the on-screen frenzy of Resident Evil Requiem. Perhaps unsurprisingly, rotary mode is even louder and crunchier. GuliKit's proprietary maglev haptic mode, the default for PC play, is the quietest and least mechanical-sounding of the bunch, and it's my personal favorite. Note that this is all based on the standard intensity setting, and there's one softer and one stronger, so you should be able to find something that works for your palms and ears equally.
One of the most luxurious features that a Switch 2 controller can have is the ability to wake up the console, and here, the TT Max has you covered. It pairs easily to the Switch 2 and will reliably wake up the console with a press of the home button, and the controller's in-box instructions are easy to follow all around. It doesn't feature a player indicator on the chassis, but it has lights to signal pairing mode and battery life between the bumpers. I haven't encountered any issues with the TT Max's lifespan, since it easily charges via a USB-C port; GuliKit says it can last up to 26 hours with the RGBs off, or 14 hours with the lights on low.
I was surprised to see that the TT Max also comes with a simple hard case perfectly molded to the controller's contours, providing protection while traveling or living with perpetually sticky kids, roommates, cats, bees, etc. The case is nothing special, but it's really nice to have.
To neatly recap, here are all of the accessories included in the TT Max's box:
- Three analog stick pairs of varying heights, one pair attached
- PC-layout keycaps
- Keycap puller
- Tension adjustment tool
- Four metal paddles, attached to the rear grips
- Two D-pads, one attached
- Hyperlink 2 wireless USB adapter
- USB-C to USB charging cable
- Protective case
- User manual (that's actually useful)
All of that comes with a sturdy, versatile and reliable gamepad that works across Switch, Switch 2, PC, Android and iOS, and still costs $20 less than the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller. GuliKit's TT Max is $70, placing it near the middle of the pack when it comes to Switch 2 controller pricing.
The TT Max is big, but it's not too big by any means. It serves as a reminder that the Switch 2 is a legitimate current-gen console, easily on par with something like the Xbox Series S, but with additional mobile functionality. The Switch 2 is a little hybrid device that's capable of handling any AAA game you throw at it, including third-party monsters like Elden Ring, Cyberpunk 2077, Resident Evil Requiem, Street Fighter 6, Diablo IV and so on. And if you do come across a game that you'd rather play on PC, the TT Max can follow you there, too.

Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence. You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton?
In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton.
There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist.
Compared to women, “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.)
While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides.
Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men.
Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women.
“Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says.
Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did.
In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty.
“We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says.

US-based AI healthtech startup Confido Health has raised $12.5 Mn (about ₹119 Cr) in a Series A extension led by Z47, taking its total Series A funding to $22.5 Mn. Existing investors Together Fund and Blume Ventures also participated in the round. Healthcare private equity investor Justin Saks has joined the startup as an investor and board adviser. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its CareOS platform across healthcare organisations with multiple sites and develop AI agents for additional workflows and medical specialities. Founded in 2022 by Chetan Reddy and Vichar Shroff, Confido Health develops AI agents to automate administrative tasks for healthcare providers, including patient calls, appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills, and payment collection. Its CareOS platform integrates with more than 50 healthcare systems, including electronic health records, practice management software, and billing platforms. This allows providers to automate tasks across their existing systems without replacing their technology infrastructure. Confido Health initially focused on voice AI for patient calls before expanding into broader healthcare administration. Its platform connects related tasks, allowing a patient interaction to trigger follow-up work such as scheduling an appointment, processing a prescription refill, or collecting a payment. The startup primarily targets healthcare groups operating across multiple sites, particularly those backed by private equity firms. Its distribution strategy involves working with private equity investors to secure introductions to their portfolio companies. Confido Health said it serves 3,200 providers across more than 1,500 sites in 27 US states, with its AI agents enabling one in 50 Americans to access healthcare. It claimed 15-fold growth since its previous funding round but did not specify the metric. The startup reported AI handling rates above 95% across key end-to-end administrative workflows. It said deployments added operational capacity equivalent to three to five full-time employees on average within three months, while patient satisfaction averaged 4.55 out of five across approximately one million tasks. The fundraise comes amid investor bets on AI applications across healthcare, from administrative automation to patient guidance and early disease detection. Earlier, Inc42 reported that AI health companion startup August AI was in talks to raise about $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners. The startup helps users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports. Earlier this year, Practo cofounder Shashank ND’s new venture Cent raised about $5 Mn from his family office OneFlow Holdings and South Park Commons. Cent uses AI and health data to detect critical diseases early. Indian healthtech startups raised $93 Mn across 13 deals in Q3 2026 till September 24.

Delhi Police return 22,882 phones under Operation Vishwas
At least 88 people, whose mobile phones were either snatched, robbed, stolen or misplaced, got their cellphones back every day this year, as the Delhi Police have recovered and returned 22,882 lost and stolen phones to their rightful owners till September 15, senior police officers said on Thursday.
With 3,010 phones returned to their owners, the southwest district police topped the list of 15 police district and four other police units – crime branch, railways, metro and Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport – in terms of tracing recovering, and returning stolen and lost mobile phones under the Delhi Police’s special drive named “Operation Vishwas.”
The IGI Airport police remained at the bottom of the list by returning only 51 stolen phones to their rightful owners till September 15, according to the Delhi Police data accessed by HT.
Data shows that the police force received 69,881 mobile handset traceability reports from the Central Equipment Identity Register (CEIR), a portal that allows people across India to block and track their lost or stolen mobile phones.
“The CEIR regularly shares information about mobile phones reported to law enforcement agencies as lost and stolen phones whenever new SIM cards are installed in the handsets and they become active again anywhere across the country. In Delhi, each police district and concerned unit receives the traceability report separately and according to cases registered in the particular district or unit,” said a senior police officer, aware of the procedures related to recovery of stolen phones.
Police data shows that between January 1 and September 15 this year, the railways unit of the city police received the maximum 9,001 mobile handset traceability reports from the CEIR followed by Dwarka police station and the Metro police unit that received 7,089 and 6,567 such handset traceability reports. The IGI Airport and crime branch units received the lowest such reports that were 92 and 937 respectively, the data shows.
Mobile phone loss reports and recovery rates
According to police, nearly 1,50,000 mobile phones were reported lost, stolen, snatched or robbed in the first seven months of 2026. Last year, the number was around 2,50,000. The Delhi Police have two dedicated digital platforms – Lost App and Theft e-FIR apps and web services – that allow people to report their lost or stolen mobile phones on their own and without visiting police stations.
The city police’s data shows that the police handed over nearly 87% of the recovered phones to their rightful numbers till September 15, with the northwest, Shahdara, and southeast districts and railways and metro police units achieving 100% handover rate, meaning all phones recovered during the period were returned to their owners.
“Recovering stolen phones and returning them to their owners has been on the priority list of the city police. Operation Vishwas was launched with the aim to restore the public’s faith in the city police, snatching and theft of phones is a common crime that affects hundreds of people daily. Each police district and unit has a specialised team for this job,” another police officer said, asking not to be named.

Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US senators and election offices
- Published
Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
They were Delaware's Lisa Blunt Rochester, California's Alex Padilla, and the two senators for New York, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, CBS reported.
Connecticut Democrat Chris Murphy was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, which was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman told the BBC.
Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings.
Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

O'Neill defiant in defeat but Celtic's 'flat-track bullies' fail another big test
- Published
Celtic manager Martin O'Neill chose to focus on the second-half positives from his side's 4-1 Europa League defeat by Benfica and insisted they can still reach the knockout stages despite their slow start.
In stark contrast, Chris Sutton branded his former side as "flat-track bullies".
Celtic have lost four of their past five games. Every high-stakes match this term - both meetings with Rangers and both European outings - has ended in a defeat.
By the time their performance improved in Lisbon on Thursday, they were three goals down and effectively already out of the contest, hamstrung by their own sloppy mistakes.
Dane Murray upended Jhon Duran to concede a penalty inside four minutes, an error which characterised the first 45 minutes.
Sebastian Tounekti then allowed Alexander Bah to run past him for Benfica's second and goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo was beaten too easily as Duran scored the hosts' third.
Camilo Duran pulled one back after the break and struck a post as the Scottish champions improved, but Vangelis Pavlidis struck Benfica's fourth late on to kill any faint Celtic hopes.
"Last thing you want to do is concede so early on," O'Neill said. "We could've capitulated, but I thought the second-half performance was terrific. We created chance after chance.
"The second-half performance gives me the determination... I think we can still qualify. We can still do it.
"We came roaring back. We could've scored a number of goals. I accept on the break they could have scored themselves, as they did with their fourth goal."
Even the most ardent Celtic supporters would struggle to share their manager's optimism given they sit 34th of 36 teams in the competition after two games.
Captain Callum McGregor admitted Celtic were masters of their own downfall in the first half.
"First half we didn't help ourselves," he told TNT Sports. "Unforced errors lead to the second and third goals and you have a mountain to climb.
"We know at this level if you don't look after the ball you're going to get punished."
'I'd pick Duran over Hogh every day of the week'
Although Celtic conceded four, the scoreline did not flatter Benfica. The Portuguese side created chances aplenty in both halves and hit the woodwork twice in addition to their four goals.
Celtic's lack of depth in defence was exposed once again in the absence of the injured Cameron Carter-Vickers as Gianluca Prestianni and Duran tormented the visitors' back four.
However, it is in forward areas where O'Neill perhaps has his biggest headache.
Club record signing Kasper Hogh was hooked at half-time and has now failed to score in 10 of his first 11 outings since joining from Bodo/Glimt in the summer.
Duran shifted inside for the second half and posed far more of a threat than his Danish team-mate.
"If I'm a creative midfield player and I've got Duran and Hogh to pick from, I'm taking Duran every day of the week," former Celtic midfielder Scott Allan said.
"He looks to get off the side of defenders, if you put a ball in the area, he's more likely to be alive to it.
"Hogh just isn't firing on all cylinders. I can take that if he's doing the other side of the game a lot better than he is.
"You can see why Martin O'Neill made the substitution at half-time and there's no doubt Celtic looked much better going forward."
O'Neill admitted he sees Duran as being better through the middle, when asked about his Colombian talisman post-match, but given Hogh's price tag he might not be inclined to pull him out of the firing line just yet.
"[Duran] has played wide at his previous clubs," O'Neill said. "But I personally feel his best position is through the middle.
"It's now a matter of us trying to fit him in and I think we can do that. It's a real battle for places now."

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer, according a statement by the Vatican on October 13, 2026
The 71-year-old spiritual leader of the Roman Catholic Church was in the operating room for about 3 hours, and the surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. The lower lobe of his right lung has been removed after the diagnosis.
The surgery was successful and there were no complications.
The pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, according to a bulletin by the Vatican.
It added that tissue tests conducted during the operation confirmed what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), lung cancer is a disease in which cells in the lung grow out of control.
Lung cancers are grouped into two main types called non-small cell and small cell.
The CDC website adds that “non-small cell lung cancer is the most common type of lung cancer” and “it grows more slowly and often doesn’t cause symptoms until it is advanced.”
The website adds that adenocarcinoma, the type of cancer Pope Leo XIV is suffering from, is the “most common type of non-small cell lung cancer” and “begins in cells in the alveoli, which are tiny air sacs in the lungs that make mucus.”
Current status of Pope Leo XIV’s health
The Pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, Reuters reports, while citing the Vatican’s medical bulletin.
It added that the Vatican had said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week, and all his public events have been cancelled until October 20.
Pope Leo was seen waving to a supportive crowd of well-wishers before heading to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. Several of his supporters shouted “auguri” (best wishes) to their religious leader before his surgery.
The Christian leader is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17, 2026, but it was not clear if the trip would still go ahead.

Karnataka has urged the Centre to extend price-control measures beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost, life-saving drugs used to treat cardiac and kidney diseases, following the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) in-principle approval to cap trade margins on certain non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines at 30% of their maximum retail price (MRP).
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader said price rationalisation should translate into direct savings for patients, and urged the Union government to extend similar measures to other essential medicines where high treatment costs place a burden on patients.
At its meeting on October 8, the NPPA gave in-principle approval to rationalise trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines identified under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. The measure is subject to finalisation of the list of medicines to be covered.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been asked to constitute an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services to recommend the anti-cancer medicines to be brought under price control. The committee is expected to submit its report by October 14.
The Centre estimates that the measure could reduce the MRP of several anti-cancer medicines by 20% to 70%, potentially saving patients around ₹2,500 crore. “The financial strain of cancer treatment often pushes families into debt, making it inevitable for them to exhaust their savings and sell assets to meet medical expenses,” Mr. Khader said.
Citing examples, the Minister said a cancer drug/injection costing around ₹3,250 was reportedly priced at ₹23,347. Medicines with a landing cost of about ₹3,000 are being sold at a cost of ₹27,000. Under the 30% trade-margin cap, the maximum price of a medicine would depend on its applicable pricing base and can substantially reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for patients, he explained.
Also Read: Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
Karnataka’s representation to the Centre
In a letter dated September 23 to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, the Karnataka government had sought national-level action after inspections in the State found substantial differences between the procurement costs of medicines and the prices charged to patients. The State identified pricing concerns involving 253 medicines and consumables with mark-ups.
Karnataka had sought the inclusion of advanced chemotherapy, targeted therapy and other expensive cancer medicines under the ambit of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, along with a comprehensive cap on trade margins for high-cost and life-saving medicines.
The State had also called for expanding the NPPA’s price-control oversight and strengthening enforcement against excessive charging and profiteering.
Disclosure of medicine costs in hospital bills
The State has also sought greater transparency in the prices charged to patients. A circular issued on October 1 asked healthcare institutions to disclose both the purchase or landing cost and the MRP of medicines in patient bills. The instructions are advisory in nature and are proposed to take effect from November 1.
Karnataka’s call follows observations by the Supreme Court questioning why the MRP of essential medicines, including cancer drugs, could not be capped at 16% above the price to retailers, as is applicable to scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
The State said the proposed 30% trade-margin cap on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines should be followed by wider action to cover other essential, high-cost medicines, including those used in cardiac and kidney treatment, so that the benefits of price rationalisation reach patients directly.

A rumor (archived) that a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee published a letter discussing why it did not award the Nobel Peace Prize to U.S. President Donald Trump circulated in October.
For example, an X user praised the letter from the alleged committee member about its deliberations for the 2026 Peace Prize, writing "This is amazing!!"
An excerpt from the alleged letter read:
Now. This year. I will not say the name, because we never say the name, but you know the name.
A certain head of state wanted this prize the way a child wants a thing in a shop window, which is to say loudly, and in public, and with the full belief that wanting it was itself the argument. He said he deserved it. He said he'd ended eight wars, a number that grew most times he said it, like a fish. He had other heads of state phone us. Israel's prime minister posted it on the internet, "Give him the Nobel." The leaders of Cambodia and Pakistan announced they'd nominated him, as though announcing it were part of it, as though we tally mentions. A man flew around the globe collecting endorsements for a Norwegian committee the way you'd collect signatures for a petition to the council about a noisy dog.
The rumor spread as the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Peace Prize to South African lawyer Navanethem Navi Pillay. Claims had circulated in late 2025 about whether Trump might be in contention for the next year's prize.
People on Facebook also shared the letter from the alleged Norwegian Nobel Committee member (archived, archived). Some users seemed to interpret the letter as authentic, though others identified it as satire. Snopes readers searched our site to investigate the letter's legitimacy.
We identified the alleged letter's original source: an X account reportedly based in Austin, Texas, that describes its owner as a "Reader. Writer. Satirist. Hacker." Therefore, we find the letter originated as satire.
The "Peter Girnus" account on X first shared the alleged letter on Oct. 12 (archived). Though the account described itself as satirical in nature, it did not include markings in its post making it obvious that the content was satire.
Aside from the account's self-classification as satire, several other details made it obvious the letter was not written by a real member of the real Norwegian Nobel Committee, which awards the Nobel Peace Prize.
The five committee members' names are publicly available on the Nobel Peace Prize's website. None of them are named "Peter Girnus."
Additionally, Snopes previously reported that Nobel Peace Prize nominations are strictly confidential until 50 years after the committee awards a prize. Therefore, a committee member would not be allowed to discuss Trump in 2026 if he made it onto the official nominations list for that year's prize. Trump received at least one nomination for the 2026 prize, as Snopes previously reported.
After sharing the initial letter on Oct. 12, the "Peter Girnus" account also shared a follow-up letter and a fake Trump Truth Social post about the fabricated letter (archived, archived).
The "Peter Girnus" account contained other fictitious letters. For example, the account included posts where the writer posed as "the United States Ambassador to a warm, strategically vital ally on the Aegean," a "Director for Energy and Sanctions at the National Security Council" and a "Joint Secretary in the Ministry of External Affairs, Government of the Republic of India."
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' descriptions of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Ganderbal, Oct 15: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah officially inaugurated the 70th National School Games on Thursday at the Government College of Physical Education, Gadoora, in Ganderbal district.
The multi-sport event, organised by the Department of Youth Services and Sports (YSS) in collaboration with the School Games Federation of India (SGFI), brings together nearly 3000 young athletes, coaches, and officials from across the country.
Accompanied by Youth Services and Sports Minister Satish Sharma, Advisor Nasir Aslam Wani, Additional Chief Secretary to CM Dheeraj Gupta, Deputy Commissioner Ganderbal, SSP Ganderbal and other senior officials, Chief Minister Abdullah declared the games open amidst enthusiastic cheer from visiting student-athletes representing states and Union Territories nationwide.
Addressing the grand opening ceremony, CM Abdullah emphasised the transformative role of sports in building discipline, fostering teamwork, and promoting unity. “ Sports play a vital role in developing self-confidence, discipline, and leadership among our youth. Events like the National School Games not only showcase athletic talent at the grassroots level but also build enduring bridges of friendship and harmony among young people from every corner of India."
Addressing the participants, the Chief Minister urged them to compete with determination, uphold the spirit of sportsmanship and build lasting friendships. He highlighted the power of sports to instil discipline, nurture confidence and empower young people across the country.
The Chief Minister highlighted the J&K Government's ongoing commitment to building world-class sports infrastructure.
Speaking on the occasion, Minister for Youth Services and Sports Satish Sharma assured that the administration has ensured comprehensive arrangements—including safe accommodations, top-tier venues, and modern equipment—for all visiting contingents. Local sports officials and community members welcomed the national-level event, noting that hosting the 70th edition of the games will inspire Jammu & Kashmir's local youth to pursue sports professionally and excel on national and international stages.
Officials said that Jammu and Kashmir is hosting nine sporting events in four disciplines from October 15 to 27, with over 3000 athletes and officials expected to participate in the events. They said that Jammu & Kashmir is hosting major events, including Wushu and Taekwondo disciplines in the Kashmir region and Fencing and Cricket in the Jammu region. The events include under-17 Wushu and Taekwondo competitions in Ganderbal from October 15 to 27, and under-17 and under-19 fencing and under-17 cricket competitions in Jammu from Nov 15- Dec 27. The competitions are part of the National School Games programme organised under the aegis of the School Games Federation of India (SGFI). “ Hundreds of elite young athletes, coaches, and sports officials from states and Union Territories across the nation are currently converging on Ganderbal. The fortnight-long championship will see competitors testing their mettle, discipline, and sportsmanship in two of the country's most rapidly growing martial arts disciplines Wushu & Taekwondo “ officials said.

Suspicious mailings to election officials, congressional offices under investigation
The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are looking into a series of suspicious mailings sent to state election officials and congressional offices. Officials say some of the mailings contained a powdery white substance.
It is not clear who sent the mail, which was sent to election officials in states including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma as well as congressional offices. According to a statement from Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams, an employee who opened a letter sent to the office on Tuesday was not injured but was taken to the emergency room as a precaution. Law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
According to a communication from the Senate's Sergeant at Arms (SAA) to congressional staff and obtained by NPR, law enforcement officials are "working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations."
Deputy Chief Inspector Brendan Donahue of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service says that the organization was able to stop the delivery of at least one of the mailings.
"Some of the letters have contained an unknown substance, and we're working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," Donahue said.
The SAA's note to staff said that all suspicious letters, packages, or substances "should be treated as potentially hazardous and handled in accordance with established safety protocols," and warned staff not to handle suspicious letters and leave the area where they are discovered.
The note said the mail could be indicated by discoloration, powder emanating from the envelope and postmarks that do not match the return address. An image included in the communication had a return address labeled "DSA" and a New York City return address.
The U.S. Capitol Police and SAA did not return requests for comment. The FBI said that the organization is "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."
"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the agency said. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters."
The investigation mirrors 2024 incidents in which more than 15 state election offices received suspicious mailings.
Now, with less than three weeks until November 3, voting officials around the country are working to carry out the midterm elections. In a statement, the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said that "those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties."

Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
- Published
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

India's telecom operators will have to introduce Calling Name Presentation (CNAP) across 4G and higher-generation mobile networks from November 1, 2026, under a directive issued by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT). The service will display the caller's name alongside their telephone number on the recipient's phone screen. The caller name will be based on the subscriber records maintained by the telecom operator with which the caller is registered. In a circular dated October 13, the DoT said telecom operators had conducted trials to introduce CNAP on 4G and higher-generation networks. "All telecommunication service providers... are hereby instructed to introduce calling name presentation service in their telecommunication networks across all service areas with effect from November 1, 2026," the circular said. The move is intended to help users identify incoming callers and address concerns around online fraud. However, the service does not amount to a blanket ban on spam calls or guarantee that fraudulent callers will be identified. Calling Name Presentation, or CNAP, is a telecom service that displays the name associated with an incoming caller's number. Under the DoT's instructions, the caller's telephone number will continue to be displayed, with the caller's name appearing in a separate field. The service will be provided to users without requiring them to make a separate request. The circular specifies that the caller's name will be taken from the subscriber data record maintained by the originating telecom service provider. For recipients who have already saved a caller's number in their contact list, the saved name will take precedence. If the number is not saved, the name recorded by the caller's telecom operator will be displayed for domestic calls. This means users will not need to install a separate application or submit an application to their telecom operator to access the service, according to the directive. The DoT has directed telecom operators holding the relevant licences or authorisations to introduce CNAP across all service areas from November 1, 2026. The initial rollout covers wireless terrestrial networks using 4G and higher-generation technologies. "Introduction of calling name presentation service in wireless terrestrial networks established using 2G and 3G technologies and in public switched telephone networks shall be considered separately, after examination of the matter," the circular said. This means the directive does not set a rollout date for 2G and 3G networks or fixed-line telephone services. The name displayed will depend on whether the recipient has saved the caller's number and whether the call originates in India or overseas. The service is intended to provide additional information about callers. However, the appearance of a name on the screen should not be treated as conclusive proof that a call is genuine. The DoT has laid down separate provisions for businesses and users with bulk connections who want a preferred name to appear on recipients' screens. A preferred name can be a trademark registered in the user's name, according to the records of the Trade Marks Registry, or a trade name registered on the Goods and Services Tax (GST) portal. The originating telecom operator must verify the name before approving it. For new connections, telecom operators must record the preferred name in the customer application form and subscriber data record. Supporting documents establishing the registration must also be submitted and verified. For existing connections, operators must establish a mechanism that allows subscribers to apply to have their preferred names recorded in the subscriber database. "For existing connections, the originating TSP shall establish an appropriate mechanism to enable the user to submit requisite application for recording its preferred name in subscriber data record, and upon examination and proper verification of such application such preferred name of such user may be updated by the originating TSP in subscriber data record," the circular said. These requirements are intended to ensure that business names displayed through CNAP are supported by verified registration records. No. The DoT circular provides an exception for subscribers who have opted for the Calling Line Identification Restriction (CLIR) facility under existing guidelines. Names of callers who have availed calling line identification restriction (CLIR) facility as per existing rule will not be displayed as part of CNAP service. The directive also leaves the rollout of CNAP on 2G and 3G networks and fixed-line telephone networks for separate consideration. The DoT circular requires telecom service providers to put technical safeguards in place while introducing CNAP. These include a security-by-design approach under which the query-response mechanism must prevent the calling name identity from being retained after the incoming call is completed. Operators must also ensure that their databases, networks and connectivity infrastructure can process caller-name queries and deliver the information in a timely manner. The directive further requires telecom operators to establish grievance-redressal mechanisms to receive and resolve complaints relating to the service within a specified timeframe. Users who find an incorrect caller name displayed can therefore approach their telecom operator through its grievance-redressal mechanism. CNAP is designed to make caller identification easier by displaying the name associated with a telephone number. This may help users assess unfamiliar calls before deciding whether to answer them. However, caller-name display alone cannot establish that a caller is trustworthy. Fraudsters may use deceptive tactics, and the service should not be interpreted as a guarantee that spam calls, impersonation or financial fraud will be eliminated. Users should continue to exercise caution when callers request one-time passwords, banking credentials, financial transfers or other sensitive information, even if a name appears on the screen. Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
The automaker has unveiled the vehicle with some crazy stunts.
Tesla has unveiled the next-generation Roadster, nine years after the company showed off its concept prototype and after years and years of launch delay. Elon Musk and the Tesla team introduced the vehicle during an event at the SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas with a stunt. It drove up a C-shaped ramp and stopped in the middle of the part perpendicular to the ground while it was hanging upside-down. Then the vehicle repeated the action and jumped off the ramp from the top and flipped, its thruster system kicking in so it could safely hover to the ground.
When they opened up the door to the driver's seat, an Optimus robot was seating there. It was, however, only for show, and the stunts were programmed into the vehicle. They explained later on that the Roadster has a suction system at the bottom of the car that enabled it to stick upside-down to the ramp. On its website, Tesla said that its multi-mode fan and ground sealing system pulls air out from beneath the vehicle to act as a downforce generator, providing suction that make holding the vehicle upside-down possible even when it's stationary.
Meanwhile, it could jump off the ramp and safely land on the ground, thanks to its attitude-control thrusters and thrusters in the rear, which use technology borrowed from SpaceX. These advanced cold-gas thrusters use all-electric actuators that enable precise thrust and can perform "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second."
Musk said the new Roadster will go into production in 2028.
Tesla first started taking pre-orders for the Roadster way back when it was first announced. Those who didn't get the chance can now reserve a unit for $5,000, with $45,000 to follow within the next 10 days for the base vehicle. As you'd expect, the thrusters and air suction system cost extra. For the "Thrust" package, which comes with the suction system and acceleration thrusters, buyers are expected to pay an additional $245,000 within 10 days of reservation. The "Rocket" version, which comes with the full-flight system, is invite-only and probably something we'll see a lot of in influencers' videos.

Priya (name changed), 32, from Kerala, had been struggling with recurring episodes of depression that affected her ability to carry out everyday activities. Despite taking medication for several weeks, she continued to experience symptoms. With her symptoms persisting, she sought further medical advice and is now undergoing repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). This non-invasive procedure uses magnetic pulses to stimulate specific areas of the brain.
Priya’s experience reveals a challenge in managing depression, say experts. While antidepressants help many people, some continue to experience symptoms despite treatment, requiring doctors to reassess the diagnosis and consider other interventions.
