Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
- Published
A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.
From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.
Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.
A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.
"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.
This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.
We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.
A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.
Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.
The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

A 19-year-old Illinois man has been accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area of the US state of Illinois. Prosecutors allege that Alexandros Paporakis spent months planning the attack, researching the intended location online and writing an eight-page manifesto that called for violence against multiple racial and religious groups. The alleged attack was prevented after two of his co-workers alerted the police, leading to his arrest before anyone was injured. Paporakis, a resident of Palatine, was arrested on October 11. He faces charges of making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, a Class 3 felony. He has not entered a plea, and the allegations against him remain unproven in court. A judge ordered him held pending trial on October 14. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30. Investigators said Paporakis worked as a cashier at a Taco Bell outlet in Arlington Heights. According to prosecutors, his co-workers reported that he frequently made racist remarks, identified himself as a white supremacist and openly discussed Nazi ideology and armed violence. According to prosecutors, Paporakis allegedly sent a co-worker an eight-page document titled “Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto)” shortly before his arrest. Court documents alleged that the manifesto contained racist slurs and hateful statements targeting people of Indian ancestry, Jewish people and Black people. Prosecutors said the document described these groups as “subhumans” and discussed a plan to kill as many people as possible. The allegations detailed in the charging documents have not been proven in court. The document allegedly described how Paporakis acquired and modified an AR-style rifle. It also outlined how he used YouTube and Google Street View to study the intended target. Prosecutors alleged that Paporakis wrote that he had been planning a mass attack for two years and had focused on the specific location for the preceding two months. The manifesto allegedly encouraged others to carry out similar attacks. Prosecutors said Paporakis described how he would appear to be an ordinary white college student while secretly embracing neo-Nazi ideology and fantasies of committing mass murder. According to prosecutors, Paporakis allegedly told a co-worker on October 10 that he “could not wait to kill Indian people” and planned to use a large quantity of ammunition during the attack. The following day, he allegedly called the same co-worker and claimed that his firearm had jammed. Prosecutors said he told the co-worker that he had quickly left the scene after the malfunction. The co-worker also received a video allegedly showing an AR-style rifle failing to fire, along with a photograph of Paporakis wearing a tactical vest. According to prosecutors, Paporakis discussed repairing the firearm so that he could “retry” the attack. He also allegedly remarked that the intended victim “was certainly saved by his God today.” Alarmed by the messages, two co-workers contacted emergency services. Police subsequently located and arrested Paporakis in a parking lot near his apartment later that afternoon. The Palatine Police Department said the investigation was continuing with assistance from the FBI’s Chicago Field Office. Singapore's non-oil exports surge 68.4% in September; growth driven by non-electronics shipments
Singapore's NODX rose by 27.6% in the first nine months of 2026.
SINGAPORE: Singapore's non-oil domestic exports (NODX) surged by 68.4 per cent year-on-year in September, extending the revised 46.1 per cent growth recorded in August, according to data released by Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) on Friday (Oct 16).
Non-electronics exports drove the increase, mainly due to lumpy exports of ship and boat structures.
Electronic NODX rose by 107.6 per cent, benefiting from robust artificial intelligence-related demand and driven mainly by disk media products, integrated circuits (ICs) and personal computers. This follows a 131.6 per cent surge in August.
Non-electronic NODX grew by 54.2 per cent, accelerating from an 11.9 per cent increase in August.
Overall, Singapore's NODX rose by 27.6 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, EnterpriseSG said.
EXPORTS TO KEY MARKETS RISE
NODX to most of Singapore's major markets expanded in September.
Exports to Hong Kong rose by 112.1 per cent year-on-year, supported by shipments of non-monetary gold, ICs and specialised machinery.
Shipments to Taiwan increased by 96.9 per cent, while exports to the United States grew 73.2 per cent.
Exports to India fell by 5.6 per cent, reversing a 23.6 per cent increase in August.
Singapore's non-oil re-exports (NORX) rose by 47.8 per cent year-on-year in September, down slightly from the 53.2 per cent growth recorded in August.
The increase was mainly driven by electronic NORX, which surged by 64.2 per cent. Non-electronic NORX grew by 22.1 per cent.
The country's total merchandise trade expanded by 50.8 per cent in September, extending August's 44.4 per cent rise.
Total exports increased by 51.5 per cent year-on-year, while total imports grew by 49.9 per cent.

Guwahati: A Kuki-Zo woman was killed and her husband injured in an alleged ambush by suspected 
Naga militants
 in Manipur’s Kamjong district on Thursday, while two other members of the community were reported missing as ethnic violence continued in the state.
The deceased, Hatneikim Haokip, was from Molnoi village.
Preliminary information suggests the group was travelling to Phaikoh to buy essential commodities when they were ambushed on the road between Phaikoh and Aishu. Hatneikim’s husband was injured, while the two other civilians who were with them remain missing.
Thursday’s attack has taken the number of Kuki-Zo women killed in the Kuki-Naga clashes to 10, including two pregnant women. The clashes followed the Kuki-Meitei conflict that continued from 2023 to 2025.
The attack came five days after nine people were killed across three districts, including two Kukis — one of them a woman — a Gorkha and six Naga men.
Since the Kuki-Naga clashes began in Feb this year, at least 22 Naga and 32 Kuki-Zo people have been killed.
Late on Wednesday night, security forces found the severed head of Naga man Ajinbou Ringkamai in Kangpokpi district. 
He was one of four Naga men killed when suspected Kuki militants attacked Makui Ashang village there on Oct 10. His head had been severed during the attack and remained missing. His headless body was taken to Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences in Imphal on Oct 11.
“The head was found in an isolated area near the site by security forces late on Wednesday night, and it was brought to JNIMS this morning for autopsy,” a senior official said.
Joint Tribes Council Manipur, a Naga organisation, had given the authorities a 48-hour ultimatum to locate the head and ensure a proper funeral.
Manipur home minister Govindas Konthoujam, speaking in Imphal on Thursday while visiting 84 BSF personnel admitted to Regional Institute of Medical Sciences with suspected food poisoning, said govt effort and security measures alone could not end the violence.
“When the general people do not have humanity, then nobody can stop killing each other. We should understand that,” he said. “Killing will never solve any problem. We should talk to each other, and all differences should be resolved through dialogue.”
He said govt was working to initiate dialogue but that society also had a role. “Security alone cannot solve the problem. We, the society and the people, should also try to restrain any kind of anger,” he said.
Separately, Lt Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of Spear Corps, visited an Assam Rifles forward post in Manipur on Thursday and reviewed the security situation. He was briefed on the preparedness of troops guarding India-Myanmar border.
India shares a 1,643 km border with Myanmar, of which 398 km is in Manipur. Fencing has started, and nearly 55 km has been completed in the state. Govt plans to finish it by 2028. Hilly, forested terrain and resistance from militant outfits that use the border to move between the two countries are slowing the work.

Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.
The Tesla Roadster flew, drove upside down, and hit 60mph in under a second
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats if it ever goes into production.
The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, trim levels, or other such mundane details. Who cares about that boring crap anyway? The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.
The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event. The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.
Early adopters quickly threw down $50,000 deposits (or $250,000 for the limited Founders Series), effectively interest-free loans to help fund Tesla’s scaling ambitions. But then Tesla seemed to forget about the Roadster, as cementing its status as the ultimate vaporware. Production deadlines slipped as Tesla prioritized mass-market vehicles like the Model Y, while also wrestling with the overly complicated Cybertruck. Occasionally, when Musk would remember that the Roadster existed, he would up the ante about its capabilities. This culminated in the “SpaceX package” that would equip the supercar with cold-gas thrusters, bestowing hover powers and a 0-60 time under one second.
Musk has also sought to downplay the Roadster’s significance, calling it a “small potato situation” that will not “move the needle in a major way financially.” He’s framed the supercar more as a joint engineering collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, even questioning whether it’s “even a car anymore” given its experimental nature. Some analysts theorize that the decision to re-release the Roadster is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger.
Tesla’s failure to bring the Roadster to market allowed other automakers to slip passed the company with their own hyper-powered EVs. Rimac has smashed performance records with the Nevera, Porsche has refined electric performance with the Taycan, and Chinese giants like BYD are producing track-ready supercars at a fraction of the cost. The Roadster is no longer shocking the world as an impossible prototype; it’s playing catch-up to an industry that spent nine years building what Tesla merely rendered.

Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
- Published
Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.
The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.
Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.
The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.
In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.
Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me."
"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.
Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.
"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.
Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.
The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.
The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.
Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.
Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

Trump signed an executive order allowing federal permitting agencies to ignore environmental protection laws in an effort to increase domestic timber and lumber production. The executive order also calls for expanding domestic logging production on federal lands. Following that executive order, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that the USDA would attempt to roll back the Roadless Rule, which, at its height, prohibited logging on approximately 59 million acres of land.
The order and proposed repeal of the Roadless Rule would not open 59% of national forests to logging. Rather, by Snopes' calculations, it would allow logging on an additional 24% of national forestland.
In October, posts on social media suggested that U.S. President Donald Trump signed an "emergency order" opening up 59% of U.S. national forests for logging. Snopes readers wrote in asking whether the rumor was accurate.
The claim resembled one we fact-checked in March 2025. Then, we investigated a Trump executive order that social media posters claimed would result in 280 million acres of forest being clear-cut. We found the claim to be a mixture of true and exaggerated information.
We came to the same conclusion on this new variant. While the claim is based partly in truth (the referenced "emergency order" is the same executive order we investigated in 2025), it also exaggerates the facts. We therefore rate it a mixture of true and false.
Here's a breakdown:
The order is real
On March 1, 2025, Trump signed an executive order aimed at fast-tracking logging on federal lands. The order, titled "Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production," directed the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management, two of the largest caretakers of federal lands, to update guidelines in order to "facilitate increased timber production," among other things.
Trump's executive order specifically asked those agencies to investigate and implement ways to increase both the speed and quantity of timber produced by cutting environmental regulations.
It asked the Fish and Wildlife Service to streamline approvals for forestry projects that could potentially be halted by the Endangered Species Act within 60 days of the order. It also asked the Agriculture and Interior departments (which control the Forest Service and BLM, respectively) to exempt "timber thinning" and "timber salvage activities" from the National Environmental Policy Act. That act, signed into law by President Richard Nixon in 1970, requires the federal government to consider the environmental effects of its proposed actions through environmental impact statements.
The executive order also encouraged the Agriculture and Interior departments to use the emergency regulations of the Endangered Species Act "to the maximum extent permissible under applicable law." Those regulations allow the act to be bypassed in situations where time is of the essence, such as "acts of God, disasters, casualties, national defense or security emergencies." (Trump's executive order was issued alongside another order declaring that importing timber and lumber poses a risk to national security.) Under the emergency regulations, the Fish and Wildlife Service provides "strictly advisory" recommendations for how to protect endangered species that can be "implemented at the discretion of the emergency response personnel."
In other words, the executive order would allow the logging industry to bypass environmental restrictions found in the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act.
The acreage
The Forest Service manages 193 million acres of land across the country (about 188 million acres of national forest). Unlike national parks, national forests were established with the purpose of permitting logging and resource exploitation as well as wildlife conservation and recreation.
If the 59% claim were accurate, then using the 188 million total acres figure from the Forest Service we would expect to find that the order opened up about 110 million acres for logging. But this wasn't the case.
The Forest Service deems just 49 million acres of its land "suitable for timber management," far less than the 110 million acres suggested by the claim.
Social media posts said NPR was the source of that figure, yet when we searched NPR's archive for stories suggesting that either 110 million acres or 59% of national forests would be opened up to logging, we found no results.
Instead, we found that the posts appeared to misinterpret or misrepresent NPR's reporting regarding a real policy change implemented by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, who was tasked with carrying out the 2025 executive order. 
According to an August 2026 news release, Rollins announced that the USDA would roll back the 2001 Roadless Rule, a policy that prohibits the construction of new roads on national forestland. Because roads are required to transport the raw materials, the Roadless Rule effectively places a limit on the number of timber and mining operations on national forestland. The news release noted the USDA would take public comment on the proposed change until Sept. 21, just before the claim began spreading.
When the Roadless Rule was first implemented, it applied to "nearly 60 million acres" of land, according to the Forest Service. We suspect this was the origin of social media users' claim that Trump's executive order would open up 59% of national forests to logging. Various sources, including NPR, reported 58 million to 59 million acres would be opened up. People may have mistaken the acreage for a percentage.
Even then, the social media posts dwelled on the wrong acreage figure, because the Roadless Rule no longer covers the original acreage. Colorado and Idaho enacted state-level Roadless Rules offering higher levels of protection for some land, and those stricter protections effectively supersede the federal rule. According to the Forest Service, taking those restrictions into account means the federal Roadless Rule now applies to only around 45 million acres of forest.
Using the correct, up-to-date acreage, Snopes calculated the rule's recision would open up approximately 24% of Forest Service land for logging. (We were unable to determine how much of that land is actually suitable for the purpose, however.)
Rollins' repeal is supported by the logging industry and several Republican governors, who claim it will prevent wildfires by allowing humans to more directly access and manage remote forestland.
The repeal is opposed by several groups, according to reports from Pew, NPR and Cal Matters. Environmental groups cite scientific research showing 80% of wildfires are caused by human activity, and therefore more human access would increase, not decrease, fire risk. This is backed up by the Forest Service's own environmental analysis on the repeal, according to Pew. Meanwhile, tribal nations claim the repeal undermines tribal sovereignty, and a spending watchdog notes that the Forest Service already has a $6 billion backlog in road maintenance. Repealing the Roadless Rule would only make that worse.
(In fact, during an phone interview for a different story on the Forest Service, Associate Chief Chris French told Snopes the maintenance backlog has been around for decades, and was part of why the rule was implemented in 2001. That detail didn't make it into the final story.)
A bipartisan group of 164 senators and representatives wrote a letter to Rollins and Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz in September pointing out all of those factors and noting that the Roadless Rule has immense public support.
The USDA is expected to make its final decision on the repeal in early 2027.

Rusty or something more? South Africa's concern after Australia loss
- Published
First Test, Durban (day five of five)
Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56
South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49
Australia won by 214 runs
South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days?
The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.
"I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning."
So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas?
Rusty batters or something more?
Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.
They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare.
Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out.
And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams.
However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters.
Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
This was an obvious step up.
In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one.
Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four.
Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging.
Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India.
Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up".
"The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said.
"Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on."
Markram & Nortje the positives
Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas.
David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46.
This defeat was not solely on the batters, either.
Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out.
Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134.
And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts.
Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four.
But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one.
The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough.
Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either.
"Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said.
"If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are."
With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust.
The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning.

A container ship has sunk near the strait of Hormuz and a second cargo vessel was reportedly sinking amid the sharpest uptick in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The surge of attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in a deliberate attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride container ship sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day while in a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was also reported to be sinking close to the strait after being previously hit by a projectile on 23 September, maritime security sources said.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine while travelling an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC) that said the ship was traveling on what it called an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The unidentified ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, the UKTMO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships from trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
The latest attacks come as ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKTMO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers while two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.

A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.
Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.

Indian woman and boyfriend get death sentence in 'blue drum' murder case
- Published
Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.
A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput.
Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder".
Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict.
The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London.
When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter.
Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed.
Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added.
A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing.
On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father.
Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station.
Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder.
"My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi.
Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her.
"My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency.
Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

) Limiting global warming to around 1.8 degrees Celsius, instead of allowing it to reach 4.4 degrees Celsius, could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life to causes such as extreme heat and air pollution, according to a new LancetCommission.
Researchers said that the true burden could be even greater and that without sharp cuts to emissions, health losses would continue to compound beyond 2100, increasingly intensify other threats, such as migration, in ways not yet reflected in these numbers.
The authors of The Lancet Commission on "21st Century Global Threats to Health", launched at the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin, Germany, examined hundreds of possible threats.
They identified 17 threats posing the greatest danger to human health and survival between 2025 and 2100. These are also the threats that can be averted through policy changes, funding decisions and innovation, they said.
The 17 interlinked "catastrophic" threats spanning diseases, social and economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict will shape the health of the next generation, the team added.
If current trends continue, the 17 catastrophic threats collectively could account for tens of billions of years of lost health, the analysis found.
Every country faces significant risks, even as the scale varied by threat and region. Within each country, people with limited resources and marginalised communities bear the greatest burden, compounded by existing inequalities, it said.
Nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI) were identified as the two threats with a potential for extinction, even as their likelihood of occurring were deemed 'low'.
Accounting for both their potential impact and probability, the commission's assessment found that action to prevent nuclear conflict could avert an estimated 133 million deaths and 9.35 billion years of healthy life lost by 2100, while action to reduce the risk of malicious AI could avert an estimated 10.4 billion years of healthy life lost.
"The estimates highlight how much health loss could be avoided in each area. Some are already imposing substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialise. Crucially, all 17 threats are interconnected, which is why they must be addressed together, not in isolation," commission co-chair Christopher JL Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, said.
"The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future," Murray added.
The other catastrophic threats to health are air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, a declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing, the authors said.
The commission also puts forth a framework to inform action before harm becomes embedded -- create and fund threat-ready health systems, increase investment in innovation and reassess threats regularly and independently, they said.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. Apollo is delaying on-cycle recruiting again this year, after a similar move last year helped push back the recruiting timeline across the private equity industry.
The private equity giant told prospective candidates Thursday afternoon that it will not recruit its 2028 associate class this calendar year, according to an email obtained by Business Insider.
The memo, signed by David Sambur, co-head of Private Equity, and Antoine G. Munfakh, deputy global head of Private Equity, said the firm will wait until candidates who started their investment banking careers over the summer are "closer to completing one full year of professional experience."
The hope, the memo said, is that this will convince others in private equity to delay their process so both candidates and employers can make "better decisions." Last year, after Apollo CEO Marc Rowan said the firm would delay on-cycle recruiting, others, such as General Atlantic also decided to pause. 
"We were encouraged that others in the industry took similar steps, and we hope more firms will do the same this year," the memo said.
On-cycle recruiting — the controversial process through which private equity firms hire junior investment bankers for associate roles a year or even two before they would start — had crept earlier and earlier in the years following the pandemic. 
Competition among private equity firms to lock up top talent pushed recruiting earlier and made the process notoriously intense. It would kick off with little warning, with junior bankers sometimes calling in sick or interviewing in the middle of the night to avoid jeopardizing their day jobs. JPMorgan's CEO, Jamie Dimon, has been a big critic of the process, calling it "unethical."
In 2025, amid rumblings that on-cycle recruiting could take place before some students even graduated from college, JPMorgan rolled out a policy that incoming analysts could be terminated for accepting future-dated private equity offers.
Apollo then decided to pause its on-cycle recruiting for 2027 associates, setting off a chain reaction that delayed the process well into this year.
Questions have swirled if the practice would kick off early again this for the 2028 class, but it appears with this latest move, Apollo is trying to slow down the recruiting timeline across the industry again.
Read the full memo below:
—-
To: Prospective Apollo Associate Candidates, Class of 2028
Subject: Apollo Recruiting, Class of 2028
Congratulations on beginning your career in investment banking. We know how exciting and demanding this period can be, and we hope you are enjoying the experience and learning a great deal.
Last June, we wrote to prospective candidates for our Associate Class of 2027 to explain why Apollo would be delaying its recruiting process. We believed then, as we do now, that young professionals should have the opportunity to develop their skills, gain meaningful experience and better understand their interests before making important decisions about their careers.
We were encouraged that others in the industry took similar steps, and we hope more firms will do the same this year. Young professionals still deserve more time to gather valuable life and work experience before making important career decisions.
We wanted to share with you that for the Associate Class of 2028, we will not participate in on-cycle recruiting this calendar year and intend to wait until candidates are closer to completing one full year of professional experience before engaging in formal recruiting for an Associate position. We believe giving candidates more time and experience before beginning the process leads to better decisions for candidates and employers alike.
In the meantime, we will continue to spend time with many of you, introduce you to our platform and share the diverse array of career opportunities available at Apollo. When our formal recruiting process begins, we intend to approach it thoughtfully and give candidates ample time to prepare, interview and consider their offers.
None of this changes our enthusiasm for meeting and recruiting exceptional young talent. Quite the opposite. Investing in our people has always been central to Apollo's success, and we remain committed to attracting and developing the next generation of investment professionals.
For now, our advice is simple: Focus on the opportunity in front of you. Learn as much as you can. Build relationships, develop your judgment, and take the time to discover what genuinely interests you. There will be plenty of time to make decisions about the next chapter of your career.
We look forward to getting to know you and hope many of you will consider building your careers at Apollo.
Best,
David Sambur
Partner, Co-Head of Private Equity and Head of Equity
Antoine G. Munfakh
Partner, Deputy Global Head of Private Equity

We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains
New research suggests brain health could be affected by consuming too much low-nutrient processed food
Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know aren't the healthiest choice.
A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.
But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.
Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health, and could even be linked to some types of cancer.
But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University, published Thursday by JAMA Network Open, signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.
The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.
People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.
But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.
Feeding the furnace
De Souza and co-author Dr. Sonia Anand, a vascular medicine specialist, examined the diets and brain MRI scans of more than 8,700 Canadian adults, with a median age of about 58, and broke them down into four groups, from those with the lowest intake of UPFs to those with the highest.
The latter cohort was made up of people who consumed nearly 45 per cent of their calories from UPFs, or the equivalent of 16 servings a day, which they self-reported in a survey listing 150 to 170 food items consumed in the past year.
By comparison, the group with the lowest consumption got 15 per cent of their daily calories from UPFs, equal to three servings.
Anand, a professor of medicine and epidemiology at McMaster, says they analyzed the scans of higher-risk participants and found that their UPF-heavy diets were associated with increased body fat and visceral fat — the kind stored deeper in the body and around organs.
"Fat tissue in the wrong places can be almost like a furnace spewing out a whole bunch of inflammatory proteins that then affect our brains," she said.
Ultra-processed foods like instant noodles are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives, preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours, rather than minimally-processed ingredients. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
Anand says the MRIs of the higher-risk group showed changes to the brain similar to silent strokes, a type of stroke that doesn't present any noticeable symptoms but damages the tissue.
These injuries add up over time and make it more likely that people could develop neurological problems, such as vascular dementia, says Dr. Michael Hill, a neurologist and professor at the University of Calgary who is not affiliated with the study.
"The more injuries you accumulate, the more likely you are to have neurological problems later in life, most commonly vascular dementia," he said.
- THE DOSE Reducing ultra-processed food intake requires rethinking our 'food environment,' experts say
- McMaster University study links ultra-processed food to range of health risks
While the damage a UPF-heavy diet may do can't be reversed, Hill says dietary changes can reduce further progression.
"Feed your brain," he said. "It's not just about your gut, right? It's about your whole body."
He says the findings are consistent with a growing body of evidence about the health impacts of UPFs.
'Eat foods that rot, not rotten foods'
De Souza notes that not all processed foods are ultra-processed and, in fact, many processed products in grocery stores have a lot of nutritional value.
"Some degree of processing is absolutely necessary in the food supply," he said. "It helps keep food safe and shelf stable."
But a can of beans, a bag of frozen vegetables or a container of yogurt are all different from a fast-food meal or a box of sugar-coated cereal.
Foods are classified using what's known as the NOVA system, where foods are determined to be ultra-processed if they are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives like salt, sugar, fats and oils, as well as preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours.
They also tend to be lower in fibre, vitamins and minerals that benefit overall health, de Souza says.
Hill says that while "one Snickers bar isn't going to hurt you," ultimately, ultra-processed food isn't going to benefit your health — especially if you're eating it regularly.
And even when people want a sugary or salty treat, he says it's going to be better if they make it at home from whole or minimally-processed foods.
"Eat foods that will rot, but not rotten food," he said.
Anand and de Souza note that their study doesn't provide the full picture of the potential toll UPFs can have on brain health and say more long-term research is needed to determine if dietary changes later in life can make a difference.
The next phase of their research will see 2,000 people who took part in the first round of scans receive a second round to determine if reducing the amount of UPFs in their diets results in changes or improvements to brain health.
Improving health literacy
Anand notes that not everyone has the time or money to prepare high-quality food, which she says is a systemic issue that would require government intervention to reduce the amount of UPFs available and make healthy food more affordable.
It's also a matter of improving health literacy, which she says would increase awareness about the repercussions of consuming too many UPFs.
Canada, she says, could follow the lead of other countries that have successfully minimized the consumption of UPFs. One such country, Chile, implemented mandatory front-of-package labels for UPFs that are high in sugar in an effort to curb childhood obesity.
She says there are things individuals and governments can do "and we need both to happen to make Canadians healthier."

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
- Published
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.
It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
But the alliance is not without tension.
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."
