India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
- Published
Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites.
The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday.
The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies.
Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny.
Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.
"Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI.
His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate.
Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses.
Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground.
The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard.
On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday).
She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar.
"Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X.
The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May.
He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change.
Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability.
The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration.
The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous.
The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this.
Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the demonstration and detained thousands of people, including CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were detained after arriving at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International AIRPORT. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some demonstrators protested at other locations. The three leaders were released on 11 October 2026 while the Supreme Court directed authorities to uphold the rights of peaceful protesters. On 12 October 2026, opposition leaders led a march towards the Supreme Court against the SIR exercise, but police stopped them before they reached the court amid heightened security and temporary metro station closures (here, here, here, and here).
In this context, a video showing people breaking through barricades and advancing is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows visuals from the protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people breaking through barricades and advancing during the protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 protests in Delhi and shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, in July 2026. The farmers were demanding 100% government procurement of moong crops at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), a legal guarantee for MSP and the cancellation of the e-token system, among other demands. The protest was later called off following talks with the government and assurances regarding their demands. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple social media posts (here, here, and here) from July 2026 featuring the same visuals from a different angle. This confirms that the viral video predates the October 2026 protests in Delhi and is unrelated to them. According to these posts, the video shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, over demands including a legal guarantee for the Minimum Support Price (MSP), 100% government procurement of moong crops and the cancellation of the e-token system. The posts also state that protesters were stopped about seven kilometres from the Chief Minister’s residence and were sitting on the road with food and water.
We then conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) stating that the farmers were protesting to demand 100% procurement of their moong (green gram) crop at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), among other demands. The farmers had marched from Narmadapuram to Bhopal, seeking the abolition of the e-token system for crop procurement and fertiliser distribution.
A report published by Dainik Bhaskar in July 2026 carried visuals from the same location and reported that a large crowd had gathered during a farmers’ protest against the moong procurement and fertiliser token system, with people breaking through police barricades and advancing. Other media reports stated that the farmers later called off their protest following talks with the government and assurances regarding their demands.
To sum up, a July 2026 video of a farmers’ protest in Bhopal is shared as showing the CJP protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
See more information on the partnership between Netherlands and WHO.

Hong Kong police will conduct round-the-clock patrols in Wan Chai from Friday as part of enhanced security arrangements for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, as delegates begin arriving in the city, the South China Morning Post has learned.

In a case of alleged medical negligence involving a 14-month-old boy who suffered brain damage following routine ear surgery, the Bengaluru Urban District Health Officer (DHO) and the Karnataka Private Medical Establishments (KPME) Grievance Redressal Authority have officially referred the matter to the Karnataka Medical Council (KMC) for an inquiry and report.
The decision follows a complaint lodged by Sampath Kumar K.P., whose son was taken to Cloudnine Hospital, Nagarabhavi, on July 26, 2026, for emergency surgical repair of a full-thickness ear laceration. During the procedure, the toddler suffered a cardiac arrest in the operation theatre and subsequently sustained severe brain injury due to lack of oxygen.
Lapses in anesthesia administration
A detailed inquiry conducted by an expert medical panel — comprising Raghunatha M. (anaesthesiologist) and Nagaraju (paediatrician) from the State-run Sir C.V. Raman General Hospital — said there were critical lapses during the administration of anesthesia.
According to the technical committee’s report submitted by doctors to the KMC, the operating room was satisfactorily equipped, but the attending anesthesiologist was “not well trained to administer anaesthesia for small children”.
Describing how the lapse led to oxygen levels plummetting, the report states that the doctor attempted to intubate the child with an uncuffed tube, leading to hypoxia, bradycardia, and eventual cardiac arrest.
While hospital logs claimed cardiac arrest was reversed within seven minutes, the expert committee stated in the report that brain hypoxia persisted for 15 to 20 minutes, causing severe, irreversible brain damage. An MRI scan performed three days later confirmed partial prolonged hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury.
Current condition and referral
Following initial resuscitation, the toddler was transferred to the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) at Cloudnine Hospital, Jayanagar, for advanced critical care.
The clinical evaluation conducted by Dr. Nagaraju noted that while the child has been weaned off mechanical ventilation and is currently hemodynamically stable, he suffers from profound neurological sequelae. The toddler remains unresponsive to verbal commands, has lost his sight, exhibits decerebrate posturing, and is dependent on Ryle’s tube feeding. He requires ongoing multidisciplinary care.
During the hearing held on October 8, the DHO and KPME Authority reviewed the expert panel’s findings and the parents’ submission. Noting that the medical panel’s findings explicitly indicate prima facie medical negligence, the Bengaluru Urban DHO, formally transferred the case files to the KMC president on October 12, for disciplinary proceedings and further action.

In May 2026, Georgia Governor Bill Kemp signed House Bill 369 into law, which would make several county-level races in some of Georgia's most Democratic counties "nonpartisan" — meaning that local candidates would run for office without party labels on the ballot. The law would only apply to five counties, including and surrounding Atlanta, the most diverse region in the state.
However, the law doesn't go into effect until Jan. 1, 2028, and as of this writing, county district attorneys are challenging the constitutionality of the bill in court. The law wouldn't apply to the entire state, which the DAs argue violates Georgia's uniformity clause.
In the weeks leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, a claim circulated that Georgia lawmakers had removed political party labels from ballots in an effort to give Republicans a leg up in counties that have seen steady electoral wins for Democrats.
Social media posts sounded the alarm, warning Georgia voters to bring sample ballots or memorize candidates before heading to the polls to avoid voting for someone on the basis of name recognition alone.
"Georgia voters- It seems our Trump loving election denying Republican led election board has decided to remove the (R) and the (D) that normally appears next to candidate's names on the upcoming midterm ballots. And you're not allowed to use your phone while voting to look up affiliation," an Oct. 4 Facebook post that was shared thousands of times read (archived). "They want you to either not vote in that category or hopefully choose the wrong one. A lot of incumbents are Republican so they're hoping you'll just choose by name recognition."
We looked into the claim and found that while it was true Georgia Gov. Bill Kemp signed House Bill 369 into law in Georgia in May 2026, making several county-level races "nonpartisan," the law would not take effect until Jan. 1, 2028 — and only in five Atlanta-area counties, not the entire state. As a result, we've rated the claim a mixture of true and false information.
The five counties' district attorneys — all of whom are Black women representing the most diverse region of the state — argue the law is unconstitutional because it's geographically limited to that region. Those counties include and surround state capital Atlanta, a Democratic stronghold.
HB 369 applies the nonpartisan distinction to counties in which the elected office of county coroner has been abolished. It's unclear precisely how lawmakers made the connection between nonpartisan coroner elections and the need to remove party affiliation labels from other candidates' names.
According to The Associated Press, state Sen. John Albers, a Republican from Roswell (an Atlanta suburb) said during a legislative session that he "believed it will promote public safety." State Rep. Trey Kelley, also a Republican, reportedly claimed that "by passing this legislation, we're giving voters the opportunity to rid themselves of district attorneys who are more concerned with playing partisan games than prosecuting and delivering justice."
In June 2026, DeKalb County District Attorney Sherry Boston announced she was filing a lawsuit challenging the law. She was accompanied by three out of the other four county DAs. We reached out to all five DA offices for comment, and a spokesperson from Clayton County responded reiterating that if the bill held by 2028, it would only deal with certain elected officials.
A June 3 statement outlining the three grounds on which Boston's lawsuit challenged the validity of the law read:
- Violation of Georgia's Uniformity Clause - The Georgia Constitution requires that laws must work the same way throughout the state and prohibits lawmakers from enacting local or special laws that change the rules for one area of Georgia. The Georgia Supreme Court has repeatedly held that laws that target just one or a handful of counties are unconstitutional.
- Violation of the Georgia and U.S. Equal Protection Clauses – Both the Georgia and United States Constitutions mandate that laws must protect all people equally. State lawmakers did not give any legitimate reason for treating the 5 metro counties, their elected officials, and their voters differently from the state's other 154 counties. They set them apart on the basis that they have medical examiners instead of coroners, which has no connection to the need for nonpartisan elections. In addition, the five counties targeted have large Black voter populations and Black female District Attorneys.
- Violation of Georgia's Rejected Bills Clause – Before lawmakers passed the nonpartisan county elections bill as HB 369, the same proposal failed a full vote of the Senate as SB 573. Before the Legislature can take up a measure it previously rejected, the Georgia Constitution requires a two-thirds vote by the rejecting chamber. That did not happen with HB 369.
Gwinnett County District Attorney Patsy Austin-Gatson, in her August lawsuit of a similar nature, wrote that the law's medical examiner distinction "is arbitrary and has no rational relation to the partisan status of county elections." The lawsuit continued: "There is simply no reason why a county with a medical examiner should have a nonpartisan election for district attorney but a county with a coroner should have partisan elections for district attorney."
We also contacted state Rep. Jasmine Clark, a Democrat from Georgia, who has spoken about the bill on her social media. In a statement to Snopes via email, Clark's office wrote that if voters want to see who and what are currently on their ballot, they can print a sample ballot at Georgia's voting information page.

The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.
“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.
Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.
That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.
Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.
“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”
Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.
Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.
The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.
“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”
The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.
“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”

A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.
That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”
Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.
“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.
Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.
Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.
Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.
In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.
“Don't talk about renewables. Don't talk about climate,” says Chris Coffey, the chief executive of the consultancy Tusk Strategies, which is running the PAC. “Pick the best issue that we can pick. And in a Republican primary, we should savage this guy for not being MAGA enough.”
Roy received a 100 percent rating from Heritage Action, the political arm of the Trumpist think tank. Coffey said he got some pushback from a few Democratic operatives, who were concerned that replacements for Roy and other PAC targets might not be any less extreme—on climate or any other issue. Without their far-right track record, the argument went, those replacements might even be stronger candidates in the general election.
“Who fucking cares? Who cares? Like, it can't be worse,” Coffey, a veteran of New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg’s City Hall, says in response. “At least we'll have extracted some payback.”
The PAC is currently putting $2 million into ads blasting GOP representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana as allegedly corrupt; it’s aiming to target Texas Republican Brandon Herrera for his “abolish old people” jokes and his plan to get rid of Social Security. Then there is the $1.5 million ad campaign about Boebert and the Beetlejuice incident. “If Lauren Boebert can’t be trusted in a room full of kids, then she can’t be trusted in the halls of Congress,” the commercial’s narrator says.
Other special-interest organizations have been running this playbook for decades. Groups supporting labor and opposing gun regulations regularly try to make examples of politicians who oppose their agenda. Green groups haven’t been as aggressive historically. That’s a problem, says Steph Bosh, the board chair of the Community Clean Energy Coalition. While her group has raised nearly $2 million to promote their favored hyperlocal candidates this cycle—and the League of Conservation Voters’ affiliated super PAC is spending another $50 million—Bosh says she appreciates that someone else is taking a less friendly approach.
“As a broad renewable energy industry, we need to be loved, respected, and feared,” Bosh adds. “We need to have a carrot, and we need to have a stick.”
James Carville, the Democratic pundit and former campaign manager, doubts the stick is big enough. “Twenty million—what the fuck do you think the carbon industry spends in a year?” he recently said to the Washington Monthly.
Roy, for his part, insisted that the PAC’s spending had played “zero role” in his race (while his campaign staff put out statements denouncing the “radical California Marxists trying to buy Texas elections”). Ralph Norman, his fellow solar target, warned about the “elite” taking out “the $1 million attack ad against me,” while Ogles complained, “they literally are trying to make an example out of me.”
“They were the difference maker,” Chris Burger, a Republican political consultant in Tennessee, says of the pro-solar group. “I don't think Charlie [Hatcher, Ogles’ primary opponent] wins if the PAC doesn't come in with $2 million.”
The Trump White House and its allies in Congress have been beyond hostile to renewables, which they believe to be intermittent sources of energy, and dominated by China. The administration has done everything it can to promote the production of oil, gas, and coal, while kneecapping renewable alternatives, from tying green projects in bureaucratic knots to pulling billions of dollars’ worth of solar subsidies and paying companies billions more to stop offshore wind farm construction. Then the Trump team tried to get other countries to adopt similar attitudes. “If you don’t get away from the green energy scam, your country is going to fail,” the president told the United Nations General Assembly last year.
But the Trumpists have been slightly less hostile to solar than to offshore wind farms, which, according to the president, cause cancer, “kill all your birds,” and drive whales “crazy.”
“While wind is dead, solar is merely in the ICU,” Richard Goldberg, a former member of the administration's National Energy Dominance Council, tells WIRED.
That has provided a small but real opening to promote solar to the America First set, especially with energy prices spiking at home, the war in Iran pushing up oil prices around the world, and the spread of AI data centers creating a borderline-insatiable need for more power.
In February, the American Clean Power Association launched a campaign to do just that, releasing a poll from former Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway’s consulting company showing that 75 percent of MAGA voters in key states supported the idea of adding more solar energy to the national mix. According to an internal memo reviewed by Politico, soon to follow were “paid media partnerships with podcasts like the Katie Miller Pod” (hosted by the former DOGE spokesperson, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller) as well as “advertorials and sponsorships with right-of-center publications.”
Katie Miller, once a consultant for Elon Musk, a renewable energy advocate, has repeatedly pushed for solar on social media since then. “Over 70 percent of the new utility-scale capacity went into states won by President Trump,” reads one of her posts. “Electricity generation is a national security issue—not a partisan one.” (Miller, who did not respond to requests to comment for this story, has previously denied receiving any funding from the clean power group.)
There’s also the data center issue. China hasn’t had problems powering its data centers, thanks in part to its widespread deployment of renewables—315 gigawatts of solar added to the grid last year, about six times more than the United States added from all sources combined. The US is in an entirely different situation. MAGA-minded promoters of solar are trying to leverage that gap to make a Trumpy argument for renewable energy. Concerns about the climate are out; fears about losing the AI race to China are in.
T1 Energy, which bills itself as one of the few truly all-American solar manufacturing companies, has hired Checkmate Government Relations, a lobbying firm led by Donald Trump Jr.’s old hunting buddy, and Tower Strategy, helmed by a former CIA operations officer, Rick De La Torre, to press its case in the administration. These lobbyists have tried to make the case that the administration’s beef isn’t with solar in general; it’s with Chinese solar. They’ve done it in the kind of pec-flexing language that’s become MAGA’s stock-in-trade.
“American-made, utility-scale solar is one of the few technologies that can be deployed at the speed and scale required” for data centers, De La Torre posted on LinkedIn. “China knows this. That is why it continues to flood markets, compress margins, and keep U.S. manufacturers on the defensive. Undercut. Outscale. Outlast.”
“Washington has a choice. Treat solar manufacturing as a strategic industry, the way we now treat semiconductors and critical minerals,” he added. Or only claim “to compete with Beijing.”
There are some indications that the argument may be gaining traction. In August, the Trump administration added a new 15 percent tariff and price floors on foreign-made solar components. T1’s CEO hailed it as a victory for domestic supply chains and manufacturing. More recently, negotiations in Congress are continuing on a bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among many other things, make it easier for solar providers to plug into the electric grid.
Which led some solar executives to question whether it’s smart for the group to beat up on Republicans, right as a few of them seem to be creeping in solar’s direction.
“We’ve been hard at work speaking to Republicans about why supporting solar and batteries helps with energy abundance and affordability. And we’ve been successful. If this [Invest in Tomorrow Coalition] becomes about going after Republicans and turns solar back into a partisan issue, that would be an epic blunder,” says Russell Gold, T1’s executive vice president for strategic communications.
Tom Matzzie, the chief executive of solar company CleanChoice Energy, is serving as executive chair of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC. Cofounders include Peter Davidson, CEO of the investment firm Aligned Climate Capital, and Michael Brune, former executive director of the Sierra Club. But it’s Larsen who supplied the lion’s share of the early money for the PAC—$6 million of the initial $7 million or so it had raised through August 31, according to federal election commission records.
He’s had an uneven record of political giving, of late. Earlier this year, Larsen spent $3.5 million to support congressional candidate Alex Bores, who was targeted by the AI industry and lost his race. Larsen’s company, Ripple Labs, has donated nearly $100 million to Fairshake, the pro-crypto PAC, which racked up electoral successes in 2024 but just lost a major fight when its preferred bill to regulate cryptocurrencies died in the Senate.
The willingness to go on the attack isn’t the only way that Larsen’s PAC differs from others in the green movement. Not that long ago, renewable advocates talked about an “energy transition” away from old, dirty fossil fuels and toward newer, cleaner ones. Larsen is suggesting instead to red-district politicians that they embrace the idea of fossil and renewable energy sources existing side-by-side, even as the PAC he funds throws haymakers at solar’s enemies.
“You could be pro oil and gas and pro solar,” he says.

A skin problem can begin with something familiar. An itch that persists. A rash that returns. A patch that looks different from the rest of the skin. What happens next often depends on where a person lives and whether appropriate care is within reach.
The Global Access to Skin Health Observatory is a landmark global study led by Esther Freeman in collaboration with the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. Published in JAMA Dermatology, it brings together data from 158 countries representing 97% of the world’s population.
For India, the findings raise questions about where specialists practise, how patients reach them and what happens when treatment is delayed.
What the numbers miss
The study proposes a benchmark of 5.63 per lakh, derived from countries reporting adequate access to dermatological care. This, however, is a reference point, rather than a universal staffing prescription. Dr. Freeman, who is associate professor of dermatology at Harvard Medical School and director of global health dermatology at Massachusetts General Hospital, places India’s dermatologist density well below the benchmark at around 0.5 to 1 per lakh people.
Ramesh Bhat, the Indian co-author of the study and professor at Father Muller Medical College and head of research at Father Muller Research Centre, Mangalore, cautions against directly comparing India with Europe or the Americas, because their health systems differ. What surprises Prof Bhat is that shortages persist despite the number of postgraduate dermatology training seats. He points to the urban-rural divide, with a concentration of specialists in urban areas, and in many cities in southern India, while rural communities face a different reality, where access even to a doctor may be limited.
The study reports that, globally, 79% of dermatologists practise in urban areas. National averages can therefore conceal substantial local gaps. “Dermatologist density gives us an important starting point, but it does not tell us whether a patient can actually receive care,” Dr. Freeman says.
When care is delayed
For Prof Bhat, the consequences are visible in clinical practice. He identifies “delay in diagnosis, wrong treatment, steroid abuse” among the problems arising when appropriate care is unavailable. He singles out leprosy as a condition where delayed diagnosis has implications beyond the individual patient. His concern brings the discussion back to what happens before someone reaches a specialist and whether the treatment they receive along the way is appropriate.
Dr Freeman emphasises the breadth of skin disease, from common infections to chronic inflammatory conditions and neglected tropical diseases. She argues that skin health must be recognised as an essential part of healthcare, with investment directed towards services that already reach communities.
The question is, how to make those services capable of recognising and managing skin disease safely.
Bringing expertise closer
“We need more dermatologists, but we cannot train our way out of this problem with specialists alone,” Dr Freeman says. Primary-care physicians and health officers already manage substantial amounts of skin disease. She advocates practical training, essential medicines and clear referral pathways, allowing common conditions to be treated locally while complex disease and uncertain diagnoses reach specialists.
Prof Bhat also proposes that medical colleges adopt villages, strengthening their links with surrounding communities. He also sees a role for the district residency programme, which takes residents into district settings, and for health camps in reaching rural and tribal populations.
These approaches sit alongside his call for rural specialist clinics and teledermatology. His emphasis is on extending the reach of existing teaching institutions and services, while giving residents the training needed to work effectively beyond major urban centres.
Making remote advice useful
“Teledermatology can be implemented,” Prof Bhat says. But he cautions that training healthcare workers must not result in unqualified practice or drug misuse. Expanding access requires clarity about who can manage a condition and when specialist assessment is necessary.
Dr. Freeman makes a related point. Teledermatology and Artificial Intelligence use need trained frontline providers, available treatment, and reliable referral arrangements. A patient requiring a biopsy, urgent assessment or specialist therapy must still be able to obtain it. “The goal is not to replace dermatologists, but to make their expertise reach much further,” she says.
A remote consultation needs to connect with treatment and follow-up. Advice alone cannot resolve the practical difficulties of obtaining medicines or reaching a referral centre.
What progress should look like
In 2025, the World Health Assembly recognised skin diseases as a global public-health priority. The next step is translating that recognition into national funding and delivery plans.
Prof Bhat’s priorities include an adequate health budget and insurance coverage for dermatological medicines such as biologics and for procedures. He also calls for better training of dermatology residents and dermatology nursing as a separate speciality within nursing education. These proposals bring together workforce development, treatment affordability and rural services, addressing several barriers to appropriate dermatological care.
Measuring progress will require listening more closely to patients. Dr. Freeman acknowledges that the Observatory relied on national leaders and health-system informants, rather than patients directly. Future work should examine waiting times, travel, affordability and diagnostic delays, alongside outcomes and quality of life.
Her planned next phase will examine selected countries more closely to understand where clinicians choose to train and practise, what retains them in underserved areas and which models improve access in different settings. “Five years from now, success should not simply mean there are more dermatologists,” she says. “It should mean that where someone lives is less predictive of whether they can get appropriate care for their skin disease.”
For India, that would mean earlier recognition, appropriate treatment and dependable referral, with fewer patients left to navigate the gaps themselves.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is assistant professor, department of dermatology, Saveetha Medical College and Hospitals, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun told CBS News that he is facing new threats to his life. Pannun, a dual American and Canadian citizen, was previously the target of a foiled 2023 assassination plot allegedly directed by a former Indian intelligence official.
According to Pannun, FBI agents visited his New York City home on Thursday to issue a warning regarding what he described as an “imminent threat to my life”.
The agents reportedly stated they are investigating leads and noted that the threat is connected to his potential travel to Canada, though they did not provide further details.
Pannun's organisation, Sikhs for Justice, is scheduled to hold a non-binding referendum in Edmonton, Canada, on Sunday, October 18. The vote invites Sikhs to decide whether the northern Indian state of Punjab should become an independent nation renamed “Khalistan”.
Addressing the situation, Pannun emphasised that the core issue is not whether he “survives another assassination plot,” but rather whether the Sikh people's right to self-determination “can be stopped through assassination threats.”
“It cannot,” he stated.
FBI agents reportedly told Pannun that the threat is connected to potential travel to Canada and are investigating leads without providing him with any further information.
The renewed threats come as legal proceedings continue for the 2023 plot. Federal prosecutors in Manhattan charged former Indian intelligence officer Vikash Yadav and Indian national Nikhil Gupta with orchestrating the attempted assassination.
Gupta pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is scheduled to be sentenced in November, where Pannun is expected to speak.
The foiled plot against Pannun coincided with the June 2023 assassination of his friend, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another prominent Sikh separatist. Nijjar was fatally shot outside his gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia.
In September 2023, Canadian authorities announced they possessed evidence connecting Indian government agents to Nijjar's murder, describing it as a violation of Canada's sovereignty.
India has officially designated Pannun, the leader of the outlawed Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), as a terrorist for his anti-India activities and continued advocacy of Khalistani separatism.
Pannun has been actively involved in promoting secessionist propaganda, inciting violence, and attempting to radicalize members of the Sikh diaspora. He is accused of funding anti-India campaigns, instigating attacks, and using social media platforms to push separatist narratives.
SFJ, the group Pannun heads, was banned in India in 2019 under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) for its role in promoting terrorism and seeking to create an independent Khalistan state. Authorities allege that Pannun, operating from abroad, continues to coordinate efforts to destabilize India and target Indian diplomatic missions.
India has issued multiple charges against Pannun, including conspiracies to carry out violent acts and threats against Indian leaders and institutions. He is also wanted in connection with threats made against Air India and Indian embassies worldwide.

LIV accuses DP World Tour of player 'interference'
- Published
LIV Golf has accused the DP World Tour of a "clear attempt to interfere" with its restructuring process, after the European tour said it would refuse membership to anyone playing on the breakaway circuit next season.
During a court hearing on Wednesday, the attorney representing LIV said that the organisation was "quite concerned" by the stance taken by the rival DP World Tour.
Rob Fitzgerald of Gibson Dunn, the attorney representing LIV, also said that the organisation would know by the end of the month if it could continue in a 'LIV 2.0' guise.
"We're continuing to monitor this situation very closely and we're quite concerned by it frankly," said Fitzgerald of the DP World Tour's position.
"The timing in particular strikes us as a clear attempt to interfere with our process with our players and potentially our reorganisation writ large.
"It also raises a lot of the same anti-competitive concerns that LIV has expressed previously regarding the way competing leagues have sought to box out and punish market participants, namely these players, from participating in LIV and really only LIV."
DP World Tour declined to comment on Fitzgerald's statement, but Guy Kinnings, its CEO, told BBC Sport on Monday that "players need to make a choice," toughening the organisation's policy on playing across the tours.
In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.
"Player freedom is the reason LIV Golf was created, and it's the foundation of LIV Golf 2.0, a league built around its players," Fitzgerald added as he continued his argument in court.
"LIV has been vocal in its belief in free agency and that the best players should have greater flexibility to compete across the ecosystem. It's unfortunate that another tour is taking an opposite view and pressuring our players with false choice."
Judge Michael B. Kaplan, overseeing proceedings in the New Jersey Bankruptcy Court, replied: "The comments I have read do raise concerns."
Responding to Kaplan's request for clarity on the timeline of LIV 2.0's creation, Fitzgerald said the "two critical pieces" were structural, relating to the investment from BC Partners, and having "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league signed up by 25th of this month".
"We are working hard around the clock both on the player front and on the structural front," added Fitzgerald.
Asked when he would be able to advise the court "one way or the other" whether LIV was "toggling to a wind-down" or going forward, Fitzgerald said: "We would anticipate that decision will be made by the end of the month.
"Once we have full clarity on LIV 2.0, the debtors will need to very shortly begin making payments to host sites, vendors and other parties, so that we can schedule and prepare for LIV 2.0 events that we anticipate will take place shortly following the emergence."
LIV filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding.
As part of the court-supervised "restructuring process", which the organisation hopes to conclude in early 2027, player contracts have been "rejected" and no players are obligated to be part of LIV going forward.
During Wednesday's hearing, 19 player contracts - including those of Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson - were rejected, after having been adjourned from a hearing last week because those players wanted clarity that contract rejection would enable them to have conversations with third parties about their futures.
LIV recruited a number of high profile players following its launch in 2021, but now owes its participants at least $45m (£33m).
Current Race to Dubai leader Patrick Reed, who left LIV in January, has said he was accepted "from day one" after rejoining the European tour.
"This year fully playing on this tour only has been something I've really enjoyed and I feel like the guys have enjoyed having me come over and playing," said Reed.
"I don't feel any different. I feel like the guys have accepted me from day one.
"I can see how some of the guys would sit there and have an issue with guys coming over and just playing the big events.
"I've come over and played everything from big events, small events, events in the middle. I feel like it hasn't been any different for me."
Meanwhile, six-time major winner Rory McIlroy said that LIV was in "such a state of flux" and that the DP World Tour had been "more than accommodating" to the players seeking to leave the competition.
"The DP World Tour are well within their rights to change the rules and regulations," said McIlroy in his press conference prior to the Thursday start of the DP World India Championship.
"This is a way to protect their business and to make the tour as strong as possible."
On Tuesday he told Bloomberg he would vote to have LIV Golf defectors back on the PGA Tour and believed the breakaway circuit was no longer a threat to traditional tours.

After a disaster like a landslide, an earthquake, or a major fire, rescue workers have to locate survivors as soon as possible, and they are increasingly using drones for this critical task—especially ultra-compact drones that can fit into the crevices of a collapsed structure. There are, however, some serious limitations to the technology.
Weighing less than a stick of butter, ultra-compact drones don’t have as much compute or power capacity as larger models, and this restricts the power of their sensors. That means if a building is filled with smoke or the disaster happens at night, the drone’s cameras and lidar will cease to function. Even a clear pane of glass can be an obstacle the drone might not sense.
Now, a research team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands—drawing inspiration from the whiskers of nocturnal animals—has developed a lightweight, tactile sensor for drones to navigate even when they can’t “see.” Some nocturnal animals, like mice and to some extent cats, can explore their surroundings using just the sensations of the environment around them on their whiskers, enabling them to move without vision. The research team wondered whether drones could do the same.
In the world of drone development, tactile navigation is a novel concept that comes with its own challenges. “For tactile sensing to work on drones, it needs to be lightweight, low-latency, and low-power,” Salwa Hamaza, a professor at Delft University of Technology, explained in a press release. Luckily, nature already did some of that innovating.
The “whiskers” Hamaza and her team crafted for the drone consist of delicate wires made of nickel-titanium, each measuring 0.4 millimeters in diameter—about the thickness of four sheets of paper. The antennae, however, were longer than the drone itself. To a palm-sized drone, the researchers attached two whiskers, each nearly 8 inches long with three small pressure sensors at the base. These can assess the bending of the wires, from which the drone estimates its distance from and position in relation to nearby barriers. All calculations necessary for this navigation are processed by a microcontroller onboard the drone, without relying on an external computer.
It may not sound too complicated, but even determining the angle at which to mount the wires was a challenge. Animals that navigate via whisker generally do not fly. Having a long protrusion, even if very light and delicate, can make the drone unstable. When moving along a wall, the researchers saw that resistance from the whisker could cause the drone to rotate and crash.
The researchers compared a total of 72 flights, testing six different angles at three different speeds. The drone flew without major incident when the whiskers were mounted at 30 degrees, 45 degrees, and 60 degrees. Of these, the 45-degree angle was adopted because it resulted in the least deviation in the drone’s orientation. They also took into account the fact that a 60-degree angle reduces the forward sensing range.
The researchers also encountered several hurdles in processing the information taken in by the whiskers. One was distinguishing between actual contact signals and disturbances caused by the drone itself, such as vibrations from the propellers. Even when filtering this noise out, about 38 percent of the drone’s detections were false positives.
The issue seemed to be drift, a phenomenon where sensor readings gradually shift over time. The research team, therefore, developed a correction algorithm that continuously estimates the trend of drifts over time—based on sensor readings when the drone is not touching anything—while in flight. When combined with the filter, false positives reportedly dropped to 0 percent.
These tests were largely done in an environment with three transparent walls arranged in a row. Whenever the tactile sensor touched a wall surface, the drone flew parallel to the wall, maintaining a distance of 60 to 100 millimeters from the surface until it reached the edge. The drone was even able to navigate when the wall was at an angle to it, something a drone with laser sensors would not be able to do.
However, in a real-world situation—like the rubble of a disaster—obstacles are not so neatly arranged. Even in your average room, a drone following a wall could easily get stuck in a corner or overlook barriers to the side. The researchers, therefore, encoded an exploration method that prioritizes moving through unexplored areas by probabilistically estimating the shape of walls. Using this method, the drone successfully found a 2.5-foot-wide exit in a small room with glass walls in 90 percent of tests.
And there is room for improvement, figuratively and literally, given that this touch system only uses a small fraction of the drone’s 192 KB of memory. “We wanted to show that touch does not have to come at the cost of size or computational power,” Chao-Shan Ye, a doctoral student at Delft University of Technology, added in the press release. “Our entire tactile perception pipeline runs onboard using just 34 KB of memory, allowing a tiny drone to sense and respond to its environment in real time.”

After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.
A fix for widespread fraud?
Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.
Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don't respond to outreach efforts by "around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections," said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.
Few details
Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.
"It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it's almost impossible to tell," said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. "That they are not being very transparent is telling too," she said of the administration.
The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children's Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.
Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants' providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.
Even so, how the move will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden's presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only states that use Healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.
"To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active," said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
How it played out
According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:
- The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.
- A broker was involved in the sign-up process.
- The plan had no monthly premium payment.
- The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.
Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers' outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn't respond.
Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting "an all-hands-on-deck" effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.
"Getting them to answer the phone isn't easy," he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.
Additionally, his team has been asked by insurers to help contact those targeted in the second phase of CMS' review. A recent case involved a client who needed to upload his new green card after his previous one expired, but language barriers meant that he had to take time off work to come in for agents to help with the process.
Information from a financial filing
CMS would not provide a list of the insurers it contacted, but publicly available documents show that New York-based Oscar Health was one.
In an August earnings call with analysts and investors, CEO Mark Bertolini said the company was reviewing the files and that "there are a number of cases where we've actually had contact" with people on the list. In other words, the company reached enrollees CMS had targeted over fraud concerns.
He did not specify how many it had reached. The company declined to comment for this article because it is in a voluntary "quiet period," when publicly traded companies limit disclosing information before the release of an earnings report.
Still, in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Oscar Health estimated that 250,000 to 300,000 of its members might be disenrolled because of the CMS effort. Nationally, the company had about 3 million members in the second quarter and reported strong profits.
Overall ACA enrollment has declined sharply, falling by nearly 3 million in the first few months of the year, due in large part to the expiration at the end of last year of the enhanced subsidies. The Trump administration has also taken some credit, saying its focus on weeding out improper enrollments and other changes, such as eliminating a special year-round low-income enrollment period, led to the decline.
CMS has also suspended some brokers for improper activity and barred new brokers from enrolling clients in ACA insurance on the federal exchange during the upcoming open enrollment period.
CMS did not respond to requests for data on the reasons it canceled enrollments. What percentage of enrollees were deemed ineligible due to incorrect income reporting or because they had other health coverage, such as through their jobs? How many because their ACA applications lacked immigration documents or Social Security numbers?
"Currently, there is no additional data to share," the agency's press office said.
But people outside the administration have been vocal.
"This was clearly phantom enrollees," said Paragon's Blase. He thinks more than 99% of the cancellations are of zero-premium coverage that people were signed up for by rogue call centers without their knowledge, or for people who don't exist at all.
Blase said the carriers had a big incentive to get hold of the enrollees because they would lose the subsidies they were being paid if the plans were canceled.
And for any people unfairly caught up, Blase and Trump administration officials say all they have to do to be reinstated is call the marketplace and provide their Social Security number or other missing information.
"Everyone has the political incentive for that process to be that easy," Blase said. "We're a month before the election."
But, as prior reporting has shown, it isn't always a quick process to get an ACA plan canceled or reinstated following an unauthorized sign-up or switch, even when a consumer discovers it themselves and reaches out to the marketplace.
Brokers and policy analysts note that some of the factors used to question enrollments — such as a plan's having no claims filed in a year — are not that unusual. Many people, for example, don't visit a doctor or hospital in a given year.
Insurers "want those healthy people in the insurance pool to help bring down the rates," said Ronnell Nolan, president and CEO of Health Agents for America, a trade group for health insurance agents. "We're against fraud, and CMS has allowed a lot of fraud to happen. But we don't want people who just didn't go to the doctor to be canceled."
And even with the outreach required by CMS, not everyone answers phone calls from unknown numbers or opens their mail or emails.
A recent marketing report found an average "open rate" on emails of 28.6%.
Policy experts also note that, while lack of a Social Security number on an ACA application could indicate a fake enrollee, it might also be an oversight, or the number might not be required, like for a child if the person applying is an adult who is not seeking coverage for the child.
"There will be legitimate people who don't have a claim or don't respond to an inquiry from an insurer," said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. "If the goal is to target fraudulent enrollment, what CMS did is better than tossing people at random, but is likely to miss the mark."

Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".

Unacceptable interference: Indian envoy rejects US lawmaker's ‘purging 130 million from voter rolls’ remark

India's ambassador to America Vinay Mohan Kwatra on Thursday criticised US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal for her “unacceptable interference” on India's electoral processes and in the country's internal affairs.
Jayapal, an Indian-origin Democratic representative from Washington state, expressed concern over reports that around 13 crore names had been removed from India's electoral rolls during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
“The remarks by [Jayapal] on India’s electoral and political processes are unacceptable interference in India’s internal affairs,” Kwatra said on X.
“India is a vibrant democracy, with robust, independent constitutional institutions and a longstanding record of free and fair elections. Always open to constructive conversation with the Congresswoman to dispel her misconceptions,” he wrote.
Jayapal said she was “deeply concerned” as she alleged efforts to remove 130 million people from voter rolls in India, drawing a comparison with efforts by US President Donald Trump's administration to undermine voting rights.
“I am deeply concerned about the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls. This appears to be a similar playbook to what the Trump Administration is doing here at home to undermine voting rights in a democracy,” she wrote on X.
About the SIR controversy
The controversy centres on the ECI's SIR, a nationwide exercise to verify electoral rolls and remove entries considered ineligible. The ECI says the revision is necessary to update voter lists by identifying deceased voters, duplicate registrations and people who have permanently shifted or cannot be traced.
Opposition parties have questioned the scale of the exclusions, claiming over 13 crore people were removed by chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar to favour PM Narendra Modi's BJP in winning elections.
The poll panel rejected the opposition's description of the entire figure as confirmed voter deletions, saying eligible electors could apply for inclusion in the rolls.
The controversy intensified after The Indian Express reported in September that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months on issues linked to the revision, registration procedures and digital electoral-roll systems. The report said the commissioners had raised concerns about decisions taken by Gyanesh Kumar without their knowledge.
What Trump is doing on voter rolls
Trump's administration has stepped up efforts to check voter-registration records and identify people it believes may be ineligible to vote.
The White House says the aim is to protect election integrity and maintain public confidence in elections. Federal law prohibits non-US citizens from voting in federal elections.
The administration has sought access to state voter-registration records and has tried to use federal databases to check voters' eligibility. These efforts have faced legal challenges, with critics arguing that inaccurate records could lead to eligible citizens being wrongly identified as ineligible.
On Tuesday, the US Justice Department gave California election officials 48 hours to review a list of people it suspected were non-US citizens registered to vote. It threatened legal action if officials failed to comply.
The department also asked officials to withhold or set aside ballots linked to the people on the list until their citizenship was confirmed. The demand came after California had begun mailing ballots to voters ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said his office was reviewing the request with state officials. He said the county had not opened the USB drive containing the names because of concerns about data security.
The Justice Department said it was enforcing federal election law. Critics, however, questioned the timing of the demand and warned that errors in government records could affect eligible voters. Being flagged for verification does not, by itself, mean that someone is a non-citizen or has voted illegally.
