In 2022, New York fined three Amish schools for not complying with a law mandating schools only accept students with updated vaccines, following the 2019 removal of a religious exemption from that law. The small schools were fined $2,000 for every student without updated vaccines every day, for a total of $118,000 before the schools sued the state.
New York fined the schools, not the children.
The New York Department of Health did not clarify to Snopes whether it had fined any other schools or whether it had continued to fine the three schools since 2022.
In early October, some social media posts claimed the state of New York had "declared war on the Amish" with vaccine requirements enforced by fines. Many Amish communities have lower childhood vaccination rates than the rest of the U.S. population, although vaccination is not universally rejected in these communities.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed the state was fining each unvaccinated Amish child $2,000 per day. The post asserted that New York Democrats took away the religious exemption often used by Amish families to opt out of childhood vaccine requirements.
Users shared similar posts claiming New York Democrats were fining unvaccinated Amish children $2,000 each day on Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers emailed us asking whether the rumor was true.
It's true that New York fined at least three Amish schools $2,000 for each unvaccinated child it allowed to attend the school each day. New York did not fine the children themselves, and it's unclear whether the state is still actively imposing fines on these schools or any other over their vaccination policies. Therefore, we've rated this claim a mixture of true and false information.
These details are outlined in a lawsuit, Miller v. McDonald.
According to the case, in 2019 New York repealed the religious exemption to its school immunization law — which applies to all public, private and religious schools in the state — after a measles outbreak in 2018 and 2019 centered around communities with clusters of unvaccinated people (PDF Page 3).
Democrats were the majority in both the state Senate and state Assembly in 2019. The governor at the time was Andrew Cuomo, a Democrat.
The immunization law prohibits schools from allowing children who do not have their scheduled vaccinations to attend the school until those vaccination requirements are met. New York audited three Amish schools' compliance with the law in 2021, and in 2022 it fined the schools for allowing children to attend who did not meet the vaccine requirements (PDF Page 7).
A school is fined $2,000 for each violation of the law every day (PDF pages 7-8). Every attending student who does not meet vaccine requirements is considered a violation, which means the school is fined for each noncompliant student every day. Prior to imposing the fines, the state sent a letter to school administrators warning it would impose the fines.
New York applied the fines under the assumption that two schools failed to comply for one day and acted as if there were only one noncompliant student attending for 10 days at the third school. That resulted in fines of $52,000 for 26 students at one school, $46,000 for 23 students at another school and $20,000 for one student at the third school, for a total of $118,000.
Notably, this amount was the total of the fines fines placed on the schools at the time the lawsuit was filed on June 2, 2023, the total fine referenced in the latest court decision on June 30 and the total fine referenced in social media posts as of this writing. A legal organization representing the Amish schools said they racked up $118,000 in total fines when announcing it would appeal the latest ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 2.
Snopes reached out to the New York State Department of Health to ask whether the schools were still racking up fines or whether there have been other schools fined since the beginning of the lawsuit. The department did not elaborate on the fines. A spokesperson told Snopes via email:
The state's responsibility is to protect public health, keep New Yorkers and their families safe and enforce the law fairly and equitably. While we cannot comment on pending litigation, the Department is committed to eliminating serious illness and unnecessary deaths caused by vaccine preventable diseases. The Department continues to provide community outreach and education on the safety of immunizations. New York's school immunization requirements are based in science and protect the health and well-being of all New Yorkers.
The lawsuit challenging this law, which does so on religious freedom grounds, has traveled up and down the court system. In 2025, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's decision to side with New York over the plaintiffs (PDF Page 5), but the U.S. Supreme Court vacated that decision and told the 2nd Circuit to reconsider the case in light of a different case the Supreme Court recently ruled on.
After considering this other case, the 2nd Circuit did not change its decision in Miller v. McDonald. That was the June 30 decision that representatives for the Amish schools are appealing to the Supreme Court once again.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked the claim that autism rates are nearly nonexistent among Amish children because Amish people allegedly rarely get vaccinated.

Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”
It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.
At a concert in 2024, Mitchell said: “Fuck Donald Trump, I love that song,” referring to the rap track by YG. She added: “I wish I could vote ... I’m a Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”
Mitchell was born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943, and eventually settled with her family in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Her earliest gigs were at folk clubs there, followed by Calgary and Toronto, where she met US folk singer Chuck Mitchell. They married in 1965 and Mitchell moved to the US. The marriage didn’t last, ending two years later, but by that time Mitchell had established herself as a mellifluous, original voice on the vibrant US folk music circuit.
She released her debut album in 1968, and soon after, using the album’s royalties, moved to Los Angeles’ Laurel Canyon where she recorded her first gold-selling album, Ladies of the Canyon. She remained based in California and currently lives in Santa Barbara.
Mitchell’s most recent studio album is Shine, from 2007. After that she spent a number of years out of the public eye, suffering a brain aneurysm in 2015 that required extensive recovery. But she returned to live performance in 2022 with an unannounced set at the Newport folk festival, and has since performed a number of all-star “Joni Jam” concerts.
A biopic about her is being prepared by director Cameron Crowe, who began work on it in the early 2020s. Earlier this year, record executive Clive Davis announced at a party that Meryl Streep would play Mitchell in the film.

School roof collapse kills at least 29, injures more than 3 dozen in Pakistan
PESHAWAR, Pakistan — The roof of a private school collapsed in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a female teacher and injuring more than 50 other people, a hospital spokesman said, as rescuers searched the rubble for anyone still trapped. Six girls were among the dead.
Several children were also trapped under the rubble in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, said Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the emergency services.
A hospital spokesman, Mohammad Asim, also confirmed the casualties, saying some of the injured were in critical condition. All the children killed or injured were age 13 or younger, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded.
Hours later, rescue officials said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews were clearing the debris. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Gov. Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause of the collapse. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children.
Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said that the three-story school had an estimated 1,200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She told The Associated Press that she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.
According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighborhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene.
A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom to drink water.
A resident, Mohammad Khan, said rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.
The cause of the collapse was under investigation. Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school's owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak.
The provincial government said that the school occupied a three-story building and that a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse.
The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, said that the government directed hospital officials to provide prompt medical care to the injured children and praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.
In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements.
"The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow," Zardari said.
He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies.
In July, a roof collapsed at a tutoring center under construction in Lahore, killing four schoolchildren.
Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs.

Shira Fischer, a physician who works in health policy in Boston, sought a speech pathologist for her child in 2022, when virtual appointments became the norm because of Covid-19.
“I read their consent and they said they were going to record and use [our appointment] for training,” she said. “And I said, no, my kid has a lisp. The last thing she wants is videos of her lisping to be used for training for who knows how long and who knows what database.”
Fischer said the clinic wouldn’t change the consent, and wouldn’t proceed with the appointment if she didn’t sign it. Eventually, she found a different speech pathologist. “It ended up being better. But what is that, that they require you to allow them to record for their training?”
Every day, doctor’s offices across the country tell patients that if they want to see the doctor, they must allow their health data to be accessible by tens of thousands of hospitals and clinics. Often, doctors give out overly broad consent forms, asking patients to agree to anything from hospitals using patient files for training doctors to using patient data for training artificial intelligence.
Practically speaking, when a patient doesn’t agree, doctors can turn them away.
Other times, doctors’ offices tell patients they can opt out of sharing their data later — by contacting an email address or mailing a physical letter — but in reality, opting out can be so difficult and confusing that it isn’t really a choice at all.
When I was pregnant with my child, I wondered why my gynecologists’ forms asked me to let another company, Phreesia, mine my health data for marketing. The authorization form was labeled “Required” even though it legally must be optional. I systematically opted out and kept my own records of this, but when I tried to confirm my opt outs with Phreesia, it said I did consent. After 81 days of back and forth, Phreesia admitted I had never authorized them to use my data. But it continued to use the misleading “Required” label on the authorization form. Months later, after complaining to the Department of Health and Human Services, and an episode of “The Indicator from Planet Money” on NPR, Phreesia changed how it labeled its forms. I found the process galling, but it spurred my curiosity, and I’ve been researching how opt outs work ever since.
In the last year, I registered as a patient at 25 clinics and hospitals across seven states and spent hundreds of hours reviewing consent forms, privacy policies, and marketing forms to see whether I could actually opt out of sharing my data.
For one hospital in Ohio, it took me 26 steps, a notary, and a flight to Las Vegas to learn how to opt out of the hospital’s many uses of my patient records. Despite my best efforts, the hospital will not follow its own policy, which ostensibly allows patients to refuse to allow the hospital to take and own photos and recordings of them.
It started last January, when I sought a second opinion on a personal health issue with a specialist at University Hospitals in Westlake, Ohio. University Hospitals is a large, nonprofit hospital system that manages its electronic health records through MyChart, a widely used patient portal. MyChart is made by Epic Systems, a health care software company in Verona, Wis., that says it has more than 305 million patient charts, coming from patients in every state and more than a dozen countries.
As I prepared for my appointment, the hospital asked me to sign its registration forms and to sign up for MyChart. In the dense terms of service, I spotted three different ways that as a patient, my data was about to be used, accessed, or shared:
- The hospital will share my health data through Epic’s proprietary health information platform, Care Everywhere.
- The hospital will share my data with CliniSync, an Ohio-based nonprofit health information exchange that facilitates the exchange of patients’ information, like lab results, across institutions.
- The hospital will own any photos, audio, or video they take of me and may use them for any lawful purpose.
In each case, I was told that I could opt out or refuse, but the process felt like it was designed to keep me from doing so. Forms and websites lacked basic contact information; customer service didn’t respond; patients were required to find a notary, and hospital staff directly contradicted their own written policies and told me I wasn’t allowed to opt out.
So I set out to see what it would truly take to say no to sharing my data, starting with Epic.
There’s no button to revoke authorization everywhere
Once a hospital makes a patient’s records available through Epic’s Care Everywhere, many clinicians who work with Epic across the country can pull up those records, with some exceptions.
The most common way doctors use health exchanges is to get up to speed on a patient who is coming to see them. Sharing patient health records through exchanges has decreased duplicative tests on patients. It also allows emergency room doctors who have never seen a patient before to immediately get their health history and allergies, which can save a patient’s life, said Saurabh Rahurkar, a former assistant professor at Ohio State University College of Medicine.
Individual hospitals can also restrict which doctors can see a patient’s files, such as by physical distance, or by adding an extra confirmation step before doctors can see the files of patients who have received psychological services.
“If you say to your new doctor, ‘Please go get my records at this place that’s 3,000 miles away,’ Care Everywhere can do that, but not if the system has the settings to only look for records within a 50-mile radius,” said Lucia Savage, former chief privacy officer at the federal health IT office.
But there are clear reasons why some patients don’t want their data to show up in these searches, and hospital protections, if they exist at all, are not always effective.
For example, a patient who crosses state lines to seek an abortion treatment may not want her records to be searchable by her providers in her home state where that treatment is criminalized.
“People who have had bad experiences with unauthorized access to their information and people who have sensitive health conditions and diagnoses, for very good reasons, are just mistrusting of the health care system,” said Julia Adler-Milstein, a leading researcher in health IT policy and a professor of medicine at the University of California San Francisco. They “don’t feel like the health care system has been a good steward of them and their information.”
For example, researchers reviewing 1,138 breach cases found that almost 10% of patient health data breaches come from unauthorized access by health care employees who forward personally identifying information to personal accounts.
Nichole Sweeney, who was recently the chief privacy officer and general counsel at CRISP Shared Services, which provides technology infrastructure to support health exchanges in more than 10 states, said she often encountered providers snooping in patient records in her job as a privacy officer: “Somebody, a provider in an office, looks up an ex, and we find that because we have monitoring software, and I have to call them and tell them not to do that anymore. They get fired sometimes.”
Cason Schmit, a health law and policy professor at Texas A&M University, warned, “We’re at a place in time where data that are being collected to help people are now being used in ways that could actively and specifically harm them.” He pointed to Immigration and Customs Enforcement use of health data for immigration enforcement. Schmit has written about the role of state policy in fostering health information exchange and its benefits to the public, such as tracking measles outbreaks.
In my attempt to opt out of Epic’s Care Everywhere, I first looked for a way to do it with MyChart. I navigated through 40-plus menu items, including the “Sharing Hub,” where I watched videos on Care Everywhere that explained its benefits but not how to restrict its uses. In the end, I found one section under “Authorize Sharing” that said I could “request that your information no longer be shared” by sending a message to customer service. I tried that. I got no response.
Then I tried emailing and calling the hospital system’s ethics and compliance department to opt out of Care Everywhere. Crickets.
After weeks of dead ends, I found something that worked. When I called MyChart’s patient support number, the representative said I could opt out by contacting the hospital’s medical records department. I called medical records, and they called back that day and confirmed I was opted out of Care Everywhere.
But how are patients supposed to know about this process? I couldn’t find “contact medical records” described anywhere in MyChart or on the hospital’s website.
I asked Epic for an interview, and they agreed to let me speak with Matt Doyle, who leads software development for Care Everywhere. Turns out, both of us were about to be in Las Vegas, for one of the largest health care tradeshow conferences in the country. I arrived early at the Epic booth, which was well-appointed among its peers in the exhibition hall with carpets and a private meeting room. Posters proudly announced that health providers exchange approximately 22 million patient records each day through Care Everywhere.
Doyle walked over from a hub of Epic employees clicking through MyChart screens with conference attendees, and led me to the meeting room along with a colleague from public relations.
“So when you check in for your appointment, the de facto position is you’re part of Care Everywhere,” Doyle confirmed, “unless you explicitly opt out.”
I recounted for him everything I tried, and how there was nothing I could click in MyChart to opt out.
“It’s not in the MyChart enrollment process,” Doyle clarified, “but as soon as your MyChart account is set up, you can immediately go opt out.”
Doyle explained that there are two levels of opting out.
“One is, ‘Revoke authorization, but I still want to be discoverable,’” he said. “And what that would mean is, let’s say today you’re in a car accident. You go to the emergency department. Your doctor’s office back in Ohio doesn’t have your authorization on file, but you’re discoverable.” Meaning, a doctor could see that a specific patient has a health record, and can ask the patient for his or her consent to access that record.
The second level of opting out is to be completely undiscoverable through Care Everywhere. In this case, doctors who work in other hospital systems can’t see any record of the patient in Care Everywhere. It’s a choice only 112 patients have made since they rolled out the ability to opt out this way in August 2025, Doyle said.
There’s one extra twist. Doyle confirmed that there isn’t a single place to revoke authorization everywhere. “You have to go to each custodian of your medical records,” he clarified. A patient would revoke access to Care Everywhere “with each place that you receive care.”
“Can you show me how to opt out?” I asked.
Doyle brought me back out to Epic’s booth, where employees have demos of MyChart on multiple screens. Doyle tried to find a demo where he could show me a new, patient-facing feature to revoke authorizations for data sharing. But the patient in the demo product had not signed any authorizations, so there was no way to show me how to revoke them.
I asked the next public relations representative who joined us if I could see it on her MyChart. She pulled it up on her phone, went to the “Sharing Hub” menu options, but we didn’t see the “Revoke authorization” button. We looked at Doyle, who then explained that only organizations that have updated their Epic software would have the opt-out methods that he described. He offered to show me on a video call the following week.
Until a patient’s health care provider updates their software from Epic, Doyle confirmed that a patient’s only option is to call the medical records department and tell them “I would like to opt out of Care Everywhere.”
A week later, three Epic representatives joined my meeting with Doyle to show me how to opt out in the Sharing Hub section of MyChart.
“There’s two different places,” explained Sean Bina, vice president of access and patient experience at Epic, as he showed me the buttons in MyChart. “One is ‘managing my record authorizations.’ And then the second is how I can prevent other organizations from requesting a record.”
After months of trying, I finally got to see actual buttons inside of MyChart that would let me opt out.
After this interview, Epic did not respond to further questions from CalMatters and The Markup about Care Everywhere, including how many current patients have the ability to see the opt out buttons inside of MyChart.
A prime example of using health data for profit involves companies that use what expecting parents search for or watch online and what they’ve shopped for to target them with baby ads.
Mary Ebeling, a sociologist at Drexel University who wrote the book “Healthcare and Big Data,” had just learned in March 2011 that her doctor could no longer detect a heartbeat in her 11th or 12th week of pregnancy.
“After learning that I lost the pregnancy, literally, I came home, and my mail carrier delivered the first issue of a year’s subscription [of the now-defunct magazine American Baby] for free,” she recalled. “I had not signed up for it — to American Baby. And I was like ‘I’m getting angry right now about it.’”
The unsolicited baby-themed marketing continued, and she eventually discovered that the data broker Experian was selling her information in a database of “new parents.”
Commercially gathered data, such as Ebeling’s online search or purchasing history, doesn’t have the same legal protections as health records at health care facilities, which are covered by HIPAA. But that protection isn’t bulletproof. Past Markup investigations have found that HIPAA-covered hospitals were sending sensitive patient data to Facebook through Meta’s tracking pixel.
Federal law also allows confidential substance use disorder treatment records to be shared in certain circumstances, such as with probation officers.
As a part of her work, Jacqueline Seitz, deputy director of health privacy at the Legal Action Center, frequently speaks with patients who use drugs, are in recovery, are living with HIV, or are in treatment for substance use disorders. She also regularly speaks with the health providers who treat them.
“When I talk to providers and I ask them what they tell patients, they say, ‘We tell patients everything is confidential.’ And that is not the right thing to say. That is not true,” Seitz said.
For patients who are mandated into treatment in order to maintain their employment, custody access, or probation, when asked, their medical records must be shared with probation officers or other legal authorities, Seitz explained. It’s why she increasingly sees electronic health records as a rap sheet.
“I don’t think people are trying to trick patients,” she said, but she regularly sees examples of health care workers not fully understanding confidentiality rules in these cases.
Opting out of CliniSync, Ohio’s statewide nonprofit health information exchange
In addition to being asked to sign up for MyChart when I registered for my appointment at the University Hospitals, I was also asked to acknowledge my participation in CliniSync.
CliniSync, Ohio’s statewide nonprofit health information exchange, facilitates the exchange of patients’ information, like lab results, across institutions. CliniSync is operated by the Ohio Health Information Partnership, an independent private nonprofit founded in 2009. Ohio’s governor designated the partnership to develop the statewide exchange.
The hospital system posts many of its forms online, so I had time to research the general consent to treatment form in advance. That alerted me to how patients are defaulted into sharing their data with CliniSync.
A quick online search for “UH privacy policy” (UH stands for University Hospitals) brought me to the hospital system’s HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices. It said I can opt out of CliniSync if I contact their privacy officer over the phone, and it gave me an email and phone number. I emailed right away. I didn’t hear back before my appointment four days later.
I also knew that CliniSync likely has its own policy, separate from the hospital system’s, so I also searched for its opt-out policy online. The instructions are simple but surprised me: CliniSync asks patients to notarize its opt-out form.
“It’s a big time suck for people. They’re going to have to spend a lot of time finding a notary. They’re going to have to pay that notary, almost certainly, unless they happen to have a friend or family member who’s a notary public,” said Lior Strahilevitz, a legal scholar at the University of Chicago who writes about privacy and teaches health law. Not only is requiring a notary burdensome, it’s also legally questionable. General guidance from the federal government states that HIPAA authorizations do not need to be notarized.
Still, I paid the $15 at UPS to get the form notarized and mailed it out.
The Ohio Health Information Partnership, which operates CliniSync, declined to respond to questions about why it requires patients to get their opt-out requests notarized.
Finally, on the day of my appointment, I tried what should have been the easiest method for patients: Asking the hospital to opt me out in-person.
When I asked the receptionist at my appointment how I could opt out of CliniSync, she said she didn’t know, but she’d run my request up the chain while I was with the doctor. When I came back, she had an answer: Patients can’t opt out. A colleague at the hospital told her through email that CliniSync “ensures that providers across various hospital organizations are able to request and access patient medical records, as it relates to medical need and treatment. This is not feasible to be ‘removed’ from clinisync.”
CliniSync does, in fact, have a form to let patients opt out. And clinic staff can sign the form so that patients don’t have to find a notary instead. It says so right on the CliniSync opt-out form.
But in my research into how difficult it is for patients to opt out of processes like this, multiple hospital staff have given me inaccurate information. I wasn’t surprised.
Strahilevitz described this as a common problem in any bureaucracy, a phenomenon known as “desk clerk law.”
“Basically, there’s what the law is, and then there’s what the person at the DMV who’s actually interfacing with the consumer thinks the law is or what the person at the Secretary of State’s office is,” Strahilevitz said. “And so I would regard your experience with the receptionist as a classic instance of ‘desk clerk law.’”
University Hospitals declined to respond to questions about whether its patients can opt out of CliniSync, and said it did not have an expert available for an interview.
After my appointment, I called the hospital’s compliance office and a few days later, I got a voicemail asking for more information over email, or for me to call them back. Since I know that Ohio law requires requests to opt out be written, I emailed the hospital with what they ask for. When no one responded, I called and emailed again.
Soon after my appointment, I got a hand addressed letter from CliniSync confirming my opt out and saying they processed it shortly after they received my notarized letter. I was pleasantly surprised, because I’ve followed many opt-out processes in the last year, and it’s uncommon to get verification like this.
Two weeks after I saw the doctor, the hospital’s compliance office confirmed my opt out from CliniSync over email.
Because CliniSync records a patient’s opt out centrally, one request blocks other providers from seeing a patient’s records through CliniSync’s network, but for many health exchanges, including Epic’s Care Everywhere, patients would have to discover and follow an opt-out process at each new provider.
Sweeney, who was the chief privacy officer and general counsel at a company that supported health exchanges in more than 10 states, estimated that a typical patient might have to opt out of data-sharing at as many as 10 different places — wherever they seek care — for their opt out to be meaningful.
In most states, she said, “the place to cut off the data exchange is at the provider because that’s where it starts.”
In some rare cases, patients do not need to go through this complicated opt-out process, because their clinic refuses to share any patient data with health databases or platforms, simply because patients haven’t explicitly consented.
Keith Smith runs the Surgery Center of Oklahoma, which markets transparent pricing and cash payment. The center does not accept insurance or Medicare, and it has tried to refuse government agencies’ requests for patient data, such as from the state health department.
“There’s no shortage of people that will claim that they have a legal right to see how many patients operated on at Surgery Center of Oklahoma had breast cancer or had inguinal hernia repairs,” he said. “And the patients haven’t consented to the release of their records.”
Because Smith’s surgery center does not accept federal dollars, he isn’t obligated to report as much information to the government. “We treat patients here as individuals. And I don’t think it’s right to violate the rights of an individual for the greater good,” he said. “All the individual cares about is that their rights have been violated.”
Refusing to let the hospital own my photos, videos, or recordings
In addition to asking me to share my patient records with multiple health exchanges in order to see my doctor, University Hospitals also required me to give it complete ownership over any photos, audio, or videos it takes of me. Its consent form states, “UH may, unless otherwise refused, photograph and/or audio or video record me or the Services I receive, including those in which I am identifiable. UH will own such images or recordings and may use them for any lawful purpose.”
I have rarely pondered the possibilities: If the doctor takes a picture of a rash on my child’s body for diagnostic purposes, would I want the hospital to claim ownership over or have broad rights to use that photo?
The consent form says I can refuse, but when I asked the hospital’s compliance and ethics office, they wouldn’t let me. “We are not able to accept modifications or partial withdrawals of specific provisions within the General Consent for Treatment itself,” said the hospital’s email. “This includes provisions related to incidental recording that may occur as part of delivering or documenting care.”
That surprised me. In hospital systems, the compliance office is usually where staff have privacy expertise. The hospital refused to follow its own policy.
University Hospitals declined to respond to questions about whether its patients can refuse giving the hospital ownership over images and recordings it takes of patients.
“It’s misrepresentation,” said Strahilevitz, the University of Chicago expert. “So I think that’s just fraud to tell you you have a right and then telling you, ‘No, we were wrong. You don’t, in fact, have that right. And now your photograph and/or audio and/or video is going to be used.’”
Fischer, who refused to see a speech pathologist because the doctor’s office insisted on a right to record her child’s lisp treatment, said she sees health providers requiring parents to agree to clauses like this all the time.
“I can’t get a link to telehealth appointments for my kids without signing agreements that include things like ‘authorize the use of photos, videos, and/or recordings’ and ‘give permission for staff (including students) to participate and/or watch for training purposes’ or other things I don’t want to agree to,” she said. “But there is no option to not sign.”
Experts say there are practical design and regulatory solutions
Colin Gray, an assistant professor at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading expert on manipulative design said, “You start from the position of defeat rather than starting from the position where you’re making a rational choice … the attitude is, ‘Well, if you really cared about your data, then you would go through the extra steps to turn it off.’ And in this case, it’s like, ‘That’s an hour of my time or 26 steps or whatever it is that I don’t have.’ And so it looks so onerous from the beginning, like, why would you even try?”
Experts like Stacey Tovino, a professor who teaches HIPAA privacy law at the University of Oklahoma College of Law, say there’s a clear and practical solution: “Amend these [federal] regulations to say covered entities shall not impose an undue burden on people trying to opt out.” Tovino suggested that when patients see that they can opt out in a form, the next sentence should include a link to do so.
Some states have laws that require this type of solution. Under New York law, for example, providers need explicit consent from patients to access their data from health information exchanges. I saw it firsthand when I registered my son for an appointment in upstate New York. The check-in screens showed me a form labelled “Health Exchange,” and asked for my consent for the physician group to access all of the patient’s medical records through Healthix, a health exchange. When I clicked “No,” the next form showed the detailed consent form with “I DENY CONSENT” selected as one of my two choices. But when a provider in Virginia, which doesn’t have a state law with explicit opt-in or opt-out requirements, informed me I had the choice to opt out, it refused to let me. My only option was to click “I accept” and to follow an opt-out process after the fact.
According to Seitz, the health privacy director who works with patients going through mandated treatment, one major challenge in privacy law is that it’s difficult to put a dollar amount on the type of harm people experience, such as when intimate details about their lives are stored in recorded therapy sessions on an unsecured database, like Confidant Health did in 2024. Individuals can’t file a civil lawsuit or sue their doctor for violating HIPAA, which means that only the federal government or state attorneys general can enforce it. As a result, Seitz said that the attitude in health care around data breaches is: “Yeah, I’m breaking the law. What are you going to do about it?”
To make privacy violations actionable, Seitz said, “I would want statutory damages. Like, every corporate defense attorney’s nightmare where it says, ‘Every breach equals $2,000,’ and then all the client has to do is show the breach, and then it’s money.”
At the end of the day, experts said one of the most important parts of the health data ecosystem is trust.
“Every single health data custodian that exists should be doing everything that we can to nurture and protect and foster the trust of those whose data we protect,” said Schmit, the health law and policy professor who wrote about how health exchanges can benefit the public. “And one thing that will absolutely undermine that trust are structures and processes that are opaque and difficult to follow, that make patients feel like they aren’t cared for.”
Alex Rosenbat is the director of sociotechnical research at CalMatters and The Markup. As a researcher and reporter, she writes about dark patterns, privacy, and product design in U.S. health care. She is the author of “Uberland: How Algorithms Are Rewriting the Rules of Work.” Read her tips for opting out of sharing your health data.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.
* With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”
Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
A ‘before and after’ photo of a freshly painted White House column was modified with AI.
As pointed out by users on Reddit, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.
The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.
Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself, while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn't always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.

On Thursday night, Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled what’s been billed as the company’s last human-driven car. The Roadster 2 is the long-awaited followup to the electric automaker’s first vehicle, the Roadster.
At a demonstration event McGregor, Texas—at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility—the new car did what Musk has long promised: With a herky-jerky burst of steam, it flew into the air. At one point, the car flipped over the automaker’s entire line-up, floating several feet over its electric semi-truck. Tesla executives said the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 1 second.
“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk said.
Tesla fans have waited a long time for the vehicle. The Roadster 2 was first announced in 2017, and at the time Tesla said the new sports car would be the fastest production vehicle in the world.
The “flying” technology is enabled by four thrusters, Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy said.
Musk says Tesla plans to enter production in 2028. The company initially promised the Roadster 2 would ship in 2020. Enthusiasts put down $50,000 deposits for what was advertised as a $200,000 car. (That deposit is worth more than $68,000 in 2026 dollars.) Some got sick of waiting. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman complained on X last year that he had trouble canceling his reservation. Musk posted that Altman received a refund in 24 hours.
Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as a carmaker and that the company is focused on building autonomous vehicle technology and robots.
The unveiling event comes at a weird time for electric vehicles. Sales of EVs have stalled in the US after the GOP-led Congress nixed federal supports. Meanwhile, the global energy crisis has EV sales booming elsewhere. Electric luxury hypercars—the class to which the Roadster 2 belongs—are in an especially tricky spot. Several luxury automakers have said that wealthy buyers are now looking for the sound and power of a typical gas-powered vehicle. Lamborghini shelved its plans to make an EV earlier this year.

Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “Klara and the Sun,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-consuming technology.
“I think we gotta put our focus on one another and put down the computers and phones,” the star told Variety on the red carpet at the movie’s world premiere at London Film Festival on Thursday night.
Ortega, wearing a stunning yellow lace dress and hair piece, added: “Remember to be present and to appreciate people while they’re standing right in front of you.”
Based on Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling 2021 novel of the same name, “Klara and the Sun” is set in a future where advances in genetic engineering have divided humans into strict social classes. Ortega plays Klara, an artificial android companion who is purchased for an ailing girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). “Klara and the Sun” is directed by “Thor” helmer Taika Waititi and also stars Amy Adams as Josie’s mother, Aran Murphy (son of Cillian Murphy), Natasha Lyonne, Steve Buscemi and more.
Popular on Variety
Waititi, Adams, Murphy and Lyonne all walked the London Film Festival red carpet on Thursday night, alongside Waititi’s wife Rita Ora, author Ishiguro and a surprise appearance from Florence Pugh, who stunned in a blue floral gown with statement sleeves. Pugh enthusiastically greeted Ortega and Adams before they all posed for photos together alongside producer Rachel Forman.
Standing alongside Ortega, Adams added that everyone she’s spoken to has gotten “something different” out of the film. “That, to me, is a really successful film that communicates something different to each viewer. So I like hearing what people get out of it,” she said.
Ortega clarified that though Klara is an “artificial friend,” she doesn’t work like the AI that we know today.
“AI I guess pulls all this information from the internet and Klara gets all her information from the real world,” she said. “So that’s a little bit different. She’s kind of like a toddler in a sense. Playing her specifically in this film was really interesting because Taika wanted a more human approach, so he didn’t want to do movement that was too robotic, maybe more sort of clumsy and unknowing.”
Ishiguro acknowledged that, since his novel came out in 2021, the world’s awareness and attitude about AI has changed greatly.
“This film doesn’t address a lot of the anxieties that you and I may have right now about where we’re going with the technology. I mean, I think quite rightly, it’s really come center stage,” he said. “I’m aware that this film is coming out into a very different world to the one that my novel came out in five years ago, and I don’t know how that will change people’s expectations or how people look at things. But I’ll say that this isn’t another film about how an AI machine seems to be nice and then becomes sinister and ends up killing all the nice people in the film. It’s not that sort of story.”
“Klara and the Sun” is set to hit theaters via Sony Pictures on Oct. 23.

The Ministry Of Communications' Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed telecom operators to roll out calling name presentations (CNAP) across their service areas from November 1, 2026. This will allow users to see the caller’s name alongside their phone number without necessarily saving contact details beforehand. The rollout follows an amendment to the definition of calling line identification (CLI) under the unified licence agreement, which will also take effect on November 1. The revised definition includes the caller’s name as recorded in telecom operators’ subscriber databases. However, contacts saved will continue to remain unchanged. CNAP will be enabled by default on 4G and higher-generation wireless networks, without requiring users to opt in. Its rollout on 2G and 3G networks and landline connections will be examined separately. Callers who have activated the calling line identification restriction (CLIR) facility to hide their identity will be exempt from this. The originating telecom service provider (TSP) must maintain a database linking subscribers’ names to their telephone identifiers, which the recipient’s operator will query to display the caller’s name without retaining it after the call ends. DoT has also allowed business and bulk-connection users to display a preferred name instead of the one in their subscriber records, provided it is backed by a trademark registered with the Trade marks registry or a trade name registered on the goods and services tax (GST) portal. These users can also request changes, subject to verification Telecom operators, including the likes of Jio, Airtel, Vodafone, must verify the supporting documents before approving the change. The guidelines require telecom operators to protect users’ privacy by ensuring caller names are not stored after a call ends. They must also ensure their networks can handle caller identification requests without affecting service quality and set up systems to address complaints related to the service. The rollout follows trials conducted by telecom operators on 4G and higher-generation networks and the TRAI’s recommendations issued in February 2024. Last year in October, TRAI supported making CNAP available by default, departing from its earlier proposal to activate the service only upon user request.

Brazil investigates Amazon wildfires that disrupt daily life
Brazilian authorities are investigating whether a recent surge in Amazon wildfires was orchestrated
SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazilian authorities are investigating whether a recent surge in wildfires in the Amazon rainforest have been set on purpose for political motives ahead of the second round of presidential elections later this month.
Fire counts across the biome, which have been near historic lows this year, have tripled since Oct. 4, when Brazilians voted in the first round of national elections. Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, won 47% of the vote, while President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva received 45%. The two will face off in an Oct. 25 runoff.
“The indications are that there has been a premeditated effort” to start the fires, Environment Minister João Paulo Capobianco told The Associated Press.
Capobianco and environmental enforcement officials flew over burned areas on Sunday and again on Wednesday. He said they observed fires in protected forest areas arranged in a distinct geometric pattern, suggesting they may have been deliberately set.
It's not clear who might have started the fires or what their motivations may be. The wildfires have particularly hit Amazonas and Para states over the past few days. Smoke has disrupted daily life in Manaus, the capital of Amazonas and the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon. Public school classes were canceled and residents were urged to wear face masks.
Conservative politicians in Amazonas state have been the most vocal about the fires, according to monitoring by Barometro, a tool developed by Brazilian climate strategy agency FALA, part of the global Climate Action Against Disinformation coalition.
The analysis examined 165 posts about fires and smoke in the state from 41 politicians, finding that nearly 55% came from the right. Over the weeks, personal publications gave way to political disputes, with local politicians claiming credit for firefighting efforts or accusing authorities of failing to act.
“The same issue serves simultaneously as a public health warning, an environmental policy agenda and a campaign tool,” the report said.
The fires have also become a point of contention outside the Amazon, in an election campaign in which forest protection and climate change have received little attention.
Deforestation in the Amazon soared under former President Bolsonaro, while Lula has brought it back down to the lowest in a decade. Flávio Bolsonaro has denied climate change but said he is an environmental defender, without offering details on protecting the Amazon or supporting forest financing. In speeches, he has called for modernizing environmental laws, which many environmentalists read as loosening them.
The Bolsonaros most popular allies — Nikolas Ferreira, a lawmaker from the state of Minas Gerais, and reelected Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcísio de Freitas, both from southeastern Brazil — cited wildfires last week to criticize Lula’s government. De Freitas said Lula’s Workers Party were hypocrites and “disappeared” while the Amazon burned.
Lula did not address the criticism but said in a video posted Saturday on X that he had spoken with Amazonas Gov. Roberto Cidade and that the federal government was sending resources to support firefighting efforts.
“The people of Amazonas can count on the federal government. We are together in this fight to protect lives, preserve the forest and support those facing this emergency,” the president said.
Susana Braz, a 35-year-old biologist in Manaus who studies how toxic ash from Amazon wildfires affects the region’s rivers, said she could not sleep in her own bed because her smoke-filled bedroom felt like a barbecue grill.
“We come home, and the house is full of smoke,” Braz said. “We go outside, and there’s smoke everywhere.”
People have tried to carry on as usual, but worsening smoke over the past 10 days has fueled frustration. “Are we really going to accept this smoke as normal, as if everything is fine and we just have to live with it?” she added.
The Amazon stores vast amounts of carbon and releases moisture that regulates weather far beyond South America. But climate change and deforestation are making it hotter, drier and more flammable. El Niño, a recurring climate pattern, can worsen heat and drought.
“Nearly all ignitions in the region are caused by human activity, mainly to renew pastures or clear land,” said Ane Alencar, science director at Brazil’s nonprofit Amazon Environmental Research Institute. “During very dry periods, those fires can escape.”
Fire counts were expected to increase at this time of year with a developing El Niño, but the timing around elections is still notable, Alencar said.
“Over the past 10 days, we’ve seen fire hot spots nearly triple compared with the 10 days before the election, mainly around Manaus,” she said. “Something happened that led people to burn more.”
João Morita, a coordinator at ICMBio, the federal agency that manages Brazil’s protected areas, has been on the front lines fighting fires in conservation areas in the Amazon. He said several factors could explain last week’s spike in the region, including residents of national forests burning crop plots, despite a ban.
“Fires start for all sorts of reasons. Some are retaliation for enforcement actions. Others are deliberately set with malicious intent. Any unauthorized burning is a crime, so there is a range of possibilities,” Morita said.
Officials and researchers have warned that El Niño’s effects on the Amazon could be worse in 2027 than this year.
In a statement to the AP, the Amazonas government said it met with federal officials over the weekend to discuss firefighting efforts and had declared a state of emergency in municipalities affected by wildfires.
“The measure takes into account worsening climate conditions caused by El Niño, with below-average rainfall and high temperatures forecast, which favor the outbreak and spread of fires,” the state government said.

The US Army is preparing for a future in which American military forces could face attacks on their own soil before deploying overseas, as drones, cyberattacks, long-range weapons and advanced surveillance technologies reshape the modern battlefield, Fox News Digital reported.
Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's acting chief of staff, said the US military could face significant challenges deploying forces against a major adversary, particularly China, if American bases, transportation networks and communications infrastructure come under attack.
"If we're going against a pacing threat, power projection will be contested," LaNeve told Fox News Digital on Wednesday.
Speaking at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, LaNeve said the military was reconsidering assumptions developed during decades of operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, when American forces could largely rely on secure bases and supply lines at home.
"During the Global War on Terror, we took a lot of things for granted, because we could," he said.
According to Fox News Digital, a potential conflict with China could expose vulnerabilities in the infrastructure needed to move American forces to the battlefield. Disruptions to military installations, transport networks and communications could delay deployments and complicate operations.
The Pentagon's latest report on China's military capabilities has warned that Beijing has positioned cyber capabilities inside US critical infrastructure networks that could potentially be used to disrupt American military mobilisation during a conflict.
The concerns come as the Pentagon increases its focus on homeland defence and the protection of military installations.
The Army's How the Army Fights operational framework is intended to establish clearer priorities for training, combat operations and the integration of new technology. It emphasises preparing forces to deploy and sustain operations even when communications, supply lines and military infrastructure are disrupted.
LaNeve said the framework would provide direction for the Army's future development.
"It was important to get this document out to provide a direction for our Army, a stake in the ground in where we're moving," he told Fox News Digital.
The Army is additionally incorporating biological incidents into routine combat training to prepare troops for disease outbreaks or deliberate biological attacks that could disrupt military operations.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink separately warned that advances in surveillance technology could make it increasingly difficult for military forces to avoid detection.
"We are rapidly heading to a point in time where, depending on what your signature is, how fast you're moving, the enemy is going to have some sense to where you are no matter where you are on the planet," Meink said.
He suggested that such capabilities could emerge within five years, possibly sooner, as China and other adversaries improve their ability to track military assets.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth criticised the Pentagon's handling of emerging military technologies under the previous administration, arguing that the US had failed to keep pace in several areas.
“On hypersonics, they took a nap. On space, they took a nap. On weaponization of space, they took a nap. On drones, they took a nap,” Hegseth said.
LaNeve, however, stressed that technological advances would not eliminate the need for soldiers to maintain fundamental combat skills.
“Soldiers are our number one platform. It is the Army's platform,” he told Fox News Digital.
The technology is intended to make troops more capable, he said, but soldiers must remain able to carry out their missions when advanced systems are unavailable.

Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.
TIRED
Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.
Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.
Exquisite Materials
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs
Wireless connectivity
Bluetooth 6.1 with Multipoint, Auracast
Wired connectivity
USB-C (supports lossless up to 24 bit/192 kHz), 3.5-mm aux (supports lossless up to 24 bit/96 kHz)
Battery life
Up to 30 hours (ANC on), up to 68 hours (ANC off)
Weight
327 grams
Codec
LDAC, LC3, SBC, AAC
Water/dust resistance
IP52
Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.
The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).
The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.
All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).
Mixing It Up
Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.
Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.
I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.
I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).
This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.
That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.
First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.
Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.
Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.
Playing in the Big Leagues
The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.
I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.
