Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

America's historic preservation law is in peril, advocates say. Here's what's at stake
It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills.
"We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966.
Now, historic preservation advocates say, the government is trying to yank the public's power away.
"Preservation, from its inception, has worked best with public and private partnership," Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, told NPR. "Over the last year and a half, the federal government has divested that responsibility."
It's a far cry from 1966, when the NHPA created a mechanism for identifying and protecting the country's historic sites — ranging from a single tree to an entire district.
Because of that law, those landmarks — today, more than 100,000 of them — are listed on the official National Register of Historic Places. And federal agencies must consult with states, tribes and stakeholders before beginning any projects that could potentially harm them, through a process called Section 106 review.
"Section 106 is in many ways the teeth behind the National Historic Preservation Act," said Elihu Rubin, a professor of architecture and urban studies at the Yale School of Architecture. "It is Section 106 that insists … that federal projects that threaten historic resources can only proceed when efforts are made to mitigate the impacts on those resources."
Section 106 has saved historic buildings from demolition and prevented development on archaeological sites, according to "success stories" recently compiled by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. But, Rubin stresses, the review process doesn't necessarily stop projects from happening — and that's the point of participating in it.
"Some of the most interesting projects that come out of it are surveys of fascinating buildings or places that will be lost," he said. "But we gain a lot from that process."
That process is now facing dual threats. A federal council packed with Trump appointees voted this summer to weaken Section 106 regulations, while a bipartisan permitting reform bill gaining traction in the Senate would significantly narrow the review process in order to speed up infrastructure and energy projects.
"It will effectively rewrite the National Historic Preservation Act in ways that, for all intents and purposes, gut its meaning and protections for hundreds of thousands of sites across the country," said Greg Werkheiser, whose law firm, Cultural Heritage Partners, is leading a coalition to protect Section 106.
"Section 106 Strong," which officially launched Thursday, says it spans 1,000 organizations — including religious, environmental and civil rights groups — and Tribal Nations collectively representing more than 9 million Americans.
"I've been involved in historic preservation and politics for 30 years, and I've rarely seen a movement come together this quickly," he told NPR. "I think Americans are simply fed up with watching their history manipulated, defaced, or destroyed as an instrument of political power."
Historic preservation law was a reaction to widespread destruction
During the Great Depression, the federal government hired workers to survey historic buildings across the U.S. They documented 12,000. But by 1965, when Johnson convened a committee to study the issue, half of those buildings had been either destroyed or damaged beyond repair.
"Folks concluded that if … we don't have some strong federal provisions, the natural instinct to just build as fast as you can, wherever you can, is going to take over," Werkheiser said.
The push for historic preservation was borne out of public backlash to post-World War II urban renewal and highway construction, which displaced entire communities and destroyed many American landmarks — including New York City's original Penn Station.
"Because so much of the funding and impetus from these projects were coming from federal housing policy, there was an idea here that there needed to be a framework put in place to identify historic resources and to — if not protect them entirely — at least to acknowledge them and then to mitigate the negative impacts," Rubin explains.
The 1966 law provided that framework. Among other provisions, it tasked every state with opening its own office to administer national preservation programs.
Native American tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations weren't included in those duties until 1992, one of the last major amendments to the law. Leaders of the Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (NATHPO) told NPR that tribal communities now risk losing the seat at the table that it took them so long to get.
"The changes that are being proposed now — both on the regulatory front and the statutory front — would represent an enormous and devastating setback not just to pre-1992, but to pre-1966 historical preservation and the state of tribal voice and perspectives being considered," said Valerie Grussing, NATHPO's executive director of legislative affairs and strategic partnerships.
Historic preservation experts maintain that Section 106 gives experts and the public visibility into federal construction projects without significantly slowing them down. In fact, the National Trust for Historic Preservation says the nationwide average for a review is 16 days, and that 98% of those reviews conclude that the project will have no adverse effect on nearby historic resources.
"At the end of the day, it's [about] whether or not the federal government can come into your backyard and to your community and do whatever they want," said Chris Cody, associate general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
These days, Cody estimates that his two-person team spends about 70 hours a week answering calls for help from local jurisdictions while also fighting federal cases in Washington, D.C. For example, the National Trust sued the Trump administration over the construction of its White House ballroom, but lost after the Supreme Court ruled the nonprofit lacked legal standing.
That's one of many of President Trump's controversial renovations — including his proposed arch and municipal golf course redevelopment — that critics say are bulldozing over historic preservation laws and norms. It's against this backdrop that the National Trust for Historic Preservation recently launched a defense fund, aiming to raise an initial $10 million to protect the places and laws now in the crosshairs.
Cody calls this a "moment of existential crisis" for preservation efforts nationwide, not just in D.C.
"There is somewhat of a trickle-down effect happening around the country, as various, I would call them, bad actors are trying to push the limits of the law in regards to historic preservation," Cody said. "It just seems to be a moment in time where everyone … who does not care about preservation or has it sublimated to other goals is trying to push the envelope."
Leggs, who leads the National Trust, said "every American should be concerned" about this trend, not only because it could spell trouble for a church or cemetery of personal significance, but because of the "wisdom, lessons, education and inspiration that is imbued in historic places" — and could be lost — to future generations.
Advocates fighting a double-headed threat look to November
The 1966 law also created the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency tasked with advising Congress and the president on such matters. Twenty of its 24 current members were appointed by Trump.
In July, the council voted to weaken Section 106 regulations in a few notable ways. It would limit what kinds of properties can be considered historic in the first place, excluding "significant landscape features" like the Grand Canyon. The change would also make public comment on new projects optional and remove the requirement to consult with Native American tribes.
Those changes are still going through the federal rulemaking process, which includes a 30-day public comment period that has not yet opened. The council next meets on Nov. 10. In the meantime, another threat to Section 106 has emerged in Congress — one that historic preservation advocates say is even more serious.
"[The regulatory changes have] been the biggest five-alarm fire for our membership and our constituency in our mission … in decades," said Grussing, of NATHPO. "And now with the proposed statutory changes, I would say it's turned into more of a wildfire."
In late September, a bipartisan group of senators introduced a bill they say will "reform the federal environmental review and permitting process" to "deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth" across the U.S. One of its provisions would streamline Section 106 in similar ways — curtailing public and tribal input, narrowing the scope of analysis and restricting legal remedies for violations.
The Senate says it plans to consider the bill when it returns from recess on Nov. 9.
These changes would be enshrined in the law, as opposed to regulations that could more easily be reversed in the future, says NATHPO Executive Director Ira Matt, a citizen of the Salish Tribe.
"A lot of the preservation community's looking at this, saying: 'We do not want to be party to these changes that are going to outlive most of our careers. We do not want to saddle the next generation with … the failures that are coming out of this permitting reform,'" Matt said.
Matt says it is "unfortunate" to see senators join forces on a bill that would restrict tribal sovereignty, particularly since its Democratic sponsors have otherwise been strong allies in tribal and historic preservation issues.
Last week, NATHPO and other tribal groups sent a letter to Senate leaders urging them to drop this provision from the proposed bill and consult with tribes about a better approach.
"Instead of bringing this permitting reform [bill], bring the promise that you'll do something next year — informed by committees, developed through consultation and in conjunction with the preservation community — where we can bring in facts, we can bring in requests, we can bring in experience to actually build something sustainable," Matt said.
Critics of the Senate bill say it actually introduces more questions and confusion about the Section 106 process. For example, it doesn't define specific terms (like what constitutes a "minor" restoration or "required metrics" for state and tribal officials to meet).
Both Matt and Werkheiser told NPR that when they asked Senate staff about this during recent lobbying meetings, they were told that Democrats and Republicans couldn't agree on definitions and expected those questions to end up in court.
"The thing that they keep saying about the bill is it's going to create efficiency and keep these controversies out of the court," Werkheiser said. "And then, on the other hand, they're like, 'Well, we haven't really done any of the work of deciding what any of this means. And so the court's going to have to sort it out.'"
Werkheiser says the bill wouldn't create efficiency by streamlining Section 106 — it would actually create "a much greater chance of controversy, objection and litigation further down the process" by excluding public and expert consultation at the start. That's one of many reasons he hopes more people will join the fight to protect historic preservation law in the weeks and months ahead.
"You can disagree about politics. You can disagree about the future," he said. "But you shouldn't have to fight your own government for the right to remember your past."

- Snopes found no evidence new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was a lawyer in the U.S. or in China.
- The rumor stems from Zacharia herself, who, asked Oct. 13 about where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), responded "when I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
- Snopes reviewed lawyer directories from the bar association and supreme courts of all 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., and found no evidence she had passed the bar examination in any of them.
- A review of Chinese rules suggested she could not have passed China's equivalent of the bar exam as a U.S. national, or practiced as a lawyer, even by the current requirements, which are looser than they used to be.
- A spokesperson for Pepperdine University confirmed in an email to Snopes that Zacharia graduated with a Juris Doctor degree in 2011.
- John Ohnesorge, an expert in Chinese law from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Snopes in an email "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the White House for more details and are waiting for a response.
In October, social media posts questioned new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia's claim that she passed the bar examination in China.
The posts emerged after several reports asked whether Zacharia had the credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., though she has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer in the past, including in an archived version of her X profile and during a television interview.
When asked Oct. 13 where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), Zacharia responded, "When I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
People on Facebook and Reddit expressed doubts, while Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, wrote on X, "Are Katie Zacharia and trump lying when they say she is an attorney?" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed and searched the website, asking us to examine whether Zacharia could have possibly passed the bar in China.
An extensive search turned up no evidence Zacharia was a member of any state bar in the U.S., nor in Washington, D.C. In addition, current Chinese law made it unlikely that she was ever in a position to pass China's examination to practice law, as she is not a Chinese national. There was no evidence that she could do when she lived there between 2011 and 2013, though China only formalized rules about foreign lawyers in 2017.
For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Katie Zacharia told Snopes in an emailed statement. Neither she nor the White House press office answered follow-up questions, nor did they share any documentation showing she could practice law as an attorney in good standing in any jurisdiction.
"Katie graduated with a JD [Juris Doctor, a law degree] from Caruso School of Law in 2011, and with a bachelor of arts in political science from Seaver College in 2007," a spokesperson for Pepperdine University wrote in an email to Snopes.
Asked whether Zacharia could have taken and passed China's law examination before 2017, John Ohnesorge, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who researched Chinese regulations of lawyers, said in an email to Snopes, "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever." 
"What she did in China was to work in an elite Chinese law firm on international business matters, and doing that kind of work does not really require being a member of a bar anywhere," he added.
We also searched lawyer directories across the U.S. and found no record of Katie Zacharia — also searching by her maiden name, Black — in any of them.
Zacharia's resumé and Chinese rules
Zacharia's LinkedIn profile indicates she worked in China between 2011 and 2013, at Zhong Lun Law Firm.
In 2020, the Chinese Justice Observer — a consulting platform and analysis outlet about the Chinese legal system — said foreigners cannot practice law in China. In 2019, China established a pilot program to allow foreign lawyers to act as legal consultants in China, not lawyers, though one condition is that the person should have practiced as a lawyer in their home country for at least two years.
Even under this program, Zacharia could not have practiced as a legal consultant as she had not practiced law in the U.S. long enough after she graduated.
Zacharia's LinkedIn indicates she later worked as "general counsel" for Fix California, a conservative organization that aims at ensuring "election integrity." It is unclear how she could hold this position without having passed the state's bar examination. We reached out to Fix California asking for more details.
A sheet of advice for French lawyers seeking to work in China from 2017 confirms that only Chinese nationals can practice law in China. In other words, any foreign lawyer practicing in China can do so only with credentials from the countries where they obtained their degrees.
However, China's current rules were implemented in 2017. Ohnesorge, who wrote a research paper in 2023 about the history of the regulation of lawyers in China, said this measure was most likely protectionistic. 
"It's true that the 2017 regulation started requiring two years of practice in a home jurisdiction in order to qualify as a foreign legal consultant, but that's best understood as a protectionist measure used to keep Chinese firms from hiring too many foreign lawyers, not a requirement that actually makes any sense," Ohnesorge said via email. "People doing the work she did aren't really practicing the law of their home jurisdiction anyway, so why require that at all?"
For further reading, Snopes covered several rumors about Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, including the claim that she said the war in Iran would be over if President Donald Trump had "better intelligence."

Menopause may not be a gradual process taking years as is commonly thought -- instead, the female body could be traversing a "physiological cliff" around the time of the last menstrual period, a new study has found.
Analysing more than 300 million laboratory test results from over one million women in the US and Israel, researchers at Weizmann Institute of Science identified abrupt changes in dozens of measures of bodily health and function, far beyond the familiar shifts in sex hormone levels and the loss of fertility.
Findings published in the Nature Medicine journal showed that the changes appeared in 52 of the 90 types of laboratory tests examined, covering nearly all body systems, including tests of bone health, liver and kidney function, and cholesterol levels.
The changes were found to be less pronounced among women receiving menopausal hormone therapy.
Further, the sudden shifts were preceded by accelerating changes in sex hormone levels that began more than a decade before menopause -- several years earlier than previously thought.
None of the abrupt changes were observed in men of similar ages, the study found.
It "revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP (final menstrual period) including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems," the authors wrote.
Because most of the abrupt changes identified in the study are associated with increased disease risk, the findings could help women take preventive steps, such as exercising and improving their diet, years before menopause, the researchers said.
"Our study extends the window for potential preventive care to almost a decade before menopause. More broadly, the method we developed may help study other major changes in life, such as puberty, pregnancy or the onset of disease," author Uri Alon, from Weizmann Institute of Science, said.
Two sets of data were analysed -- results from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted over more than two decades, and medical records collected over around 20 years by Israel's health insurer Clalit.
The researchers said that such large datasets are rarely used in menopause research because they generally lack information about the age at which women had their last period.
To overcome the limitation, the team developed a computational method which they said is inspired by astronomy.
Just as astronomers can sharpen an image by mathematically correcting distortions caused by a telescope, the new method removed the 'blur' in medical data caused by differences in the age at which women reach menopause, the researchers said.

Trump is taking his midterms anger out on Ukraine
The Ukraine-Trump-SpaceX debacle, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: Is Trump turning on Ukraine?
What’s happening? Ukraine says its access to Starlink, the satellite internet system run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, and Starshield, the military version of the same technology, is being throttled as President Donald Trump’s animosity toward the country mounts.
Why is Trump angry with Ukraine? Trump has been hot and cold on Ukraine since he returned to office, but his current anger is driven by oil prices and successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — particularly ahead of the US midterm elections.
Last week, Trump announced a US-Russia diesel deal, which has elicited bipartisan anger and probably won’t do much, if anything, for diesel prices in the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticized the deal, leading Trump to lash out and call for Zelenskyy’s replacement.
Over the weekend, Trump also announced an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” between Ukraine and Russia that doesn’t really seem to exist. “Both parties have agreed,” he wrote. “Do not break it!” (Russia appears to have broken it the same day, while Ukraine is complying for now.)
Is Ukraine actually to blame for high oil prices? Partially, but not primarily; as the BBC explains, while Ukrainian refinery strikes play a role, ongoing disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf oil industry from Trump’s war with Iran have had a greater impact (though Trump has tried to shift the blame to Ukraine).
Why is Starlink so important? Starlink and Starshield provide vital communications infrastructure in Ukraine, especially on the battlefield. The technology is also used to control offensive and defensive Ukrainian drones, which have emerged as a key part of Ukraine’s military efforts against Russia.
What’s next? Despite the fact that neither Russia nor Ukraine seemingly signed on to Trump’s “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” and Russia is still attacking Ukrainian energy facilities, Trump is trying to bind Ukraine to it: The US has reportedly threatened to suspend US intelligence sharing, which has helped give Ukraine early warning of Russian missile attacks, if Ukraine strikes more Russian refineries.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

According to The Washington Post, Omar said that requests to change her birth year were due to it being incorrect, not to cover up the truth. We found evidence to support that she was 17 in the year 2000.
As U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., entered the final weeks of her reelection bid in October, federal agents searched her home in a criminal investigation reportedly related to claims that she or her father may have lied on immigration paperwork when she sought to secure legal status in the U.S. decades earlier.
In an Oct. 12 statement on X, Omar said called the search "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." It is unusual for a federal agency to publicly investigate someone running for office so close to Election Day.
Following the search, numerous social media posts claimed Omar was not a minor in 2000 — the year she reportedly became a U.S. citizen after her father naturalized — saying that official records indicated her birth year was originally listed as 1981 before it was later changed to 1982. Some of the posts said this indicated citizenship fraud.
We looked into the evidence and found that while her birth year was changed in official records, according to The Washington Post, she said this was to fix incorrect information rather than cover up the truth. We found other pieces of evidence indicating she could've indeed been a minor in 2000, including her high school yearbook and reports by reputable news outlets in 2018.
Omar has long maintained that she was 17 when she became a citizen in 2000 — receiving citizenship by default, according to U.S. law, after her father was naturalized.
In 2018, two years after she first ran for public office, articles by The Associated Press and The New York Times reported she had become a U.S. citizen in 2000, when she was 17.
In addition to the 2018 news reports, we found a high school yearbook showing Omar was a junior in 2000 and that she was in the graduating class of 2001. While not definitive proof, it supports the claim that Omar was not yet an adult when her family applied for citizenship.
Omar attended Edison High School in Minneapolis. As a member of the class of 2001, she was listed under the "Juniors" section in the 2000 yearbook.
(Classmates.com / Snopes illustration)
Her family fled Somalia in the early 1990s during the country's civil war, eventually arriving in the U.S. in 1995 before applying for citizenship five years later.
Archived versions of her profile in official records, such as the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, show that at one time, Omar's birth year was listed as 1981 — which would have made it unlikely for her to be a minor in 2000.
The circulated posts above took screenshots of an archived version of that website along with the current version (archived), noting that her birth year was changed from 1981 to 1982.
A note on the current version of her profile read:
Her birth year is correct. It is incorrectly reported as 1981 in other sources. As of May 24, 2019, Rep. Omar's congressional staff are working with Wikipedia and the U.S. House to correct her birth year in those sources.
In a emailed statement to Snopes, David Schmidtke, deputy director of the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, confirmed that "congressional staff contacted the library regarding her birthdate."
"However, we do not have supporting documentation, as the information was 'self-reported,'" he wrote. "The library does not independently verify birthdates before publishing or updating them."
We contacted Omar's office seeking comment on the speculation surrounding her birth year and have not yet received a response. We will update this story if we do.

SC to issue orders on preventive steps taken by Centre to curb online child sexual abuse content
SC agreed to issue orders on preventive steps to be taken by the Centre and other stakeholders against child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) online
The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to issue orders on preventive steps to be taken by the Centre and other stakeholders against child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) online, citing the seriousness of the matter.
The order was passed after the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) submitted a draft Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to the court. “As part of the future preventive action required to be taken with respect to dissemination of CSEAM content, MeitY has drafted an SOP for the intermediaries for prevention, direction, removal and reporting of CSEAM content to a government portal (Sahyog),” the ministry said.
The SOP has been prepared in consultation with the ministry of women and child development (MoWCD) and other stakeholders, besides the ministry of home affairs (MHA) and department of telecommunications (DoT), the affidavit said.
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta appearing for Centre said, “We are serious about this matter. There were discussions that took place based on which we have given our suggestions on how to tackle this problem. We require some more time to finalise the SOP.”
The bench said, “This is a very serious matter. We want the Union government to take it seriously. We will pass an order. You study our order. We will suggest you some things that will be helpful for you.”
The court posted the matter after a month to allow the Centre come up with further developments on preventing CSEAM online.
The Centre’s affidavit gave examples of how in an instance, MeitY issued notice in July 2026 to the Meta’s compliance officer regarding dissemination of paid advertisements promoting CSEAM. The proceedings are still underway. Meity said it has been regularly communicating and coordinating with various stakeholders, including the intermediaries, regarding the need for enhanced monitoring, reporting and removal of CSEAM content.
As part of these efforts, Centre pointed out that in February this year, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 were amended to incorporate specific due diligence obligations for preventing and reporting CSEAM content on their platforms.
The Centre was responding to an order passed by the court last month in a petition filed by Just Rights for Children Alliance (JRCA). The petitioner sought compliance of a 2024 judgment and a uniform SOP to be framed to ensure timely reporting by intermediaries.
The judgment passed on September 23, 2024 held that social media intermediaries have a duty to report cases of child abuse and exploitation to the local authorities under Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act.
The verdict held, “In view of the salutary object and the mandatory character of the provisions of Sections 19 and 20 of the Pocso read with Rule 11 of the Pocso Rules, we are of the considered view, that an intermediary cannot claim exemption from the liability under Section 79 of the IT Act for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, unless due diligence is conducted by it and compliance is made of these provisions of the Pocso.”
It further stated that the compliance required includes not just removal of child pornographic content but an immediate report of such content to the concerned police.
The JRCA application said that Instagram carried paid advertisements promoting CSEAM, raising concerns over compliance of the top court’s judgment. The petitioner sought a comprehensive mechanism to ensure effective implementation of obligations of social media platforms and prevent the online circulation and exploitation of children. It sought a uniform SOP for intermediaries covering detection and mandatory reporting of CSEAM, preservation of evidence and inter-agency coordination among relevant agencies.
It further demanded prompt uploading of offenders’ particulars to the National Database of Sexual Offenders (NDSO), timely action by law-enforcement agencies on every report received from an intermediary, and initiation of criminal proceedings against intermediaries that fail to comply with mandatory reporting obligations, in accordance with law.
The petitioner even sought the establishment of a centralised online reporting portal to facilitate reporting of CSEAM by intermediaries.

US president Donald Trump said Washington was holding talks with Moscow and Beijing aimed at denuclearizing the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.

BookMyBai co-founder Anupam Sinhal has revealed the disturbing incident that prompted his company to stop providing domestic workers to Bollywood celebrities nearly a decade ago. In an interview with Hindustan Times, Sinhal recalled how a worker arrived at the company’s office with burn marks on her body after an incident involving an iron. “The Bollywood celebrity decision was taken the day a worker stepped into her office and she had burn marks on her body through the clothes iron because she accidentally burnt the clothes of that particular celebrity while she was ironing her clothes,” Sinhal said. The incident, he explained, became a turning point for the company. “That is when we thought enough is enough and now we are not doing this anymore,” he added. The account highlights the vulnerability of domestic workers, whose employment often takes place inside private homes, away from public scrutiny. Sinhal’s remarks also raise questions about the safeguards available to workers when they face mistreatment at work. Asked whether the restriction remained in force almost 10 years later, Sinhal offered a qualified answer, “Yes and no.” He said BookMyBai continues to refuse requests from celebrities who approach the platform directly. However, exceptions can be made when a trusted contact personally vouches for a prospective employer. “If a celebrity contacts us directly that she needs a domestic helper, we flat outrightly refuse that we will not be able to provide you with the service because we have a blanket ban on this,” he said. Sinhal cited Soni Razdan, actor Alia Bhatt’s mother, as an example of someone whose recommendation could lead the company to accept a request. He clarified that Razdan, rather than Bhatt herself, contacts the company in such cases. The distinction, according to Sinhal, is between an unsolicited request and one supported by a trusted reference. Despite the restrictions, Sinhal said some celebrities treat their domestic staff with consideration and generosity. He named Alia Bhatt and Dia Mirza among those who, according to him, have shown respect towards their workers. He also mentioned filmmaker Farah Khan, casting director Shanoo Sharma, cricketer Rohit Sharma, Sherlyn Chopra and actor Tina Datta. Sinhal recalled that Bhatt had given ₹50 lakh to a cook placed through the company, asking him to use the money to buy a house. He said the worker subsequently purchased a home in Virar. “There are very, very good employers who are there in the celebrities also, but they are a handful,” he said. Sinhal also described less severe but concerning situations involving wealthy employers, including domestic workers being expected to remain awake until 4 am during parties, even when they did not wish to do so. Sinhal said employer behaviour had improved considerably since the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent lockdowns. When part-time workers could not travel to employers’ homes, families had to manage household responsibilities themselves. That experience, he suggested, helped employers recognise how much they relied on domestic workers. He also pointed to a change in language, saying workers were increasingly described as “domestic workers” rather than “servants”. For Sinhal, the shift reflected a broader change in how their role was perceived. While he said major incidents had become less frequent among the households served by his company, his account underlines the importance of treating domestic work as employment that demands dignity, clear safeguards and accountability. Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds
- Published
BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.
Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.
BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.
Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.
Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.
For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.
A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.
How does the IDF investigate incidents?
The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.
A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.
In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.
In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.
The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", external, had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.
These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.
Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.
In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".
It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".
The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.
Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.
Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.
Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own".
"That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."
Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments.
"[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.
Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.
He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".
Gaza
Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.
BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.
Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.
A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.
BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".
In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".
Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.
Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."
It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."
Deadly attack on school building
One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.
The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque.
The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around.
Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military.
The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review.
West Bank
BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law.
More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, external. BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured.
One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation.
Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house.
The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.
Lebanon
BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon.
The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities.
One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children, near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry.
Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review.
Long running investigations
Michael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation".
Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential."
Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC), said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded."
She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate".
"If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added.
Methodology
BBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026.
We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined".
This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above.
This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents.
We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed.
We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents.
For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report.
We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests.
For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken.
For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website.
This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website.
This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search.
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

In a major executive shakeup, Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix after 10 years at the streamer, most recently serving as its chief content officer.
She will be replaced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice, as first reported by Puck. As chief content officer, Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions.
Bajaria’s exit comes amid a significant workforce reduction at Netflix. Around 1,000 employees (6% of the company) were laid off this week in what marks the company’s largest axing to date. Netflix‘s film VP Doug Belgrad and film director Sheroum Kim were also pink slipped as part of the restructuring.
Popular on Variety
“I want to thank Bela for a decade of dedication, innovation, creativity and leadership,” Sarandos, Netflix’s co-CEO, said in a statement. “She led enormous changes at Netflix. She helped broaden our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports, in addition to crafting and running a world class, global slate of films and series. I’m incredibly grateful for everything she’s done to help Netflix entertain the world.”
Bajaria joined Netflix in 2016 after she was let go from NBCUniversal, where she was president of Universal Television. In that role, she had produced shows that aired on Netflix, including “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” and “Master of None.” Sarandos first brought in Bajaria to help Netflix launch an unscripted division, as well as licensing and studio co-productions. Bajaria was later elevated to head of global in 2020 as Cindy Holland exited the company, and named chief content officer in January 2023.
Under her watch, Bajaria oversaw popular TV series including “Bridgerton,” “Squid Game,” “Adolescence,” “Beef,” “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” as well as films like “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Frankenstein.” She also pushed Netflix into more live sports and events like “The Roast of Tom Brady” and deals with the NFL and WWE.
But in recent months, as Netflix growth has slowed, so too has the aura around its original programming. The streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy awards this year — down from 30 in 2025 and quite a distance from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44. All told, 2026 was Netflix’s lowest Primetime Emmy haul since 2016.
Rice’s own ousting at Disney in 2022, by then-CEO Bob Chapek, was a huge shock to the industry given his stature at the company. A well-regarded executive, Rice was most recently chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the Walt Disney Company. There he oversaw ABC, FOX Broadcasting, Fox Sports, ABC News, ABC Studios, Disney Channel, Freeform, FX Networks, Hulu, National Geographic, Onyx Collective, Disney Television and Twentieth Century Fox Television, with more than 300 shows and 4,000 hours of television a year. Programs during his tenure included “The Simpsons,” “American Idol,” “Modern Family,” “This Is Us,” “The Bear,” “Abbott Elementary,” “Shogun” and “Only Murders in the Building,” along with ABC News programming and sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals.
Since he was let go from Disney, Rice worked as a producer on movies such as Jason Reitman’s “Saturday Night,” “28 Years Later” and “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” at Sony, as well as “Warfare” and Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” at A24. He is currently producing Alex Garland’s “Elden Ring” and Sonoya Mizuno’s “Stages,” as well as as well as the opening and closing ceremonies for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Earlier in his career, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group, and Fox’s lead executive on the Hulu board. He also worked at Fox Searchlight Pictures and worked on indie favorites like “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Juno,” “Little Miss Sunshine” and “Sideways.”
“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad,” Sarandos said. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives. I’m excited to welcome him to Netflix as chief content officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love.”
“Netflix has fundamentally changed the way stories are made, shared and experienced around the world,” Rice said. “They’ve shown again and again that they’re willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I’m excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere.”
Mike Schneider contributed to this report.
More to come…

Microsoft President and Vice Chair Brad Smith has warned that the Trump administration's move to restrict green-card access for skilled foreign workers could weaken the US technology sector and push talent towards other countries, Politico reported.
In an interview with Politico's Decoded, Smith said blocking pathways to permanent residency for highly skilled immigrants could cripple the US technology industry for more than a generation. His remarks came less than a week after US Vice President JD Vance announced that the administration would bar Microsoft and seven other companies from seeking green cards for skilled foreign workers.
Smith also rejected Vance's allegations that Microsoft had abused the H-1B visa programme to avoid hiring American workers at higher salaries, describing the claims as "completely off base".
He said the US should be concerned about sending signals that could encourage talented artificial intelligence and software engineers to pursue opportunities in other countries rather than remain in the US.
Smith also argued that Microsoft's green-card applications largely concerned long-serving employees rather than new hires, attributing the situation to a lengthy backlog in processing applications. He said someone had failed to provide Vance with accurate information about the company's figures.
Microsoft defends hiring and pay practices
Smith denied that Microsoft paid foreign-born employees less than American workers. According to Politico, he said the company follows the same compensation system for all employees, irrespective of their immigration status.
He also pointed to Microsoft's domestic hiring, saying the company employed more than 9,000 US-born workers last year. Smith argued that this contribution had been overlooked in the administration's criticism of its use of skilled-worker visas.
The Microsoft executive called on the White House to reassess its position in light of what he described as a more accurate account of the company's hiring practices.
What is PERM programme
The Donald Trump-led US administration on October 8 suspended the PERM programme for certain IT companies including Microsoft, TCS, Infosys, Wipro and Cognizant among others.
The suspension bars the affected companies from submitting new PERM applications and stops the processing of pending applications, according to reports.
The Permanent Labour Certification programme, known as PERM, is a process run by the US Department of Labor that allows companies to sponsor foreign employees for US green cards, which grant permanent residency.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s plan to deport a member of Congress
The investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar just became more alarming.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump wants to deport a member of Congress.
What’s happening? On Monday, Homeland Security officers raided the Washington, DC, home of US Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) in an investigation reportedly tied to immigration paperwork filled out by her father when she was a minor.
That was, at the time, more than enough cause for alarm. Trump’s animosity toward Omar, who is Somali-American and an outspoken critic of the administration, is well-known, and the raid is an extraordinary violation of the Justice Department’s usual rule to avoid taking visible action around politically sensitive cases within 60 days of an election.
On Wednesday evening, however, we learned more about the raid from the Wall Street Journal. The Omar investigation, the Journal reported, is explicitly aimed at stripping Omar of her citizenship — and thus her ability to hold office — and deporting her.
How would they do that? Omar came to the US as a refugee when she was 12 and became a US citizen when she was 17. The Trump administration’s investigation is said to focus on whether she or her family misrecorded her age in order to more easily gain citizenship.
The government cannot unilaterally denaturalize a citizen, however; it would have to ask a court to do so.
What’s the context? Historically, it’s rare for the US to strip citizenship from naturalized US citizens. But doing so at volume has been a major, if less visible, priority for the second Trump administration.
As of earlier this year, NBC News reported, DOJ was targeting hundreds of people for possible denaturalization, and has reportedly hoped to put forward hundreds of new cases per month (though successfully stripping them of citizenship is another matter).
Why does this matter? Trump’s campaign to bend the traditionally nonpartisan DOJ into a tool to punish and harass his enemies has been one of the major stories of his second term.
Even if it never advances beyond Monday’s raid, an investigation targeting Omar’s citizenship with the eventual goal of deporting her from the US represents a new and even more dangerous evolution of that effort — and it threatens to move the US to a far darker place, where citizenship and the rights it guarantees are predicated on the president’s goodwill.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
