The CEO of Compass Pathways said Wednesday that the company, which is preparing to complete the submission of its psychedelic therapy for regulatory review this quarter, will “go slow before we go fast,” warning that negative patient or provider experiences early in the launch could damage the broader sector.
As the psychedelics field races toward its first potential approval by the Food and Drug Administration, the executive, Kabir Nath, underscored that a cautious rollout would be essential. But he also said the mental health field was on the brink of a major change.
“I think this is a really big deal for patients, for providers, and incidentally for Compass Pathways as well,” Nath said, speaking in Boston at the STAT Summit.
Compass is preparing to complete a rolling FDA submission this quarter for COMP360, its synthetic psilocybin treatment for treatment-resistant depression, with aims to launch early next year.
Nath said the company expects its treatment, if approved, to be subject to an FDA risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, or REMS, and is investing in training for providers who would administer the drug.
Unlike conventional antidepressants, which can take weeks to work and require daily dosing, psilocybin has shown the potential to produce rapid and lasting improvements after just a handful of administrations, Nath said.
In Compass’s Phase 3 trials, roughly a quarter of patients experienced a clinically meaningful response after a single administration of COMP360, which involves a roughly six-hour supervised session. That figure rose to about 40% after a second dose three weeks later. Nath said the company’s longer-term data suggest that patients who respond to treatment can experience benefits lasting as long as a year after two or three administrations.
But Steven Hyman, a Harvard University professor and former director of the National Institute of Mental Health, cautioned that significant scientific questions remain about psychedelic treatments, including how to establish their efficacy in clinical trials.
One challenge is that patients who receive a psychedelic drug often know they have received it because of its distinctive effects, potentially compromising the blinding of trials. This was one concern when an MDMA-based therapy from Lykos Therapeutics was rejected by the FDA in 2024.
“The unblinding remains a challenging problem,” Hyman said.
He raised another fundamental question: whether the psychedelic experience itself is necessary for the drugs to work.
Some companies are developing compounds designed to produce antidepressant effects without hallucinations or other intense subjective experiences. If successful, such treatments could potentially be prescribed for patients to take at home, eliminating the need for lengthy supervised sessions.
“It would be nontrivial if you could separate these, because then somebody could write a prescription and send somebody home,” Hyman said. “But we don’t know.”
That question also has implications for psychotherapy, which has traditionally been considered an important component of psychedelic treatment.
Nath said Compass deliberately separated psychotherapy from its clinical trials, arguing that the company’s responsibility is to develop a drug rather than dictate how physicians provide psychological care. He noted that an analysis of recorded treatment sessions found that roughly 80% of the time was spent in silence.
Hyman said psychotherapy following a psychedelic experience could nevertheless help patients process powerful emotions, memories, and other psychological effects. But he emphasized that researchers have yet to determine how much of the clinical benefit comes from the drug’s pharmacological effects and how much from the experience itself.
The discussion also touched on the risks of moving too quickly to bring psychedelic treatments to market – particularly since officials in the Trump administration have expressed support for accelerating their development.
Hyman said the field’s credibility would depend on rigorous research, responsible marketing, and long-term safety monitoring.
“I don’t mean this as a pun,” Hyman said. “But being really sober about the way this research is presented — the only way to gain credibility is to be absolutely rigorous.”
He drew a comparison to cannabis, where early perceptions of safety did not anticipate all the risks associated with increasingly potent products.
Even if COMP360 wins approval, another major challenge will be ensuring that patients can afford and access the treatment.
Asked about potential pricing relative to Johnson & Johnson’s Spravato, an esketamine treatment for depression, Nath said Spravato provides a reference point but declined to commit to a specific pricing benchmark.
The treatment’s costs would extend beyond the drug itself, given the need for several hours of monitoring in a clinical setting. Nath said Compass has spent years working on reimbursement mechanisms for that monitoring and is engaging with commercial insurers and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to secure coverage.
For Hyman, the promise of psychedelics is clear, particularly given the limitations of existing depression treatments. But their emergence also underscores how much psychiatry still needs to learn about the biological underpinnings of depression and why patients respond differently to treatment.
“We’re awash in subjectivity still,” he said, pointing to the lack of objective biomarkers that could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit from a given drug.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.

The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Though movies about disruptive tech founders are nothing new, 2026 has been unusually stacked with features that take a much more critical look at how Silicon Valley is reshaping our reality. Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoningframes Mark Zuckerberg as a robotic villain whose ambitions are destabilizing society. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything paints a damning picture of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares for her ongoing stint in prison. After years of being widely celebrated as a visionary, you can see how the larger narrative around Elon Musk has shifted in projects like Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary. And while Luca Guadagnino’s Artificialis a dark comedy, it is also a character study that makes Sam Altman look like a manipulative sociopath.
The tech backlash is now in theaters
Between The Social Reckoning, You Can See Everything, Musk, and Artificial, filmmakers are taking Big Tech to task.
The tech backlash is now in theaters
Between The Social Reckoning, You Can See Everything, Musk, and Artificial, filmmakers are taking Big Tech to task.
Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.
Especially when you compare them to classics like The Social Network, the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but The Social Reckoning builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by whistleblower Frances Haugen, the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful executive who wields autocratic control over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.
What The Social Reckoning lacks in timeliness (The Wall Street Journal began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health and the relationship between Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s Musk documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.
Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling. X has blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the Musk ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.
Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is a longtime Donald Trump supporter and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year. Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.
Guadagnino’s Artificial — which was originally going to be released by Amazon — also faced unexpected marketing challenges this year. The streaming giant backed out of its deal to distribute the film this past June, just months after announcing that it was investing $50 billion in OpenAI. All of that made it seem very much like Amazon and other studios financially involved with AI companies might be cooling on the idea of releasing projects critical of the technology’s creators. Now that Artificial has begun screening and people have a sense of how it takes Altman to task, it’s easy to see why Amazon didn’t want to have its name attached. More than anything else, that decision may be what convinces people to see Artificial in theaters when it releases widely on December 25th, and OpenAI’s impending IPO could make the movie’s messages about Altman feel that much more relevant.
What sets Fielder’s You Can See Everything apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison, and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that she defrauded Theranos investors. Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.
That central tension turns You Can See Everything into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of her recent PR campaign, and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.
It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or seen in Hulu’s The Dropout. Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes You Can See Everything feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.
Even though some of these films have been box office flops, their existence reflects a larger cultural shift in how people are thinking about modern technology and the powers behind it. Hollywood has spent years poking fun at and mythologizing founders, and portions of the industry are finally beginning to take a more critical view. As we continue to deal with the fallout of things like Elon Musk’s tenure at DOGE and OpenAI’s quest to bake generative AI into every aspect of our lives, audiences’ appetites for movies like these could grow. And with all of these founders racing to monopolize the next tech frontier, the entertainment industry will probably have plenty of source material to draw from.

As the competitive AI race pushes tech workers into long hours, the head of OpenAI's new Dots product says AI gives people another option: work a whole lot less.
Alexander Embiricos, who leads OpenAI's enterprise product and helms the new Dots agent tool, told a crowd at TechCrunch's Disrupt conference on Thursday that AI's capabilities have created something of a fork in the road for workers. You can grind to meet the moment. Or you can use AI to kick your feet up a little.
"We basically have a lot more choice now," he said.
Embiricos made the comments after a reporter asked about when AI systems will actually deliver more free time. The reporter shared an anecdote where an OpenAI employee used a ChatGPT mobile feature to work in their car and on a plane — not exactly liberated by the new tech.
Embiricos said that the moment has already arrived where a worker can "outsource" tasks to AI and do less work. Then again, some people are so excited about AI's potential that they feel like it's an "interesting, ripe moment" to put in extra hours.
"I think that's why a lot of people are motivated to work very hard right now. That includes myself," he said. "But I think actually there is this choice, and there's totally this other setup where you could delegate a ton more things."
OpenAI is billing its Dots tool as a workplace assistant, always on and capable of proactively handing tasks and sorting to-dos. Embiricos uses his Dot often in Slack, he said, engaging on various threads.
His perspective illustrates how early companies are in their journey to adopt AI tools. Most companies have not yet automated their work tasks, and many workers are still debating how much to use the tools. Early AI adopters, meanwhile, can sprint through some work that used to take days or weeks, especially in software engineering.
Embiricos summed up the situation he feels workers are in: "You either choose: do you expand the ambition of what you can do, or do you do less? I do think we're there."

No, Rome was not built in a day, but it was built at breathtaking speed, its temples, amphitheaters, and aqueducts rising with the help of a magical blend of volcanic ash and lime. Today, that miraculous mortar has a less than enchanting name: concrete.
The surprisingly hopeful quest to fix concrete
Scientists are racing to reinvent concrete before we pour millions more tons of it.
“Romans lived through a true architectural revolution, and at the foundation of this revolution, literally, was a concrete discovery,” said Admir Masic, a materials science professor at MIT who made waves a few years ago for unearthing the fast-hardening secret sauce for why Roman concrete is so durable. “They were able to take a pile of dirt and mix it together, add water, and turn it into solid rock of any arbitrary size. It literally changed everything.”
And yet, for a millennia after the fall of Rome, the world largely forgot about concrete, until, in the 18th century, an English mason found that mixing limestone and clay could form a paste that hardened underwater. Another few decades later, concrete as we now know it was reborn, and once again, it changed everything.
In the centuries since, concrete has come to reshape our way of life, with disastrous results for the climate. What early concrete evangelists didn’t realize was that the modern way of producing the substance released giant amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. As it has become increasingly central to modernity, it has helped fuel environmental catastrophe.
Today, however, a new generation of concretophiles like Masic have pored over the poured mixture in search of another miracle, a greener, more durable kind of concrete. And they’ve found multiple answers, from concrete that can heal its own cracks — as the Pantheon has for millennia — to electroconductive concrete capable of storing energy to a blend that allows concrete to soak up more CO2 than it emits.
Together, they suggest that in a not-so-distant future, concrete — yes, concrete — one of the dirtiest substances ever concocted, could help save the planet, transforming our built environment while actually intervening in the climate for the better.
How concrete built (and polluted) the modern world
It’s no wonder that luminaries of the neo-concrete age, Thomas Edison among them, marveled at the stuff just as their Roman predecessors had. They saw it as a harbinger of utopia, of a world in which anything and everything — a home, an interstate highway, a water pipe, a subway system, or a grand piano — could be molded and poured for a fraction of ordinary costs.
“As to concrete dogs to stand warningly in the front yard and concrete cats to purr stonily under a concrete kitchen range,” the New York Times teased Edison in 1911 when he described his plans for a concrete home finished with concrete furnishings, “he made no announcement.”
The beguiled inventor’s utopian vision of a world remade by concrete would come true in more ways than he realized. Yes, it changed the way we build forever. Muddy roads and rotting wooden sidewalks gave way to smooth gray pavement, and newly cast sewer systems saved millions of lives in the deathly dirty cities of the early industrial era. Concrete, when poured over rods of steel, proved strong enough to prop up colossal skyscrapers that Julius Caesar could only have dreamed of.
But there was a trade-off: Every time Edison fired up his trademark 150-foot kilns, scorching the limestone inside into blistering pebbles of cement clinker, he released hundreds of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Yankee Stadium was built not by Babe Ruth’s swing alone, but with around 30,000 cubic yards of Edison concrete, whose creation released at least 5,400 tons of CO2, the equivalent of driving a gas-powered car 12.5 million miles, or to the moon and back more than two dozen times. But this is nothing compared with the roughly 30 billion tons of concrete the world now uses each year, enough to have turned the gluey gray goo into the second-most used material on Earth. (The first is water. Glug glug.)
The Anthropocene has been built atop a foundation of concrete, its weight eclipsing the biomass of all living things, and its annual carbon tab responsible for up to 8 percent of global emissions, the equivalent of the entire country of India. Critically, unlike the astonishingly enduring remnants of Rome, our modern concrete decays quickly, so it must be repoured time and time again, which only makes it more environmentally catastrophic.
But it doesn’t have to be this way, not anymore.
“The future of concrete is to think differently, to go away from claiming that cement is bad,” Masic told me. “Our goal is to turn this around and make concrete part of the solution instead of being a problem.”
This is why we can have nice concrete
Per ton, concrete actually emits far less CO2 by volume than other materials like aluminum, steel, plastic, or glass.
The problem is that we use so much of it, even a slightly negative footprint can quickly become enormous. But “the upside is,” said Sabbie Miller, a professor at UC Davis who focuses on sustainable concrete, “if you’re able to come up with some small change, then those small changes will also scale” in ways “that could have a huge effect on modern society and its burdens on the environment.”
One of those solutions takes a cue from the Romans, who made concrete differently than we do today. Their once-mysterious method ensured that hulking structures like the Colosseum or the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built during Augustus’ reign and still in use today, could survive for millennia while New York City’s Brooklyn-Queens Expressway or the Washington Bridge crumble after just a few decades of use.
It’s not just that we drive cars over our concrete freeways while the Colosseum has been mostly free of even the bulkiest chariot wheels for millennia. The answer, according to Masic’s research, lies in the Romans’ ingenious recipe for cement, the glue that binds concrete together. When the ancients brewed a batch of cement, they left big white chunks of dormant lime in the final mixture. Later, if a crack formed, any water would react with the idle lime, filling the fissure with new stone. Our modern concrete has no such lime clasts, meaning that if water seeps into a crack, it degrades the structure from within, rusting the rebar that made our big towers possible, leading to a grim condition known as “concrete cancer.”
Masic has recently turned his research into a startup called DMAT that reserves unreacted lime in concrete, giving it self-healing properties he says could extend a structure’s lifespan by about 50 percent, which in and of itself would reduce its carbon footprint by 40 percent. If the construction industry normalized such concrete or other mixtures that emit, say, half as much CO2 as usual, it would keep hundreds of millions of tons of it out of the atmosphere each year.
But why stop there? Some startups have gotten much better in recent years at producing concrete capable of quite literally breathing in more CO2 than it emits in a process that takes advantage of concrete’s natural porousness. It could, in theory, turn our cities into concrete rainforests by turning the material into a storage reservoir. As Miller put it, “what if we can use our concrete to undo some of our environmental damages that we’ve already caused?”
In the Bahamas, the startup Partanna has already built what it’s called the world’s first carbon net-negative home, an unassuming 1,250-square-foot abode that the company claims will sequester 182.6 tons of CO2 in its lifetime, the equivalent of hundreds of trees. Meanwhile, Masic’s lab has been piloting ways to turn concrete into a giant battery, capable of storing solar power during the day and releasing it at night, a green innovation that could cancel out its own carbon footprint within a few years of use.
Masic believes that electroconductivity could be key to catalyzing a new era of concrete — more so even than his neo-Roman ventures. “It might hold the secret,” he said, “for turning a bad guy into something amazing.”
But as promising as these innovations are, it will take time for them to ripple out from model homes and into the concrete that actually surrounds us. American concrete startups have lost billions of dollars in federal funding and expected procurement contracts under the Trump administration. Some states, most notably California, are helping to pick up the slack, but investment still lags behind potential. There’s also the challenge of convincing builders running on paper thin margins that their old ways of doing things might fit better in a new mould.
But concrete’s staggering scale means that we can’t afford to keep pouring it without considering its ugly trade-offs. More importantly, perhaps, we can’t afford to miss out on the opportunity that such a mammoth, transformative material presents to change everything yet again.

Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he's still not fit to lead
- Published
President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all of the documents and answers key questions.
The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.
Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.
In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered.
"One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said.
"I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.
"I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."
Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology.
"Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added.
"What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."
Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.
It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.
Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, Hewitt added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."

Uefa still searching for candidate to stand against Infantino
Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.
Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.
Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.
But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.
Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.
She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.
"I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added.
"We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have opportunity to vote according to how they feel."

Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
- Published
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"
Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).
"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."
When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.
A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.
Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.
The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"
The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.
This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.
"I really like it here."

The Vigilance Investigation Bureau (VIB) on Thursday (October 15, 2026) conducted simultaneous raids at Rural Works Department’s Executive Engineer’s four locations in Chhapra, Patna, Katihar and Darjeeling in connection with a case of amassing disproportionate assets (DA) to his known sources of income.
The Bureau has registered a DA case against Rural Works Department’s Executive Engineer Chandra Shekhar Singh whose four locations have been raided and searched. Mr. Singh is posted at the Department’s Quality Testing Office in Chhapra, the headquarters of Saran district.
A special vigilance team searched the Department’s office in Chhapra, Flat No. 103 at Vamika Apartment on Jagdev Path in Patna, his residential house in Lohiya Nagar, Katihar, and a private property in the Phansidewi police station area of Darjeeling district in West Bengal. The raids continued until late evening.
During the searches conducted so far, the vigilance team recovered ₹3 lakh in cash from his flat in Patna and ₹2 lakh from his house in Katihar. Gold and silver jewellery weighing approximately 250 grams was also recovered from his Katihar residence.
The amount of movable assets suspected to have been acquired illegally may increase after the completion of the searches.
According to the vigilance investigation, Mr. Singh is accused of possessing illegal assets worth ₹1.10 crore in excess of his known sources of income.
An FIR (No. 121/2026) was registered at the Vigilance police station on October 13, 2026, in this connection. The case has been registered under Section 13(2), read with Section 13(1)(b), of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as amended in 2018.
During the search of his Katihar residence, investigators reportedly found documents relating to the purchase of 92 decimals (31 kathas) of land in the Phansidewi police station area of Darjeeling district in the name of his wife, Shweta Kumari.
The land was purchased in several parcels, notably all during the same year, 2021.
The area where the land is located is considered an upscale locality in Darjeeling and lies alongside a national highway. A three-star hotel is also situated near the property. The market value of the land is reportedly estimated to be worth crores of rupees. Its actual market value is currently being assessed.
In the property declaration submitted to the government for the financial year 2025-26, Chandra Shekhar Singh reportedly did not disclose any details of this land (31 Kathas). The matter is being investigated separately.
During the vigilance bureau’s investigation, documents relating to other properties, bank accounts and jewellery were also reportedly found. Their examination is currently underway.
The total value of the alleged illegal assets will become clear only after the preliminary investigation and search operations have been completed.

On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.
Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.
Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.
“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”
The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.
“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.
During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)
“The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.”
Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Integrity Partners, which is believed to own Candiru’s assets, following sanctions by the US government in 2021, also did not respond to requests for comment.
Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.”
The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says.
A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.”
Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The milliseconds-long process can result in advertisers collecting huge volumes of data about your device, your location, and browsing history, plus a whole lot more. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.
The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech.
The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. These include NATO and United Nations networks, as well as lawmaking bodies in Europe, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, plus armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden.
Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight.
“The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.”
Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging.
“Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

I’ll admit it up front: I don’t like procedures. I’m fine doing them to other people. Having one done to me is different. For 10 years I treated my colonoscopy the way some people treat a check-engine light. I knew it was there, I knew what it meant, and I kept driving.
Every birthday there was a reason to wait. I was too busy, I had no symptoms, I’d get to it next year. I’m 55 now, which means I spent a full decade telling patients to do what I wouldn’t.
Two groups finally wore me down. The first was my wife, who is persistent and usually right, a combination I find exhausting. The second was my colleagues, who brought it up in the lounge more often than you’d think. Once a doctor’s wife and his co-workers are on the same side, the argument is over.
Seeking counsel
Before any big decision, I call my senior partner. He’s been my mentor for years, and he has the sharpest wit of anyone I know. He’s also, as I learned that day, almost no help at all.
I told him I’d finally decided to schedule the colonoscopy. He paused, and then said: “It’s a good thing you called. Now I’ll know why you’re walking funny the next day.”
I hung up, wondering why I keep calling him. I also quietly saved the whole speech, word for word, so that I can pass the same useless advice to the younger doctors in our group. Some traditions deserve to continue.
Why we do this at all
Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide, accounting for approximately 10% of all cancer cases and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally. . In India, it accounts for about 65,000 new cases a year and is rising, especially in cities, and with no national screening programme, too many cases are found late. Nearly 38,000 Indians die of it every year. It is also one of the few cancers we can actually prevent, not just catch early.
Most colon cancers start as polyps, small growths on the lining of the colon. Over roughly 10 years, some become malignant. That long, quiet stretch is the opportunity. If you find a polyp and remove it, the cancer never gets a chanc’e to start. A colonoscopy is one of the few screening tests that also serves as treatment.
A brief history
Colonoscopy is younger than you might guess. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, William Wolff and Hiromi Shinya in New York used new flexible fiberoptic scopes to examine the whole colon. Dr. Shinya also developed the wire-loop snare to remove polyps through the scope, so they no longer had to be removed through open abdominal surgery. That was a revolutionary change.
The landmark evidence came from the National Polyp Study. In 1993, Sidney Winawer and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that removing adenomatous polyps sharply cut the rate of colorectal cancer compared with what would otherwise be expected. In 2012, a long-term follow-up in the same journal showed that removing polyps reduced colorectal cancer deaths by about half. Our whole screening approach rests on those two papers.
The recommended starting age in the United States has also come down. Rising rates in younger adults led guidelines to lower it from 50 to 45. That leaves people like me with no excuse.
The alternative
Think about what skipping it looks like. A polyp grows unnoticed for years, and colon cancer often gives no warning until it’s advanced. Then the symptoms come: bleeding, a change in bowel habits, weight loss, fatigue, anaemia. By that point the conversation is about surgery, chemotherapy, and staging scans.
For some patients it means a colostomy, where the bowel is brought out through the abdominal wall and stool goes into a bag, sometimes permanently. For too many, it means dying of a disease that a simple screening test could have prevented.
Put that way, a day of inconvenience looks like a bargain.
The prep and the procedure
Every patient will tell you the procedure is easy and the prep is the hard part. They’re right.
I’ll spare you the details. You either already know, or you’ll find out soon enough. The good news is that the prep has come a long way. The dreaded jug is no longer your only choice, and tablet preps have made the whole thing far more bearable. If your doctor offers them, take them.
The next morning was close to anticlimactic. I checked in at the outpatient centre, changed into a gown that and got an IV. A nurse went through the usual checklist, and we chatted about nothing.
Then came propofol.
If you’ve never had it, here’s what it’s like. A warm flush rises up your arm, a brief awareness that something is about to happen, and then nothing. No dreams and no sense of time passing. One moment you’re listening to the anaesthesiologist, and the next you’re in recovery with a cup of juice, asking whether they’ve started yet.
The verdict
My gastroenterologist is also a friend, and he was completely professional from start to finish. He was calm and thorough, and he put me at ease. He came by recovery to tell me he’d found one polyp and removed it. It will go to pathology, and I’ll come back for surveillance on whatever schedule the results call for.
That polyp had probably been growing for years while I made excuses. Now it’s gone. That’s the point of screening: find it before it becomes cancer.
The bottom line
It really isn’t that bad. The prep is unpleasant for a single night, and easier than it used to be. The procedure takes less time than your commute, and the sedation is the best nap you’ll take all year. It may keep you from getting cancer. That’s a pretty good trade.
If you’re 45 or older and you’ve been putting it off as I did, talk to your doctor about getting screened. Colonoscopy isn’t the only option. You can do stool tests at home, and your doctor can walk you through other options. The best test is the one you’ll actually do. Doing nothing is the only wrong answer.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is Director, Interventional and Structural Cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and Clinical Assistant Professor of Medicine, Florida State University dinarab@yahoo.com)

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

The Keralam Assembly on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) referred the Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, which aims at ensuring the rights and protection of the elderly, to the Finance Subject Committee for further scrutiny.
The Bill, piloted by Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and care givers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
Opposition alleges Constitutional breach
However, the Opposition alleged that the provision that a copy of a Bill to be tabled in the Assembly should be made available to members at least three days before had not been fully complied with. N.K. Akbar, MLA, in a point of order, alleged Constitutional violation, failure to calculate the financial burden correctly, violation of Supreme Court directives on advanced medical directives with regard to the Bill’s provisions on execution of ‘living will.’
The LDF government had brought out a policy for the elderly, set up a commission for them, and prepared an elderly budget. “So, the Opposition is not against the Bill. But, serious legal issues exist,” he said.
The Chief Minister, who holds the portfolio of the Department of Senior Citizens, contended that special Acts could contain penal provisions. Moreover, the finance memorandum in the Bill clearly specified recurring and non-recurring expenditure. The government would not incur any particular expenditure in setting up senior citizen unit and forums as proposed in the Bill. The Supreme Court guidelines would be incorporated when Rules for the Act were framed, he said.
The Speaker ruled that the Bill was published in the Gazette on October 10 and its copies circulated among members the same day.
During the discussion on the Bill, the Chief Minister reiterated that “the measure of a civilised society was how it treated its senior citizens”. If the Bill were to be passed, the Keralam Assembly would become a model for the world, he addded.
Focus also on silver economy
Referring to demographic changes and migration of children and youth outside Keralam, he said the population of the elderly in the State was expected to be double the national average by 2036. However, the government was focussing not only on the welfare of the elderly, but also “silver economy” so as to transform the challenges posed by the rising elderly population into an opportunity.
The United Democratic Front (UDF) government had set up a dedicated department for the elderly. Government interventions were planned to ensure active and healthy ageing, tapping into the skills and knowledge of the elderly, conducting a survey of all elderly in the State and their health status, setting up a volunteer corps, registration and monitoring of care homes, and training and certification of care-givers, he said.
“No one should feel they are alone. They should be protected and their rights ensured,” the Chief Minister said.
He also explained the rights and principles that informed the drafting of the Bill.

White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
- Published
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."
She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.
Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.
In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

A tailoring course offered by Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) has helped eight hearing-impaired women move from depending on their families for money to earning an income of their own. Together, they have set up Colours, a stitching unit at Nilambur that gives them a way to put their skills to work and support their families.
Sabna V.K., Ramya A., Afeefa K., Sameena M.K., Nimmy N., Rajeena P., Salma V.P., and Sajeena C. began ‘Colours’ after completing the assistant dress maker course at the Nilambur training centre of JSS, Malappuram.
Before joining the course, all eight were homemakers. The training introduced them to tailoring and gave them the skills to take up stitching work. They decided to build on what they had learnt by starting a business together.
Now, the women share the work at Colours and earn through their tailoring skills. Their income helps them meet household expenses and reduces their dependence on their families for financial support.
“Earlier, we depended on our families for money. Now, we can earn through our own work and contribute to our household expenses,” they said.
Starting a business together has allowed them to put their skills to use while sharing the responsibilities of running the unit. Their experience shows how vocational training can help women with disabilities find work and build a livelihood.
For the women, the course was a step towards earning on their own. The stitching unit has given them an opportunity to use their skills in everyday life rather than letting their training end with a certificate.
“We learnt tailoring through the course. Starting Colours gave us a chance to use those skills to earn,” they said.
JSS, Malappuram, provides skill training to people from disadvantaged communities, with a focus on women and persons with disabilities. Its courses aim to help trainees find work or start small businesses.
JSS chairman P.V. Abdul Wahab, MP, said skill training could help women become financially independent. “It gives women the skills to earn and support their families,” he said.
JSS director V. Ummer Koya said the aim was to help trainees turn their learning into a livelihood. “Training makes a difference when people can use their skills to earn a living,” he said.

Israeli firm used ads to enable espionage, Canadian researchers say
Ads left millions open to 'zero-click' spyware attacks, Citizen Lab says
An Israeli advertising agency has placed ads seen by millions of internet users that have left them open to spyware attacks, according to a new report from the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab.
The report, released on Thursday, alleges that Discover-Tech intentionally operates a platform that allows its "partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" with spyware.
Those partners can then "push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements," it says.
Over a four-month period, Discover-Tech ads appeared on more than 120,000 websites and more than 75,000 apps in dozens of countries — endangering the security of "national-security-sensitive networks," such as government ministries, armed forces and multilateral organizations such as NATO, according to the report, which was released alongside an affiliated investigation by U.S. cybersecurity firm Confiant.
Ron Deibert, Citizen Lab's director, said the findings are a "worst-nightmare" scenario, with "two poorly regulated and highly abused industries" — targeted advertising and mercenary spyware — coming together.
"It's a recipe for disaster," Deibert told CBC News. "It's global espionage that we've uncovered on a massive scale."
'Zero-click' attacks
Rights groups have raised concerns for years about companies that sell spyware to anyone, oppressive governments in particular, wishing to spy on the public, journalists, political figures and other perceived critics.
Experts also have speculated that what's known as the targeted ad ecosystem — where data brokers and advertising firms bid in real time to place ads on apps and websites — could be used for espionage.
But Thursday's report marks the first time researchers have documented how "zero-click" spyware attacks can be enabled by targeted ads, Citizen Lab says.
"Zero-click" means that users don't need to click on a link or actively do anything for their devices to be targeted with spyware.
"The moment [the ad] is rendered, their device can be hacked, so there's really no defence against this, short of not using a smart phone or [not] connecting to the internet," Deibert said. Such infections can be hard to detect.
The report said some Discover-Tech ads also appeared on the websites of news outlets, including CBC, BBC and the New York Times. But Deibert says there's not much those organizations could have done to prevent it.
"It's just the advertising ecosystem working as intended," he said.
Discover-Tech did not respond to CBC News's requests for comment via a contact form on the company's website.
Chuck Thompson, the head of public affairs at CBC, said in an email that the public broadcaster's logs have "no trace of having delivered any ads," from Discover-Tech. CBC escalated to Google, which operates systems for ad sellers, "to verify and provide answers," he said.
Al Jazeera targeted
Citizen Lab said it was able to confirm a targeted spyware attack on Al Jazeera: At least 45 of the Qatar-based news outlet's devices were infected with spyware via Discover-Tech's ads in 2024 and 2025, the report said.
When spyware is implanted, the operator behind the hack can take control of the device. "They can turn on the camera, turn on the microphone, and track someone's geolocation, so it's kind of like God-like capabilities," Deibert said.
The researchers linked the zero-click attacks on Al Jazeera "with high confidence" to spyware from Candiru, an Israel-based firm that the report said has rebranded as Integrity Labs.
In 2021, the U.S. Department of Commerce sanctioned Candiru "based on evidence that [it] developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used these tools to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers."
CBC News could not immediately find a way to reach Candiru on Thursday. The Reuters news agency also said its attempts were not successful.
An Al Jazeera spokesperson condemned the targeting of its staff by such spyware as 'deliberate attack on journalists and on press freedom.' (Malak Harb/The Associated Press)
An Al Jazeera Media Network spokesperson told CBC News in an email that it "strongly condemns the targeting of our staff with mercenary spyware."
"This is a deliberate attack on journalists and on press freedom," the spokesperson said, adding that while Al Jazeera would not speculate on who deployed the spyware, it is calling for "a full, independent investigation to identify those responsible and hold them to account."
Push for investigations
Qing Tan, an associate professor at Athabasca University in Alberta, said the Citizen Lab report raises "very concerning" questions, including around personal privacy. "A majority of people don't realize this could happen to them, so this is a very big issue," he said.
Citizen Lab researchers said their findings should push ad vendors to "significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers."
They also called on regulators around the world to "investigate whether the rights of their citizens, as well as applicable privacy and security laws were violated."

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada did not immediately respond to emailed questions about whether it intends to investigate the report's allegations or take any immediate action.
A Google spokesperson told CBC News in an emailed statement that it blocked Discover-Tech from its ad platforms "for systematically violating" the company's policies, and that it has set up warnings "to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group," they said.
IAB Europe, a European association that develops frameworks for digital marketing and the advertising ecosystem, also said Thursday that Discover-Tech was suspended from its list of global vendors for violating its terms.

Buying energy drinks in public is embarrassing. Every time I see someone scanning the cooler for their favorite flavor of Monster or Ghost, I guess which accompanying vape flavor they've picked out, and I know others are making the same assumption about me when I’m scoring a can of Celsius to beat back a hangover or get lifted before a 10-hour bartending shift.
The good news is that it’s easier than ever to purchase your favorite cans from Amazon, and the great news is that you don’t need to put on your Crocs and Cookie Monster jammies to do it. Throw in a nice little discount for buying in bulk and setting up auto-delivery, and you’re basically being paid to not leave your house. The future is here, and it is jacked up on B vitamins, red dye, and taurine.
As a devoted coffee drinker, I often feel like the misquoted New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael when I see neon-colored tallboys of high-octane energy drinks usurping shelf space from my favorite Dr. Pepper and Mountain Dew variants at my local Sheetz. Energy drinks are big business—they raked in close to $20 billion in the US in 2023—yet I don’t know a single person who drinks them on a regular basis.
A good cup of coffee is hard to find at odd hours in the middle of nowhere. Energy drinks, on the other hand, are as no-fuss as it gets. At any hour of the day you can pick out an eye-catching can that boldly advertises its caffeine content, plunk down a few bucks, and shoot into space in just a few swigs. Homebodies and deal junkies don’t even need to leave their domiciles to cop excellent deals with lightning-fast shipping on their most beloved brands, provided they’re Amazon Prime members. I love value, convenience, and caffeine, so I finally caved.

4. Naked
The realm of low- or no-calorie energy drinks offers two options for sweeteners: an unwieldy list of chemicals with confusing names, or allegedly “natural” options like stevia and monkfruit. The former camp commands the lion’s share of the market, but the latter is ascendant and willing to pay a premium for an energy drink with as few ingredients as possible. Liquid Death burst onto the scene in the late 2010s with a concept so simple you’d kick yourself for not thinking of it first. In that span, the very concept of what a “rockstar” even is has been rewritten ad infinitum, with the most current iteration functioning as an ideal assembled from poptimism, monoculture, consolidation, and psychopathic “stanning.”
In other words, the model followed by musicians—forming bands to meet strippers to do drugs with—has been blown up completely, and consumers' appetites for branding that’s hitched to that ethos have bottomed out accordingly. Rockstar is now owned by Pepsi, and the flavor of this energy drink that is famously not Red Bull tastes exactly like you’d expect it to with this in mind. A nondescript citrus flavor serves as a poorly made Trojan horse for high fructose corn syrup and a synthetic aftertaste that’s hard to tolerate unless you’ve been chain-smoking Parliaments most of your adult life.
Notes: Partying with a can of Rockstar is a white-knuckle affair that commonly leads to grinding teeth, anguished pacing, and an overwhelming urge to argue with strangers on the internet about how the music of Buckcherry is actually good. This is the kind of energy drink that’s only appropriate to drink after midnight before you’re about to do even worse things to your body.

28. Black Rifle Energy
Black Rifle Coffee Company was founded in 2014 by a former Green Beret with a mission to “serve coffee and culture to people who love America.” That’s a noble goal taken at face value, and no reasonable person would argue that military veterans shouldn’t reap some sort of financial benefit from a commercial enterprise that so brazenly hitches its wagon to their valor. This is America, however, and a business that’s as invested in selling culture as it is a consumable product is immune from the perversions of hyper-partisanship and the cheap thrills of owning the libs. Between Black Rifle's pledge to hire 10,000 veterans as a direct response to a similar pledge made by Starbucks to hire just as many refugees; the Blue Lives Matter-adjacent aesthetic of its merch; and its weekly podcast, which serves as a hyper-macho who’s who of conservative politicians, venture capitalists, and manosphere snake oil salesmen, it’s easy to guess which side of the aisle butters BRCC’s bread.
Notes: Freedom Punch is the least offensive option one would find in BRCC’s mixed 12-pack, which also includes Project Mango, Wild Frost, and Ranger Berry. I liked the above-average carbonation level, but the vague hint of Tahitian Treat at the front of the gulp immediately dissipates into a tingly chemical aftertaste followed by a dry mouthfeel that’s a little bit concerning. I would reach for this if I were suffering a stomach bug and avoiding things with pronounced flavors, or if Alex Garland’s 2024 film Civil War came to life and a roving gang of right-wing marauders rolled by and threatened to beat my liberal ass unless I proved my fealty to their king. Two hundred milligrams of caffeine is not nothin’, but it’s stretched a bit too far across the can's volume to really pack the wallop I’d need to outrun Landry and his crew of Pantera-loving degenerates without having to stop to pee along the way. This isn’t the energy drink America needs, but it might just be the energy drink it deserves. Sigh.

Others Tested
Ardor Tropical Mango (12-Pack) for $38: This is the best of all the Ardor flavors we tried, and it still tastes like someone rinsed out a glass that contained a mango White Claw with plain seltzer. It’s 99 percent flavorless. On the bright side, this may be drinkable if you have food poisoning and need to get caffeine in you without throwing up. I copped a bigger buzz watching commercials for Mountain Dew Kickstart on YouTube. This one is a hard no all around.
Key Keytone Energy Drink Pineapple Passionfruit (12-Pack) for $45: Key is an “all natural” energy drink that’s very proud of its vegan and keto-friendly ingredients. It’s made with Avela, which is described as a “ketogenic ingredient intended for adult use” on its incredibly vague fitness-adjacent website. That’s all well and good if chasing ketosis is your hobby. If it’s not, you should run as far away from this beverage as possible. The initial hit of flavor is a muddled medley of faux-sweetness akin to woo-woo sugar replacements like Stevia or monkfruit, but what comes next is nowhere near as merciful. The astringent aftertaste hits somewhere between the final coat of goop your dental hygienist doles out and that last can of Mom Water that’s left in the cooler after a long day at the pool. The impact of so many foreign substances definitely had me feeling a certain kind of way within just a few minutes, but my attention swung wildly between work tasks, domestic minutiae, and creeping dread about our country's unraveling social fabric.
How I Tested
Across the span of a year, I sampled different energy drinks from an amalgamation of readily available gas station staples, brands the Amazon algorithm was pimping extra hard that day, everything in the Whole Foods end cap that advertised its caffeine content, and a couple oddballs from the past you probably don’t remember.
I graded on taste, which is obviously subjective, and the palpable effects of the caffeine after knocking back a can at 8:30 am every day, after my daily 1.5-mile run with my dog. The extra cans were deployed two hours into shifts at my part-time bartending gig. I took one day off from the experiment due to gut-wrenching stomach pain and horrible night sweats. If there’s a Ghost-addled gamer in your basement as you read this, please consider offering them a wellness check, or a refill on their tendies at the very least.
