Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections, and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.
That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.
It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.
White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)
The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.
Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.
Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.
“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.
The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.
But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.
With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.
"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”
The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.
Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."
On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.
And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.
Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.
But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.

CitizenLab details new spyware triggered by online advertising
It requires 'no interaction' from victims to infect devices.
A new type of spyware dubbed "AdFection" is infecting phones and computers via global online advertising networks, according to a new report from Citizen Lab. The attack is unique in that it can infect devices just by showing an ad, with no need for the victim to click on a link or file. The researchers said that AdFection is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads.
The ad-infiltrating technology was reportedly developed by Israeli company called Discover-Tech. Researchers said it has been used to target journalists and staff at the Al Jazeera news network, along with officials and employees at organizations including NATO, the European Commission, NVIDIA and Arm.
"Discover-Tech has leveraged the advertising ecosystem for years to turn trusted websites and popular apps into a zero-click spyware delivery platform," Citizen Lab senior researcher Bill Marczak told The Financial Times. Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm but instead serves as a "bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem," Citizen Lab's report states
Google was among the major ad platforms targeted by the spyware, but it has now suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list. "Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies," the company said in a statement.
Targeted online advertising is a highly desirable medium to spread malware because it's prevalent on the web globally. It works though an automated real-time bidding auction system that lets advertisers compete to show ads to specific internet users. Discover-Tech's software used the system instead to profile and de-anonymize such users before targeting them with spyware, the report states. Victims were then sent malicious malware code buried in innocent-looking ads.
Discover-Tech reportedly displayed 442 million ads on more than 120,000 websites, including the BBC and New York Times, along with mobile apps like Duolingo, Badoo and Grindr. The ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure and national cyber agencies. Citizen Lab researchers found login records on Discover-Tech's site, including details belonging to employees of the spyware maker Candiru.
The discovery is "surely just the tip of the iceberg," Marczak said in the blog post. "If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it's time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether." Discover-Tech and other players in the scheme have yet to comment.

Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
- Published
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.

The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, Ipac, which counts members from all the UK’s major parties, says.
In an endorsement, the former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
While the report accepts that “disengagement was not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
It identifies emerging technologies such as AI as posing new challenges, in terms of disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The Guardian has contacted the UK government and the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.
Yes, the company that popularized the “keeper test” is known for abrupt exits. But despite Netflix’s recent stock struggles, many considered Bajaria too big to fail.
Word of her ouster leaked before the executive had the chance to address most of her internal teams — an announcement dovetailed with news of her incoming replacement, the venerated film and TV executive Peter Rice. As the former general entertainment chairman of the Walt Disney Company, Rice’s bona fides are clear — “I wish I bought stock this morning,” one huge talent rep said about Netflix’s new hire — but it doesn’t explain how Bajaria fell out of favor so fast.
One word that came up in nearly a dozen conversations with industry players this afternoon about Bajaria’s pink-slipping: “scapegoat.”
Netflix is obviously against the ropes again, after slowing user engagement on the service rattled Wall Street investors and layoffs came this week as a sacrifice to the share price. But Bajaria’s dismissal makes it clear, according to the numerous sources we spoke with, that content is once again going to take it on the chin.
“People always blame the content,” said the source, “but you don’t lay off 1,000 people unless there’s a big problem with the business model.”
Bajaria’s exit echoes similarly shocking removals in Netflix history — notably that of Cindy Holland, the company’s first content queen who oversaw flagship hits like “House of Cards,” “Stranger Things” and “The Crown.” Holland was ousted in 2020, when Sarandos combined English-language and international content under Bajaria (elevating the latter to the largest autonomous content job in the streamer’s history).
Holland, one insider with knowledge of Netflix observed to Variety, built a business of boutique hits. Bajaria’s foresight was sharper, investing in local language productions and building up Netflix’s global presence (almost two dozen international offices were opened during Bajaria’s reign). She is also credited internally with pushing the streamer into live entertainment. Bajaria was on the “ground floor” of licensing deals with WWE and the NFL, which have proven significant draws for the ad-supported tier of Netflix subscribers, per the source. Her talent relations were on par with others at her level (Bajaria was ubiquitous at premieres and launches in film and TV, most recently at Sarandos’ side at the L.A. premiere of Ben Affleck’s “Animals”).
“The problem isn’t engagement,” said yet another person with knowledge of Netflix. “It’s that the only lever to pull for revenue growth is raising the subscriber price. How’s that Bela’s problem? Where’s the CFO and the CEO?”
Interestingly, we hear that Rice came into play only a few weeks ago when he was reported to be interviewing with Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz for a top position at that newly combined company. The lunch meeting, one source familiar with the men said, was called so Kreiz could request that Rice replace him on the board of his former company Mattel. Regardless, it alerted the town that Rice was done with semi-retirement (a producing deal with A24) and ready to come back to a big job. Another hot Thursday rumor said that Rice also met recently with NBCUniversal about a post there. One source familiar with NBCU said there was no job in play for Rice under Donna Langley’s expansive umbrella, so it’s unclear what he would’ve met about. A spokesperson for NBCUniversal had no comment.
Another lunch may have proven consequential in Bajaria’s exit. Earlier this year, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was spotted breaking bread with HBO chief content officer Casey Bloys. Was Sarandos courting Bloys for a top job at the streamer, perhaps to take the job then held by Bajaria? Soon, the spin machine reframed the meeting as a friendly gathering, floating the idea that it was a pitch for Bloys to sign a production deal under Bajaria if he did not want to find a way to work at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. At a Bloomberg conference last week, Sarandos downplayed the meeting: “He’s a good guy,” he said about Bloys. “For some reason, we had a very well-publicized lunch.”
Perhaps. But in hindsight, now that Sarandos has leveled the ax on Bajaria after 10 years, is a lunch ever really just a meal? Rice’s recent focus has been as the head of ceremonies and content for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games, a role that now be ending as Rice focuses on a more urgent task. The exec has been on the open market in the years since he was let go at Disney. He’s seen as the rare exec who has spent time heading up both major film and TV businesses, so the job of chief content officer at Netflix, where he’ll oversee both, makes sense. He’s also well-liked and respected from his time at 20th Century Fox, heading up Fox Searchlight and later the Fox network, and eventually becoming president of parent company 21st Century Fox prior to Disney’s acquisition.
“Surprise” was also a common refrain both inside and out of Netflix on Thursday about the turn of events. But a few hints had already been out there: Netflix is set to report its Q3 earnings next Tuesday, so such a move would have to be made beforehand. And with co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters not going anywhere, the sacrificial lamb next in line was Bajaria. Observers speculated that the Q3 results are likely to be extremely disappointing for the streamer, which is already facing some tough headwinds.
At that same Screentime event, anyone reading between the lines might have guessed that Sarandos was getting antsy with Netflix’s current low-growth status. In particular, he was asked about Netflix’s slower growth (2% year-over-year growth in user engagement during the first half in 2026). “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said. Turns out Bajaria’s exit was a part of that change. Now all eyes turn to Rice’s plans for Netflix, and whether those plans will include some of Bajaria’s lieutenants, such as U.S./Canada head of scripted series Jinny Howe and film lead Dan Lin.
Bajaria may also have hit thin ice with Sarandos after the streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — its worst showing since 2016 and down from 30 in 2025. That’s quite a turn from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44.
Along with the Emmy slump, Netflix hasn’t premiered a culture-defining hit in the vein of “Stranger Things” in quite some time. But it’s still fielded some of the most-watched programs of the year, including “His & Hers” and Season 4 of “Bridgerton.” Bajaria is known for her keen creative eye, honed over the years at places like CBS and NBCUniversal (where she was ultimately head of Universal TV before moving to Netflix in 2016).
“In her decade at Netflix, Bela’s impact has been undeniable — from attracting new talent, bringing live sports, concerts and events to driving the company’s global expansion and push into new areas of entertainment,” WME co-chair Richard Weitz tells Variety. “Her relationships with talent have been integral in Netflix’s relationships with A talent across the platform. Simply put, she’s been transformational and I know her worldwide team and the talent who have worked with her will miss her.”
Rice will not inherit a bus of happy campers. He’ll have to galvanize a team that lost a slew of executives Wednesday as a result of pink slips; on the TV side, that included Carolina Garcia, who has been let go as director of original series after a decade with the streamer.as well as scheduling head Andy Kubitz, Lisa Lang McMullen (director, overall deals, series), Andrew McQuinn (director, original series), James Oh (director, original drama series) and Jason Pan (manager, original series creative development).
The remaining film group appears safe for now, as Lin’s team saw a major sacrifice in VP Doug Belgrad earlier this week. Morale will need tweaking, budgets adjusting and a slew of new lunches will be scheduled. What you can count on, per one of the streaming insiders, is that “eventually, everyone’s time comes at Netflix.”

The rising tide that has been the Drive to Survive effect has lifted more boats in motorsport than simply Formula 1’s. Sportscar racing is enjoying its own surge in popularity internationally at races like Le Mans in France, but also in North America in IMSA’s WeatherTech Sportscar Championship. For one thing, multi-hour, multi-class racing lends itself better to the age of streaming and second screens than it did linear broadcast TV, and fans are taking advantage of that: IMSA’s audience grew by more than a third domestically and almost a quarter internationally last year.
Having some of the coolest-looking cars racing today certainly helps, whether that’s the (mostly) hybrid prototypes or the GTs, racing versions of road-going cars from Porsche, Ferrari, and others. And it definitely helps that fan access at the races is virtually unmatched, with open paddocks and grid walks that now see huge crowds get up close to the cars just before the start of each race.
“I think we’re just scratching the surface,” said IMSA President John Doonan. “I think besides the people that are here on the ground, the people watching, people engaging with us on social media, I’m seeing the passion come out more. Just on the grid walk, these fans coming up and being so excited to be here.” The series has certainly been making an effort, among other things getting local high school students exposed to the industry and starting a partnership to train more mechanics with ASE.
IMSA’s 2026 season wrapped up at the start of the month at Road Atlanta in Georgia. Although the 10-hour Petit Le Mans is now the regular finale, the race predates the WeatherTech series as well as its predecessor, the American Le Mans Series, first being held in 1998 after Elan Pharmaceuticals founder Don Panoz got a bright idea to invite the cars that raced at the French enduro to come here to the US. It worked and led to some classic races; no one who watched it could forget Allan McNish’s recovery drive in 2008, clawing back two laps after crashing on the way to the grid to hunt down and beat the Peugeots. (Don’t take my word for it, watch it for yourself.)
I wasn’t kidding about the crowd on the grid walk.
Credit:
Jake Galstad/Lumen via Getty Images
I wasn’t kidding about the crowd on the grid walk.
Credit:
Jake Galstad/Lumen via Getty Images
2026’s running was perhaps not quite an all-time classic. As often happens, weather played its part, suppressing the crowd size and making life complicated for the teams and drivers on track. Nearly four hours were spent neutralized behind the safety car, with 16 cautions that prevented this year’s race from ever really developing a rhythm. The first half of the race was dominated by the Acuras, and the BMWs were also strong, but in the end victory went to one of the two Porsche 963s—believe it or not, the marque’s first prototype Petit Le Mans win (although in 2015 a slower GTLM Porsche 911 RSR managed to take overall victory).
This being the real world, things in sportscarland aren’t entirely easy. The war in the Middle East has disrupted both the World Endurance Championship—the series built around the 24 Hours of Le Mans—and a new Asian Le Mans series. And as always, at the top level, the sport is dependent upon manufacturer largesse, something that usually vanishes in the face of worsening economic outlooks. Porsche cut its factory prototype program in half last year, parking the two cars it had campaigned in WEC and leaving just the two cars running in IMSA. Betting heavily on an EV transition that hasn’t come to pass, plus the effect of Trump’s tariffs on US-generated profits, are mostly to blame for the decision to pull back.
But Porsche is not the only one; Alpine announced earlier this year that it was retiring from the WEC at the end of this year. There were hopes that the program might be saved by Geely, the Chinese automaker that owns Lotus and Volvo. Sadly, just today it emerged that it’s unlikely to happen, and two more cars will fall off the grid at the end of the year. Acura is also calling time on its GTP program in IMSA, preferring to focus its motorsports efforts on IndyCar. In doing so, it almost certainly means there will be no Honda presence at Le Mans in the near future, something many fans had hoped to see.
Then again, the end of those other programs does mean room on the grid for others to join. This year saw Genesis enter the WEC, and next year both Ford and McLaren are joining WEC as well. So the trajectory is positive.
Next year McLaren returns to endurance racing.
Jakob Ebrey/Getty Images
Next year McLaren returns to endurance racing.
Jakob Ebrey/Getty Images
But this is the last we’ll see of Acura for now.
Jake Galstad/Lumen via Getty Images
But this is the last we’ll see of Acura for now.
Jake Galstad/Lumen via Getty Images
Next year McLaren returns to endurance racing.
Jakob Ebrey/Getty Images
But this is the last we’ll see of Acura for now.
Jake Galstad/Lumen via Getty Images
One reg to rule them all?
That all three factory efforts have chosen the IMSA-written LMDh technical regulations rather than Le Mans’ own Hypercar ruleset says something. Hypercar gives OEMs greater technical freedom, including the option to have all-wheel drive hybrid systems or use bespoke batteries, whereas the LMDh rules mandate common hybrid systems and gearboxes, as well as requiring each OEM to start with one of four approved carbon-fiber chassis.
The lack of spec components in Hypercar was definitely a factor when Ferrari chose those rules for its 499P, as well as Toyota with the GR010 (now TR010) and Peugeot with the 9X8. Aston Martin’s road-derived Valkyrie, too. But going that route is more expensive than using some common parts, and is that extra cost even worth it when the cars all have performance balanced to roughly the same lap times anyway? That process has just enough friction that we still haven’t seen a 499P race in IMSA despite the US being Ferrari’s largest market.
“We’re fortunate that Aston Martin saw the opportunity to come [to IMSA]. I think we absolutely 100 percent need one set of regulations. I think our vision is that LMDh by sheer vote has been the choice of the OEMs,” said Doonan. “I think rules stability is really important, and this has always been a laboratory for advancement in an authentic way, but I think the more stable that we can make the platform rules-wise is only going to help its stability and longevity,” he said.
The good news is that most stakeholders also agree that having two sets of regs is daft and that from 2030—when the current rulesets expire—everyone should be reading from the same sheet.
“The way to go forward is to have one category. And everybody behind the scenes… there’s a lot of talks, a lot of meetings, and they’re going exactly that way,” said Urs Kuratle, head of Porsche’s prototype program. “On the other hand, with the big success sports car racing had in the past four years, we also have great races in the WEC with the Hypercars. We have record crowds, both sides of the Atlantic. So that basically proves that concept also works. And if it was the enabler, the two different congregations or regulatories or whatever, that was the way to enable the sports car renaissance, then it was a good success. If you would ask, it would have been clever to do it with one rule set from just beginning, the answer would also be yes. But it worked,” Kuratle told me.
What does this sport look like in five years?
Credit:
Brandon Badraoui/Lumen via Getty Images
What does this sport look like in five years?
Credit:
Brandon Badraoui/Lumen via Getty Images
It looks likely that IMSA’s approach will win the day. “We see the next set of regulations as being an evolution of LMDH, and there’s got to be a way to have everybody see the value of what has happened with LMDH. And the OEMs did by saying, “Well, geez, I could run in the top category in a pretty cost-effective manner,” Doonan said. “Without being repetitive, stability is critical in so many areas of this right now because when headwinds that we don’t control come, my hope would be that this would be… a place where automakers can come market, Michelin and Motul can come market,” Doonan said.
One reason some of us love prototype racing is that in many cases it really has improved our road cars. Direct technology transfer from the racetrack to the road is less common than it was, but still happens—Porsche’s T-hybrid engine and its electric turbocharger are directly descended from Porsche’s 919 Hybrid race car, for example.
In the future, it’s more likely that software will be the place to look to see it happening. That’s something IMSA has been accelerating, offering the vast amounts of data generated during its races to researchers and developers to work with. “Now IMSA Labs has opened up this whole new opportunity to come into this space, use the data that we generate to prove out or build out new software solutions, business solutions, AI, predictive analysis. All of those things can happen here in real time, in a controlled environment, in a regulated environment,” Doonan said.
“The OEMs have told me point-blank learnings from the hybrid system on the GTP cars, more so the strategy of how the hybrid is being implemented are immediately being utilized in product development for road cars, flat-out. And that’s been told to me by OEM representatives. We still have to allow things like that to be authentic and real in sportscar racing, in my opinion,” Doonan said.
The #6 Porsche Penske 963 finally got Stuttgart a prototype win in Atlanta.
Credit:
Porsche
The #6 Porsche Penske 963 finally got Stuttgart a prototype win in Atlanta.
Credit:
Porsche
“It should be a technology which is also transferable to the roadcar business or for any OEM. I think that’s an important thing,” Kuratle said. “It has to be something the fans would love to see. But I make a stupid example now: whether or not you develop your own fuel pump. A fan in the grandstand doesn’t really care. So it does not matter if everybody has the same cheap pump in the cars. These are things which should be avoided in the future. But all the environmental topics have to be touched. We cannot burn shitloads of fuel on all these things,” Kuratle said.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

Withings wants new users to pay $100 a year to sync with Apple Health
The smart health company is gating third-party app syncing to its own subscription plan for new users.
Withings has found itself in hot water with its customers after adopting an expensive policy change this week. According to a post on the company's support forum, Withings appears to be gating the ability for users to sync their data with Apple Health to its own subscription service. Current users don't seem to be impacted, but accounts made after October 13 need to be Withings+ members to automatically connect their information to Apple Health or another similar third-party app. The Withings+ plan costs $100 a year.
Many of the responses to the original post are from existing users criticizing the change to apply this additional charge to new customers for what is a comparatively simple feature. A reply labeled as "Official response from Withings" confirms the change, though stating that after the 13th, "automatic sync to third-party apps is part of Withings+." Rather than allowing the automatic sync, new free users will need to manually export and upload their history any time they want to access their latest Withings data in another platform. We've reached out to Withings for additional comment and will update if we receive a response.
Withings is primarily known for high-end smart health gear. The company recently released the Body Scan 2 scale, which costs $600, while the mid-range version will still run you $280.

El Salvador's Bukele unveils plan to free up to 50% arrested under state of emergency
President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador announces a plan to release up to 50% of those imprisoned under a state of emergency
SAN SALVADOR, El Salvador -- Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele announced a plan to release up to 50% of the people imprisoned under a state of emergency under which authorities arrested more than 90,000 people since March 2022 in a campaign to wipe out violent criminal gangs.
The emergency, which was declared after a spike in violence, has drastically reduced the country's homicide rate while also suspending fundamental rights, including the right to be informed of the reasons for detention, the right to access legal counsel and the right to visitation.
Human rights groups have condemned the emergency, saying it has led to widespread arbitrary arrests, and they have repeatedly called on Bukele to end the measure. The president has justified the measure as necessary to reign in warring gangs MS-13 and Barrio 18.
The president’s plan announced Tuesday night would focus on releasing people who were considered gang collaborators, a blanket term that can include anyone from gang lookouts to people who make extortion payments.
“There are many people who have indeed committed crimes, but their crime was collaborating with gangs,” Bukele said. “They deserve to be in jail, but we come from a country where collaborating with gangs wasn’t so unusual, and if we were to arrest everyone who collaborated with gangs, we would have to arrest 20% of the population.”
Without going into details, the president indicated that authorities plan to analyze cases to determine potential early release with monitoring, which could benefit half of those detained during the state of emergency.
Human rights organizations have registered more than 6,000 complaints during the emergency and documented the deaths of at least 575 people in government custody.
For some, the potential release of thousands of prisoners doesn’t go far enough to repair the damage of their prolonged imprisonment.
“The victims of arbitrary detentions don’t just deserve to recover their freedom, but they also deserve to be compensated for the harms caused by the State of El Salvador: the physical and mental harm that imprisonment causes, family suffering, loss of work or studies, reputational damage, among others,” wrote exiled Salvadoran lawyer Bertha Deleón on X.
Bukele dismissed criticism from national and international rights groups, saying that they should take the side of the victims of gang violence.
He defended the need to maintain the state of emergency, but expressed his intention to end it eventually.
Homicides have drastically decreased under Bukele, according to government figures, down from a peak of more than 100 murders per 100,000 residents in 2015 to 1.3 per 100,000 in 2025. However, the government has narrowed the definition for homicides to exclude killings by police, murders in prisons and bodies found in unmarked graves.

New Delhi, Oct 16: The government on Friday cut the windfall tax on diesel exports and raised the levy on petrol exports for the fortnight beginning October 16.
The duty on ATF exports has been retained at Rs 10.5 per litre for the fortnight.
The Special Additional Excise Duty (SAED), along with the road and infrastructure cess, on diesel exports will now be Rs 8.5 per litre, down from Rs 16 per litre.
The duty on petrol exports has been hiked to Rs 2.5 per litre, from Rs 0.5 per litre, for the next fortnight.
The Finance ministry in a notification said the duty hikes will be effective from October 16.
Amid escalating tensions in West Asia, the government imposed an export duty on diesel and ATF on March 27 and revised the rate every fortnight.
Beginning May 16, the levy was imposed on petrol exports.
The ministry also said that there is no change in the existing duty rates on petrol and diesel cleared for domestic consumption.
The windfall tax was levied to increase domestic availability of the fuel amid the war in West Asia.
It was also aimed at preventing exporters from taking undue advantage due to price differences as global crude oil prices had risen since the war began.
The windfall tax was intended to ensure domestic availability of petroleum products by disincentivising exports amid the West Asia crises.

Rumors that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security allegedly illegally used water from New Mexico in order to aid in construction of its border wall circulated in October.
Specifically, people claimed that DHS had issued a waiver to remove the state's protections and ownership of the water wells despite ongoing disputes with land owners and lawsuits against the federal government's actions regarding its construction plans.
The claim was true.
On Oct. 2, the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued a directive — available to read on the Federal Register — that it was "necessary to waive certain laws, regulations, and other legal requirements in order to ensure the expeditious construction of barriers and roads in the vicinity of the international land border in the state of New Mexico."
Included in the waiver was the entirety of the New Mexico Water Code.
The directive further described the El Paso Sector, a Customs and Border Protection jurisdiction that includes all of New Mexico, as an "area of high illegal entry" to justify the move.
A spokesperson for CBP, which is part of DHS, told Snopes via email the agency was "coordinating with the State of New Mexico and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to develop a broader groundwater management strategy" and stressed the importance of how "water is required for road construction, concrete production, and dust suppression associated with border wall construction."
They wrote that "CBP recently instructed the barrier construction contractor to pause on the installation of any new groundwater wells in collaboration with the State of New Mexico and as an initial step in minimizing or avoiding impacts to groundwater water resources," adding they were committed to working with local landowners.
A spokesperson for New Mexico's Office of the State Engineer told Snopes via email:
We have informed the CBP that all water used for the project must come from permitted sources, and we have instructed them in how to do that. To date, they have been unwilling to do so, and they continue pumping water from illegal wells. Therefore, while a pause in drilling new wells is a good first step, more must be done to ensure that New Mexicans' water supply is not threatened by this project.
The agenda for a meeting of New Mexico's Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Oct. 6 showed that Nathaniel Chakeres, general counsel at the New Mexico's Office of the State Engineer, made a presentation regarding the illegal drilling and resulting waiver, which he called "unconstitutional."
Searchlight New Mexico, an investigative journalism outlet, quoted Chakeres as telling the committee that "the water of New Mexico is owned by the public for appropriation by private parties. That's in our constitution, and the federal government accepted that constitution when we became a state." Snopes attempted to locate video of the committee meeting but was unable to.
The committee's website appeared to host the minutes from its meetings for public review, but none were available for the meeting in question as of this writing.
In Chakeres' presentation, as one local report pointed out, he "shared an image of an open well casing that sat roughly six inches above pooled surface water," which meant "the next rain storm could send oil, gas or construction chemicals into the groundwater."
That report, by Source New Mexico, quoted Chakeres as saying, "It's appalling. We were shocked when we came out and saw this. No New Mexico drillers drill wells like this."
New Mexico's battle for water at the border
The battle between the state and the federal government's attempts at border wall construction first made headlines in June when the government attempted to seize land belonging to a Roman Catholic diocese in New Mexico after the church refused to agree to an acquisition, leading to a lawsuit.
In July, area farmers met to discuss the issue of federal drilling on the border, voicing their concerns over a dwindling water supply and "unmonitored tapping of border aquifers."
In August, the Office of the State Engineer threatened to revoke licenses of the companies contracted by the Trump administration for the border wall project.
One local news report wrote the officials had found multiple "unauthorized" wells in protected water basins, along with possible safety violations, with one that had the "imminent risk of groundwater contamination."
CBP reportedly agreed to stop drilling following the voicing of these concerns, however, by the end of August, the state sued the federal government and the border contractors, citing that no formal effort was made to cease the drilling. The ongoing legal struggles led to the introduction of the waiver on Oct. 2.
When reached for comment, DHS also provided a statement from CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott that was first released in August, discussing an unrelated CBP project in southern Arizona in which the department is cutting through tribal land for construction. The department has not yet responded to a follow-up about what, if anything, the statement about the Arizona project has to do with the situation in New Mexico.

After a special executive magistrate court released CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 11 after a one-day preventive detention, several pro-BJP social media handles claimed that the trio had been granted bail on the condition that they would not take part in any protest for a period of one year. Those making such claims included retired Major Manik M Jolly, Right wing Wire, and BJP-supporting troll handle RiseOfBurnol.
Subsequently, a copy of an alleged bond began circulating on social media, bearing the name of Abhijit Dipke and the seal of the executive magistrate of New Delhi district.
It was claimed that this Dipke had signed the bond at the time of his release. BJP leader Radhika Khera shared a photo of the said bond while quoting an X post in which Dipke had claimed that he had not signed any such bond.
Sharing this picture, Facebook user Riju Dutta, who claims to be a ‘politician’, took a dig at Dipke, remarking that these people are supposedly revolutionaries.
Several users shared the same image on social media platforms.
Fact Check
We first checked Delhi Police’s official X handle. In their post, Police stated that Deepke, Ranka and Das were placed under ‘preventive arrest’ on October 10, 2026, and were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, 2026. “A bond of ₹50,000 was furnished to ensure the maintenance of peace and good behavior for one year, and the Special Executive Magistrate Court released them.”
Preventive arrest u/s 126/170 BNSS of Sh. Abhijeet Dipke, Sh. Ashutosh Ranka and Sh. Saurav Das was done on 10.10.2026. All due legal procedures were followed and they were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt on 11.10.2026.
A bail bond as Surety Bond of ₹50,000/- was filled for maintaining peace and good behaviour, for a period of one year, and they were released by the SEM Court.
— Delhi Police (@DelhiPolice) October 11, 2026
Nowhere in this police statement was it mentioned that their release was conditional on Dipke or the other leaders not participating in any protest for one year. There is also no mention of Dhruv Rathee in the statement.
In other words, police did not state that Rathee was required to sign a bond. The YouTuber himself refuted the viral claim on his X account, stating that he did not sign any bond or undertaking to secure his release.
I did not sign any bond
I did not sign any undertaking
I did not sign any condition for release
For all the media houses ^
— Dhruv Rathee (@dhruv_rathee) October 11, 2026
Examining the viral document clearly, we noticed several discrepancies:
- According to the police statement, the three individuals were produced before the special executive magistrate (SEM) court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, whereas the alleged bond bears the date of October 10.
- The SEM Court falls under the South West district of Delhi, while the alleged bond mentions the New Delhi district.
- The spelling of “Satyamev Jayate” in the center of the Executive Magistrate’s seal on the alleged bond is incorrect.
We checked the image using OpenAI’s ‘Verify OpenAI-generated content’ tool, which revealed that it was created with the help of AI.
Advocate Sautik Banerjee, who appeared for Deepke, Das and Ranka in the SEM court, told the media that the magistrate had not imposed any conditions on them. They were released on a personal bond with one surety.
Delhi: On the SEM Court releasing CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Saurav Das, advocate Soutik Banerjee says, “The magistrate has not imposed any conditions on them. They have been released on a personal bond with one surety” https://t.co/UI6OgPt2nL
— IANS (@ians_india) October 11, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, Banerjee explained, “Breach of peace refers only to activities that are not sanctioned by the Constitution and do not enjoy protection as fundamental rights. If the Constitution grants the freedom of speech and expression, the right to form associations and hold assemblies, or the freedom of movement, then restrictions can be imposed on these rights only within the scope of ‘reasonable restrictions’ that are rational. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly stated, peaceful protests are permitted, and one is always free to organize or participate in them; this cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a breach of peace.”
Sautik Banerjee sent us a bail bond format from the special executive magistrate (West District), Delhi, which looks entirely different from the document in the viral image.
Overall, the claim that Sourav Das, Abhijit Deepke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Dhruv Rathee were released on the condition that they would not participate in any protests for a year is false. Furthermore, the image of the bail bond bearing Abhijit Deepke’s name, which was shared by several individuals, including BJP leader Radhika Khera, was generated using AI.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.

New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia didn't pass the bar exam
Zacharia has faced scrutiny over her resume and legal background
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is defending her legal background, while acknowledging that she did not pass the bar exam.
In an interview with the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia said she was preparing to take the California bar exam at a time when she had just gotten married and was preparing to move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.
"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia said.
She said the results of the bar exam, which she did not pass, were "somewhat inconsequential" because she would not need to be a barred attorney while living in China.
Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny for calling herself a "lawyer," said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.
"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."
Zacharia said she will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House role.
Showed 'ample deference' to Trump
Zacharia also spoke to Human Events about her start to her new job as press secretary — including her truncated inaugural press briefing on Tuesday.
She said she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing and that the plan had always been to keep it short because U.S. President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.
"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Zacharia said. "So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."
The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed on Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said.
"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.
Trump called her about job
She also revealed details about how she secured the White House press secretary job. Zacharia stressed that she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, which became vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.
Zacharia, who was a communications adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, said she closely monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.
"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job. I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."
Zacharia says that U.S. President Donald Trump called about the press secretary position on Oct. 7. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Then on Oct. 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.
She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.

Your flu shot can’t wait
Some parts of the country are already seeing case levels typical of late fall or early winter.
Flu season is starting earlier than usual this year, which I know from reviewing federal data. But I also know it because I woke up with body aches and chills last night, mere days before I’d planned to get my flu vaccination (!).
Already, some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. In Washington state, for instance, doctors are reporting seeing as much flu now as they usually would around Christmas.
Flu activity overall is still low, to be clear. But as of October 7, infections were rising in all 50 states. And flu is spreading before many people — like, say, me — have received their annual vaccine.
Epidemiologists don’t yet know why the flu arrived early this year, or why cases first started rising in Western states like Washington, California, and Nevada. It’s possible that a mutation is helping this year’s flu variants evade existing immunity, one virologist told NPR. International travel could play a role, too: Flu cases also spiked early in Japan and other parts of Asia.
We don’t need to know why the flu arrived early to take some basic precautions, though. So today, we’re talking through some practical tips for coping with an early flu season.
Go a little deeper
An early flu season doesn’t necessarily mean a worse season — but even a moderate season can do serious damage. Last year, influenza sent hundreds of thousands of people to the hospital and caused tens of thousands of deaths, including almost 200 among children.
The first and best way to avoid those kinds of harms is by getting the flu shot, which reduces the risk of serious illness by an average of 40 to 60 percent. In the US, people aged 6 months and older are typically told to get the vaccine by October’s end.
In light of the early onset, however (it takes two weeks to build up full immunity), you might instead want to get your shot ASAP.
There are some everyday precautions you can take, too — many of them familiar from the Covid-19 era. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, for slightly longer than feels appropriate. Mask when you’re sick or might encounter someone else who is.
And don’t neglect the good habits that support your overall health: getting enough sleep, drinking a lot of water, and eating a balanced diet. (There’s very little evidence for trendier interventions, like supplements, saunas, cold plunges, or the infused herbal baths that my kooky former yoga teacher used to recommend.)
If you do get flu symptoms, reach out to your doctor early — especially if you’re older, pregnant, immunocompromised, or otherwise at higher risk for complications. Prescription antiviral medications, like Tamiflu, prevent the flu virus from spreading inside your body so that your immune system can clear it. But they work best within 48 hours of symptom onset.
To be clear, you needn’t take my word on any of this; I’m just another voice in the public health cacophony! Besides, recent polling suggests that my particular voice — that is, the voice of someone who works in media — is not quite as persuasive as it used to be. (Ditto medical websites and government health agencies.)
But if you have doubts or questions about vaccines, there is someone much closer to home you can consult: Ask your doctor (or nurse or pharmacist) about the flu shot’s risks and benefits. They’re best positioned to break the science down and apply it to your health. In hindsight, mine surely would have told me to stop delaying my shot for a more convenient weekend.

WASHINGTON — U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow specialty pharmacies to produce certain peptides, a class of largely unregulated injections that have become popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers.
Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services submitted a peptides “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a posting Thursday on a government website. The plan was sent to the Office of Management and Budget, which reviews federal rules and regulations with the potential for significant economic impact.
HHS officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Peptides are the building blocks of more complex proteins, triggering hormones inside the body needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.
But the ones at issue here haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. Nevertheless, they have gained a foothold among Americans interested in bulking up, looking younger or boosting energy. Those uses are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration and most of the data on peptides comes from animal studies.
Before joining the administration, Kennedy publicly declared that “FDA’s war” on peptides and other wellness products would soon end.
After becoming health secretary, Kennedy said U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans were increasingly turning to “gray market” peptides made in China and other countries. Those products remain widely available for purchase via online platforms like TikTok.
The White House filing doesn’t give specifics of the new policy, but two people familiar with the plan say it is intended to allow pharmacies to temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, a chemical promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The update is the latest indication that Kennedy and other Trump administration officials are looking to ease access to unproven products that are popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Some of the biggest MAHA figures sell peptide injections and supplements.
The FDA previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances that are too risky to be compounded by pharmacies. Possible risks include contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth, according to the FDA.
But earlier this year, Kennedy directed the agency to reconsider a short list of chemicals that have been widely promoted by wellness influencers and fitness celebrities.
In July, a panel of external FDA advisers recommended the agency drop its restrictions on six of the seven peptides put before them. That recommendation went against the scientific conclusion of FDA’s staff scientists, who reiterated that none of the peptides had been studied enough to establish their safety and effectiveness.
The new policy sent to the White House would essentially assure compounding pharmacies — specialty businesses that mix customized medications that aren’t available from traditional drugmakers — that they won’t be targeted for producing certain peptides, according to the people familiar with the plan. That approach, known as enforcement discretion, allows the FDA to selectively choose to not enforce some of its own regulations.
Formally adding the peptides to FDA’s list of drugs that are safe for compounding would require federal rulemaking, a process that could take years and involves multiple rounds of public comment. It was not immediately clear if the administration still plans to pursue that process.
The proposal was quickly praised online by some Kennedy allies who sell peptides.
“This is huge,” Brigham Buhler, a wellness clinic operator who sells peptides through an online service, posted on X. “This isn’t about whether you’re for or against peptides. It’s about whether you’re for or against MEDICAL FREEDOM.”
The panel of outside experts that met in July was selected by Kennedy’s health department and included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers and Noom. Both companies recently announced plans to offer peptides to their customers if the federal government eases access. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth $2 billion to $3 billion.

For entrepreneur Akhila Vijayaraghavan, whey has always been a convenient way to get 100-120 grams of protein every day. “I train regularly, so it was an easy addition to my routine and helped me consistently hit my protein intake,” she says. This is why she couldn’t help but notice how much whey prices have increased over the last few months “I understand that there are broader supply and import issues behind the increase, particularly because India is so heavily dependent on imported whey. But for a consumer, the result is pretty simple: something that used to be an everyday purchase suddenly feels expensive,” she says.
For instance, a kilogram of True Basics and Whole Truth whey concentrate, which once cost around ₹2500 last year, has gone up to around ₹3500, a clear leap of nearly ₹1000, points out Akhila. Other brands aren’t far behind, either. Optimum Nutrition, the protein brand associated with numerous elite athletes, including Neeraj Chopra, Rishabh Pant, and Priya Punia, is currently pricing 4 kg of its Gold Standard 100% Whey Protein at ₹17,649, while the same amount of MuscleBlaze’s Biozyme Performance Whey is ₹13,999, an over 20% jump from last year, when they were about ₹15,000 and a little over ₹10,000 respectively.
Several forces
According to Vijay P, operations and procurement manager at Chennai-based OMG Labs, a functional nutrition brand offering both whey and plant-based protein products, this sudden hike is not the result of a single event, but of several forces coming together. Though India has a large dairy industry, we still do not produce enough whey for the protein supplement industry because much of our dairy processing focusses on products like milk, curd, paneer, and ghee rather than large-scale cheese production, Vijay explains. “Whey is mainly obtained as a by-product of cheese manufacturing, and because domestic availability is limited, we depend significantly on imports.” This means that when there is a shortage or price increase in the international market, it directly affects the Indian market, says Vijay.
“Freight costs, currency fluctuations and other import-related costs also add to the final prices,” he says. For instance, whey isolate prices, which were ₹2,200 per kilogram exclusive of GST in December last year, now cost around ₹3,400. “Apart from the whey, we also have to account for the flavours, packaging, other raw materials, labour and manufacturing costs, which have pushed the overall finished product cost to ₹4,200-5,000 from ₹3,000-36,000, depending on quantity and customers.”
The price spike also stems from a significant increase in demand for dietary protein that current supply just can’t meet. “We are going through a protein bubble right now where everyone is talking about it, so everyone is aware of and looking for protein,” says Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath.
Given that the Indian diet is notoriously protein-deficient, most of us may need a scoop or two of a protein supplement to get the ideal amount of protein, “about 1.25 to 1.75 grams of protein per kilo per day,” says Raj, pointing out that our meals consist largely of carbohydrates, fat, and some vegetables. Even though most Indians do eat meat — a recent National Family Health Survey (NFHS) found that 70-80% consume meat, fish, poultry, and eggs — for many of us, it does not happen regularly enough to meet daily protein needs. “In India, a non-vegetarian is essentially a vegetarian who eats a little bit of meat, so we still rely on vegetarian protein sources,” says Raj, the co-founder of The Quad and founder of The Slow Burn Method, a sustainable weight-loss coaching programme.
Additionally, while other new protein options exist in the market, for instance, functional dairy products like Greek yoghurt and protein milk, gram for gram, even with the increase in costs, “it roughly costs you the same amount of money as whey (if it is a concentrate or blend, isolate is a little more), around 6-7 rupees per gram of protein,” he says.
That is why people like Santosh Raghavan, an entrepreneur also based in Chennai, prefer whey protein to hit their daily goals. Given that he does not cook meat at home, “whey gives me the best protein-to-calorie ratio, allowing me room to eat other whole foods too. It is also convenient post-workout since I can have it immediately for recovery and absorption, without needing to wait for a meal to be prepared,” he says. And yes, he also likes the supplement’s taste. “It helps me think I have had some dessert, which is great for a guy like me, with a sweet tooth.”
The rise in whey prices, however, has influenced his choices considerably, he says. “I used to be loyal to a couple of brands, but now I have become brand agnostic. I just look at the label and pick up what is affordable,” says Santosh, who has also experimented with vegan protein, “which didn’t work for me,” and fermented yeast protein, “which I found decent.”
Options and opportunities
This trepidation among long-time whey users seems common, as Aditi Mammen Gupta, the co-founder of plant-based protein powder brand Origin Nutrition, points out. Earlier, people who used whey regularly often found the transition difficult, “but the thing is, plant protein was very different. Now, with new technologies and processes, plant protein has become much better in terms of taste, texture, mixability...everything really,” she says, pointing out that skyrocketing whey prices have led to “a lot of people shifting to plant protein. They seem to be quite happy with plant, especially when they discover that when they stick to it for a while, they feel a lot better.” As a business, given this shift, Origin is all set to expand its product range, says Aditi, who believes, “I think it is a really exciting time to be in the plant protein space.”
While rising whey prices will likely push more people to try affordable, equally effective plant- or yeast-based options, the consensus is that whey will continue to have a strong user base. “Whey still has strong demand because it is well established in the fitness and sports nutrition market,” says Vijay, while Sahil Kukreja feels that whey offers distinct advantages that justify the premium. “Whey provides all nine essential amino acids, is highly digestible, and is naturally rich in leucine, which helps stimulate muscle protein synthesis. That makes it an efficient protein source, particularly when someone wants a substantial protein serving in a relatively small volume,” says the co-founder of The Func Lab in Mumbai, a functional nutrition start-up that manufactures whey, plant protein, and electrolytes.
As the whey conversation goes beyond sports nutrition, it is now also being used in everyday beverages, snacks, and foods. “Healthy ageing and weight management are expanding the consumer base, while GLP-1 usage adds to this demand because reduced appetite makes getting adequate protein more challenging,” says Sahil, adding that he would, however, be careful not to attribute the entire price increase to GLP-1s.
But Sahil feels that the whey protein shortage challenge may also be an opportunity for the domestic industry to strengthen whey recovery and processing capacity. “Sustained whey premiums will also encourage innovation in plant proteins and other protein sources. That requires investment in collection, quality systems, and specialised processing — not just higher milk production,” he says.
Vijay, too, agrees that the crisis could prove a “strategic opportunity” for India to build a stronger domestic whey ecosystem. “Indian dairy and nutrition companies are moving in this direction, with major players investing in whey and value-added dairy products. This could reduce our exposure to international supply disruptions and foreign exchange movement.” However, given that capacity-building takes time, for the time being, “whey protein is likely to remain a strategically important and relatively expensive ingredient for the Indian nutrition industry.”
And despite rising costs, whey remains the preferred option for consumers like Akhila because of its familiarity, taste, texture, and convenience. “I know it works well for me as a practical way to get more protein,” she says. What has changed, however, is how often she turns to it, cycling it with other protein sources, including fish, meat, eggs and low-fat paneer, “because the price makes daily use harder to justify. At the current prices, I am much more conscious about when I actually need it, rather than automatically having it every day.”
