Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Rubio urges restraint over Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions, civilians killed
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is calling for de-escalation in the Horn of Africa amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia
NAIROBI, Kenya -- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called for de-escalation in the Horn of Africa amid fighting in northern Ethiopia and heightened tensions with neighboring Eritrea.
Rubio spoke by phone with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Wednesday, urging dialogue under a peace deal agreed between Ethiopia and Eritrea in 2018. He said the region could not tolerate more conflict, according to a statement from the State Department.
Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region in recent weeks has effectively shattered a 2022 peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war. Ethiopia has accused Eritrean troops of occupying parts of its territory, while Eritrea condemned Ethiopia for what it called a declaration of war.
Human Rights Watch has received reports of civilians killed and injured by shelling in southern Tigray, Laetitia Bader, the group’s deputy Africa director, told The Associated Press in an interview Tuesday.
She said shelling also forced some health facilities to close and called for independent monitoring, restored communications and safe humanitarian access. Her account did not identify who carried out the shelling.
Near the border, a resident reported that Eritrean soldiers withdrew Monday from Fatsi, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the Ethiopian border town of Zalambessa.
“The last time I saw Eritrean soldiers was when they left late this morning,” Hayelom Gebretsadkan, a three-wheeled taxi driver from Zalambessa, told the AP on Monday. He said the soldiers headed toward the border and there was no active fighting in Fatsi. Later that day, he said Ethiopian federal forces had moved into the town.
In a letter to the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos accused Eritrea of deploying troops across the border and said Ethiopia was taking measures in self defense. He did not specify those measures, identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting the allegations. The AP could not independently verify the claims.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urged the council to condemn what he called a “deplorable declaration of war” by Ethiopia. His response did not confirm or deny the alleged troop crossings.
Rubio told Abiy in their call that “all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions.”
The dispute also reflects tensions over Abiy’s pursuit of access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.
The countries’ armies fought together against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front during the 2020-2022 war, which caused about 500,000 civilian deaths from violence, famine and the collapse of health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium.
Last week government-allied fighters entered Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, after the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front announced its withdrawal. Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to Mekelle on Sunday after suspending all flights there for days.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.

Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.

"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."

I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

A year-long celebration of renowned clinician, teacher, and humanitarian, the late K.V. Thiruvengadam will kick off in his centenary year on Sunday (October 11, 2026). The celebrations, in memory of Prof. Thiruvengadam’s extraordinary impact on medicine both in Chennai and beyond, will focus on restoring the art of listening to the patient, examining at the bedside, thinking before ordering a test, and finally, and dwelling on the fundamental question of what it means to be a good physician in an age of extraordinary technology.
K. Vardachari Thiruvengadam, fondly known as KVT, was born in 1926. He graduated from Government Stanley Medical College in 1950 and taught for 31 years both at his alma mater and at Madras Medical College, and subsequently at private institutions. His core areas of specialty were chest medicine, allergies and infectious diseases. His career coincided with a period when medicine was rapidly expanding, but his students remember that he did not teach bedside examination as a ceremonial ritual — he taught it as a way of thinking, listening to the patient, and asking the right questions.
Prof. KVT was a scientist as well as a clinician. He received formal training in chest diseases in the U.K., under the Colombo Plan. He published nearly 100 papers in national and international journals. Among the many areas of his research were chikungunya fever, neurological complications following influenza and amoebiasis. He also investigated traditional medicines in allergic lung and skin diseases. He worked for decades in the government system, among the poorest in society, and believed that government service could achieve extraordinary things when doctors had the willingness to serve. For him, medicine was a social responsibility.
Enduring legacy
Prof. KVT’s awards and recognitions were numerous, and included the Padma Shri in 1981 and the Dr. B.C. Roy Award for Eminent Medical Teacher, alongside multiple other distinctions. But perhaps the most enduring aspect of his legacy is in the number of students who remember him and his teachings and went on to become teachers and leaders themselves, committing to his principle of what you learn and experience must be passed on to the next generation.
The centenary year celebration’s objective is not merely to celebrate him, but to translate his philosophy into medical education. The commemoration is not an argument against technology, but an argument against technology without context, and for the need for human clinical reasoning to be paramount.
The proposed celebration aims to take to medical students and postgraduate doctors the importance of history-taking, clinical examination, clinical reasoning and their role not only in diagnosis and management, but also in medical research.
On October 31, the third Prof. K.V. Thiruvengadam Memorial Oration will be delivered at Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, by S.R. Chandra, on ‘The Patient Speaks, the Doctor Thinks and the Research Begins’, alongside a national conference on movement disorders.

BOSTON — Three former Food and Drug Administration chiefs lit into the Trump administration Wednesday, criticizing the now former FDA officials who oversaw a massive staffing exodus and robbed the agency of institutional knowledge that will take years to restore.
“DOGE will go down as one of the biggest disasters in American history,” Rob Califf, former FDA commissioner under Presidents Obama and Biden, said during the STAT Summit, referring to the Elon Musk-led initiative that conducted mass layoffs of government employees. The DOGE cuts of 3,500 workers preceded a larger staff exodus under the tumultuous leadership of former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who resigned in May. White House official Heidi Overton has since been nominated to replace Makary, though she has yet to face a Senate confirmation vote.
Califf’s sharp tone was echoed by Scott Gottlieb, who served as commissioner for part of the first Trump administration, and Ned Sharpless, who was acting commissioner towards the end of the first Trump administration. Sharpless called the cuts “arbitrary” and said that the companies he works with as co-founder of Jupiter BioVentures often now find themselves in meetings with more junior and less experienced drug and medical device reviewers.
“You lost a lot of institutional memory,” Gottlieb added.
The panelists offered some optimism, however. The former officials said the agency may be turning a new leaf with departures of certain high-profile officials, who they did not name, but include Makary and former top drug and device regulators Vinay Prasad and Tracy Beth Høeg.
“I think the sowers of chaos came and went,” Califf said. Gottlieb, in particular, praised Kyle Diamantas, the agency’s top food regulator who is now acting commissioner, and FDA’s policy lead Grace Graham, who he said are encouraging the agency to get “back to the basics.”
“Now we have, I think, sensible leadership that’s doing smart things in the organization. I think things have gotten back to people feeling confident that the regulatory agency is making rational decisions,” Gottlieb said.
But even with new leadership, the former officials warned that rebuilding the agency will take time. They advised Overton, if confirmed, to focus not just on rehiring staff (which the agency has already started), but on reassuring officials that they will be protected from political meddling or further firings.
“Recruit, support, and defend the workforce,” Gottlieb said. “That will bring them back.”
They also offered advice on how to restore trust in federal agencies, a top-of-mind topic for public health officials since the Covid-19 pandemic. Sharpless lamented “errors” made in public communication by federal officials on vaccines during the pandemic that linger today.
“During the pandemic, number one is, don’t politicize a vaccine, and, you know, that didn’t last very long,” he said.
Califf and Gottlieb more pointedly addressed health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long history of sowing distrust in vaccines. Since becoming Health and Human Services secretary, Kennedy has aggressively tried to reform existing vaccine policy. Within the FDA, that has included pushing for renewed reviews of vaccine safety and efficacy, including post-market surveillance. Last year, when Makary was still commissioner, the FDA added safety warnings to mRNA Covid-19 vaccines about a rare heart inflammation side effect.
Kennedy “is just actively still eroding public confidence in these issues,” Califf said. “It’s going to be hard to overcome that until he’s moved on to some other job.” Gottlieb added that he had been critical of Kennedy since his nomination, which he said resulted in him needing to hire extra personal security for his safety.
But Califf also said that distrust in federal health agencies goes beyond Kennedy and reflects the frustration Americans have with high health care costs.
“If I would just get one biotech exec to say you know what, our drugs are too expensive,” Califf said. “You just never hear that and you know you wonder why people are upset and going to other sources of information.”
At the same time, all three urged the FDA to focus on its core mission, rather than trying to tackle some of these policy issues.
It is not in the FDA’s mandate, Sharpless said, to change drug prices or address vaccine hesitancy, but rather work in statute to prioritize safe and effective medicine.
“And if it sticks to its sort of statutory role, it’ll be fine,” he said.

Pentagon will not livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter: Trump
U.S. president made the announcement on social media
U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice-President JD Vance said he wouldn't watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But, he continued, "any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."
The Pentagon has said Hasan's execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose."
The announcement earlier this month from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan's execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.
It also came as capital punishment already faced renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived an execution attempt by Tennessee that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalization.
The Pentagon on Thursday declined to elaborate beyond Trump's statement.

Livestream decision backlash
Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.
But he continued: "Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration's decision to livestream Hasan's execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered."
Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, in Louisiana, voiced similar sentiments.
For his part, the U.S. president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth's announcement that it would be public.
"Well, they're making a determination about that," Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream.
As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: "He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
The cancellation comes less than three weeks before elections to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress, as voters increasingly register disapproval of Trump's policies in opinion polls.
Sen. John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called the cancellation "the right move" in a statement.
13 killed in Fort Hood shooting
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, at a military base in Fort Hood, Texas.
An Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, Hasan walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment.
He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, but it's not clear whether or not he will. An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment by Reuters.
The U.S. military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since the Second World War. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

In a move aimed at addressing a long-standing policy gap, the Department of Expenditure under the finance ministry has directed all ministries and departments to conduct a comprehensive review of government employees’ pay fixation orders, service records and pension-related details four years before retirement. The aim is to prevent excess payments from being detected too late for recovery, two government officials said.
The move follows a large number of proposals received by the department seeking waivers from the recovery of excess payments made to government employees due to incorrect pay fixation, increments and benefits under the Assured Career Progression (ACP) and Modified Assured Career Progression (MACP) schemes.
The new norms make compliance mandatory and provide for accountability in cases of failure. Heads of offices have also been asked to ensure that service records, qualifying service, salary details and other pension-related information are verified before pension papers are sent to the accounts office.
The development assumes significance given India’s 3.65 million civilian central government employees and 3.39 million pensioners, according to data provided by Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary in a written reply to the Rajya Sabha on 25 March 2025.
The Union government’s expenditure on pensions and other retirement benefits rose 12.3% to ₹3.46 trillion in FY25 from ₹3.08 trillion in FY24, according to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG). Defence pensions accounted for 45.57% of the total outgo in FY25, followed by civil pensions at 33.57%.
Ministries and departments have also been asked to establish monitoring mechanisms to track compliance and periodically review audit and verification records, particularly for employees nearing retirement. However, both officials declined to disclose how many waiver proposals had been received.
Queries sent to the spokesperson of the finance ministry and the secretaries of the Department of Expenditure and the Department of Posts remained unanswered till press time.
According to the first of the two officials cited above, the new instructions were issued after consultation with the Controller General of Accounts.
“Now, government departments must check pay fixation orders issued after an employee’s promotion, annual increment, financial upgradation or other pay revision within three months of the order being issued or by the end of that financial year,” this official said.
Earlier, pay fixation orders were not subject to a specific mandatory audit timeline, although departments were responsible for ensuring that employees’ pay was fixed correctly.
The new instructions aim to detect errors earlier and prevent excess payments from accumulating before they are identified.
Experts’ view
Experts said the move was a step in the right direction.
“Timely scrutiny of pay fixation orders can help detect discrepancies before they lead to substantial excess payments, while clear accountability will encourage departments to strengthen their internal checks and financial controls,” said Arun Kumar Jha, former Indian Economic Services officer and chancellor of the National Institute of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, Ranchi.
“The new guidelines should strengthen financial discipline across government departments and help identify pay fixation errors at an early stage. Regular audits and clear accountability will be key to preventing excess payments and ensuring greater accuracy in salary and pension calculations,” said DP Majhi, former director of the Dr Ambedkar Foundation, an autonomous body under the ministry of social justice and empowerment.
Service verification
The revised norms also mandate periodic verification of employees’ qualifying service under Rule 30 of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 2021, with any discrepancies in service records to be rectified promptly.
Rule 30 of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 2021, refers to the verification of a government employee’s qualifying service to determine the service period that counts towards pension benefits.
To ensure compliance, the government has made it mandatory for the Internal Audit Wing or the concerned Pay and Accounts Office to certify that pay fixation orders have been checked, the second official said.
“If errors or excess payments are found after the pay fixation orders have been certified, the concerned Pay and Accounts Office and/or the Chief Controller or Controller of Accounts will be held responsible,” this official said.
“Once a certificate confirming the correctness of pay has been issued, no recovery of any nature can be made from the employee for the period covered by the certificate. Any loss to the exchequer arising from incorrect pay fixation may instead be recovered from the office that approved the certificate.”

Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
- Published
Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".
He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.
Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.
The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

Brazil’s Senate has approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours without cutting salaries
SAO PAULO -- Brazil’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment Wednesday to reduce the country's maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours without a salary cut, a move backed by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who hopes it will boost his standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the Oct. 25 presidential runoff.
Lula is expected to sign the shorter workweek into law next week after the measure passed the Senate in two rounds of voting with the same result: 75 to 1 out of 81 members. The sole vote against it came from former Vice President Hamilton Mourao, who served under President Jair Bolsonaro.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who opposed the initiative until early this week, voted for it remotely as he campaigned in southern Brazil. Analysts and politicians say his allies in the Senate stopped blocking the popular move so he wouldn't be hurt in his neck-to-neck race against Lula.
The amendment gives businesses 14 months to adopt the shorter workweek, which was a key sticking point in the negotiations. Many business leaders and lawmakers wanted the changes to be made gradually over 10 years.
The constitutional amendment establishes a 40-hour weekly limit and two rest days without reducing pay. More than 37 million workers could benefit from the new rules, according to the government.
Brazil's president was quick to celebrate the decision.
“Today is a day to celebrate a historic achievement for millions of workers,” Lula said in a statement. “This means having more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, take care of yourself, and enjoy life. Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve to have time to live.”
Many senators chanted Lula's name after the vote, while Bolsonaro supporters quickly left the chamber.
“Didn't I say this was going to work?” Davi Alcolumbre, the president of Brazil's Senate, told a leading senator of Lula's Workers' Party after the result. He timed the decision to take place between the first and the second round of the election, which benefits the incumbent.
Recent polls indicated widespread support for the measure, despite the opposition of many business owners. Many Bolsonaro allies said in their remarks they see the cost of living going up because of the new schedule.
Lula has taken a number of steps in recent days to shore up support before the runoff, including new fuel tax cuts, the extension of existing subsidies, the pledge to pardon debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses with the federal government, the decision to block signal for cellphones around prisons, and a boost in payments of a welfare program for university students.
The change in the workweek system is regarded as the pinnacle of those initiatives.
Bolsonaro, who bested Lula by 2.2 million votes in the first-round election, reversed his long-standing opposition to the measure on Tuesday. He previously advocated for a more flexible payment-by-the-hour regime, called for individual negotiations between employees and employers and repeatedly called the legislation election-motivated.
Hours after announcing his support for the change, Bolsonaro told business owners that the new Congress, where his party could reach a simple majority with other allied parties come February, could review the measure, local newspaper O Globo reported.
The approval of the reduced workweek was a theme in dozens of pro-Lula protests taking place nationwide since last week. Some celebrated the Senate vote on Wednesday in streets of Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo.
“We needed the people out on the streets,” said Lunna Normande, 23, during a protest with hundreds of people in Rio. “We will continue to be on the streets until this inhumane work week ends.”
Lula's government has been working on the proposal since last year. “Any change made in an election year can be considered an electoral measure,” said Carla Beni, an economist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation, a think-tank and university.
People working in the shadow economy, such as freelancers and delivery drivers, will not be affected by the new legislation.
The momentum behind this reform reflects a growing trend across Latin America. Neighboring countries such as Chile and Colombia have recently enacted landmark legislation to shorten their respective workweeks to 40 and 42 hours, which emboldened Brazilian labor groups to seek the same.
In February, Mexican lawmakers approved a proposal by President Claudia Sheinbaum to trim the 48-hour workweek. Working hours will be shortened gradually to a 40-hour workweek by 2030.
Chile in 2023 passed the so-called 40-Hour Law, which reduced its workweek to 40 hours as of last year. It applies to all workers under Chile’s Labor Code, without reducing pay.
But Argentina has bucked that trend under President Javier Milei and may extend its 48-hour workweek.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the protest and detained several protesters, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. A Delhi court ordered their release on 11 October 2026, while the Supreme Court intervened over restrictions on public movement and allegations of unlawful detention. On 15 October 2026, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court, stating that police imposed restrictions at 45 Metro stations (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming it shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over a CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over the CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: The viral video dates back to 16 October 2025 and shows a heated exchange between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and advocate Mahesh Tiwari, not a confrontation with the Chief Justice of India over the CJP protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. The exchange occurred during court proceedings concerning a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues. The Jharkhand High Court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari, which were later dropped after the court accepted his unconditional apology. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals from October 2025. According to these reports, a heated exchange took place between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and Advocate Mahesh Tiwari on 16 October 2025, following which the court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari. The proceedings were being streamed live when the incident occurred.
The incident began when a lawyer sought relief for his client, a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues of Rs 1.30 lakh. Justice Kumar questioned the manner in which the lawyer was seeking relief and explained how the matter should be argued in accordance with court ethics. He also said that the Bar Council chairman should take note of the lawyer’s conduct. Tiwari, who had been standing at the back of the courtroom, then joined the argument, stepped forward and pointed at the judge.
A report published by NDTV on 23 January 2026 stated that the Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, criticised Advocate Mahesh Tiwari for challenging the criminal contempt proceedings initiated against him by the Jharkhand High Court. The Supreme Court asked the High Court to take a sympathetic view if Tiwari apologised. Subsequently, a report published by The Indian Express on 19 February 2026 stated that the Jharkhand High Court dropped the contempt proceedings after accepting Tiwari’s unconditional apology. The High Court observed that an advocate with more than 40 years of legal practice was expected to exercise greater restraint and was as much an officer of the court as the presiding judge.
To sum up, an unrelated courtroom exchange video is shared, showing a lawyer confronting the CJI over the CJP protest against Gyanesh Kumar.

Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.
Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.
Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.
Eradicating rats and replacing coconut plantations with native forests and brush could give some atolls a “fighting chance” to persist at the rate of sea-level rise expected toward the end of the century with about 2° Celsius (3.6° Fahrenheit) of warming, Graham said.
The findings provide more evidence that nature restoration can buffer the impacts of global warming. For example, restoring wetlands and forests dampens swings between wet and dry spells, reducing flood and fire hazards. Restoration efforts can also slow global warming by supporting natural carbon storage.
On the 28 atoll islands Graham’s team studied, strengthening the dynamic system of seabirds, native vegetation, and reef systems starts a virtuous cycle, as ecosystems become better able to sustain themselves and build resilience to growing impacts.

Stand-up comedians have always had a reverence for what they like to call a “comic’s comic” — a fellow comedian who works with such distilled purity and edge, diving head-first into the gnarly metaphysics of comedy, that the comics end up worshipping him more than the public does. (He’s the stand-up-comedy equivalent of an ultimate cool indie-rock cult band.) Gilbert Gottfried was a comic’s comic. So are Larry David and Doug Stanhope and Maria Bamford. And Norm Macdonald was one too, except that as you watch Judd Apatow’s juicy and haunting documentary “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald,” you realize that there was a special thing about him. He was a comic’s comic…who everyone else loved too.
As the movie demonstrates, Macdonald’s credentials as a comic’s comic were unassailable. We see his very first network television appearance on May 9, 1990, on “Late Night with David Letterman,” where he did a bit about the devil commanding someone to kill his family and chop them into bits and stuff the pieces into a duffel bag. (Then the killer learns that the devil is a friend who was kidding.) He speaks in that familiar halting deadpan; he already knows how to draw the audience into his head.
Popular on Variety
On “Saturday Night Live,” where Macdonald, starting in 1993, spent four seasons as one of the all-time great hosts of Weekend Update, he returned, over and over, with a bluntly obsessive fixation that couldn’t be denied, to the subject of O.J. Simpson, and to the fact that Simpson had murdered his wife. Why was this funny? Because every time Macdonald made a joke of it, his assertion of O.J.’s guilt was a way of tapping back into the shocking unreality of it. His every O.J. joke had the effect of a giddy slap. He would not relent, and that wound up getting him fired from “Saturday Night Live” (Don Ohlmeyer, the president of NBC’s West Coast division who was responsible for axing Macdonald, was O.J. Simpson’s best friend). Now that’s a comic’s comic thing to do.
On “SNL,” and in his legendary litany of late-night talk-show appearances, and in his stand-up routines, Norm Macdonald had an oxymoronic quality — a slightly disconnected aggression, where he would zero in on a topic, and a joke, that he knew would be prickly, and that might take him “over the line,” but he couldn’t help himself. He had to say the naughty thing, to blurt out the forbidden. Telling that joke would be a catharsis; it would be comedy. Not telling it would be defeat.
At times, he had a streak of Andy Kaufman’s antisocial hostility, as if comedy was his way of testing both himself and the audience, seeing what they would accept, and seeing if they would accept him. A strange thing that emerges in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is that Macdonald was a compulsive liar, in both his stand-up act and his life, the two planes of existence sometimes entwined around the same deception. That’s part of why he always seemed a bit of a space cadet. You could never really tell whether he meant what he was saying. We learn that he never went to high school…and also that he did (and graduated when he was 14)…that he never went to college…but actually did as well. On the eve of the pandemic, he described himself to an audience as “a young 68” (he was 60 at the time). He also describes himself, to Larry King, as “deeply closeted,” and when King asks if that means he’s coming out as gay, he says no, he’s straight…and then indicates that claiming to be straight is an expression of how closeted he is. You can hear Andy Kaufman chortling in his theater-of-the-absurd heaven.
Yet the thing about Norm Macdonald is that he executed all this with a smiling charm and a winsome agreeability that made him irresistible to a wide swath of fans. He wasn’t a prickly punk — more like a transgressive Teddy bear. In the early days, including the “SNL” years that made him famous, he was quite handsome, with a lean face and twinkly eyes and dimples and a coif of curly hair and a killer grin that made him look like the slightly goofy cousin of Paul Newman. Fifteen years before Norm Macdonald, Chevy Chase had been the first break-out superstar of “Saturday Night Live,” transforming his own Weekend Update quizzicality into big-screen celebrity, and he accomplished this not because he was a great actor but because he had a sublime detachment coupled with tall preppie good looks that he used ironically. His handsomeness was part of the joke, as well as the cushion for it.
Macdonald, though, didn’t use his looks in that way; they just kind of existed alongside the bratty edge of his comedy. And so when he was booted from “SNL,” he acted like he’d been kicked off a cliff. He was still out there in the culture, but he floundered around, and this, as the documentary captures, was related to his strange and slippery personality: his compulsive sincerity (which meant that he didn’t quite know how to package himself), his compulsive put-ons (which meant that he was actually scared to show who he was), his compulsive insecurity (which meant that he didn’t truly believe in himself as a star), mixed with an element of self-sabotage (his way of confirming all those anxieties about himself).
After all of that, “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is rooted in what a beloved comedian Norm MacDonald was, and still is. In the opening montage, several people, like Howard Stern, reference the rabbit hole you can get into just by going onto YouTube and watching clips of Macdonald on late-night talk shows. He had countless appearances that were gems, because he always invested his talk-show time with a spark of danger. He couldn’t just be a straight shooter, but he had to make his put-ons feel real. At times, he was as philosophical as Lenny Bruce — but Bruce talked about religion only to mock it, whereas Macdonald, at one point, reveals that he’s a Christian who’s a true believer. (This is a man who would introduce his sidekick as someone who jerked off punks for $15 under a bridge.) It’s all part of his mystery.
The movie is spanked along by clips of Letterman, Jerry Seinfeld, Conan O’Brien, and Dave Chappelle, and Apatow, working with the editor Jake Hostetter, assembles the comedy snippets in an entrancing way, so that we feel the underground sprawl of Macdonald’s career. He could be a great impressionist (his Bob Dole on “SNL” may have helped turn the 1996 presidential election; his Quentin Tarantino was inspired). He kept doing stand-up, but didn’t require the comedy stage to be great; just talking to Jane Fonda on his video podcast, “Norm Macdonald Live,” he was insanely funny. We see his appearance change quite a bit over the years, as he evolves into a puffier version of himself, something that happened in part because he spent his last nine years secretly fighting leukemia. (He died in 2021.) Yet the audience stayed with him — at least, more than the entertainment industry did.
Macdonald wasn’t the first “incorrect” comedian to run afoul of the comedy police, but it felt like he was the first such comic of a certain day and age (namely, ours). He should have had his own late-night talk show, but when he learned that he was up for one — and that he had been passed over for the yuppie dullard Craig Kilborn — that was a sign that his comedy was ruffling feathers. At the same time, he cultivated incorrectness in a way that could be mindless. When he went on “The View” and said that Bill Clinton was guilty of “murder,” he claimed that he was just doing a bit, but since the “bit” fed into right-wing conspiracy theory, it seemed like an episode of sour derangement. And when he defended Roseanne Barr, after her racist tweet in 2018, he did it out of loyalty (one of his first gigs was as a writer for “Roseanne”) but in a tone-deaf way, as if what she’d said in her tweet was some trivial joke. (It was not; it was egregious.) All of this fed into the perfect shitstorm that was The Decline of Norm Macdonald.
We pretend that comedy is just fun, a means to an end — the end being to make you laugh. But the few who are chosen to be “comic’s comics” occupy that rarefied stratosphere because they know that comedy is more than laughter, and that laughter is more than we give it credit for. You laugh for a lot of reasons, but one of those reasons can be when an idea goes off in your head like a small bomb. That’s why comedy can tickle your soul, snap you back to life, cleanse you. And that’s the kind of comedian Norm Macdonald was. He had a devilish gleam, but he provoked a laughter that lifted you up, landing on the side of the angels.

Cold weather and high prices could flip the Senate
Bad news for the GOP in Maine and Alaska.
Throughout his second term, President Donald Trump has saddled his party with no shortage of political liabilities — from the mass pardons of January 6 convictions to ICE killings of US citizens to questionable Reflecting Pool redesign choices.
For voters, however, there is one stain on Trump’s record more unsightly than all the rest: his failure to reduce Americans’ cost of living.
As the midterm campaign enters its home stretch, Americans’ expenses are rising — and the GOP’s prospects are consequently dimming.
Last month, consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than they had been one year earlier, according to a Consumer Price Index report released on Wednesday. That represented an acceleration in the inflation rate, one driven largely by skyrocketing fuel prices: Gasoline was 9.1 percent more expensive in September than it had been in August. As a result, America’s average real wage has fallen by 44 cents since January.
In less than three weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, this newsletter is partnering with our colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November.
Last week, we tackled the data center backlash. And this week, we’re digging into affordability.
Go a little deeper
These upward trends in prices aren’t lost on voters. In a recent Pew Research survey, just 21 percent of Americans said economic conditions were “excellent” or “good” — while 65 percent said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse.
The high cost of living is weighing on Republican candidates in all battleground races. Maine provides just one example of how potent the issue could prove on Election Day.
From one angle, the state’s Senate race might seem like a gimme for Democrats. Kamala Harris won Maine by nearly 7 points in 2024. Thus, in 2026 — when Democrats are poised to win in a national landslide — one might expect the party to easily triumph.
But Republican incumbent Susan Collins is an unusually formidable foe. The race has been a dead heat, with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson leading by just 2 points in a recent Suffolk University poll.
Fortunately for Jackson, Mainers’ energy bills are expected to soar in the campaign’s final weeks, plausibly increasing voters’ appetite for change in the process.
Maine is America’s second coldest state and unusually reliant on oil for home heat. As autumn advances, its residents will use more heating oil, thereby driving up both their personal bills and market prices. Thanks to the global energy crunch, a gallon of such fuel is already nearly twice as expensive as it was this time last year.
Jackson has been hitting Collins on the issue relentlessly. That could put a chill in Collins’s reelection odds — and thus, the GOP’s hopes of retaining Senate control.
➨ Other races to watch:
- Similar dynamics are playing out in perennially icy Alaska, where Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has hammered incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan for his complicity in sky-high diesel prices, which many Alaskans use for home heat.
- In Ohio’s Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown has tried to pin rising electricity bills on Republican Sen. Jon Husted, due to his support for data center development.
- And in Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has attacked his Republican rival, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, for supporting “this disastrous war in Iran that’s driving up our costs.”
In other news
- A brief ceasefire ends: Ukrainian drones attacked a Russian oil refinery early Thursday, days after Trump demanded both Russia and Ukraine halt such attacks.
- Execution livestream canceled: Trump canceled a plan to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad.
- On the podcast: A recent rash of violence between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis threatens to destabilize the region — and make the Iran war much larger. Listen to the whole thing here.
One link for later
Rethink confidence. Research shows confidence is good for your job and good for your romantic prospects. Unsurprisingly, then, a whole industry has sprung up teaching people to be more confident. One writer signed up to work with a confidence coach for the first time, and ended up doubting that her self-doubt was all that bad.
Before you go…
- Did you know…there are four state laws regarding real estate and paranormal activity in the US? That’s because purported hauntings are just one of many factors that can affect home prices.
- Today’s trivia: What is the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword. Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.)
- Yesterday’s trivia: We asked which percussion instrument is famously played by Mississippi State University fans at home football games. That would be the cowbell.

Xreal's new flagship One Pro+ AR glasses offer better brightness and increased comfort
There's still no camera here, so they won't be confused for pervert specs.
Xreal just released an upgrade of its popular One Pro AR glasses. The One Pro+ is a minor refresh, but offers some welcome quality of life improvements.
First of all, it's brighter than ever before. The One Pro+ reaches 1,200 nits of peak brightness, compared to 700 nits for the standard One Pro. It also includes AI HDR upscaling tech to improve the visuals.The company has upgraded its 2D-to-3D conversion algorithm from 30Hz to 60Hz. This is for adding depth to 2D content, which is similar to the spatial imaging system available with the Apple Vision Pro.
Finally, there's a newly designed nose pad to maximize long-term comfort. The company promises this pad will improve overall stability, but not at the expense of field of view. This is actually the feature I'm most excited about because there's a huge difference between wearing AR glasses for 20 minutes and hunkering down for two or three hours of work. They tend to get uncomfortable pretty fast.
Other than that, these are still Xreal One Pro glasses. They offer the same X1 spatial computing chip and a 57-degree field of view. This is not a bad thing, as we enjoyed the original One Pro. They are great for productivity, via screen mirroring, and watching stuff. We actually said they intrigued us in ways that Meta's glasses never did.
To that end, there's one missing feature here that's a mainstay with Meta. The Xreal One Pro+ AR glasses do not have a camera, so people are unlikely to suspect you are wearing pervert glasses. Xreal's new specs are available right now and cost $600, which is the same price as last year's One Pro.

Nvidia and Apple have each pledged $25 million towards US President Donald Trump's proposed White House ballroom, as private donations for the project have reached $333 million, The Washington Post reported on Thursday.
The report raised questions about the interests of companies and wealthy individuals funding the project. The Post said the vast majority of the money had come from donors with interests before the federal government. It also reported that companies or executives of firms holding federal government contracts during Trump's second term accounted for half of the total funds raised.
Who all donated
The Adelson family, long-time financial supporters of Trump and the Republican Party, also pledged $25 million, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, according to the report. Trump himself was not listed among the donors.
The White House declined to disclose details of the donors. Spokesman Davis Ingle said the contributions came from a broad range of American companies and defended the fundraising effort, arguing that critics would also object if taxpayers were made to pay for the renovations.
Nvidia said it was proud to contribute to a nonpartisan trust serving Americans, adding that its support for the US was independent of business interests. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told The Post.
Ballroom funding draws scrutiny
The scale of the project and the administration's approach to fundraising and disclosure have attracted criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who have raised concerns about transparency, potential donor influence and compliance with established ethics and oversight practices.
Trump initially said the estimated $400 million project would be financed by him and wealthy donors. He later sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and additional security features, but the request was unsuccessful.
The planned 90,000-square-foot ballroom is intended to accommodate about 1,000 guests. Trump has said it would include bomb shelters, medical facilities and defences against drones and missiles, framing the project as a national security requirement, Reuters reported.
Opposition from preservationists
The development has also faced opposition from preservationists and other critics, who argue that Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing to make way for the structure.
In August, the US Supreme Court allowed construction to continue while Trump challenged a judicial order seeking to halt much of the development. In a dissenting opinion, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful".

The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.
The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said two Russian drones violated Romanian airspace and struck two chemical tankers, setting the ships ablaze. Rescue crews were searching for at least seven missing sailors.
“The situation in the Black Sea is serious,” he said. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Moscow claimed debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire.
Ukraine also struck back at Russia’s military, hitting four Sukhoi Su-34 fighter/bomber jets and damaging two more, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s military said it had used a Neptune cruise missile to strike an airfield in Russia’s southern Voronezh region.
“These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs,” Zelenskyy said, publishing a satellite photo of the damaged airfield.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three people and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration.
“Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” he said.
Later, the British defence secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart Pete Hegseth that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.
The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.
On Thursday, a group of US senators from both major parties sent a letter to the Pentagon demanding it investigate whether the satellite and intelligence services had been deliberately restricted, and whether the Trump administration was responsible.
“We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities,” they wrote, according to the New York Times.
The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Zelenskyy, when asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a leading critic of Zelenskyy in the US.
On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has been the subject of a number of Snopes fact checks since President Donald Trump picked him to be a part of his administration ahead of his second inauguration. Hegseth's official remarks as defense secretary, like his actions, have tended to be brash and controversial.
We've put together a collection of articles about some of the more provocative quotes attributed to Hegseth, sometimes accurately, sometimes not. The topics include rules of engagement, women's right to vote and so-called "kamikaze dolphins."
