In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

A woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.
Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.
A 43-year-old woman allegedly contaminated it with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance, a police spokesperson said on Thursday.
“The curry had been shared among employees and consumed without issue during a morning tea break,” police said.
“After the meal, the accused accessed a chemical storage shed and later entered the staff lunch room where the food was kept.”
At lunchtime, the alleged victim went to eat some more of her curry.
When she opened the container, she spotted bright green granules in the food.
“After tasting a small amount, (she) experienced numbness to her tongue,” the police spokesperson said.
It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.
Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.
She has been charged with one count of unlawful act or omission with intent to harm (endangering the life, health or safety of any person).
She is scheduled to appear before Armadale magistrates court on 5 November.
Police declined to provide further information about the relationship or the workplace.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Ukrainian forces had their access to the technology restricted this week after Trump announced a new diesel deal with Russia

Elon Musk has blamed Donald Trump for restrictions introduced on Starlink speed for members of the Ukrainian military.
The service provided by Musk’s company SpaceX provides broadband internet and has been used for government and military communications by Ukraine in the war against Russia.
The outage came amid Trump’s demands for Ukraine to completely halt long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Polish foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski accused Musk of “playing politics” on Wednesday but the tech billionaire has now denied he was involved in the decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
He had previously said that “no matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals... We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt betrayed by the decision in an interview with Piers Morgan and that the shutdown meant “people would die” as a result.
Several combat missions failed on Tuesday evening as a result of the shutdown, an adviser on military technology to Zelensky told The Guardian.
A US official told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved in the Starlink limitations.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
“This is not the right side of history,” Zelensky said on Piers Morgan Uncensored. Asked if he felt betrayed by decisions made over the last week, he said: “Really, yes.”
The outage came just as Ukraine was hit by ballistic missiles, despiteTrump’s insistence that there is an energy ceasefire in place between the countries.
Poland has said that it pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscription, which is crucial for guiding long-range drone strikes that have severely disrupted Russian logistics.
The restriction came amid Trump’s decision to lift sanctions against Russia and allow global diesel exports, with the US to buy 300,000 tons of the fuel.
He faced criticism from several corners including from the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who told Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”

The 27 Best ‘American Horror Story’ Characters, Ranked
“American Horror Story” has given audiences a lot to chew on over the years: wildly inventive themes, sadistic imagery, over-the-top performances and gleefully macabre mythology.
But arguably its greatest contribution to television since its debut in 2011 is its characters, an ever-expanding company of ill-fated spooks and kooks who rarely find a happy ending, and yet we relish in watching their descent into whatever brand of hell the series is conjuring that season. The citizens of this connected universe of horror storytelling, from creators Ryan Murphy and Brad Fulchuk, are ultimately what stitch it all together, and have proven to be the enduring draw for audiences left wanting more from their favorites.
For its 13th season, “AHS” has banked on the bedrock of those characters by dipping back into its stable of actors and their alter egos for a mashup season. The satanic-centric story has been a chaotic exercise in fan service, with varying degrees of success. When it works, there are undeniable pleasures in seeing characters thought to be done and dusted come back for one more shot at a good line reading or an uncanny interaction with someone who shares their face. Many of those characters are on this list, some elevated by the extra screen time and some demoted for disrupting a previously perfect storyline.
As “AHS” plays the hits for 13, let’s rank the best characters from the series. The following list isn’t necessarily a grading of performance, but rather character arc, impact and sheer entertainment value. It should also be noted that “AHS13” focuses almost exclusively on characters from the first eight seasons, with good reason. Even for their flaws, those characters are the series’ best work. More recent seasons were considered for this list, but frankly, “AHS” hasn’t aged all that well –– even though some of its characters have.
- Coco St. Pierre Vanderbilt (Leslie Grossman) Grossman has been making a meal out of Murphy-scripted roles since she appeared on “Popular,” his first series, as Mary Cherry, so “AHS” is better off with her among its ranks. But she doesn’t get enough credit for taking so-so characters within this world and really making them sing — or scream. Take Coco St. Pierre, a Beverly Hills-bred socialite who thinks she has survived the “Apocalypse” only to learn she is really a mind-wiped witch hidden right under the nose of the Antichrist. But her power is the ability to detect gluten, and that’s not a joke. She’s a witch who believes she has nothing to provide her coven. Rather, she functions as a supportive sister who contributes to morale as much as magic, until her time comes. Stay with us here, because in “AHS13,” Coco uses her gluten spidey sense to take down the Zodiac killer by inducing diabetic shock. None of those words have ever been spoken together before, so Coco deserves her flowers for making history.
- Montana Duke (Billie Lourd) 
	Lourd has played a number of major roles in “AHS,” chief among them Mallory, one of its most powerful, if not the most powerful, witch. But with all due respect to that character, Lourd has never been more fun than when she was trying on the bleached blonde wig of Montana Duke, the aerobics instructor turned right hand of the Night Stalker in “1984.” The second she tore down a mouthy student in her Midnight Manerobics class, we were hooked. Did she go off the rails when it was revealed she was behind some of the slashing at Camp Redwood? Sure, but to be fair, no one was innocent that season. At least she had deranged fun with it. By the end, she becomes the eternal Walmart greeter standing at the gates of the camp. Which makes sense because she’s the only one from this season we’d ever like to encounter again.
- Nora Montgomery (Lily Rabe) Among the tragedies plastering the walls of the Murder House like wallpaper, few were as gut-wrenching as that of Nora Montgomery, played in her “AHS” debut by fan-favorite Rabe. Nora’s mad doctor husband Charles (Matt Ross) built her the lavish home that would become a hellish prison for so many, and her spoiled and needy attitude didn’t exactly start it off on the right foot. Rabe’s prickly characterization of Nora as a woman who craves motherhood only to push it away when it gets tough could have been unforgivable. But she still managed to make the audience care for Nora when her son was dismembered, and again when Charles decided to Frankenstein him into a monster of reanimated horror. The bewildered Nora constantly wandering the halls, unaware she is what haunts them with the melancholy of her unfulfilled life, left a stain that still lingers.
- Miss Evers (Mare Winningham) The kindly but deranged laundress tending to the soiled sheets of the Hotel Cortez is never a leading figure in Season 5, but she benefits from “Hotel”’s talent for giving its sprawling supporting cast a taste of main character energy. Devoted to mastermind serial murderer and hotel designer Mr. March (Evan Peters), Miss Evers was a tragic figure of 1920s Los Angeles who found hope in the grand vision of her maniacal boss. Winningham had single-episode appearances in “Coven,” “Freak Show” and “Cult,” but here she is central to the understanding why the Hotel Cortez is a mecca for the lost and/or depraved. Her monologue in the finale is a beautiful evolution from willfully agreeing to March’s murder-suicide evasion of justice, to her long-awaited epiphany that an eternity spent serving an ungrateful man isn’t worth the time.
- Beverly Hope (Adina Porter) Is TV news reporter Beverly Hope a good character, or is Porter just that good of an actor? Regardless of the answer, no “AHS” list is complete without the Emmy-nominated powerhouse, and there’s no better role than the one she was nominated for. “Cult,” as a season of storytelling, is as uneven as it is heavy handed in its post-2016 election nightmare. Yet it’s hard to take your eyes off Porter’s rage-filled reporter who finds purpose in the murderous promises of Trumpster and aspiring cult leader Kai Anderson (Evan Peters). Porter found in Beverly a recognizable discontent and fury that both sides of the aisle wrestled with in the aftermath of 2016. Despite her blood-soaked misdeeds, Beverly became a somewhat sympathetic figure once she was confronted with the all-too-real disappointment people find in the idols they glorify, who break promises as quickly as they make them. Ultimately, Beverly was a hero for snuffing out Kai, even if she is the one who helped first inflate his ego.
- Agnes Mary Winstead (Kathy Bates) A decade later, who could have predicted “Roanoke” would be the most controversial season of the series? Still, it will always get credit for its creative structure, as a sharply rendered true-crime docuseries that switches halfway through to damn the actors of said series to their own nightmarish fates. At the switch, audiences meet Agnes Mary Winstead, a devoted thespian who has taken her role as the Mad Butcher of the Roanoke Colony too far and comes back to stalk the co-stars and crew that spurned her. Bates’ unhinged embrace of Agnes’ psychosis was genuinely thrilling. But it is also a rather pointed commentary on actors who disappear into their roles, showing the lonely spectrum of skill and sadness one can face when committing to the craft. Her execution by the cleaver of the real Mad Butcher was also pointed.
- Dandy Mott (Finn Wittrock) “Freak Show” was pretty clear on its stance of who you should call a freak, and that was Dandy Mott, the privileged mama’s boy whose beautiful looks masked a deep-seated evil and callous hatred for life –– human or otherwise. Wittrock’s portrayal of one of the franchise’s most vile characters is a fan favorite because Dandy was a sicko who didn’t need to be supernatural to be scary. From killing animals to robbing the world of Patti LaBelle, Dandy was a demented person with the means to explore it. Training under Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch) certainly didn’t help Dandy overcome his lethal case of only child syndrome with a dash of FOMO. But he got his due in the end, proving some evils can be curbed with old-fashioned karma and Houdini’s famous Chinese Water Torture Cell tank.
- The Countess (Lady Gaga) Getting Lady Gaga to succeed Jessica Lange as the grand high bitch (compliment!) of the “AHS” franchise, at least for the “Hotel” season, was an inspired choice. Giving her a character worthy of her gravitas and flare for the dramatic was a taller order. In hindsight, The Countess is more of a vibe than a character. She glided in and out of the shadows of the Hotel Cortez, feeding on Angelenos, tourists and the scenery as she made the dark souls of the hotel quake with fear. She was a living tribute to Gaga’s own prowess for fashion and fame, and proud embodiment of the misplaced fear she inspires in those who don’t understand her. The Countess was a vampire-ish villain, so it was OK that she was essentially there suck all the air out of any room she was in –– and Gaga delivered.
- Tate Langdon (Evan Peters) Not a single thing Tate Langdon does in “Murder House” should be commended. Even his attempt to gently ease Violet (Taissa Farmiga) into the idea of her own death is riddled with self-serving delays. Yet, Peters is able to inspire, in his first “AHS” role, a deeply complicated empathy for the last person who deserves it. Sure, Tate had a rough upbringing with less-than-desirable parents, but murdering your classmates to work out those feelings is nothing short of reprehensible. The passing of time since “Murder House” (and America’s frustrating cycle of school shootings) has only further hindered any redemptive qualities in Tate. But the fact that audiences even tried to find some means of liking him in the first place laid the groundwork for similar ill-advised character evaluations in future seasons. Tate was a trailblazer in that way, forcing those who fell under his spell to question their own tolerance for evil.
- Papa Legba (Lance Reddick) Not everyone can be the Big Bad in the “AHS” universe. Someone has to strike fear in even the darkest hearts, and Papa Legba (the late Reddick) has a knack for it. Originally summoned in “Coven,” he has the power to grant immortality in exchange for your eternal soul. He’s the Gatekeeper of the Spirit World, a job he executes with a sinister smile. Look no further than his sick sense of humor in designing a two-for-one eternal hell for enemies Marie Laveau (Angela Bassett) and Delphine LaLaurie (Bates). Reddick’s performance infused the character with a certain ie ne sais quoi no one can replicate, but after the actor’s death in 2023, Orlando Jones stepped in for Papa’s return for “AHS13”–– and did his predecessor justice.
- Moira O’Hara (Frances Conroy and Alexandra Breckenridge) “Murder House” set the tone for what this show could do, and one of the more memorable characters trapped on the fateful Los Angeles property was Conroy’s Moira O’Hara, the housekeeper cursed to dust its mantles for all eternity. Conroy gave Moira a quiet resolve that became a saving grace for Vivian Harmon (Connie Britton), who saw her as the old soul she was. Conversely, Breckenridge imbued Moira with a seductive allure when seen as the younger temptress by Ben Harmon (Dylan McDermott). Two sides of the same coin, Moira took the audience’s hand and gently walked us into this world, and for that, she will always be among our saints.
- Queenie (Gabourey Sidibe) 
	Try as they might, multiple seasons of “AHS” have attempted to extinguish the fire that is human voodoo doll Queenie, and none have been successful. A descendant of both the Salem witches and the New Orleans voodoo community, she walks in both worlds and is among the stronger connective threads of the franchise’s mythology having appeared in “Coven,” “Hotel,” “Apocalypse” and “AHS13.” A child of foster care, Queenie has clung to the family she found at Miss Robichaux’s Academy. Even when she questioned her place among them and felt the temptation of her voodoo roots, she found her way back to “Coven” leader Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson). But Queenie should be celebrated most as one of the best “AHS” scene partners. Whether it’s with her fellow witches, or tormenting the racist disembodied head of Delphine (Bates) or beating Mr. March at cards in the Hotel Cortez, she is a fiery constant in a franchise that needs it.
- Hypodermic Sally (Sarah Paulson) There is something cancerous about “Hotel,” and it is best represented by Paulson’s turn as Hypodermic Sally. As tarry and disagreeable as the drugs she injected into her veins, Sally brought a bitterness to the Cortez that could have been unpalatable. Yet, she wore viewers down to her ways as the voyeuristic jester of the hotel. She was no stranger to the pain of its story, and she often contributed to it, but there was also a lightness to her, thanks to an often side-splitting humor in her nastiness. It’s as if she found, in death, the home that eluded her in life. Plus, a fleeting scene of her cuddled up in bed lit only by the light of her phone has become a meme that embodies an entire generation of doomscollers.
- Elsa Mars (Jessica Lange) Full disclosure: Fraulein Elsa Mars moved up this list after her return in “AHS13,” simply because she made the most of her one scene. Some worried the wannabe actress never got her comeuppance after “Freak Show.” But her singular appearance as a minion of Satan, resurrected at his whim to perform for a crowd that could care less, was her own form of hell –– and it is “AHS13” at its sporadic best. Charged with throwing bad women of history into the flames of hell was an amusing ritual, but her razor-sharp disdain for Margaret Thatcher (also played impeccably by Lange) was the funniest thing this show has done in years. In her original run, the Nazi Germany survivor abandoned the outcasts who trusted her to give them a safe space in a world. Lange has long said this was her passion role for the series, and she exited stage left (for a while at least) after Elsa’s swan song. What she left behind was a stunning stage presence (see: her David Bowie cover “Life on Mars”) and a special breed of bad that many characters inherited by virtue of her existence.
- Misty Day (Lily Rabe) Rabe’s achingly naive swamp witch Misty Day is not unlike the fragile animals she can reanimate with her gifts. The world wasn’t kind to her delicate disposition, and yet she found acceptance and shelter among the girls of Miss Robichaux’s Academy. This sensitive soul getting one of the show’s crueler fates — trapped in hell dissecting a frog on a loop — gave “Coven” palpable stakes and grim consequences that later seasons have unfortunately undone. We want Misty safe and sound, but her loss was gutting in the most effective way. Perhaps her greatest gift is that anytime she is around, the White Witch herself, Stevie Nicks, tends to appear for an acoustic set — and that’s never a bad thing.
- Mr. March (Evan Peters) Some of Peters’ best work in all of “AHS” is done from behind the pencil-thin mustache of Mr. March, the brains and brutality behind the Hotel Cortez. This trickster god of a character who bathed in his own horrific acts of violence has become unexpectedly central to our understanding of the franchise’s mythology. In “Hotel,” he convenes the Devil’s Night serial killer dinner party, and eventually he collects souls from various corners of this universe in “AHS13.” He is among the few to enjoy his eternal damnation, spent serving as the bloody legend he always wanted to be. He’s a psychopath who revels in his own madness, and loves holding court whenever the laws of this supernatural universe allow.
- Myrtle Snow (Frances Conroy) Myrtle Snow did more with a single word than most later-season “AHS” characters did with a whole storyline. The Witches Council alum turned sage advisor to Miss Robichaux’s Academy served, perhaps, the series’ best example of pure camp when she chose “Balencegia!” as her final word before burning at the stake. But she’s more than her (faux) end. From under her crimped rustic red mop, Conroy has turned a supporting character into an icon with candor and staunch loyalty for her fellow witches. These days, she exists mostly to shade those threatening the “Coven” witches and advocate for their charred end. She had to endure that fate, why shouldn’t they?
- Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson) Paulson’s most revisited character has become somewhat of a patron saint of the “AHS” series. Initially timid compared to her barn-burner of a mother, Fiona (Lange), Cordelia rose to become the Supreme the “Coven” witches needed. She was strong without being cruel, capable without alienating the next generation and forward-thinking for the sake of the coven. Her anguish about putting her girls through the deadly test of the Seven Wonders, and the losses she suffers along the way, has built the character into a pillar of strength in an ominous world, one that is still allowed to occasionally tremble under the pressure. Since she was one of the few to benefit from further exploration in “Apocalypse,” hopefully “AHS13” leaves Cordelia’s legacy intact.
- Madison Montgomery (Emma Roberts) 
	“AHS” continues to retcon the story of faded-starlet-turned-bitchy-witch Madison Montgomery with repeated appearances. But initially, she was a vessel for the angst and anger that came with being a young woman unsure of how to wield her literal and metaphorical powers. Her unwavering cynicism made her eternally viral “Surprise, bitch” moment such an enduring classic, and “Coven” initially treats her as a lost cause. Then “Apocalypse” turned her into a reluctant hero, and now “AHS13” has fully bent her trajectory toward foul-mouthed savior (which culminates in lighting a cigarette off the charred corpse of Jeffrey Dahmer … because, sure). She’s best when she is at war with her fellow witches as much as herself, but her impact is undeniable. Just look at who continues to stand beside Cordelia in her various battles against dark forces. Like it or not, Madison is here to save the day.
- Sister Jude Martin (Jessica Lange) As its second installment, “Asylum” had a lot to prove to launch “AHS” into an anthology series, so it threw everything at the audience: aliens, religion, musical numbers, Nazis. But no character goes through it like Sister Jude, a ruthless nun running from a murky past who reigns over Briarcliff Asylum with an iron fist and a cabinet full of wooden whips. Her fall from grace, becoming an institutionalized shell of herself after being subjected to the very electroshock therapy she once prescribed, proved that Sister Jude reaped what she sowed. But like the best “AHS” characters, she had enough complexity that her rather sweet ending also felt justified. Jude’s reckoning with her own horrors made her the rare person you love to loathe and hate to watch leave.
- Delphine LaLaurie (Kathy Bates) “AHS” can create all the creatures and demons it wants, but some of the worst threats already exist in the real world — and New Orleans nightmare Delphine LaLaurie is one of them. A murderer, enslaver, sadist and racist, “AHS” did Madame LaLaurie a service she didn’t deserve: It cast Bates to play her. Throughout her run in “Coven,” part of which was just as a disembodied head, Delphine is repeatedly and rightfully held to task for her unrepentant disregard for others. When she watches President Barack Obama on TV and bristles at being made to serve Queenie, you realize even hell isn’t hot enough for her.
- Lana Winters (Sarah Paulson) No one runs toward the screams of “AHS” quite like Lana Winters. To her credit, things couldn’t get much worse for Paulson’s intrepid journalist after she was admitted against her will to Briarcliff; subjected to electroshock and conversion therapy to reverse her queer identity; raped, imprisoned and impregnated by a serial killer named Blood Face (Zachary Quinto); and then left to kill the resulting child years later after his own killing spree. Lana’s story could have been relentlessly depressing, but instead she became an imperfect beacon of resilience. She let her ambition for fame and recognition drive her after escaping Briarcliff, but who can blame her? Later appearances in “Roanoke” and “Cult” proved she got what she always wanted: a career spent calling out injustice and evil.
- Marie Laveau (Angela Bassett) By Season 3, “AHS” needed a spark of life to shake things up, and Bassett brought it with a sizzling superiority as famous voodoo queen Marie Laveau. The series had fleeting brushes with real people before (see: the legends of The Black Dahlia and Anne Frank), but Marie was among the first to be a main character in the story. Bassett brought to this voodoo icon a banshee scream for respect as one of New Orleans’ most important historic figures. Her messy methods, killer instincts and incredibly potent threats, exquisitely conveyed by Bassett’s seething line delivery and body language, made her a force to be reckoned with, and a character who levels up this series every time she returns.
- Fiona Goode (Jessica Lange) The mean streak of Fiona Goode is something unrivaled in the “AHS” universe. A blistering presence from her first scene in “Coven,” she is a menace to anyone with a pulse, even her own kind. The fact that Fiona wasn’t a cartoonish villain is a true testament to why Lange was such a great match for the early seasons of “AHS.” Fiona was selfish, vain, scared, reckless, witty, proud and literally soulless, as revealed by Papa Legba. Lange played every one of those as if it was her defining trait. But her danger lay in the fact that she built any semblance of self on the power she was given, only to watch it slowly slip away to another. Her punishment at the end of the season was humorous, yes, but it worked because hell came for her well before Fiona was damned to it. A knotty-pine eternity with the Axman was just the cherry on top.
- Liz Taylor (Denis O’Hare) Although he had been part of “AHS” since the beginning, O’Hare wasn’t given something worthy of his depth until “Hotel” introduced audiences to the lavishly drawn Liz Taylor. Adorned in the kind of glamour and confidence that only comes from a well-earned journey of self-discovery, Liz Taylor is among the few selling points of the Cortez. The keeper of the secrets and the queen of the side eye, Liz managed to bind together the mismatched souls of the hotel. When she decides to end her life on the grounds of the Cortez instead of letting cancer take her, everyone trapped in its walls came to welcome her –– even The Countess, who was never more merciful than when she encouraged Liz to embrace her true identity. O’Hare deserves tremendous credit for the compassionate humanity he wove into Liz, and “Hotel” is better as a season and as a tourist trap because her company is among its amenities.
- Sister Mary Eunice (Lily Rabe) Rabe is the most underrated ringer of “AHS” players for sheer volume of classic characters. Viewers first meet “Asylum”’s meek Sister Mary Eunice as she fumbles her way through a day as the second in command to Sister Jude. Her desperation to earn her place at Briarcliff makes her an easy target for the disembodied soul of the devil, who straightens Mary’s spine, fills her with hate and a penchant for sowing chaos. Rabe’s ability to make Innocent Mary and Possessed Mary feel like two distinct characters in one vessel is extraordinary, oscillating seamlessly between gentle soul and gleeful hellion who just wants to watch the Christians be eaten.. Mary makes other “AHS” monsters look like child’s play, and the loss of her light — even in the eyes of Nazi Dr. Arden (James Cromwell), one of those monsters — reiterated the price so many paid at Briarcliff and throughout “AHS.”
- Constance Langdon (Jessica Lange) There is nothing the “AHS” audience hungers for more than Constance Langdon. A human horror in a series of supernatural terrors, Lange’s first (and best) role in “Murder House” remains unmatched. No wonder Murphy and company couldn’t resist anchoring “AHS13” in her resurrection as a servant of Satan with nothing better to do than help bring about the end of days for the hell of it. All she wants out of it is a misguided maternal request to be reunited with her children, Tate and Addie (Jamie Brewer), whom she repeatedly failed. But nursing the gooey corpse of the devil is hardly her worst trait. During her “Murder House” run, Constance was the acid-tongued neighborhood gossip, the negligent mother of a bad seed, the jilted wife with a gun, the jaded silver-screen wannabe who watched her dream wither on the vine, and perhaps most dangerously, the lost soul desperate for a purpose. With her Southern drawl and bigoted worldview, Constance was and remains the promise of the show’s title. For all its murderers, aliens, witches, vampires, cults, clowns, diseases, demons and carnies, she is the horror story worthy of America — a flesh-and-blood human who’d rather watch her neighbors die than be inconvenienced.

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.
“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”
Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.
Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”
Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”
Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.
On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:
It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.
I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.
On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:
It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.
I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?
In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.
OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:
I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.
I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.
I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.
On the future of Hollywood:
I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.
But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.
On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:
I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.
It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.
Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.
On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:
I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

Gianni Infantino: FIFA president apologises for World Cup sell-off plan - but FA and other European leaders still want him to resign
Gianni Infantino has apologised to the FIFA Council for his World Cup sell-off plan; FIFA president was speaking in Zurich on Thursday morning; the FA is among European leaders who still want him to resign, while UEFA has called on Infantino to release documents related to the scheme
Thursday 15 October 2026 20:38, UK
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan at a three-hour FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on Thursday - and the Peace Prize he awarded to US President Donald Trump looks set to be ditched.
Infantino's expression of regret for not telling the council about his plans earlier was not good enough for European football leaders, including FA chair Debbie Hewitt, who still want him to resign.
UEFA wants Infantino to release all documents relating to the plan as they believe the 20 per cent stake in all future FIFA tournaments was being sold for a knockdown price.
- Infantino abandons plans to sell off stake in World Cup
- Pressure to resign increases on Infantino with news he received £1.3m in 2024
Meanwhile, the FIFA Peace Prize, which Infantino handed to Trump in December, is likely to be scrapped, with FIFA's Football Social Responsibility Committee assessing the award and reasons for it.
The Peace Prize was only introduced in 2025, meaning Trump is the award's sole recipient to date. News of its expected scrapping emerges despite FIFA saying last year the award was to be "bestowed on an annual basis".
During the meeting, Infantino also faced scrutiny on the decision to suspend the one-match ban of USA striker Folarin Balogun during the World Cup. It was determined FIFA's Legal Committee will review disciplinary procedures, with their findings - and those on the Peace Prize - to be presented at the next council meeting in December 2026.
FIFA has also announced plans - through the FIFA Surplus Solidarity Programme - to use some of its reserves to more than double the level of planned funding for the 2027-2030 period to $6.35bn (£4.79bn), including around $25m (£18.8m) to each member association. That idea will also be examined in December.
What happened with the World Cup sell-off plan?
After this summer's World Cup, Infantino abandoned a controversial plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private equity investors after fierce opposition from football's governing bodies.
FIFA had announced it was seeking to launch FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would bring together the sale of FIFA's commercial rights - including broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing - with the operational delivery of its tournaments.
Infantino had then given football associations until September 19 to back his proposals to sell off part of FIFA to private investors with a £30.1m incentive to accept.
But the controversial proposals received fierce criticism from UEFA, CONCACAF (the North American, Central American and Caribbean association) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).
Infantino 'not fit to be FIFA president' if he avoids questions
FA chair Hewitt has called on Infantino to answer questions about his World Cup private investor plan and the Folarin Balogun case.
She said Council members had not received answers to "anything we had specifically requested" regarding FFE or the Balogun incident, where the United States striker's one-match ban was suspended following a call to Infantino from US President Donald Trump.
Hewitt told reporters in Zurich: "The man has to answer those questions, and if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president, and that was what was shared in the meeting.
"He's told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it's up to him to do that, and do that in the open way."
Saying sorry 'not enough for European football leaders'
Analysis by Sky Sports News chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:
"It's not enough for European football leaders, because make no mistake, they have had enough of Gianni Infantino, they want him out.
"They just think this is the final scandal in a long list of scandals - and don't forget what Infantino was doing this summer behind the backs of the FIFA Council, who are effectively the FIFA Board.
"He was negotiating to sell a stake, not just in the World Cup, but all future FIFA tournaments forever more. A 20 per cent stake, he was going to set up a new company, and the company was valued at just $20bn (£15m) when the World Cup this summer made $15bn (£11bn).
"So, European football leaders are convinced he was trying to sell off the World Cup on the cheap. They have gone to the courts to try and force him to release all documents about this plan he had come up with. They are saying today [Thursday], including the chair of the FA, Debbie Hewitt, that basically sorry is not good enough, we need to see the documents, we want to see all the figures, you've got to be transparent, you've got to release all these documents.
"And I think the reason they are so desperate to get their hands on those documents is because they know it will be a massive scandal if they have the evidence to prove the FIFA president was selling off a stake in FIFA tournaments to people with close ties to President Trump for a knockdown price. That would be a big, big story."
FIFA Peace Prize set to be scrapped
FIFA is reviewing its Peace Prize and the controversial award is set to be scrapped later this year. US President Donald Trump was handed the inaugural award by Infantino in Washington last December before the World Cup draw.
Nobody knew why Infantino suddenly decided that FIFA needed a Peace Prize and how and why it was decided that it should be awarded to President Trump. The bizarre award was widely seen as a way for Infantino to flatter Trump after the US President missed out on winning the Nobel Peace Prize.
A final decision on whether to scrap it will be taken at the next council meeting in December after an assessment is carried out by FIFA's Social Responsibility Committee.
Wenger and Figo among potential Infantino rivals for presidency
UEFA still wants to put forward a candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency.
Infantino is hoping to be re-elected for a fourth term next year, without facing a challenger for the third election a row.
UEFA wants him to resign after he became embroiled in a long list of controversies and scandals, but Infantino believes he still has enough support from around the world to win again at the election in Morocco in March.
Arsene Wenger, Luis Figo and Michelle Kang have been mentioned as potential candidates but it remains to be seen whether any of them are prepared to challenge Infantino.
Anyone who wants to take on Infantino has until November 18 to declare their candidacy.
It may be in the best interests of challengers to declare their intention to stand as late as possible in order to give Infantino and his supporters less time to prepare for taking on a rival.
Former Arsenal manager Wenger is respected around the world but he has shown no interest so far in leading FIFA.
He has been happy working as FIFA's global football development chief since 2019, although he did release a statement in August criticising Infantino's plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup. He was appointed to his role by Infantino and has supported some of the FIFA president's most controversial projects, such as a biennial World Cup and an expanded Club World Cup.
Luis Figo has launched a scathing attack on Infantino in a newspaper column, calling for his resignation in the wake of the World Cup sell-off scandal. The former Real Madrid and Barcelona star has the profile to pose a challenge, but his role as a UEFA adviser since 2017 could make it harder to secure the votes he would need from football associations around the world to replace Infantino.
Lyon, London City Lionesses and Washington Spirit owner Kang has also been mentioned as a potential challenger but there have been no indications that she is preparing to take on Infantino.
What is the FIFA Council?
The FIFA Council has 37 members made up of:
- FIFA president Gianni Infantino
- Eight vice presidents including UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and the presidents of the other five confederations. FA chair Debbie Hewitt is also a vice president
- 28 other members elected by the FIFA member associations

Guwahati gets northeast’s first visa application centre, will ease travel hassles, says CM Himanta
Set up by VFS Global within the Inter-State Bus Terminal (ISBT) complex at Khanapara, the centre will enable residents of Assam and the northeast to apply for visas
Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Thursday inaugurated the northeast’s first visa application centre in Guwahati.
Set up by VFS Global within the Inter-State Bus Terminal (ISBT) complex at Khanapara, the centre will enable residents of Assam and the northeast to apply for visas to Cyprus, Egypt, Ireland, Japan, Malta, Morocco and the United Kingdom. The facility will also accept Schengen visa applications, which allow travellers to visit 29 European countries.
“Residents of Assam and the rest of northeast had so far been required to travel to Delhi or Kolkata to apply for visas to foreign countries. With the opening of the new centre, they will now be able to apply for visas to several countries from Guwahati itself,” said Sarma.
The CM said the centre would make international travel services more accessible to people across the northeast and bring several countries closer to the region.
He described the initiative as an important step towards facilitating international travel, adding that its benefits would extend beyond Guwahati to all eight states of the northeast.
“The centre in Guwahati would assist applicants in completing the visa application process in accordance with the prescribed rules and procedures. However, the decision to grant or reject a visa would rest solely with the embassy or consulate of the concerned country,” said Sarma.
Highlighting the growing operations of Lokapriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport in Guwahati, the CM said direct flights were already operating from Guwahati to Dubai, Singapore and Bhutan, while a flight service to Bangkok would commence on October 27.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Tesla's Roadster is back. Now, it kinda flies, and I'm not just being hyperbolic about its speed.
(Although, I guess, that would be a fair read, too.)
On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the second-generation Roadster. It's capable of doing "crazy gymnastics," Musk said, like hopping off the ground and spinning in the air. The prototype also sprints from standing to 60 mph in 0.8 seconds, Tesla claims — and the automaker said the production model will be even quicker.
Will the two-door electric sports car be street legal? Who knows.
Instead, the car is accomplishing something more tangible — and more obviously Musk-like: make Tesla look like the kind of company that can build things other companies cannot. That's a useful message for Wall Street and for the engineers Tesla wants to hire.
Tesla is already valued far more like a tech company than a traditional automaker.
For years, investors have bet heavily on its ambitions in autonomy, artificial intelligence, robotics, and robotaxis. A flying (or, at least, hopping) Roadster does not prove those businesses will work, but it makes Tesla's technological ambitions more legible.
Musk also has long treated product spectacles as recruiting events, too.
At a 2019 Neuralink presentation, where he announced that the company had successfully implanted sensors in rats' brains, he said the "main reason for doing this presentation is recruiting." Ahead of Tesla's 2021 AI Day, Musk posted on X that "convincing the best AI talent to join Tesla is the sole goal."

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, also agrees that Thursday's Roadster reveal was an exciting technical feat for up-and-coming tech talent:

Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma has called for a ban on power banks on flights to and from India after a power bank caught fire aboard an IndiGo(InterGlobe Aviation Ltd) aircraft carrying 191 passengers from Delhi. In a post on X, Sharma questioned why airlines and aviation regulators had not prohibited power banks on flights, citing safety concerns linked to fire incidents involving the devices aboard aircraft. He also referred to the existing requirement for passengers to keep their devices in airplane mode, adding that he would prefer a ban on power banks on flights to and from India. His post has brought renewed attention to power bank safety during air travel and the measures needed to prevent onboard fire incidents. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has prohibited the carriage and use of a specific power bank model on flights, PTI reported. In a communication dated September 29, the aviation regulator banned the “MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 power bank”, citing a recent fire incident involving the device. Specific details about the incident and the manufacturer of the power bank could not be ascertained. Explaining the decision, the DGCA said that, in view of the recent fire incident and the potential safety risks associated with the device, the power bank should not be “carried or transported on board the aircraft, whether as passenger baggage (including checked-in and cabin baggage) or as cargo, on any flight to, from or within India”. There have been multiple incidents involving power banks catching fire aboard aircraft. On October 11, a passenger's power bank kept in the overhead bin of a Chennai-bound IndiGo aircraft caught fire, following which the plane was diverted to Hyderabad airport, where it landed safely, according to sources. The incidents have brought attention to the safety risks associated with power banks during air travel and the regulatory measures governing their carriage and use. In 2025, India recorded 55 deaths by malaria, 131 deaths by dengue, and 27 deaths by kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis or black fever), according to Union Health Ministry data, whereas there is no single comparable and comprehensive national measure of its annual human rabies mortality, even as the country looks to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by the year 2030.
While a community-based study led by researchers from the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases recently estimated that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year, the Health Ministry’s Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme-Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP-IHIP) system reported 21 deaths by rabies in 2022, 50 in 2023, and 54 in 2024.
In contrast, the Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022, and 271 in 2023. The MCCD system, however, covers only medically certified deaths and does not capture all registered deaths.
These figures are not directly comparable — the IDSP-IHIP is a disease surveillance system, while the MCCD captures medically certified causes through civil registration. At the national level, the MCCD covered 22.3% of registered deaths in 2022, and 22.0% in 2023. Neither system, therefore, provides a complete national count — underscoring the gaps in India’s rabies mortality surveillance.
The government table, sourced to IDSP-IHIP, had recorded one death in January 2025 but did not provide a figure for all of 2025. The government’s published table, labelled ‘Human Rabies cases (Death)’, gives the source as IDSP-IHIP.
ICMR for its study surveyed 3,37,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States and estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including about 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers used the community survey, laboratory data, and a probability decision-tree model to estimate the number of people who progress from an animal bite to rabies and die. The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual deaths, and not a count of deaths recorded in hospitals or by government surveillance.
The difference between the two datasets is substantial. The 54 deaths reported through government surveillance in 2024 is less than 1% of the study’s estimated annual toll of 5,726.
“The two figures, however, are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The figures therefore highlight a large gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality,” a senior Health Ministry official said.
“Lack of consolidated data is a challenge in rabies eradication. Very often cases and deaths occur in areas of the country where they are not measurable. Vaccination of stray dogs, stringent post-exposure vaccination for humans, and disruption of the rabies chain is essential to curb the problem,” Nirmal Kumar Ganguly, medical scientist, public health expert, and former ICMR chief, speaking exclusively to The Hindu, said.
The National Centre for Disease Control itself says efforts are continuing to make human rabies a notifiable disease across India, and that all States have been asked to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
The Health Ministry has also acknowledged the surveillance challenge, with deaths occurring outside the formal health system posing an additional difficulty in capturing the full burden of disease.
Meanwhile, the Lancet study found important gaps even after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received the anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear, with infected dog bites causing most human transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that domestic dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmission. Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths every year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia.
The WHO estimates that India accounts for 35% of rabies deaths globally and 59.9% of rabies deaths in Asia, underlining the country’s significant contribution to the global burden. Children are particularly vulnerable. The WHO says 40% of people bitten by suspected rabid animals are children under 15 years. Rabies is entirely preventable through timely vaccination of dogs and prompt post-exposure care.
The ICMR-funded study states that although there has been a substantial decline in human rabies deaths over the past two decades, India needs to fast-track its actions to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 by adopting a focused ‘One Health’ approach — integrating human and animal surveillance, ensuring timely administration of the full course of post-exposure prophylaxis, and accelerating dog vaccination across the country.

Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working?
- Published
The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
Why did we see heavy scorelines?
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Is the competition good enough?
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.
The UN health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.
WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.
Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.
“Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said.
WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia.
Russia has denied any such second case.
