The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, presents an opportunity to strengthen Keralam’s response to population ageing. The Government of Keralam’s initiative to introduce this first-of-its-kind legislation in the country is a welcome step towards protecting the rights and well-being of senior citizens.
By recognising dignity, independence, safety, participation and access to care, the Bill provides a foundation for moving beyond welfare and towards a comprehensive, entitlements-based approach to ageing.
Central principle
A central principle of the Bill is ageing in place, enabling older persons to remain in their homes and communities for as long as possible, with institutional care as a last resort. This requires supporting families through accessible health care, community-based services, trained caregivers, rehabilitation, and social support. Care must be organised as a continuum, responding to changing needs rather than only during crises.
Equally important is the shift from managing dependence to preventing or delaying avoidable functional decline. The Bill’s provision for standardised care assessments, incorporating intrinsic capacity and functional dependency, is particularly relevant. Linking these assessments with primary and community health care could enable earlier identification of changes in mobility, cognition, sensory function and daily activities, followed by timely interventions that help preserve independence.
Addressing critical gaps
The Bill also addresses critical gaps in the care ecosystem through provisions for registration and regulation of care institutions, caregiver training and certification, and minimum standards of service delivery. These measures must be accompanied by appropriate supervision, continuing education, fair working conditions, and support for family caregivers.
The proposed district-level institutional mechanisms offer an opportunity to strengthen accountability, grievance redressal, and coordination. The Bill also introduces penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for specified violations, reinforcing the importance of compliance and protection of senior citizens’ rights.
The effectiveness will depend on clear responsibilities, adequate resources, effective enforcement, and convergence across health, social welfare and local self-government systems.
An age-ready Keralam must be measured not only by the institutions and services established but also by whether older persons can maintain their functional ability, remain connected to their communities and live with dignity, independence, security and purpose.
The next priority is translating legislative provisions into accessible, equitable and quality services, particularly for older persons living alone, those with disabilities or dementia, and those without adequate family support.
Overall, the Bill presents a robust framework for geriatric care. Its efficient implementation can help set an effective precedent that can be replicated nationwide.
(Prof. (Dr.) Sudha Chandrashekar is CEO, Swasti - The Health Catalyst, a not-for-profit global organisation in the field of public health).

A six-year-old girl, Nina Manes, and her mother, Tali, are being credited with helping alert passengers during a mid-air emergency aboard a Flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Flydubai flight FZ1073 was carrying 174 passengers when an Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the Indian captain, Capt. Smit Machchhar, in what authorities described as an apparent attempt to crash the Boeing 737 MAX 8. According to the account of the incident, Nina had asked her mother to take her to the forward restroom. While standing outside, the two heard a commotion and screams coming from inside the cockpit. Tali described seeing “blood all over the cockpit" and witnessing intense fighting moves. After hearing his daughter's screams and realising that an emergency was unfolding, Nina's father, Tzvika Manes, the CEO of Bank Leumi's underwriting division, and two other passengers rushed forward to enter the cockpit and subdue the attacker. The severely injured captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing a group of passengers to enter, overpower the co-pilot and restrain him. The passengers also helped stabilise the situation after the aircraft had plunged thousands of feet. An off-duty pilot travelling on the flight subsequently helped fly the aircraft to a safe emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and defence officials have since praised the bravery of the captain and passengers, crediting their actions with preventing a potential mass-casualty disaster. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke to Captain Smit Machchaar, the Indian pilot who was seriously injured after being attacked by his co-pilot aboard the Dubai-Tel Aviv-bound Flydubai flight. During the conversation, Machchaar shared details of his experience during the incident and spoke about what gave him the courage to act during the emergency. The prime minister praised the pilot's bravery and wished him a speedy recovery. One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don’t react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain.
“Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min’s team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect.
Microdroplet chemistry
Min’s lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.”
Many animal studies have tied microplastic toxicity to oxidative stress, which is caused by ROS. So the team wondered if the boundary between water and plastic might do something similar. “We got inspired by that field,” Min said.
In the first test, the team stirred polystyrene powder into water containing methyl orange, a yellow dye that ROS break apart. Over 10 days, the solution faded almost to colorless, losing nearly 90 percent of the dye. In ethanol or other solvents, the dye stayed intact. Min and his colleagues concluded that whatever chemistry polystyrene was undergoing needed water to happen. So they ran more tests.
Water under stress
First was electron spin resonance, a technique that directly detects radicals—atoms or molecules with an unpaired electron that makes them particularly reactive. The polystyrene powder and water mixture contained hydroxyl radicals, a highly reactive ROS.
Next, the team used a fluorescent sensor that lights up only when it reacts with hydroxyl radicals. “You don’t see it, but once it reacts with local ROS, it turns into a bright color,” Min said. Under a microscope, the glow concentrated on the surfaces of the plastic particles and kept building over time.
The effect was not unique to polystyrene either. Scientists tested six common plastics—polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, PVC, PET, and acrylic—and all of them generated radicals. The most water-repellent plastics, polyethylene and polypropylene, were the most active, while PET and acrylic, which contain chemical groups that attract water, were the least.
“The simplest answer is the most water-repellent ones change the water structure the most,” Min said. In ordinary, or bulk, water, each molecule is held in a network of hydrogen bonds with its neighbors. But a few layers of water molecules pressed against a water-repellent surface lose some of those partners. “Their structure is no longer the regular water structure. They are perturbed, and their energy is also significantly increased,” Min said.
Water always contains a small number of hydroxide ions, and turning one into a hydroxyl radical requires stripping away an electron. In bulk water, that costs a lot of energy. But simulations run by the group showed that, at a polyethylene surface, hydroxide ions short on hydrogen bonds needed far less energy to form radicals. On top of that, the plastic surfaces build up a negative electric charge in water, which further lowered the energy cost.
But Min’s team still had doubts to address before making any conclusive claims.
Ruling out the dirt
Min’s earlier work on microdroplet chemistry has drawn a lot of criticism, with some researchers arguing that the reported reactive chemicals come from contamination or measurement artifacts.
To avoid similar objections, Min and his colleagues used several independent detection methods. They also added a detergent-like surfactant that coats the plastic and disrupts the water layer at its surface. They found that the more surfactant they added, the weaker the plastic’s electric charge became and the fewer radicals it produced. “We only change one parameter while keeping all the rest [the same],” Min said. “We’re using exactly the same plastics, the same water, the same everything.”
Impurities, Min explained, are typically stable molecules with no reason to spontaneously generate radicals. He is careful not to overstate it, though. “To be absolutely clear, we cannot 100 percent rule out the involvement of impurities,” he said. “But our controls and our theoretical computation studies highly suggest that this is intrinsic to the microplastic-water interface.”
Finally, the team tested if this interface chemistry matters for biological molecules. And it most likely does.
Proteins and blood cells
Proteins and DNA can gather on plastic surfaces, and lysozyme, a common test protein, also began clumping into aggregates there. Adding caffeine, which mops up radicals, largely stopped the clumping, pointing to the radicals as the cause.
Mouse red blood cells that touched polystyrene particles broke into fragments, and the damage from each type of plastic tracked how many radicals it produced. The effect also persisted in blood serum.
Min stressed, though, that this indicates that microplastics make people sick by generating ROS. While animal studies often point to ROS as possible roots of oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, ROS can be produced in many ways, including through basic metabolic activity.
Min admitted comparing the magnitude of this effect to the impact of ROS our own cells make is rather tricky.
A local problem
“If you are really at the interface, you could be significantly affected by this effect, whereas if you are just a few microns away, you don’t feel it anymore,” Min said. Exposure is another unknown here. Min also emphasized that no one can yet say how many microplastics an average person takes in each year from food, water, and air.
The plastics in the study were mostly fresh, lab-bought powders, unlike weathered particles we encounter in the environment. In the team’s tests, older particles with more oxidized surfaces produced somewhat weaker signals. “This aging process is very heterogeneous,” Min said. “Some microplastic particles were made 50 years ago, some were made five days ago.” Finally, there is the question of size.
Microplastics are usually defined as particles smaller than five millimeters, while the minimum cutoff varies between 100 and 1,000 nanometers. Min’s team did not test how variation in microplastic particle size affects water-interface chemistry, but the researchers suspect it might play a role. The same mass of plastic broken into nanoparticles has far more surface area, which might make the effect larger. “This may be another reason for nanoplastics to be more dangerous,” Min said.
The researchers argue that if water-repellent surfaces drive the water interface chemistry, plastics could be designed to be less water-repellent, either by changing their molecular structure or including additives. First, though, the team wants to focus on the question their study left open. “We definitely want to see how much this effect is directly contributing to disease or biological problems in animals and humans,” Min said.
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) has some advice for fellow lawmakers: unapologetically support the biotech industry, vilify insurance companies, and focus on making America a biotech research haven, instead of relying on protectionism.
Right now in Washington, it’s popular to support protectionist policies against China in industries like tech. China is rapidly gaining on the U.S. biotechnology industry, and there is bipartisan support to extend those protections to the biotech sector.
Auchincloss said that approach hurts America’s competitiveness.
“Washington needs to fix itself and worry less about what China is doing because China is going to be excellent,” he said at the STAT Summit in Boston on Thursday. “But we can be even better.”
That attitude aligns with the views of the biotech industry and its investors. America cannot stop China from becoming a biotech powerhouse, the thinking goes, so Congress should invest in the domestic biotechnology industry and speed research and development.
Auchincloss plans to introduce a bill that would adopt the approach taken by the Australian government, which has sped up the clinical trial regime in part by allowing early-phase trials to bypass pre-approval evaluation by the national regulator. It will never be as cheap to conduct early-stage trials in the U.S. as it is in China, Auchincloss said, but it should be as fast.
He said he’s also interested in cracking down on pharmacy benefit manager business practices, reforming the 340B hospital drug discount program, and creating small business grants.
Although drugmakers have become a popular target of lawmakers, Massachusetts lawmakers should boldly promote the industry, which plays a crucial role in the state’s economy, Auchincloss said.
“Some advice from a six-year veteran of Washington, D.C.: You do need a villain, and the villain is the insurance company,” he said during the conversation with STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.
Another villain, in his eyes: Russ Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who Auchincloss said considers science a “blue state subsidy.” The OMB proposed empowering the White House to override the recommendations of peer reviewers, terminate grants at will, and exercise more latitude in the type of research federal agencies support.
Auchincloss also took issue with the Food and Drug Administration’s Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program. Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary created the program, and it has come under scrutiny from industry stakeholders and public health advocates.
Auchincloss said it politicizes decisions that should be guided by transparent, well thought-out standards. For example, Makary awarded vouchers to psychedelics after podcaster Joe Rogan texted President Trump about research around ibogaine.
“If Washington behaves that way, there’s nothing that we’re going to do about Beijing that’s going to save our biomedical leadership,” Auchincloss said. “Because ultimately, what makes us great is high, clear, transparent standards paired with the world’s best talent getting funded to pursue curiosity-driven research.”

Chinese chemicals and machinery in EU crosshairs as leaders back more trade curbs
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen floats safeguards as member states fall in behind two-track strategy to deal with China shock
Chemicals and industrial machinery were identified as the top priority industries the EU needs to shield against Chinese imports during a meeting between the EU’s top leaders in Brussels on Thursday.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the bloc’s 27 member states that the EU should consider quickly introducing safeguard measures, which can involve import quotas and tariffs, to shield these sectors from a wave of cut-price alternatives from China, according to people familiar with the discussion.
Her motion was endorsed by influential member states, including France, Germany, Belgium and Denmark, while the wind turbine industry was also mentioned during the debate as one that needs intervention to alleviate pressure from Chinese imports, one of the people said.

Netflix has hired a new content chief after a stock slump and struggles to grow its viewership.
Bela Bajaria, who's overseen Netflix's movies and shows since 2023, is leaving the company after almost a decade, the company announced on Thursday.
She'll be replaced on October 26 by Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney executive, Netflix said. Rice was the head of Disney's TV arm, where he oversaw Hulu and networks like ABC, Disney Channel, and FX.
The news arrived the day after the streaming giant laid off about 1,000 employees on Wednesday, its biggest round of layoffs in four years.
Bajaria "led enormous changes at Netflix," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a statement, crediting her for helping the streamer broaden its content mix to live events and sports.

I was reporting on the ground near Connaught Place, close to Rajiv Chowk metro station, when Delhi Police detained me and several other journalists at around 11:20 am on October 10, 2026.
Delhi Police and central security forces had cordoned off the area around Jantar Mantar, preventing protesters and journalists from approaching the designated protest site. I was filming the police action and speaking to people present at the scene when officers began pushing and shoving individuals standing at the intersection of Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Several people were holding placards to express their dissent when police arrived and began detaining them.
While I filmed the detentions, one officer thrust his hand towards me and attempted to grab me. I showed him my press card. He backed off but continued gesturing aggressively. On camera, I asked him what legal guideline or constitutional provision allowed him to detain or attempt to assault a journalist on duty. He became enraged, and a heated exchange followed. The police then detained several journalists, including me.
We were shoved into a bus and driven across the national capital. When we repeatedly asked the officers which legal procedure they were following to detain us, they did not respond. They also refused to tell us where we were being taken.
The journey lasted around two hours. We travelled along Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, crossed the Yamuna, passed Shahdara flyover and Burari, and eventually reached the Delhi-Karnal highway. We became increasingly concerned about our destination. At 8 am, when I had begun reporting on the ground, I had noticed several police vehicles bearing HR and UP number plates. Our apprehensions grew as the bus continued along the Karnal expressway for another 20 minutes or so.
During the two-hour journey from Connaught Place towards neighbouring Haryana, we were not provided with sufficient drinking water or other basic necessities in the scorching heat. We managed to get some water only when a truck driver passed his bottle through the bus window. However, packed food, including bananas, biscuits and kachori, were already available on the bus.
Around 2 pm, we arrived at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana, Delhi, approximately 65 km from Connaught Place. The stadium had been converted into a detention centre, where around 100 people detained from different parts of Delhi were being held.
I began documenting the situation inside the detention centre, speaking to detainees and trying to understand the circumstances in an area that had been without internet connectivity since the previous night.
A Cockroach Janta Party coordinator, reportedly picked up from his residence in Burari around 3 am on October 10, described his experience to me. “No food, no proper water, and a contingent of police officials who were not cooperating with anything since I was detained,” he said.
The stadium, usually filled with the sounds of athletes and cheering fans, now echoed with protesters’ slogans. “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chor” (The vote thief needs to resign) rang out across the premises.
A few minutes later, another bus brought in a group of protesters. They alleged that the police had shoved them into the bus and assaulted them. Despite this, they continued raising slogans against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the BJP-led Union government. Those detained included supporters and activists of the Muslim Students’ Federation (MSF), the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), and leaders of the Communist Party of India (Marxist).
CPI(M) leaders Sujan Chakraborty and Manik Sarkar, the former chief minister of Tripura, were also at the detention centre, along with several other leaders from across the country. Sudip Dutta, general secretary of the Centre for Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a prominent national trade union affiliated with the CPI(M), had also been detained and brought to the stadium.
I spoke to a student from Delhi about how they intended to pursue their demands. Aman, an AISF member, said voter deletions and irregularities in Form 6 could affect future generations of voters.
“See, this issue of voter deletions is going to impact the upcoming generations who are going to vote tomorrow. As college students, it is our responsibility to make our peers aware about these issues. After today, we would hit the classrooms, reach out to our friends and make them aware of how this issue of ‘vote Chori’ that has come to light is going to impact them and the generations to come,” he said.
Another student, Ali, spoke about police brutality and the use of central security personnel to curb the right to protest.
“We were picked up from Minto Road. The police had barricaded the entire area. Around ten police officers were charging at a single protester, and dragging them to the police van. CRPF, BSP, ITBP, CISF, and even Uttar Pradesh Police are on duty. Why is the government acting like this to curb the voices of the students,” he said.
I spent another hour documenting events at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, where protesters continued raising slogans despite being detained. Around 3:30 pm, after repeated negotiations with police officers, I was released along with another journalist.
As we left the premises, we were asked to provide our personal details. When we identified ourselves as journalists, several officers appeared astonished and initially thought we were lying. They believed us only after we showed our press cards.
The exchange lasted around ten minutes. It became clear that the officers at the detention centre had received no instructions or communication informing them that journalists were also being detained.
During the four to five hours I spent under detention, the same ort of resentment came up in every conversation: Allegations, an investigation and protests against Gyanesh Kumar had prompted the Union government to take preventive measures in the name of maintaining law and order. These measures were so extensive that people seeking reforms to Indian democracy were being detained. The scale of the restrictions was equally alarming.
Metro services, railway stations, roads and shops in parts of Delhi were directed to be shut down, affecting daily commuters, roadside hawkers and shopkeepers. Internet services were also suspended within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path area and in and around makeshift detention centres across Delhi. Internet connectivity was suspended in the area surrounding Rajiv Gandhi Stadium as well.
A shopkeeper in Bawana, near the stadium, told me that the internet shutdown had caused significant losses because customers could not make online payments. The preventive measures affected not only protesters but also ordinary people, disrupting the lives of commuters, daily-wage labourers, shopkeepers, railway platform-based workers, auto drivers and others going about their daily routines.
Why was Delhi being subjected to what resembled a state of emergency?
Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution guarantees individuals the right to express their opinions and protest, subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions and the rights of others. The government can also take measures to maintain law and order. But how far can such measures legally and constitutionally extend?
I continued to think about these questions as I travelled to Samaypur Badli metro station, approximately 17 km from the detention centre. The 30-minute journey offered no concrete answers.

On Thursday, Donald Trump called off the Pentagon’s highly controversial plans to livestream a firing squad execution that is still on schedule for December 3.
Trump supports the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood. But sources close to Trump told CNN that the president was blindsided last week when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the event—which is the first US execution of a soldier since World War II—would be livestreamed.
Backlash to the livestream was immediate and crossed political divides. On the morning Trump canceled the plans, an ABC News poll found 8 in 10 Americans were against the livestream, including a 55 percent majority of MAGA Republicans.
Insiders told ABC News that Trump feared that “broadcasting the execution could super charge anti-American propaganda or reflect poorly on the US.” Privately, Trump had remarked that “he did not initially know that Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down,” CNN reported. As one Army officer appalled by Hegseth’s announcement explained in a separate CNN report, livestreaming the execution “takes away everything America stands for.”
“The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable,” the officer, who was deployed multiple times in the Middle East, told CNN.
Livestream risked identifying US soldiers
On Truth Social, Trump confirmed that Hasan “will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.” Families of victims will still be able to watch the execution, but the execution will not be broadcast for the public.

Data centers house computer servers for storing and managing data. The rise in artificial intelligence has led to an increase in the construction of massive data center buildings to support the technology's training and intense data requirements.
The recent boom in their development has been unpopular with many people in the United States, particularly when those structures are being built in their local area.
While data centers did exist prior to the development of AI as it's known today, little attention was paid to them before. With the American public now more widely scrutinizing the structures, Snopes has been researching numerous claims about them, particularly their construction and potential impact on local communities and the environment.

Google’s philanthropic arm Google.org has committed $15 Mn in funding to nonprofit organisation The/Nudge (formerly The/Nudge Institute) to support the growth and digital enablement of Indian MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises). The initiative aims to develop scalable AI tools that can help small businesses improve access to formal credit, discover new markets and navigate compliance requirements. Besides, an open call for proposals to identify innovative solutions addressing challenges faced by MSMEs is also on the cards. The initiative also includes a multilingual AI platform to train talent in Tier III and Tier IV towns in job-ready skills and connect them with small businesses. “By partnering with The/Nudge, we are putting open digital tools directly into the hands of small business owners, ensuring that India’s economic backbone is equipped to lead this technology shift,” Preeti Lobana, VP and country manager at Google India, said. The initiative also aims to establish open standards that can help Indian MSMEs become more competitive, creditworthy and visible in global markets. The funding comes amid growing efforts to leverage AI for improving productivity and expanding access to digital services among small businesses. For MSMEs, AI-powered tools could help simplify operational processes, improve access to information and address some of the barriers that limit their ability to scale. India’s MSME sector continues to face structural challenges in accessing formal finance, expanding market reach and navigating compliance requirements. For smaller enterprises, limited access to business information and digital tools can further complicate these processes. A World Economic Forum report published in October 2025 estimated that AI adoption could unlock $490-685 Bn in economic value for India’s MSME sector. Amid this, digital lenders have increased focus on MSMEs, which often have difficulty in raising formal credit despite being the country’s second largest employer. New-age NBFCs like Indifi Capital, Techfino, Lendingkart, FlexiLoans, Aye Finance, among others, are leveraging tech to address this issue and provide credit to MSMEs. Prior to this, Google.org announced a $1 Mn grant to help improve news literacy in India and fight back against misinformation and fake news, in 2020. It has also given a grant of $3 Mn to non-profit organisations in India in 2018, to provide quality education in India through elearning.

An increase in killings of women in Cameroon spurs protests
Elementary school teacher Geraldine Achiah died in Cameroon after allegedly being beaten by her husband
YAOUNDE, Cameroon -- Geraldine Achiah, an elementary school teacher in her 30s, died barely two months into her marriage in September. Her relatives allege her husband beat her over a marital dispute and demand justice in what they say is a gender-based crime.
Her only child, Courage Abombi, 18, fondly remembers her support for his dreams of becoming a mechanical engineer. “My mom died an unexpected and painful death,” said Abombi, who had to take a university entrance exam a day after his mother’s burial.
Achiah, who died in September, is one of nearly 70 women who were killed in Cameroon this year for reasons related to their gender, the Ministry of Women's Affairs says. That's up from government estimates of at least 50 in 2023 and 67 in 2024. The rise in such killings has sparked protests and calls for government action as many of the killings remain unsolved while others go unreported.
Manfred Amambua, Achiah’s husband, has denied killing his wife, the police said. He has been charged with murder and is in jail awaiting trial.
Femicide — the killing of women and girls for gender-related reasons — in Cameroon is mostly driven by economic dependence, unequal control over family property and lack of adequate laws in what's widely viewed as a patriarchal society, activists say. The crisis reflects a global pattern with an estimated 50,000 women and girls killed by intimate partners or relatives in 2024, U.N. data shows.
Femicide cases in Cameroon have reached a “cruel” and “alarming” proportion, Women’s Affairs Minister Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa recently told the state broadcaster as she promised more action from the government.
“The current economic situation in the country is not helping matters. With limited resources, many women tend to endure violence in their marriages, hoping that their men will change, which is not usually the case,” she added.
At the root of the crisis is inadequate laws to punish offenders and a poor judicial system, activists say. While Cameroon’s Penal Code recognizes crimes such as rape, it does not have explicit laws or provisions on femicide, leaving judges to rely on general laws on harmful acts.
It is a common trend across many African countries where femicide is addressed through general homicide laws rather than expressly defining it as a distinct offense, although some have taken limited legal or policy steps that acknowledge femicide.
The Cameroonian government is working on a new bill that would establish femicide as a standalone criminal offense while also strengthening broader protections against gender-based violence. For rights groups and activists, that is only one of several hurdles to stop the killings.
Cases can be delayed with different tactics, including intimidation, corruption and procedural mistakes that can reduce charges or even lead to acquittals, said Carole Grace Mbarga, a Cameroonian rights activist.
“When investigations drag on, evidence deteriorates, witnesses lose confidence, and families become discouraged,” she said.
Even when convictions in such cases happen, the punishments are usually light and short of expectations, such as in 2025, when a man who pleaded guilty to killing his wife was handed a suspended five-year sentence and a fine of 52,000 CFA francs ($90).
Family and friends recently gathered in Yaounde for the burial of Achiah, who had just married her husband in July.
Her relatives are grappling with the loss and told the AP they’re not only worried about justice for her, but also for other victims of femicide.
“I pray that justice will follow its due course and that her killer will face the law,” Abombi said.
The AP obtained hospital records that noted Achiah had “several bruises on her face and lips” before she died.
Ndzana Bienvenu, an officer involved in investigating the case, said police gathered other evidence including phone footage of her and her husband after the alleged beating, as well as blood-stained bedsheet.
“We want justice for our daughter who died a violent death. This was a teacher who imparted knowledge on thousands of young Cameroonians,” said Regina Ngukum, Achiah’s cousin.
Anti-femicide protests have been held in major cities in the country, including Douala and Yaounde, with thousands demanding more action from the government.
The proposed law against femicide is expected to be submitted to parliament for consideration in November. But in addition to the law, systemic barriers and support for victims should also be addressed, said Laura Sen, one of the protest organizers.
For many Cameroonian women who face violence at home, they often have to contend with hardship and stigma, especially when they already have children.
In the case of Achiah, her child said he is praying for justice for her death and “that her killer will face the law.”
“She keeps appearing to me in a dream, consoling me not to despair and that she is still with me,” he said.

Aboard an icebreaker, a writer got a closer look at the Arctic's 'Sea Change'
As polar ice melts in the Arctic, shipping lanes are opening up, making the region a new zone of superpower competition. Writer Rana Foroohar got an up-close look aboard the USS Healy, a Coast Guard icebreaker. She says that traversing the North Pole by ship — once a "largely conceptual" route — is now becoming a "real possibility" for two or three weeks a year.
"If you are taking one of these Arctic routes, you can save as much as 40% of the time it would take you to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and depending on the price of oil, that's a heck of a lot of money," she says. "China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest."
In her new book, Sea Change: America's New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Foroohar makes the case that the "High North" may become as critical to world shipping as the Suez or Panama canals. But she also notes that beneath the Arctic waters are large deposits of oil, natural gas and rare earth minerals, as well as underwater cables, which carry a large part of the world's intercontinental information flow.
"Undersea cables have become a real touchstone in wars and conflicts around the world," she says. "So you are seeing a race to lay down new cable, and who can get there fastest, and then who can potentially commercialize and even militarize areas where those cables have been laid."
Foroohar describes the Arctic Circle as one of the few areas of the globe where countries and companies can still "hunt" for territory and "duke it out potentially with rivals." And she predicts more conflict in the coming decades as the region continues to warm.
"There is going to be more commerce done through this area. There is gonna be greater military interest in the area, and all of that matters because it really is in America's backyard," she says. "I just think that everything in the High North is going to be higher priority for America in the future."
Interview highlights
On increased international interest in the Arctic
China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest. And that's very interesting because it starts to dovetail with something that's happening in U.S. policy, which is more of a sense of we need to protect what's close to home. And so if you look at things that way, then you have the U.S. and China coming into much closer geographic conflict. Whether or not it would ever be a hot conflict, I hope not, but certainly competition in that area.
On the debate over rights to resources in international waters
There's some debate over that. There is something called the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which governs maritime activities, including those in the Arctic. It has ... rules about where you can mine, how you can mine, who gets what. But the U.S. never signed on to that convention. Various presidents from Clinton to Bush [to] Obama did support it, but key Republican senators opposed it, basically on ideological grounds, the notion that no international body should have sovereign right over what the U.S. does. ... And so it makes it much more of a free-for-all as to who gets what in the Arctic. And then you throw in the fact that Russians and Chinese don't always play by the U.N. rules either.
On how Arctic power struggles are part of a larger global trend
It's kind of part and parcel of a bigger collapse of international rule and a pendulum shift from globalization to something that is much more about regionalization and spheres of power ... and influence, which is exactly what's happening in the Arctic, which to me is so interesting, not only just for itself, but because it's a mirror into what's happening in other parts of the world. Some of the same conflicts over territory and mineral rights and ports that you see in the Arctic now are also happening in Latin America or West Africa or parts of the South China Sea. So it's a bit of a bellwether for geostrategy more broadly. …
And then there's this — kind of largely theoretical up until now, but becoming more realistic — trans-polar route where right now it might be a couple of weeks that you could consider going right across the pole, but if global warming continues the way it seems to be going in the next decade or two, that could turn into a month, two months, three months. And so who's going to control that area? This is what's up for stake now.
On what it's like to be onboard an Arctic icebreaker
You begin to feel and hear the ice as it is being broken by the ship. And I remember being down on the mess hall, which is a couple floors down from the waterline, and I was sitting eating my lunch and you begin to hear this shhhhhh kind of sound, like something traveling through sound, and then it becomes squeaky, like fingers on chalkboard, and you can kind of feel vibration and it gets louder and louder and you're like, "Wow, there are only 12 inches of reinforced steel between me and death." That's very sobering.
On the region's changing climate
I actually touched base with some of those scientists several months after we had come off of the Healy, and they were starting to go through that data and look at it. And there is some real scientific data showing that these areas are changing. They are warming. They are becoming different than they have been in the past. And that affects all kinds of things. It affects the kind of fish that could live there. It affects wind and wave patterns that you might get, which could in turn affect things like the Canadian boreal forest fires that I experience in my home in Brooklyn, New York. You would think that has nothing to do with the Arctic, but it actually has everything to do with what's happening in the High North.
Therese Madden and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

Walsh vomit & Ponga pain - the physical toll of World Cup opener
- Published
If anyone doubted the physical commitment of rugby league's greatest stars, they only needed to watch an exhausted Reece Walsh doubled up and vomiting during Thursday's epic World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand.
And during the Kangaroos' dramatic 24-22 victory in Sydney, there were plenty of other examples of that commitment - aside from the normal rough and tumble this punishing sport regularly delivers.
New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga bravely battled on for 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm before almost having to be scraped off the pitch minutes before hat-trick hero Jack Bostock's winning try for the Kangaroos.
Mitchell Moses initially tried to run off a calf issue before being forced from the field just after the break, while Australia captain Isaah Yeo demonstrated his durability against a powerhouse Kiwis pack, having elected to delay surgery on his injured pectoral muscle just in order play in the tournament.
But understandably, much of the focus was on the star full-backs - Ponga and Walsh.
The Kangaroos number one was playing for the first time for eight weeks after recovering from an ankle injury.
- Australia edge New Zealand in epic World Cup opener 
  - Published4 hours ago
And he delivered a superb try-saving tackle on Ponga during the first-half before scoring a with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.
"Walshy was very good tonight having not played for eight weeks," said Australia head coach Kevin Walters.
"I thought he was really good. That try-saving tackle he did is equal to anything that he can do an attack, and then he comes up with a couple of big plays in attack as well.
"He's cramping and vomiting and all sorts of things. He didn't have the energy to kick the goal. He's a chucker [he throws up]. People get nicknames and his nickname is 'Chucker'.
"He's not an endurance athlete. He's a power athlete and he had some big efforts there a couple of times, back-to-back and we've seen him do that before."
Yeo added: "For Reece to come back in a contest like that with some of those plays is a massive effort after not playing for eight weeks. It won't get spoken about enough but it is really hard to do at this level.
"He has just got the ability to just make people miss. I think he made two people miss on the one move but he's just one of those players that can just break a game open, and we probably needed that."
New Zealand suffer Ponga blow
Having finally fulfilled a long-held desire to represent New Zealand, Ponga's night was going sweetly - he scored two tries that included one trademark run from deep and elusive step that left Walsh clutching at air - but it ended on a bitter note.
For one thing, Australia swiped victory from the grasp of Stacey Jones' team. For another, Ponga's futre participation in the World Cup is now in serious doubt.
Speaking after the game, Jones admitted that the Newcastle Knights man would now have medical checks after playing on for a quarter of the contest with an injury sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster.
"It's a possible fracture of the arm but he's going to go for scans and we're not going to make a call on him right now where he's at," said Jones.
"He had a pretty good game.
"I think he played on for 20 minutes, he toughed it out. It's a tough one. They scored a try and that's when we were told what it possibly was and that he would have to come off.
"He couldn't catch the ball or anything like that, he was in a lot of discomfort."
Should Ponga be ruled out it would be a huge blow to New Zealand's hopes of winning a second World Cup, 18 years on from their first.

ECI directs officers to provide political parties with searchable PDF voter rolls
The Election Commission has directed officers to provide recognised political parties with searchable PDF copies of draft and final voter rolls, excluding voters’ photographs.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has directed electoral registration officers to provide recognised political parties with hard copies and searchable PDF versions of draft and final electoral rolls for each polling station, with the digital copies excluding voters’ photographs.
The October 15 directive applies to the Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls in 17 states and Union Territories and also requires officials to share lists of additions, deletions and modifications.
“ERO, immediately after draft and final publication, in accordance with Rule 11(c) & 22 (c) of the Registration of the Electors Rule, 1960 (RER, 1960), shall supply free of cost two copies (one hard copy & one soft copy in readable PDF format) of each separate polling station to every recognised political party,” the poll body said.
The order also directs officials to share lists of additions, deletions and modifications to help parties track changes in voter records.
The directive comes amid controversy over the ECI’s revision of electoral rolls, with Opposition parties raising concerns about transparency and the risk of eligible voters being excluded.
The Commission currently uses scanned images in PDF format to display electoral rolls. Readable digital copies can be searched and analysed more easily, helping political parties check voter names and scrutinise changes at the polling-station level.
The controversy dates back to a 2018 Supreme Court case filed by Congress leader Kamal Nath, who sought voter lists in text format to help identify duplicate and bogus entries ahead of the Madhya Pradesh Assembly elections. The Election Commission opposed the demand for searchable PDFs, citing privacy concerns and the risk of data mining.
In June 2025, Rahul Gandhi and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge demanded consolidated, digital and machine-readable voter rolls for the 2024 Lok Sabha and Maharashtra Assembly elections, along with version histories and timestamps showing changes to the rolls.
The party also sought CCTV footage or videography from polling booths after 5pm on election day, citing questions about the rise in final voter turnout. Congress said access to the data would allow it to conduct its own analysis.
The ECI had then rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated and maintained that electoral rolls had been supplied to recognised parties during the regular revision process. It also argued that the demand for machine-readable lists was not tenable under the existing framework.

Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, report says
Trump’s Homeland Security Secretary has suggested that authorities are examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork

Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone was seized and more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued, including to some of her relatives, as part of a federal investigation into the Democratic lawmaker, according to a new report.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar's immigration paperwork, a source told The Associated Press. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday, just weeks before the November midterms in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on" related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker's financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar's home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Psst—I’m going to let you in on a little secret as a smart-home editor. Even though I now own the much-lauded Ecobee Premium ($260) smart thermostat, I had an Ecobee3 Lite for eight years, and I loved it just as much. It's everything you need a smart thermostat to be, without weird add-ons you'll never actually use, like occupancy detection and a built-in speaker for podcast streaming. (Unless you regularly listen to Uncanny Valley on your thermostat, in which case, you do you.)
The Ecobee3 Lite has a touchscreen and app control and is compatible with Ecobee sensors if you want to split the temperature difference across floors in your home. However, many people simply want to be able to turn their thermostat on and off from their phone and have the ability to set schedules. For this, the Lite has you covered.
Though it's been formally rebranded as the Essential and now runs $140, the OG Lite is still available refurbished straight from Ecobee. During the brand's fall sale, it's just $120 with free shipping—and it comes with the same three-year warranty as a new model.
If you've been wanting to upgrade your thermostat but missed Prime Day and don't want to wait until Black Friday, you may want to take a peek at this sale, which ends Wednesday, October 21.
Refurbished versions of the Enhanced ($170) and Premium ($220) thermostat models are available as well, plus packages that include Ecobee security accessories. I have tried most of the brand's add-ons and find Ecobee to be a bit buggy as a security and smart-home ecosystem (not the best, but also not the worst); however, I do heartily recommend the smart thermostat alone.
If you already have an Ecobee thermostat, you can also score a set of not-refurbished security sensors for $50, or the Ecobee video doorbell for $130, which lets you see and speak to visitors through your phone—or thermostat.

Trump ballroom's biggest donors were overwelmingly tech and telecom companies
Records also show that taxpayers are footing some of the bill.
The Washington Post has obtained a list of all of the major donors to President Trump's ballroom project thingamajig. The big reveal? The tech, telecom and crypto industries are the primary benefactors here, donating over $183 million for the audacious ballroom that nobody wants or asked for.
The biggest donors are NVIDIA and Apple, who each committed $25 million. The same goes for billionaire Charles Ergen, the co-founder of Dish Network. NVIDIA and Dish have both benefited significantly from Trump policies during this second term. As for Apple, it has been scrambling to curry favor with Trump so as to avoid some of those endless tariffs.
Exclusive: A list reveals all the major donors to President Trump's White House ballroom, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member. https://t.co/y3ivMy1NKk
— The Washington Post (@washingtonpost) October 15, 2026
Nearly every other major tech company has also donated millions each to the project, including Microsoft, Meta, Palantir, Google, Amazon and Cisco, among others. This isn't exactly surprising, given that most of these companies were also heavily involved with funding the president's inauguration in 2025.
Republican megadonor Sheldon Adelson also gave $25 million and companies like Blackrock, Lockheed Martin, Gemini and Coinbase gave millions. There's also $77 million in funds unaccounted for, as ballroom donations aren't subject to public disclosure or campaign finance rules. It could be anyone or any entity from anywhere. This money is funneled to a "nonprofit" that the president directly controls, just how the constitution envisioned it.
Absent from this list of donors? President Trump. He has repeatedly vowed to help pay for the project, once saying "it's being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine." There's no money trail here with his name on it.
However, we'll be spending some of our cents to turn the now-demolished East Wing into a gaudy ballroom for the world's richest people to dance inside of. The Washington Post has also found American taxpayers could end up paying for around half of this thing when all is said and done. This is especially worrisome, given that the expected budget for the ballroom recently shot up to $600 million.
This being a Trump project, there are even more troubling potential connections between the President and some of these donors. Joseph Popolo Jr. donated $1 million to the ballroom just after being chosen as the ambassador to the Netherlands. He did not report this donation. Trump cabinet member Kelly Loeffler and her husband promised $5 million. Brandon Lutnick gave stock worth more than $2.5 million. That's the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Finally, there's Isabela Herrera, who donated $2.5 million. This is the daughter of international banker Herrera Velutini, who was indicted by the Justice Department on bribery charges and pleaded guilty. His daughter made the first payment installment of $835,000 in October, 2025 and her father was pardoned by the president in January.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle expressed frustration that this list of donors was published and vowed that the administration will "relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give." He also said that reporters are just looking for "fake conflicts of interest."

Pope Leo XIV, 71, was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after doctors detected a small, localised nodule in his lung during medical examinations. He underwent surgery on October 13 at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, where surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung. Two days after surgery, doctors reported good recovery in the operated lung.
According to the Global Cancer Observatory, an estimated 2.48 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer worldwide in 2022, and approximately 1.82 million died from the disease that year. A 2025 analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimated that 1.26 million new cases of lung adenocarcinoma occurred worldwide in 2022, accounting for about half of all lung cancer cases.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Lung adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the most common category of lung cancer. It develops from glandular cells that produce substances such as mucus, which helps keep the airways moist. The cancer usually begins in the outer parts of the lungs, in cells lining small airways or the tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen enters the bloodstream.
The disease develops when changes in the DNA of these cells disrupt the normal controls on cell growth and division. The affected cells multiply uncontrollably and form a tumour that can invade surrounding lung tissue. As the cancer progresses, cells may enter the blood vessels or lymphatic system and spread to lymph nodes or other organs, including the brain, bones, liver and adrenal glands.
Lung adenocarcinoma is not a single, uniform disease. Tumours can have different genetic changes that affect how they grow and respond to treatment. Some changes allow cancer cells to keep multiplying by activating specific growth pathways. Others may make the tumour sensitive to particular medicines. This biological variation is one reason why doctors need to examine the characteristics of each tumour when planning treatment.
Adenocarcinoma can grow slowly in some people, while other tumours are more aggressive. Its behaviour depends on factors such as the tumour’s cellular features, genetic changes and stage at diagnosis.
Who is at risk?
Smoking is a major risk factor for lung cancer, but it is not the only one. Lung adenocarcinoma can also develop in people who have never smoked.
Exposure to outdoor air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter, is another important risk factor. These tiny particles can travel deep into the lungs, where prolonged exposure may contribute to inflammation, cellular damage and changes that increase the risk of cancer. The 2025 IARC analysis highlighted the contribution of air pollution to the global burden of lung adenocarcinoma.
Other risk factors include second-hand tobacco smoke, radon and certain substances encountered at work, such as asbestos. A family history of lung cancer may also be relevant.
Having one or more risk factors does not mean that a person will develop cancer. People without known risk factors can also develop the disease.
What are the symptoms?
Lung adenocarcinoma may not cause noticeable symptoms in its early stages. In some cases, it is detected during imaging performed for another reason. When symptoms develop, they can resemble those of common respiratory illnesses.
A persistent or worsening cough, chest pain, breathlessness, coughing up blood, unexplained weight loss and fatigue are among the symptoms that may occur. Some people may also develop repeated respiratory infections or a change in their voice.
If the cancer spreads beyond the lungs, symptoms may depend on the organs affected. Spread to the bones, for instance, may cause pain, while involvement of the brain may lead to headaches or other neurological symptoms.
These symptoms can also occur in conditions other than cancer. However, persistent or unexplained symptoms should be assessed by a doctor.
How is it diagnosed?
Doctors begin by assessing a person’s symptoms, medical history and risk factors, followed by a physical examination. A chest X-ray may reveal a suspicious area, while a computed tomography (CT) scan provides more detailed images of the lungs and can help identify the size and location of a tumour.
Depending on the findings, further imaging may be needed to determine whether the cancer has spread. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan can help identify areas of suspected cancer activity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), particularly of the brain, may be recommended in certain cases.
Imaging alone cannot confirm lung adenocarcinoma. A definitive diagnosis generally requires a sample of cells or tissue, obtained through a biopsy or a procedure such as bronchoscopy. The sample is examined by a pathologist to determine whether cancer is present and identify its type.
Once the diagnosis is confirmed, doctors determine the stage of the disease. This involves assessing the size of the tumour, whether nearby lymph nodes are affected and whether the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. Lung cancer is commonly classified into stages I to IV, with stage IV indicating that it has spread to distant parts of the body.
Doctors may also recommend molecular testing of the tumour. These tests look for genetic changes that may help guide treatment, including alterations in the EGFR gene and changes involving ALK, ROS1 and other genes. Testing for a protein called PD-L1 may also help doctors assess whether immunotherapy is likely to be useful.
What are the treatment options?
Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer, the tumour’s characteristics, the person’s general health and whether the cancer can be removed safely. Different treatments may be used alone or in combination.
For early-stage lung adenocarcinoma that has not spread beyond the lung, surgery is often the main treatment. Depending on the tumour’s size and location, surgeons may remove a small section of the lung or an entire lobe. For people who cannot undergo surgery, stereotactic body radiotherapy, which delivers radiation precisely to the tumour, may be an option.
When the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or structures, treatment may involve a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted drugs. Treatment before surgery may help shrink the tumour, while treatment afterwards may reduce the risk of the cancer returning in selected patients.
For advanced lung adenocarcinoma, molecular test results can help doctors choose the most suitable treatment. If the tumour has a specific genetic alteration for which an effective medicine is available, targeted therapy may be recommended. These drugs act on particular molecules or pathways that help cancer cells grow.
Immunotherapy works differently. It helps the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells. Depending on the tumour’s characteristics, it may be used alone or alongside chemotherapy. Chemotherapy remains an important option for patients whose tumours do not have a genetic alteration that can be treated with targeted drugs. Radiotherapy may also help control the disease or relieve symptoms.
Advances in diagnosis and treatment have expanded options for some patients, including those with advanced disease. However, outcomes vary widely, and survival statistics cannot predict an individual person’s response to treatment.
When the cancer cannot be cured, treatment may still slow its progression, prolong life and improve quality of life. Supportive and palliative care can help manage pain, breathlessness, fatigue and other symptoms. It can be provided alongside cancer treatment and is not limited to end-of-life care.
Can it be prevented?
Not all cases of lung adenocarcinoma can be prevented, but reducing exposure to known risk factors can lower the risk of lung cancer. Avoiding tobacco, stopping smoking, reducing exposure to second-hand smoke, improving air quality and limiting exposure to carcinogens are important measures.
Screening with low-dose CT can help detect lung cancer before symptoms appear in certain people at high risk, particularly those with a substantial history of smoking. Recommendations depend on factors such as age, smoking history and local clinical guidance. Screening is not recommended routinely for everyone, and a normal chest X-ray does not rule out lung cancer.
Recognising persistent symptoms and ensuring timely access to diagnostic tests can help people receive appropriate care earlier.
