At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northern Pakistani city of Peshawar.
As panicked parents and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble.
Most of the victims were under 13 years old and from low-income households. At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, the regional director of emergency services.
Television footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to waiting ambulances as people crowded the alley where the school stood.
The roof of a higher floor collapsed on to classrooms below, crumpling two storeys of the building, a rescue official said. “The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher,” said the Lady Reading hospital spokesperson, Mohammad Asim. Three children remained in critical condition with head injuries, while most of the injured taken to the hospital had been treated and discharged, he added.
The incident took place at 8.48am local time (0348 GMT) and the rescue operation lasted for four to five hours, Khattak said. “It was a weak building structure,” said the Peshawar police chief, Mian Saeed. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse.”
Saeed said the school’s owner had been arrested and an investigation launched. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.
Distraught relatives accused the school of ignoring concerns about the building’s condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.
The school was located in a poor, crowded neighbourhood of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Pakistan’s president imposed a state of emergency on Sunday, saying the provincial government had failed to tackle Islamist militancy from neighbouring Afghanistan, an allegation it denied.
Pakistan spends less than 1% of its approximately $450bn (£340bn) GDP on education, leaving many families dependent on low-cost private schools.
Many of those schools operate from poorly maintained rented buildings with limited oversight, contributing to recurring safety concerns. In June, at least 14 children died when the roof of a tutoring centre housed in a dilapidated building collapsed in the eastern city of Lahore.
There was no immediate comment from school officials.
The country’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, expressed sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims’ families, his office said.
Jawad Ahmad, whose son and daughter survived the incident, said the news had left him devastated. “It felt as if someone had shot me in the chest when I learned that the school building had collapsed,” he said.
The province, governed for years by the party of the jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, has frequently been at odds with the federal administration. Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, imposed a new governor on the province when he declared the state of emergency on Sunday, sharpening the tensions.

Permanent outdoor lights are the perfect solution to a holiday season's worth of lights, and will last you for years to come. The name suggests exactly what they are: a type of string light designed to stay up all year instead of coming down after the occasion you hung them for, whether it's the holiday season or a big party that inspired you to deck out your front porch.
Whether these lights are truly “permanent” is up to you, since you can choose to anchor them to your home with either screws or adhesive. Note that they may not be a fit for every home's architecture—you will need eaves, and preferably flat ones, to hide the thick cords. Our favorite options are from Govee ($300, 100 feet) and Eufy ($350, 100 feet); both are great sets you can cut and splice to customize to your home's roofline. My favorite affordable set is from Cync ($117, 100 feet)—it's easy to use and install and has lots of great color options.
No matter which set you choose, these lights are made for year-round enjoyment, though they shine best in the holiday season. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck uses hers in the post-holiday season to display her husband’s favorite sports team colors, while I'm currently using mine to backlight the giant spiderweb spread across my balcony for Halloween. We're both looking forward to switching over to Christmas color schemes soon, and you can too after picking up one of our favorite sets below.
Updated October 2026: I've updated this guide with current pricing as we head into the holiday season, and added a new section about the lights we're testing next.
What Are Permanent Outdoor Lights?
Permanent outdoor lights are exactly what they sound like: outdoor lights meant to be permanently affixed to your home, so you don't have to go up and down a ladder every Halloween and Christmas season. They're similar to smart Christmas lights like those from Twinkly ($125) and Philips Hue ($220), and other smart lighting options like Philips Hue's smart bulbs ($90), in that they connect to an app and have custom color control.
The lights we recommend below are all DIY-friendly, but you can also hire a professional to affix them to your home. Some higher-end brands, like JellyFish and Gemstone, are for professional installation only. Hiring an installer is recommended either way if you have harder-to-reach eaves or a trickier home design, which may add considerably to the overall cost.
What Your Home Will Need
The most important thing to check is if your home is even compatible with permanent outdoor string lights. If your home has any of these features, installation should work for you:
- Accessible roof eaves, often found on one- or two-story homes
- An outdoor ceiling, like a porch roof
- Flat, smooth materials, including glass, cement, wood, or metal, under the eaves (or other spots on your home's exterior that would make sense for lights to live permanently, like a porch covering or pergola)
- Access to an outlet, ideally an outdoor one that's at least partially covered to protect the control box, or the ability to run the cord to one inside a garage or other interior space
Most one- and two-story homes can accommodate permanent outdoor lights, since they typically have roof eaves accessible on both levels. Govee, for example, claims its permanent outdoor lights ($300) will work on everything from cottages and tiny houses to large homes and even mansions. (I'm sad to report that no, I did not have a mansion available for our testing.) Eufy (another set we recommend!) warns that certain paints, including those with texturing, could prevent secure adhesion of its permanent outdoor lights ($350).
Most permanent outdoor lights come with multiple options for attaching them to your home, ranging from sticky tabs to more permanent options with screws, though some brands may require you to buy anchors separately. Some of our testers used sticky options with success, while others chose to use the included screws to ensure the lights wouldn't move. It depends on your home style and personal comfort as to which style you'd like to use. We've tested sticky adhesion for the better part of six months in the Midwestern US with great success, but obviously, tape isn't as permanent as drilled anchors.
Here are the home styles for which installation of permanent lights will be a struggle or may require a professional for installation:
- Homes and properties with a stucco exterior
- Homes with no roof eaves of any kind
- Homes with cross-style eaves that don't allow for flat adhesion
- Three-story homes with no eaves on the lower levels
- Townhomes and condominiums that don't allow for permanent changes, or don't have rooflines to fit these light styles
I live in a three-story, stucco-covered townhouse, which disqualifies me from installing most permanent outdoor lights. The stucco makes it impossible to stick anything to it, and I have an HOA that forbids “permanent changes” to my exterior, so they frown upon me drilling. And, most important, I don't have the right eave design with my townhouse to hide the strip of lights when they're off.
But that doesn't mean I have zero options (more on what I can do instead below). Still, if you want the full-home look, you'll need a home with a more standard roof.
What to Look for in Permanent Outdoor Lights
Most permanent outdoor lights look pretty similar, with puck lights on a string. How different can they be, right? Well, we've found a couple features that really make a set stand out.
Cut-and-splice abilities. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck has tried two different sets of permanent lights on her home, and she finds the ability to cut and splice the lights to be a key feature. Many homes have varied architectural features like peaks, gables, and sections without eaves, so the ability to cut out pucks and splice the cord ends back together creates a much more customized and professional look. Our favorite sets from Govee ($300, 100 feet) and Eufy ($350, 100 feet) both include this ability.
Weatherproofing. Every model needs an IP (weatherproofing) rating to survive outside, so if you don't see one, don't buy those lights. There's usually a lower rating for the control box compared to the rest of the lights, so be sure you can put that somewhere that's a little less exposed to the elements. (As mentioned above, make sure you have an outdoor outlet, and check if there's only one on a certain side of your home in case it limits your installation options.)
A range of installation options. You'll want a set that comes with plenty of options for your own installation, including adhesive and drilled mounting options. What you need will vary based on your home design and materials; e.g., you'll want adhesive for homes you can't drill into. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, who tested a couple of different permanent lights, liked sets with screw-on holders that the puck-style permanent lights can slide onto.
Controls for individual lights. This should be a no-brainer, but some cheaper lights won't offer this ability or have more roadblocks to customized control. Make sure you'll have easy individual controls, or you might find yourself frustrated with the design results of these lights. It's similar to design controls that you'd see on smart bulbs and smart string lights.
A great app. This goes hand in hand with the need for individual light control—a good app determines whether that and other features are accessible. Govee and Eufy, two of our favorite permanent outdoor lights we've tried, both have good apps that are easy to use and come with preloaded light themes. These tech companies make more than just outdoor lights, including other favorite gear of ours, so they're a good brand to trust to make a usable product and app. We also like Lepro's more affordable lights, though the app had some extra hoops to jump through to get to controls, while Lumary's app was a brutal experience for our tester.
What Time of Year Should You Use Permanent Outdoor Lights?
Most people are interested in this style of lights for the fall and winter, and it's the time of year I've found myself using it the most. That's a great time to set them up and use them, since you've got Halloween and Christmas decor that the permanent outdoor lights could complement with colorful holiday scenes. The days are also shorter, so you've got more nighttime hours to take advantage of these lights.
They’re a fun way to deck out your home for a sports game, especially for major games like the Super Bowl (WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, a resident of Washington state, was surprised to discover just how many people in her neighborhood had permanent lights this past February) and the World Cup, or for smaller holidays like St. Patrick's Day or the Fourth of July. They're a fun way to jazz up your home's curb appeal in the evening year-round (though if you have an HOA, you might have to check your rules about displaying lights regularly) or add a little pizzazz for your next outdoor party. No matter what you use it for, there's no wrong way or wrong time of year to use these lights.
Our Favorite Permanent Outdoor Lights
We've tested a handful of permanent lights on different homes and have a few clear favorites. These are all options we recommend, provided your home's exterior meets the constraints mentioned above.
These lights from Govee have been one of our top picks in our smart Christmas lights story for a reason, and they're still our favorite at this price point for everything you'll get with them. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill tested the 100-foot string that came with six sections, plus an extension code. He used adhesive and screw clips to secure the light pucks and cables, and found installation easy. This is a set that you can cut and splice, but he says that isn't a task for the faint of heart. The lights have an IP67 rating, and an IP65 rating for the control box. The busy companion app has everything you could want: color controls, tons of Scenes (Govee's lighting effects), scheduling, and even a music sync option (though that felt a little gimmicky). There's Matter support, and Govee can connect to Alexa and Google's ecosystems for voice control. Simon says he would like these lights to be closer together and the design to be a little more subtle, since you can see the cords pretty easily.
★ New Model Out: There's an updated version of these for 2026, the Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro (100 feet, $280), which I'll be testing this fall. This set has similar weather ratings and sizing options, but promises more than 100 modes and has an AI tool to design custom lighting, called AI Lighting Bot 2.0. Stay tuned for my next update on how these lights turned out.
WIRED reviewer Kat Merck has tested two sets of permanent outdoor lights on her home, and Eufy's S4, which incorporates RGB with both warm and cool whites, is by far her favorite. She's found the app incredibly easy to navigate and find the features she wants, from preset holiday scenes (120!) and colors to schedules and brightness adjustments. There's even an AI feature that lets you create customized light shows based on moods and scenarios. They were relatively easy to install on her home, which has nonstandard architectural features, as this set has extensions and can be cut and spliced. She says the lights aren't quite as bright as the Lumary Max set below, but the brightness is adjustable. There's also a radar motion sensor included, though she was never able to get it to work. The Eufy S4 set also works with the Matter protocol, so it's compatible with Apple, Google, and Alexa's smart home ecosystems. It's got a waterproof rating of IP67 like the Govee set above. They've been on Kat's house for the better part of a year now, and are still working well with no issues.
Cync, from appliance maker GE, makes affordable smart bulbs and other smart lights I like, so it's not a huge surprise that I also appreciate the brand's Smart Eave Lights. They were easy to install with 3M sticky strips already on the individual lights, and since my eaves are out of safe reach on my townhouse, I used the lights on my balcony railing with great success. One piece of the 100-foot set (it comes with four strings, plus an extension) was the perfect length to loop around my 9-foot-long railing. The set quickly connected to the Cync app, and the power cord is nice and long to make it easy to reach wherever your power outlet is. It has a waterproof rating of IP65.
These lights have been on my balcony for about a year now, and have had no issues, even after months of leaving them off. I've been able to easily reconnect to them whenever I want and get the light colors and routines set up for whatever holiday or event I'm celebrating.
If You Can’t Install Permanent Outdoor Lights
Not every home is a good fit for these types of lights. I haven't yet found a permanent light set that can attach to my home, so here's what I've used instead for a similar result.
Twinkly's smart string lights have a weatherproof rating of IP44 for both the lights and the power supply. This means they're splash-proof but not waterproof, so you can use them outside, but make sure they're somewhat protected. I love how much you can customize these lights. You'll use the app to take a photo of how you've set up your lights, whether that's around a Christmas tree, around your balcony's railing, or along the front of your house, and then you'll be able to customize the lights and pattern based on how you arranged them. There are tons of fun light designs already in the app, and you can make your own. It's a good option if you can only do string lights but want smart capabilities. These lights are also compatible with Amazon’s, Google’s, and Apple’s ecosystems. Twinkly also makes an icicle-style smart light string ($110), which I love using outside too; they hung over my garage door for the holiday season. I'm on my third year of using this set and it's still going strong.
More Outdoor Lights We’ve Tested
Cync Outdoor Light Strip for $154: I was really hoping this would be a good solution for outdoor lights for my balcony, but this light strip is heavy and tall and is better designed to line a yard versus sticking onto the side of a railing. It comes with grass stakes.
Lepro’s EE1 AI for $450 (300 feet): These permanent outdoor lights are sold out right now, but they are another more affordable option when the shorter length is available. They aren't as cheap as Cync, however, and you will have to get around the app's AI to really get the most out of it. Right now only the longer set is in stock, too, making it more expensive to invest in.
Lumary Outdoor Permanent Lights Max for $331 (105 feet): Lumary's lights were frustrating and limiting for our tester. The app wasn't intuitive or easy to use, and our tester actually had to have the power box replaced after she tried to connect the lights to a different phone. She liked how bright the lights were and that there’s a physical remote, but the app, power box shutdown, and installation limitations compared with other sets (no splicing ability, installation recommended from the left) make this one we’d skip. Lumary has since released new versions, and is now on its third iteration with the Lumary Permanent Outdoor Lights 3 ($220, 100 feet).
What We’re Testing Next
We're looking at testing a few permanent outdoor lights this fall and winter. Here are the sets on our list to hopefully test: the Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro ($280, 100 feet), the Nanoleaf Permanent Outdoor Lights ($200, 49 feet), and the Hampton Bay Permanent Outdoor String Lights ($89, 50 feet).
FAQs
What Are the Cons of Permanent Outdoor Lights?
The main downside to permanent outdoor lights is the cost. These sets usually cost significantly more than a light string, even the smart ones. That's because they're designed to last longer on your home, and the more expensive sets allow you to cut and splice the cords to perfectly fit your home instead of dangling strings and extra lights. It's an investment, but one you can enjoy year-round.
Are Permanent Outdoor Lights Worth It?
Yes, because you'll install them once and be good to go with every holiday in your future: Christmas! Halloween! Your fave sports team headed to a big championship match! Your kid's graduation (or your own)! Similar to how smart bulbs can give you so many options inside your home, the possibilities are endless and something you'll be able to use and enjoy year-round.
When Should You Buy Permanent Outdoor Lights?
There's no wrong time of year to use these lights, but I often see them on sale during events like Prime Day and Black Friday. I've seen them sporadically on sale throughout the year without special holidays and events attached to the sale, so it's worth checking regularly to see if a set you like gets a surprise discount. But the easiest time to aim for is one of these deal events. I'd recommend aiming for Amazon's summertime Prime Day or early fall deal event (last year it was called Amazon Big Deal Days 2025, but we'll see if it gets the same name this year) so that you can have your permanent outdoor lights in time for Halloween and Christmas.
How Does WIRED Test Permanent Outdoor Lights? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?
WIRED tests permanent outdoor lights on the homes of our reviewers. We've tested these lights on three different homes in separate areas with serious weather: Washington state, Missouri, and Scotland. We've also tested a set in the more mild climate of Southern California. We install these on the homes themselves and leave them up for at least a few weeks, if not months and years (depending on performance), to see how they hold up. Our picks remain on our homes for long-term testing, as these lights are supposed to be permanent, and used sets are safely disposed of.

Emerging out of stealth mode, robotics startup Origin has raised $20 Mn (around ₹189 Cr) in a funding round co-led by Accel and Zacua Ventures. The round also saw participation from Unilazer Ventures, Schema Ventures and Z21. Angel investors from Anduril, Skild AI, 1X and Tesla also participated in the fundraise. As part of the investment, Zacua Ventures’ founding partner Vivin Hegde has also joined the startup’s board as a director. The startup said that the fresh capital will primarily be utilised to deploy its flagship OG-1 robot and build a fleet of construction robots. A chunk of the capital will also be used to support “large-scale” pilots with customers in the US and Europe and explore new use cases for bots. “We think of Origin as a time machine for construction, helping crews complete work faster while moving the industry toward autonomous job sites. Wall finishing and painting are only our starting trades; our ambition is to automate the full range of interior trades so contractors can build faster with consistent quality,” said Origin cofounder and CEO Yogesh Ghaturle. Founded in 2025 by Ghaturle, Ashish Daga and Tushar Makkar, the US-headquartered startup develops autonomous robotics for construction work. It aims to address widespread labour shortages in the construction sector and claims that its robots can work 3X faster than a human. Its flagship robot, OG-1, is currently capable of automatically completing wall-finishing tasks such as applying compound, sanding, and priming. The startup claims to have already deployed its robots at construction sites in New York, adding that its bots are also being deployed across commercial spaces, apartments, data centers, hotels and warehouses. Under the hood, OG-1 is powered by a proprietary foundation model that the startup calls a construction action model. The model integrates a reasoning system to plan complex sub-tasks, an action policy to help it navigate autonomously and a controller for feedback-driven movement. Going forward, the startup plans to deploy 150 robots by the end of 2027. It is also exploring additional pilots for its offerings in countries like Germany, Sweden, France and Saudi Arabia. Origin also noted that incoming investor Zacua will support its expansion plans through its network of contractors, developers and manufacturers. With the latest fundraise, Origin is eyeing a piece of the global construction robotics sector, which is projected to become a $12 Bn opportunity by 2036. Back home in India, startups like Pace Robotics and Flo Mobility are also raising big bucks to take a lead in the burgeoning space.

When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.
Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.
AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.
Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.
When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)
Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.
“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”
Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”
Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.
Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

South Africa hope to host first African Olympics
- Published
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.
Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.
The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.
Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.
After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.
The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.
Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.
Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.
The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.
Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.
Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.
Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.
The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.
Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.
Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.
The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.
The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.
The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

‘Dictatorship’ vs ‘Aasteen ka Saanp’: Mixed political reactions on Imran Khan being asked to leave India
The Mumbai Police directed Imran Khan, an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, to leave India by October 28 for protesting against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
A notice by the Mumbai office of the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) directing actor Imran Khan to leave India before October 28 triggered many political reactions, with some backing the move and others opposing it. While several Opposition leaders came out in Khan's support, some BJP leaders backed the Mumbai Police move.
The notice came days after Khan was briefly detained for participating in a protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Opposition parties in Maharashtra criticised the ‘leave India’ notice. Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT) leaders accused the government of being “dictatorial” and curbing dissent while the BJP defended the action, saying foreign nationals should not participate in India’s political protests.
Deep Dive
The notice directs the 43-year-old ‘US national’ to depart from the country, alleging that he has contravened provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025.
‘Freedom being snatched away’
Congress leader Nana Patole described the action as an example of dictatorial rule, alleging that people who speak against the government are increasingly being branded as traitors. “Not just actor Imran Khan, but anyone in the country who speaks against the government is labelled as a traitor by people sitting in the government,” Patole told PTI.
The former Maharashtra Congress president also alleged that people’s freedom was being curtailed and questioned the removal of voters’ names during the SIR exercise. “People’s freedom is being snatched away,” he said, adding that citizens should be able to express their views and participate in protests without facing restrictions.
"Nowadays, in order to hold a protest also, you need to pay money. If you want to express your opinion, you must pay. This is a dictatorship. If you do not have the right to voice your opinion in independent India, then the Narendra Modi government is running a dictatorship," the former MP said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also criticised the action, alleging that the government was apprehensive about protests against the SIR exercise.
“The government is scared if Imran Khan is asked to leave the country for participating against the SIR protest in favour of the youth,” Raut told reporters.
He pointed out that several Bollywood personalities held foreign citizenship and questioned the government’s approach towards foreign nationals living in India. Raut also referred to former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh amid mass protests in August 2024, and asked why the government had not asked her to leave.
NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule also came out in support of Khan, arguing that people should have the right to participate in protests.
“Everyone has the right to protest. Now, someone will say that he (Khan) has a foreign passport. Many of my friends live abroad. They also protest,” Sule said.
Questioning the action against the actor, the Baramati MP asked what offence Khan had committed by participating in the demonstration. She also contrasted the action against him with the continued presence of politicians facing serious criminal allegations in public office.
The Congress, NCP (SP) and Shiv Sena (UBT) are part of the Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA), the opposition alliance in Maharashtra.
BJP backs action against actor
The BJP defended the police action, saying that foreign nationals should not participate in protests concerning India’s domestic political affairs.
BJP MLC Parinay Fuke welcomed the notice and alleged that people arriving from other countries to participate in demonstrations over the SIR exercise were attempting to create unrest.
“Imran Khan is a US citizen. Coming to this country and agitating and speaking of name deletion in SIR — such people are ‘aasteen ka saanp’,” Fuke told ANI, using a Hindi expression meaning “a snake in one’s sleeve”.
He said the Maharashtra government and Mumbai Police knew how to deal with such individuals and called for action against foreign nationals from the US, Pakistan and Bangladesh who, he alleged, were participating in such protests.
BJP leader Kirit Somaiya had earlier sought action against Khan following his participation in the protest. Somaiya alleged that foreign nationals involved in such demonstrations were attempting to create discord and thanked Union home minister Amit Shah and Maharashtra CM Devendra Fadnavis for the action.
"Imran Khan is an American citizen; what is he doing in India? His very purpose in coming here is to spread discord. For the past few weeks, certain individuals—who receive funding from Pakistan and the United States—have been engaging in such activities," he told ANI.
BJP leader Jafar Islam also backed the move, saying that if Khan was a foreign national, he did not have the right to participate in political protests. He added that the law was taking its course and should be allowed to operate. “I was unaware that he was a foreign national. If he is, he does not have the right to protest,” Islam told ANI.
Maharashtra minister of state Yogesh Kadam defended the police action, saying foreign nationals must abide by the conditions of their visas. “When you enter a country, a visa is usually issued, and certain conditions are stated within it. You cannot violate those conditions. If any violation occurs, the relevant act applies, and a notice is issued accordingly,” Kadam told reporters in Mumbai.
He said he was not aware of the exact contents of the notice but maintained that the law could not be overlooked simply because the person concerned was an actor. Kadam added that the government would take appropriate action if further complaints or issues came to light.
What happened at the protest?
Khan, 43, who has acted in several Bollywood films and is the nephew of actor Aamir Khan, participated in the October 10 demonstration at August Kranti Maidan, where protesters demanded CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over concerns surrounding the SIR of electoral rolls.
Police briefly detained the actor during the protest. Following his detention, Khan shared a photograph apparently taken inside a police vehicle, captioned: “Apparently I’m going for a drive.”
Speaking to the media, Khan said he had attended the demonstration as a resident of Mumbai and was not there to put forward any specific demands.
“I don't have demands. I am here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I am here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted. Why are people's voices being suppressed? That is why I am here,” he said.

Rally champion gets hero's welcome in home county
- Published
New world rally champion Elfyn Evans has been given a hero's welcome by hundreds of supporters at a celebration event in his home county.
The driver from Dinas Mawddwy in Gwynedd drove his Toyota world rally car from the village to a stage in the middle of nearby Dolgellau, before meeting fans for autographs and photographs.
The celebrations ended with a driving exhibition by Evans - where he took First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth for a spin - in the high-powered car around Dolgellau's main car park.
Evans became the first Welsh driver to become world champion, and during the event, he thanked the fans who had supported him since he started his career as a teenager.
Evans said he felt "very lucky and honoured" that the event was arranged, and hoped his success would build "some awareness of the sport".
He added he was taken aback by the cheering from pupils.
"Of course we're used to it on events, but to have it at home is a bit surreal in a way," he said.
"It's a small community, obviously everyone around my age knows me as Elfyn so there's no fuss.
"But maybe for the kids they're only used to seeing me on TV so it's a bit of a different reception."
But he said being champion wouldn't change much in his day to day life.
"Life at home is exactly the same, we still have the same battles to get the kids to school every morning as any other family," he said.
"I will continue to give my best, current or past form won't alter that. I'm still hungry to try and achieve more in the sport and my approach won't change."
Wales' First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth was among the supporters at the celebration event and said Evans was "a true champion".
"To become a world champion is no mean feat," he said.
"He has shown such consistency, such quality over the years - came so close, we felt his pain year after year.
"I had a feeling this year he could do it, and now we are seeing what this means not just to his home area but to the whole of Wales. A true champion a true hero here too," ap Iorwerth said.
Son of former rally driver Gwyndaf Evans, Elfyn - before this year's victory - had finished runner-up in the world championship five times.
The World Rally Championship sees teams battle across multiple events, and various countries and surfaces.
It is one of motorsport's most spectacular and demanding disciplines, taking drivers and cars to the limit across some of the world's most challenging terrain - from snow and ice to gravel, asphalt and extreme heat.
During the final rally of this season in Sardinia, it looked like Evans' main rival and teammate Oliver Solberg would deny him the title once again.
But two corners from the finish line on the last stage of the rally, Solberg slid off the track, sparking jubilation amongst Elfyn Evans's fans.
As part of the celebrations, Evans visited his former school Ysgol Bro Idris earlier on Thursday, where he met pupils and teachers.
Esme and Lois, both 12, said the experience was "amazing".
Esme said she felt "so lucky" that the world champion had visited.
"We're such a small place, but we have such amazing people here," she added.
Louie, 13, met him during the event and "spoke about how much the car was worth and how it felt to see him come first".
He watched him win, and said "it's shows what Wales can do".
Oscar, 13, liked Evans' car, which was on display at the school.
"I'm proud of him for doing what he's done, and he deserves more I reckon."
The school visit was followed by the event in Dolgellau's Eldon Square, where crowds had gathered despite the persistent rain.
Most of the supporters were local, but some had travelled significant distances to be at the event.
When Elfyn Evans spoke from the podium, he thanked his family for supporting him throughout his career, saying his grandfather had "taught me to drive probably far too early".
Wyn Williams from Llanrwst and Neil Pringle from Betws-y-Coed were in Sardinia when Evans clinched the championship.
Williams said the celebration was "the icing on the cake after being in Sardinia".
Pringle added that the evening was "fantastic" and that the first minister's presence "shows what this means to Wales".
"This is for Elfyn, his family and the country."
Heledd Edwards travelled from Talerddig to Dolgellau and described Elfyn's perseverance as an inspiration.
Several members of Elfyn's family were also in the crowd. His aunt, Lowri Edwards, had travelled from Glan Conwy, saying she was immensely proud to have a world champion in the family.
"We're absolutely thrilled, to be honest. He's come so close and been terribly unlucky, finishing second five times - we're absolutely thrilled."
Dolgellau Town Council helped organise the celebration, with Deputy Mayor Nia Wyn Evans, saying: "We are absolutely thrilled and delighted to be able to welcome Elfyn back as a world champion; there's a real buzz in the town."
Evans' victory comes at the end of an era for the high-powered Rally1 cars.
From next season, the world rally championship is introducing new technical regulations which aim to encourage new manufacturers to compete in more affordable and sustainable vehicles.
It will be a new challenge for the drivers and their teams, as Evans sets out to defend his title.

Arizona university to 'part ways' with coach who oversaw training where Matthew Mayich collapsed
Arizona State University hires ex-NHL coach Dave Hakstol to replace Greg Powers
Arizona State University (ASU) says it will "part ways" with the hockey coach who oversaw the training at which Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on a hot day this August.
ASU has “reached a mutual agreement to part ways with hockey coach Greg Powers,” officials said in a statement Thursday, adding that former NHL coach Dave Hakstol will replace him.
Mayich, an NHL prospect drafted by the St. Louis Blues, remains in hospital in serious condition, his family’s lawyer, Robert Carey, said Thursday.
In an initial review released last month, ASU official James Rund wrote that Mayich collapsed at a training at ASU’s Tempe campus just before 8:30 a.m. Aug. 20. The review also said coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.
ASU then said it would commission an independent review, to be conducted by former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales.
Mayich's family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances around the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to his collapse. Mayich's parents say he was healthy prior to the workout. The family's lawyers said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.
Family says Powers should cooperate with investigation
"Our focus remains where it has been since August 20, on Matthew, and making sure what happened to him is fully understood and never happens to another player," the Mayich family said in a statement through Carey Thursday.
They said Bales's investigation must continue "with its full scope, gathering all digital evidence and covering everyone involved in that morning’s workout and in approving it, and its findings must be made public."
"Coach Powers’s departure should not limit his cooperation or anyone else’s, and the players who have spoken up must be protected," the family added. "We wish Coach Hakstol, his staff, and the players a safe and successful season."
Seven of Mayich's teammates anonymously sent a letter to ASU's president Michael Crow on Sept. 28, disputing some findings from the school's review of the workout that led to his collapse. Players alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.
It urged that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."
Powers had been ASU’s head coach since 2015 and, in 2022, signed a five-year contract extension through the 2026-27 season. He was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 30, ASU said in a statement. ASU assistant coach Mike Corbett was appointed to lead the team.
University hires Colorado Avalanche assistant coach
Before ASU announced hiring Hakstol on Thursday, he had been working as an assistant coach for the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche. He previously worked as a head coach with the Philadelphia Flyers and the Seattle Kraken, as well as an assistant for the Toronto Maple Leafs.
ASU Athletics Director Graham Rossini also announced that former NHL player Matt Greene, who played for the Los Angeles Kings and Edmonton Oilers, would join the team as an assistant along with current assistant, Jimmy Mullin. Corbett’s status was not announced.
Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issued its first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.
Two months later, Israel has still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined to comment.
Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.
Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.
But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.
“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.
The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, whom Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.
Though many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.
On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.
There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.
A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.
Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing about 1,400 people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.

Nobody on a factory floor wakes up wanting AI, Internet of Things (IoT) systems or a smarter dashboard. Their job is simply to keep machines running, production moving, and compliance headaches at bay. For factories, this also means keeping track of groundwater extraction, air quality and other metrics, which regulators now expect enterprises to monitor and report. For decades, this grunt work rested on manual readings. A flow meter installed on a borewell would tell a factory how much water was being pumped out. Someone would note the reading, compile it and submit it to the relevant authority. The system worked, but it was slow, fragmented and vulnerable to inaccurate reporting. Now, as regulatory expectations shift towards IoT-based monitoring of industrial assets, this challenge of compliance has become more urgent. Enterprises may not necessarily care about deploying another layer of technology, but they care about avoiding the fines and disruption that follow non-compliance. Another major issue facing enterprise compliance is that most manufacturers, which supply industrial monitoring equipment, are not built to offer software, AI and connected-device capabilities. “Industries had long relied on flow meters for manual readings. When IoT monitoring became mandatory, they turned to their existing flow meter vendors for compliance support. However, most OEMs lacked expertise in IoT, AI, and software,” says Ubiqedge cofounder Visat Patel. This is where Mumbai-based Ubiqedge appears to have found its niche. Founded in 2024 by Patel, Archit Khandelwal, Akhilesh Thorat and Hetvi Shah, the startup is building a full-stack artificial internet of things (AIoT) platform for monitoring and managing industrial infrastructure. Its hardware platform, KLEON, and AI-powered software layer, SAMASTH, are designed to help industrial equipment makers and system integrators convert conventional machines into automated systems. Earlier this year, the Mumbai-based startup raised ₹10 Cr in a seed round led by Piper Serica. A Second Shot At Industrial IoT For Patel, Ubiqedge is his second attempt at building an industrial IoT company. An alumnus of IIT Bombay, Patel began his entrepreneurial journey in his final year of college. He holds two patents – one in biomedical devices and another in agritech. Before Ubiqedge, he founded Ushwa, an IoT startup that operated for nearly eight years before it was shut down. By his own admission, Patel said that the technology was sound, but the go-to-market (GTM) approach was wrong, and the business couldn't scale past a certain point. This experience left the founders with a clearer understanding of why industrial IoT deployments often fail to move beyond pilots. “We identified that while AI and IoT tools are good individually, industries aren't very comfortable engaging with this technology. A lot of large companies have deployed this tech at a cost of ₹50 Lakh or a couple of crores, gotten a good overview, but then nothing concrete has come out of the solution. This has weakened industry confidence in the technology's scalability,” Patel said. Determined not to repeat the past mistakes, Patel regrouped his founding team, including Khandelwal, Thorat and Shah, to rethink industrial IoT deployment from the ground up. The four cofounders quickly zeroed in on three persistent bottlenecks. Technology creators lacked the bandwidth to support varied industrial use cases OEMs also lacked the expertise to develop IoT and AI layers around their machines Technicians on the ground were often intimidated by complex connected systems. Ubiqedge was built around solving this three-way problem. Rather than asking factories to adopt a new tech stack from scratch, the startup was envisaged with the idea of making industrial AI and IoT simple enough to deploy at scale. Turning Machines Into Connected Assets To overcome traditional enterprise sales resistance, the startup deploys a novel distribution strategy. Ubiqedge doesn't sell directly to factories. It sells to OEMs and system integrators, who then bundle Ubiqedge's hardware and software with their own equipment. Powering this bundled model is a plug-and-play tech architecture designed to upgrade legacy machinery without disrupting existing operations. At the heart of Ubiqedge’s tech stack is KLEON, a hardware device that is integrated with industrial equipment. It reads the data generated by the equipment, stores it and sends it to the cloud. The device can communicate with nearly any sensor protocol and can operate through SIM connectivity, Wi-Fi or LAN. Take a factory borewell as an example. The flow meter attached to the borewell measures the volume of groundwater being extracted. Ubiqedge’s device connects to this meter, captures the reading and transmits the data to the cloud. The software layer, SAMASTH, then converts that raw information into a usable operating and compliance system. It can show the factory owner live groundwater consumption, retain a year of historical data, automatically forward required data to government servers and send alerts when usage approaches a limit set by the owner. The system can go a step further. Using the same hardware-software combination, a factory can automatically shut off the borewell pump once the licensed extraction limit is reached. In this sense, the startup is not merely digitising a flow meter, but turning it into an automated compliance tool. “A common failure mode with tech adoption is offering technology that just notifies you of a problem without doing anything about it. We always deliver a baseline ROI (return on investment) automatically, without requiring further action,” Patel said. The startup currently caters to four use cases: smart water management, solar photovoltaic remote monitoring and control, smart concrete management and air-quality monitoring. Separately, Ubiqedge is also working on an AI-driven configuration layer to make its platform more adaptable for OEMs and system integrators. The idea is to let a client describe a new use case in a prompt: which sensors need to be connected, which data points need tracking and what kind of dashboard needs to be created. The system would then generate the relevant firmware (the software layer that runs on the hardware) as well as the analytics dashboard, without requiring programming. This could make it easier for factories to deploy solutions across specialised industrial needs without waiting for custom engineering work for each new application. Smart Hardware, Steady Margins On the business front, Ubiqedge operates on a dual-revenue model. Besides one-time hardware sales, the startup also earns revenue from its software via an annual subscription model. Piggybacking on the distribution networks and customer relationships, the Mumbai-based venture claims to have already onboarded more than 100 direct customers, over 8,000 end users and roughly 30,000 devices deployed through its OEM and system-integrator network. On the back of this, the startup claims to have closed FY26 with a revenue of around ₹7 Cr, with double-digit profit margins. It also claims to have been cash-positive since its first year of operations. Going ahead, Ubiqedge plans to expand its footprint globally, with an eye on the Middle East first. But the road ahead may not be easy as the AIoT startup eyes its next stage of growth. While its servers are currently hosted in India to comply with domestic data localisation norms, moving overseas will require the startup to set up dedicated regional data infrastructure in each of these geographies. Hardware adds another set of constraints. While manufacturing is outsourced to Indian contract manufacturers, Ubiqedge still relies on Chinese connectivity chipsets. Any supply disruption, price volatility or component shortage could affect delivery timelines and margins. The startup’s dependence on OEMs and system integrators, rather than factories, also limits its control over sales cycles, installation quality and the end customer relationship. Ubiqedge must ensure that its partners can explain, deploy and support its products without turning the implementation into a complex project. But Ubiqedge’s biggest challenge will likely be overcoming the scepticism that industrial clients have developed after years of expensive but underwhelming IoT deployments. For now, with a cash-positive business and a fresh seed round, Ubiqedge is looking to deepen its presence in India while preparing for overseas expansion. The bigger test will be whether its partner-led model can scale across industries and geographies without losing the simplicity that forms the core of its pitch.

Kakatiya Knights and Mighty Marathas stayed clear on top of the standings, both reaching 10 points after beating Rajputana Royals and Chola Chiefs, respectively, in Archery Premier League Season 2 on Wednesday.
Earlier in the day, Prithivraaj Yodhas downed Chero Archers to move into third place on eight points.
In the final match of the day, Chiefs’ woeful run of form continued as they remained rooted to the bottom of the table with just one win in seven matches, suffering a fifth straight defeat. In complete contrast, Marathas, who had started the season with two losses, have now won five on the trot and appear to be the team to beat.
The last time Prithviraaj Yodhas and Chero Archers met, three Sudden Death tiebreakers were needed to decide a winner. But in the reverse fixture, Yodhas made light work of Chero Archers and registered a convincing 5-1. Yodhas were led by some superb shooting by 16-year-old recurve archer Gatha Anandrao Khadake, who shot 58 out of a possible 60, and Asian Games compound medallist Ganesh Thirumuru (59).
With this win, Yodhas arrested their own mini slump while Chero Archers – who had started the season brightly- have now suffered three straight defeats.
Carrying on from where they left off in their previous meeting, it appeared as though there would be very little to separate Yodhas and Chero as they tied the first set 75-75. But the second set would slip away from Chero as Kumkum Mohod was left with little time to shoot the final arrow and she could manage only a 7, while Yodhas finished the set strongly with four 10s.
USA’s Casey Kaufhold then replaced Kumkum ahead of the third set but she started with a 8 that opened up a window for Yodhas, who saw Gatha step up once more with two 10s in that set. Matias Grande calmly closed out the set and match 77-74.
In the second match, not for the first time this season, Royals had two of the best-scoring archers in the match but when it mattered, Knights came up with clutch arrows, led by the impeccable Neeraj Chauhan, who has emerged as one of the stories of the APL season with his consistently high scores while shooting last in each set. While his 8 in the first set could have proved costly, Royals’ Mete Gazoz missed the 10 by the smallest of margins to give Knights the first set.
The second set would turn out to be the best of the night as all eight archers were in sensational form but Neeraj’s final X gave it to the Knights 79-78. The Royals showed a hint of a fightback by taking the third set, but the Knights sealed their win with Neeraj anchoring with another 10. The local franchise also had Jyothi Surekha Vennam in fine form as she shot 78 from her eight arrows.
For Marathas, the strategy since getting off to a slow start has been ‘attack, attack, attack’ and they found a new hero on the night in recurve archer Simranjeet Kaur, who shot a sensational 59 out of 60. With Dhiraj Bommadevara in good form again, Simranjeet’s scores propped up the Marathas even more with compounds Mike Schloesser and Parneet Kaur doing their bit. The Chiefs, who brought back Chikitha Taniparthi into the starting lineup, struggled to get going once again as they lost all three sets.
On Thursday, as the league phase heads into its business end, Prithviraaj Yodhas will hope to capitalise on Chola Chiefs’ inconsistent form and move closer to the semifinals in the first match. Defending champions Rajputana Royals will face the red-hot Mighty Marathas in the second match, and the day’s action will conclude with local franchise Kakatiya Knights facing Chero Archers in what could be the match of the day.

The national telemedicine consultation helpline e-Sanjeevani has integrated an AI-enabled clinical decision support system for healthcare providers. This is just the latest example of AI’s increasing integration into medicine and medical care worldwide, and in India. As AI begins to influence clinical decisions, such as reassurance, referrals, or investigations, its regulation has now become an urgent patient-safety question. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation’s (CDSCO) July 2026 guidance on software in medical devices becomes important in this context. The document brings software (including AI-enabled) used for a medical purpose into a clearer approval pathway. However, it explicitly says that it reflects existing practice and is not a new regulatory control.
What is MedTech?
Medtech refers to instruments, apparatus, implants, software, or related devices used for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, or treatment, whose primary action is not achieved through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means. A thermometer, glucometer, blood pressure apparatus, pacemaker, dialysis machine, and CT scanner are considered MedTech. Software is the set of instructions that makes a digital device work. A digital blood-pressure monitor, for example, uses embedded software to control cuff inflation, read pressure sensors and calculate the final BP value. Within software are algorithms, which are step-by-step rules that convert inputs into outputs.
AI (built on advanced algorithms such as machine learning and deep learning models) learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses them to make inferences. All AI depends on algorithms, but not every algorithm is AI. Netflix and YouTube recommendations are familiar examples of algorithms. But a medical algorithm is not a film recommendation. AI may reduce workload, improve consistency and extend specialist support to places where it is scarce. But a false positive can send a healthy person through anxiety and unnecessary tests, while a false negative can do the opposite. A model trained on one population, or one hospital network, may behave differently elsewhere. So, a model that works in Boston is not automatically ready for Bihar.
Risk before labels
India currently regulates medical devices by stretching the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which was intended mainly to penalise spurious drugs. In 1982, an amendment allowed the government to classify devices as ‘drugs’. The Medical Devices Rules, 2017, established the first dedicated rulebook. The rules introduced four classes - Class A for low risk, B for low-to-moderate risk, C for moderate-to-high risk, and D for high risk. The manufacture of devices under classes A and B is generally handled by State licensing authorities, while the central authority regulates manufacture of devices under classes C and D as well as the import of all classes. In 2020, all devices meant for medical use, including software, came under the law. While AI does not create a fifth class, the risk it poses depends on its intended use and the consequences of incorrect output.
The July guidance translates this risk-based approach classification specifically to software as Software in a Medical Device (SiMD - embedded in or controlling hardware), or Software as a Medical Device (SaMD -where the software itself performs the medical function). Software that only stores or transfers patient information is treated differently from one that influences diagnosis or treatment. Standalone medical software is assessed according to both the severity of the clinical situation and the extent to which its output guides medical decisions. Software intended solely for general wellness or routine tracking of body parameters may remain outside the medical-device framework.
Proof followed by surveillance
Validation for AI-enabled devices is sought uniquely. The CDSCO seeks evidence of a sound clinical association between the output and the condition; whether the software technically produces the intended result, and whether it performs clinically in the population and setting (deployment) where it will be used.
Developers are expected to describe training, validation and test datasets, including demographic, geographic and clinical diversity when using AI. Models developed outside India may require justification and validation in representative Indian populations. Bias, generalisability and subgroup performance matter because even ‘95% accurate’ means little without asking — accurate at what, in whom, and against which reference standard? Approval is also a continuous process as algorithms can be retrained, software can be upgraded, while performance can drift. The CDSCO discusses change in management, retraining, rollback, version control and post-market surveillance of the system.
Guidelines, not law
India’s AI regulation is outlined in policy papers of NITI Aayog, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. In 2018, NITI Aayog released the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, which named health care a priority. ICMR then, in 2023, issued ethical guidelines for AI in health care, stressing the need for accountability, fairness and patient autonomy. In November 2025, the Electronics & IT Ministry’s AI Governance Guidelines chose not to propose a separate AI law, leaving each sector’s regulator to act.
In February 2026, the Health Ministry launched the Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India (SAHI), which addresses governance, data, validation, deployment and monitoring of AI across healthcare. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has developed AI-specific lifecycle approaches, including predetermined change-control plans for defined future modifications. Europe combines medical-device regulation with the EU AI Act, which adds requirements for high-risk AI such as risk management, data quality and human oversight.
Way forward
The new guidance raises a larger question: can a technology that decides who is sick and who is sent home be governed by guidelines alone? India’s guideline-led approach has enabled regulators to move quickly without waiting for Parliamentary legislation. While its insistence on Indian data is ahead of many similar guidelines elsewhere, a dedicated statute for AI-enabled medical devices could make Indian validation mandatory for high-risk tools, clarify liability, and create a public registry of approved AI devices.
The question is whether technologies that can influence life-and-death decisions should continue to rely on guidance built on an 80-year-old law or be governed by a clear statutory framework that patients and clinicians can trust.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
- Published
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.
The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.
Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said restrictions to Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.
The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.
But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".
Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.
After the unexpected restriction to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection on Tuesday, there were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame. But owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this, suggesting it was the Trump administration's doing. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, referring to the the military-focused version of Starlink.
They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions".
