  - Published2 days ago
Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.
European leaders have also rallied around Zelensky, with the matter expected to dominate their summit in Brussels later on Thursday
The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.
Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.
Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin.
He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week. "We didn't destroy any relationship."
Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.
But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.
Ukrainian officials have said they were not warned before a speed limit was imposed on the Starlink uplink, whose sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US Department of Defense (DoD) contract.
Musk wrote on Wednesday that the systems were owned and controlled by the US government and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [Trump]."
The Trump administration has not commented on the issue. The BBC has approached the White House and the DoD for comment.

Desperate to clear toxic haze, Indonesia to douse its skies with dry ice
- Published
As toxic smog continues to billow from wildfires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands, authorities are looking at an experimental way to disperse the haze.
A trial on Thursday will see an aircraft scatter pellets of dry ice - solid carbon dioxide - in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions worst hit by the haze.
Indonesia is battling its most dire wildfire season in a decade, as an unusually strong El Niño has exacerbated drought conditions and made flames harder to put out.
Amid increasingly urgent efforts to clear the hazardous air, authorities in Indonesia and neighbouring Malaysia have turned to various weather modification methods.
These include cloud seeding, a technique that speeds up the natural process of water vapour condensing inside of clouds by dispersing compounds such as silver iodide to form ice crystals.
Authorities have been carrying out such operations for weeks.
But Thursday's dry ice trial is different.
Rather than interacting with clouds to trigger rain, the dry ice is meant to "break down" haze in the lower atmosphere "so that it can rise upward", said Dudung Abdurachman, the coordinating minister for political and security affairs.
"If this trial is successful, we will continue with other areas that are central to the haze, such as Central Kalimantan and its surroundings."
The trial will involve 1.5 tons of dry ice, according to authorities.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for agencies to step up efforts to extinguish the wildfires and mitigate the impact of toxic smog billowing from the hotspots.
New cloud seeding operations are also set to take place in Central Kalimantan - another haze-stricken area - on Thursday and Friday.
Meanwhile, firefighters on the ground are continuing to tackle out-of-control blazes and authorities have deployed dozens of helicopters to extinguish the wildfires - though these operations have at times been disrupted by poor visibility in the haze.
Residents across Kalimantan and South Sumatra are bearing the brunt of the toxic smog, with air in many cities turning a dusty amber.
Pollutants have also drifted across borders to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia, raising public health concern as air quality scores soar to unhealthy levels.
In parts of Malaysia with particularly hazy air - including its capital Kuala Lumpur and the city of Johor Bahru, near Singapore - local authorities have conducted their own cloud seeding operations.
Last month, Indonesia granted permission for Malaysian agencies to enter its airspace for cloud seeding operations along the countries' shared border.
More than one million wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia this year, burning almost 900,000 hectares of land, according to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.
Much of the public frustration is directed at agricultural companies that burn vegetation as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
Indonesian police have named more than 200 individuals and nine companies as suspects in connection with the fires.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

Bend (Oregon), Oct 16: A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school, authorities said.
Authorities found the suspect dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to a hospital in critical condition, Krantz said.
The attacker, identified as a Bend resident, forced his way into the school by shooting at locked doors, police said. He was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The first 911 call came just before 1 pm from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.
Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, Miller said.
Police said they did not know if the attacker knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation.
The school in Bend, Oregon, which is more than 100 miles (160 kilometres) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.
At a news conference Thursday night, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was “absolutely broken” and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.
Reunification of children with their parents was ongoing early Thursday evening. [AP]

Microsoft says it made Windows 11 zippier, especially on PCs with less RAM
The company also unveiled a revamped Photos app that testers can try now.
Microsoft has been working on some Windows 11 updates that it's starting to bring to all users after testing them with Windows Insiders. Among other things, the company said it made the operating system up to 20 percent more responsive, in part by improving memory efficiency and management. For instance, Windows 11 "can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, helping your PC stay responsive as you open more apps or browser tabs," Navjot Virk, Microsoft's corporate vice president of Windows Experiences, wrote in a blog post.
Virk noted that PCs with 8GB of memory may see "an especially meaningful difference." That's welcome, given that it's increasingly expensive to upgrade RAM in a PC. You can largely blame AI data centers for gobbling up as much memory as possible and jacking up prices for normal people. Microsoft, of course, is heavily involved in that, so improved memory management and efficiency feels like the least the company can do to mitigate the RAM crisis.
One thing Windows 11 will do on PCs with 8GB or less of RAM is to only load widgets when users actually open them. Microsoft says that'll free up over 200MB of memory for other tasks.
Microsoft says it should also be faster to pair AirPods with PCs as part of improvements to Bluetooth headphone reliability. Windows Hello logins are said to be easier, faster and more reliable too.
Windows Insider testers can now try out the revamped, AI-powered Search that the company unveiled last week. They can carry out thousands of actions directly through Search, which Microsoft is effectively turning into a chatbot.
Other updates for Insiders include a new Photos app with a revamped gallery that can pull together snaps from local storage, OneDrive and iCloud. The built-in editor is said to load 25 percent faster. The native viewer loads 30 percent quicker too, Microsoft claims.

U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall sought a $4.2 million earmark to resolve a water rights dispute in Kansas in 2024

A long-standing conflict over water rights in rural Kansas, which has pitted local agricultural interests against conservationists and endangered a vital wildlife sanctuary, prompted intervention from Sen. Roger Marshall.
According to public records, Marshall, an outdoors enthusiast, requested $4.2 million in federal earmark funding for infrastructure upgrades intended to boost water flow into the Quivira National Wildlife Refuge.
However, he did not disclose that his personal property, Rattlesnake Ranch, sits directly adjacent to the preserve and stood to benefit from the project.
The sanctuary has long drawn hunters every autumn, attracted by hundreds of thousands of migratory waterfowl. Yet as farming in the region expanded, increased crop irrigation strained the local water supply, reducing the volume reaching the preserve.
While Marshall sought the 2024 funding to balance farmers' and conservationists' needs, ethics experts noted the initiative created a conflict of interest that could boost his land's financial value.
The request also contradicted the Republican senator's staunch stance against earmarks, having voted four times to eliminate them while calling such appropriations wasteful taxpayer spending and "not American."
Although the specific bill containing Marshall's earmark request failed to pass, the refuge's funding was ultimately approved last year through broader spending legislation he supported.
Millions in taxpayer money could flow past senator's own ranch
Public records indicate that a federal plan will pump water from a separate watershed through a pipeline into Rattlesnake Creek, alongside Marshall’s property, before it flows directly into the refuge.
The allocation came as Marshall prepared for a reelection contest this November that once seemed certain. President Donald Trump won Kansas by 16%, and voters there have not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
However, the race has narrowed significantly, prompting Republican groups to invest millions in advertising to counter Democrat Adam Hamilton, a former Republican who serves as head of the nation’s largest United Methodist church.
Marshall’s office refused to allow the senator to speak with The Associated Press for an interview and failed to respond to specific questions regarding his property.
"All the water for this project would go into Quivira Wildlife Refuge," spokeswoman Payton Fuller said in a brief statement. "Rattlesnake Ranch would not benefit from it."
She added that the project would "literally save farms" and "supply water to the refuge in drought years."
From railing against 'pork' to requesting millions in taxpayer money
A senator’s decision to request federal funding has drawn criticism as a potential conflict of interest from both a government watchdog organization and a water rights expert.
Burke Griggs, a former state water rights attorney, noted that waterfowl hunting is "big business" in Kansas and federal money will help "establish a steadier water supply than (the Quivira Refuge) has had since the 1970s."
"That will increase the value of the land," observed Griggs, a law professor at Washburn University in Topeka, Kansas, who has donated money to Democrats. "Think about it: If Quivira doesn’t have water, we don’t have as many ducks and waterfowl staying in that area for hunting season. That would absolutely diminish the value of the property."
Craig Holman, a registered lobbyist with Public Citizen, a nonprofit advocacy group seeking greater government accountability, stated that Marshall "should not be involved in any legislative effort that provides a direct or substantial financial benefit to himself. He should have recused himself."
Holman noted Senate rules forbid members from seeking earmarks where the "principal purpose" is furthering personal financial interests. In this case, Holman said, he did not believe the earmark violated the rule because the project would also benefit the refuge and farmers.
Marshall’s efforts to secure funding represent a departure from a long-held stance.
He had railed against such appropriations, arguing colleagues should have to defend their earmark requests on the Senate floor and describing a Democrat-sponsored spending bill as "full of so much pork" and "dripping with grease."
"I’m going to do everything I can to blow up the process so that no one does earmarks," he told reporters in 2021.
Though he sought an earmark in 2024, he voted this past January to strip such funding from a spending bill.
From hunting grounds to commercial property, Marshall's ties run deep
The region surrounding the preserve has deep connections to Marshall and his family. At one point, he held full or partial ownership of more than 1,000 acres (405 hectares) near the Quivira Refuge, which he previously described as a hunting "mecca."
According to financial disclosures filed with the Senate, these real estate holdings produced a consistent stream of revenue over the years through building rentals alongside oil and gas leases.
After his election to the Senate, public records show that Marshall significantly trimmed his land holdings near the refuge.
Rattlesnake Ranch remains among his current holdings, registered as a business entity in Kansas and designated as a commercial property featuring a rental building. Official records show that Marshall holds a 20% stake in the ranch and serves as a company director.
Fuller, a spokeswoman for Marshall, said Rattlesnake Ranch is not used for hunting waterfowl. However, she did not respond to questions regarding the underlying nature of the business or the commercial application of the land, which records indicate Marshall co-owns alongside campaign donors and hunting companions.
Marshall, who entered the Senate in 2020 after serving two terms in the House, regularly posts online images of game he has killed.
Regional news reports have highlighted both the senator’s conservation efforts in the territory and his hunting of sandhill cranes near the preserve. "I hunt as often as I can," he told Lone Star Outdoor News, per an article published on his Senate website in 2022.
A shrinking water supply fuels a political and environmental showdown
A growing dispute over water rights between agricultural producers and conservationists has put the sanctuary at risk in recent years.
Expanding farm operations, along with severe drought, have depleted essential water supplies needed by waterfowl.
Under Kansas state law, water rights fall under state jurisdiction. Farmers were angered in 2023 when President Joe Biden’s Democratic administration, through the Fish and Wildlife Service, asked Kansas to guarantee adequate water for the refuge. That action would have compelled farmers and other users to cut back their consumption.
Marshall and fellow Kansas elected officials celebrated when the Biden administration retreated from the plan. Lawmakers, including Marshall, promised to craft a remedy that would aid the preserve without penalizing agricultural interests, ultimately leading to his earmark.
"As a property owner along Rattlesnake Creek for three decades," he said in a statement issued at the time, "protecting our local agricultural communities and the environment is something I take very seriously."

Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Infectious Diseases Foundation.
"In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates."
As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency.
Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk.
"It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says.
The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response.
"The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots, a history of measles.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors.
If you were born before 1957
People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
"It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected.
That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S.
If you were vaccinated before 1968
People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus.
If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine.
If you only got one dose of the MMR vaccine
At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today.
Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says.
If you're in a higher-risk group
One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them.
But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says.
Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose.
While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications.
No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says.
She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age.
If you really don't know your immunization history
If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
"It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says.
Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost.
Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose."
After all, it's much better to be protected than infected.

'Onion cartel' in Philippines fined $28m for price shock
- Published
Filipino authorities say they have fined six companies 1.76 billion pesos ($27.9m; £21m) for forming an "onion cartel" that caused the price of the vegetable to skyrocket.
In 2022 the price of onions, a staple of Philippine kitchens, surged to a record 800 pesos per 1kg, surpassing the country's daily minimum wage and overtaking the price of meat.
The crisis put pressure on then newly-elected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who had promised to bring down surging food prices.
The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) said Wednesday the fine against the companies, comprised of onion importers and storage and shipping firms, was the largest since its formation in 2016.
For months between late 2022 to early 2023, onions disappeared from restaurant menus and became the object of smuggling attempts.
The bulbous vegetable even became something of a status symbol, having been used on at least one occasion as a wedding bouquet.
Authorities approved the emergency import of onions and Marcos vowed to go after those behind the shortage, saying there were "Filipinos dying from starvation and poverty because of what they are doing".
The crisis ended as local bumper harvests entered the market later in 2023 and prices stabilised.
A parliamentary committee tasked to investigate the price crisis said a cartel was behind the "artificial" surge in onion prices.
The PCC said evidence retrieved during raids on the companies showed that the six firms had collectively controlled nearly 50% of all approved import clearances for onions in 2020 and 2021.
The companies were involved in an "illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage, and whole sale distribution", the commission said.
The hefty fine shows a "commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct", the PCC said.
The commission also said that offenders may also be criminally prosecuted by the Department of Justice.

NEW DELHI: 
Reliance Industries
 has welcomed 
Elon Musk
’s Starlink to India, saying it has never feared competition and that its own satellite services are also in the queue.
The statement comes as a response to Musk’s repeated allegations that vested interests were obstructing Starlink’s entry into India. Reliance, however, stressed that all companies must comply with Indian laws and regulations, adding that priority is to serve the people.
In a statement released on Friday, the company said India’s investment and innovation landscape was open to both domestic and foreign players, with the same regulatory process applying to all applicants.
“In light of recent remarks about Reliance and the Indian market, we wish to place the facts on record. Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. That openness rests on the rule of law. As the Government of India has stated, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign. 
Jio
's own satellite services await clearances.”
The statement posted on X further stated, “At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best. Jio itself entered India's crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer. In just ten years, Jio has earned the trust of over 530 million customers and given Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world.
We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land.”
Musk accuses Reliance of opposing Starlink’s entry
Reliance’s statement came after SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk accused the Indian conglomerate of benefiting from the existing market structure and alleged that arguments against Starlink’s entry were contradictory.
In a post on X, Musk had said, "The ridiculous arguments by Ambani’s army of Internet shills make no sense. On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor! This is absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole."
Musk argued that greater competition would give Indian consumers more choices, even if it reduced the profits of existing players. However, he said, this would not necessarily threaten their businesses.
"The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business," he wrote.
Musk had previously alleged monopolistic practices in India’s telecommunications market and questioned the regulatory barriers facing Starlink’s commercial launch in the country.
In another post, he directly addressed the government, writing, "Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India. Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?"
The government has denied Musk’s allegation that Starlink was being discriminated against at the instance of a “local oligarch”.
Government asks Starlink to comply with law
Union communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said that there is no question of allowing a monopoly in satellite communications. He also said three entities are in line for final approval for commercial licences.
Scindia said that India was close to taking a final decision on the pricing framework for satellite communication services. All licensed operators, including Starlink, must meet security requirements before beginning commercial operations.
Starlink is yet to receive clearance to launch its services in India because it has not agreed to comply with regulations requiring satellite internet providers to establish domestic infrastructure, a senior government official said earlier this week.
The government has no objection to the company rolling out its services once it addresses security concerns and agrees to establish local base stations, sources said.
A base station is a radio transmitter and receiver that acts as a local hub, or the “first hop”, connecting end-user devices to a wireless network. The requirement to establish base stations is intended to help authorities ensure compliance with the law.
Reliance Jio, Sunil Bharti Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Musk’s Starlink are the three entities planning to launch satellite communication services in India.
Bharti Enterprises chairperson Sunil Bharti Mittal has also said that Airtel’s satellite venture, Eutelsat OneWeb, could receive regulatory approval before Starlink because it applied earlier and is further along in the process.

Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with her third child: 'This one releases in December'
The star previously gave birth to twins in 2023 at the age of 48
Hilary Swank may be 52, but it's not slowing down her family — the Yellowjackets star has announced she's pregnant with her third child.
The two-time Oscar winner is already mom to two children with her husband, Philip Schneider. After freezing her eggs at age 37, she welcomed twins Aya and Ohm in 2023 when she was 48.
Swank dropped the news on Wednesday with a light-hearted Instagram video showing her family dancing in a dark room with glow sticks on their bodies to make them look like stick figures. In the video, Swank turns around to reveal a tiny glow-stick-figure in a circle on her belly.
"A lot of people have been asking what project I'm doing next," she wrote in the caption. "This one releases in December," she added, with an emoji of a baby angel, suggesting this is when the baby is due.
Swank has previously spoken about how happy she is to have waited to have children, telling Women's Health in 2025 that she feels she's a different parent than she would've been even in her early 40s.
"I'm much more patient. I'm much more understanding," she said. "And I have my career that's already established, so I'm not divided. I'm able to really sink in and be present with them and be a hands-on parent."
The American actress won her first Oscar at 25 years old with her starring role in the 2000 film Boys Don't Cry, following it up with a second best actress Oscar for the 2004 film Million Dollar Baby. Most recently, she appeared in the Netflix series Away and Showtime's Yellowjackets.
She's also spent the past few years lobbying the California government to pass bills requiring manufacturers to disclose ingredients in diapers and in prenatal vitamins.
Swank isn't the first celebrity to welcome kids in her 50s. Pop icon Janet Jackson and supermodel Naomi Campbell both had children at age 50, in 2017 and 2021 respectively, with Campbell welcoming a second child at age 53. Brigitte Nielsen, of Beverly Hills Cop II fame, gave birth to her fifth child and only daughter in 2018 at the age of 54.
Late pregnancies a growing trend
Advanced maternal age pregnancies — defined as occurring past the age of 35 — are becoming more common in North America.
In 2021, a quarter of mothers were 35 or older when they gave birth, compared with just 16 per cent 20 years earlier, according to Statistics Canada. In the U.S., federal data shows 21 per cent of births in 2023 were to those aged 35 or older, up from nine per cent in 1990.

Natural pregnancy is possible at any time before menopause, but the chances go down as you age.
Anne Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child, telling Access Hollywood in July she was "overjoyed" that it had happened.
"When you get to a certain age, that hope looks like it's about one per cent to two per cent," she said. "It's a blessing that we do not take for granted."
Anne Hathaway, 43, seen on the red carpet last month in New York City, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)
The majority of later-stage pregnancies like Swank's are possible through modern technology such as egg-freezing or in vitro fertilization (IVF), which can cost tens of thousands of dollars.
Egg-freezing allows families to press pause by extracting and preserving eggs from the ovaries at a younger age, before the eggs degrade in number and quality, which happens naturally with aging. The eggs can be stored at fertility clinics for decades, if desired, before being reimplanted when a person decides they're ready to try to conceive a child.
Developments in medical care have made pregnancy and birth safer over the years, but medical experts caution that the risk of complications with pregnancy still increases at an advanced maternal age.
And although egg-freezing is growing in popularity in Canada, providing more options for when to start a family, the procedures averaged $12,000 to $15,000 in 2024 — not quite accessible for every Canadian.

Bollywood actor Imran Khan will challenge the legal notice issued to him to leave the country by October 28. As per PTI, Khan is likely to file the plea in the Bombay High Court by Friday or Monday over alleged violation of the Immigration and Foreigners Act. The controversy stems from Khan's participation in protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai. Khan, a US national and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, received a notice from the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) after his detention at the demonstration. The OCI scheme was introduced in 2005. It is only applicable to eligible foreign nationals of Indian origin. Unlike its name, OCI status does not confer Indian citizenship or permit dual citizenship in India. As an OCI cardholder, an individual of Indian origin may remain a foreign national and hold passports issued by their respective countries, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). Quick answers to key questions No. OCI status is for eligible foreign nationals of Indian origin and does not confer Indian citizenship or allow dual citizenship in India. OCI cardholders receive a multiple-entry, lifelong visa and are generally exempt from FRRO registration. They have parity with NRIs in certain economic, financial and educational matters, subject to applicable conditions. The OCI rules described in the articles do not specifically list protest participation as an activity requiring prior permission, but the rules do not settle whether every protest is permitted. OCI holders cannot claim Article 19’s freedom of speech and peaceful assembly on the same basis as Indian citizens. Yes. OCI cardholders remain foreign nationals subject to Indian immigration laws, and OCI registration can be cancelled on specified grounds. A complaint or allegation alone does not establish that an offence occurred or that removal is justified. The FRRO issued the notice after Khan, a US national and OCI cardholder, participated in a Mumbai protest and was detained. The notice alleged a violation of immigration law; Khan said he would challenge it in the Bombay High Court. According to an MHA notification dated March 4, 2021, OCI cardholders are entitled to a multiple-entry, lifelong visa to visit India and are exempt from registration with FRRO, irrespective of the duration of their stay. The same notification also specifies parity with Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) in certain economic, financial and educational matters, subject to applicable conditions. However, OCI cardholders must obtain special permission for specified activities such as research, missionary or Tabligh work, mountaineering, journalism, selected internships or employment at foreign diplomatic missions in India, and visits to protected, restricted or prohibited areas. Under Section 7B of the Citizenship Act, 1955, OCI cardholders are not entitled to all rights reserved for Indian citizens. OCT holders do not have rights like the right to vote or contest parliamentary and state legislative elections, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. Article 19 of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully, applies specifically to citizens. This is where Imran Khan's rights as an OCI cardholder may remain controversial. The notification from the MHA does not particularly list participation in political protests or demonstrations among the activities for which an individual under OCI status requires prior permission. The notice was sent to Imran Khan following a complaint against him by former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya. Somaiya told PTI, “I had filed a complaint regarding this matter. Imran Khan is an American citizen. No foreign national can engage in Indian politics or participate in illegal political activities in India. Over the past few weeks, we have seen foreign powers, foreign funding, foreign individuals, and foreign organisations attempting to create disorder in India. Imran Khan also picked up a flag, and therefore, a person of this kind has no right to stay in India.” “Whether it is Imran, Yusuf, Iqbal, or Amir Ali, money comes from Pakistan, and major American companies also provide funding here. These people want to create instability in India by working together with what I would call ‘Dimagi Naxals.’ I welcome the decision taken by Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis. I had filed this complaint, and a decision was taken within five days. Now, Imran Khan can approach whichever court he wishes to. He is not an Indian citizen, and therefore, he cannot claim such rights here. Action will be taken,” he added. An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in ChatGPT owner OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, logging its worst performance since July.
The sell-off comes after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher than expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid, said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said earlier this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where Shanghai’s CSI 300 slipped as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.
In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

A shooter is dead and at least two people, including children, have been taken to the hospital following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday afternoon.
Officers were alerted around 1 p.m. local time after receiving a 12:59 p.m. report of a shooter firing into a car outside the facility, according to police. Emergency crews brought the injured to a local hospital. Within a minute of the initial call, law enforcement received multiple 911 reports of an active shooter inside the building.
Bend Police arrived at the scene by 1:02 p.m. — just two minutes after being notified that officers needed to respond to a critical scene — and the shooter was down seconds later. Officials noted that the gunman may have been shot by a bystander, though the suspect’s identity, total victim count and specific weapon used remain under investigation.
The incident prompted an immediate lockdown of the school while police vehicles, fire trucks and ambulances swarmed the grounds. Authorities are working on safely evacuating roughly 40 staff members and 450 children enrolled at Silver Rail Elementary to a designated reunification point at Journey Church.
“As you can imagine, the process of getting all of those people safely out of the building and down to Journey Church is a real challenge,” police told reporters during a news conference, asking for patience while officers thoroughly clear each section of the school. A large crowd of parents and community members gathered outside as the search and evacuation continued.
Federal authorities are also aiding local police with the response. FBI Director Kash Patel stated on social media that the bureau’s Portland field office is on the scene to support the investigation, adding that the agency “will make every resource they need available.”
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek similarly said she was “closely monitoring the situation at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend,” expressing gratitude for the first responders on site and promising further updates as more information becomes available.
The Bend Police Department is serving as the lead agency on the investigation.

Opera's lightweight Air browser is back, unbothered, moisturized, in its lane
New soundtracks and breathing exercises are designed to encourage mindful browsing.
Opera has relaunched its very mindful Air browser with a host of new anti-distraction features. The audiovisual makeover is designed to help you focus better on what you're actually supposed to be doing, rather than encouraging you to wander into yet another free time-draining Reddit rabbit hole.
The first new addition is music. Opera seemingly knows that people turn to ambient playlists when they're trying to concentrate, so it's built its own. Air Soundscapes give the browser a soundtrack split into four moods: Focus, Relax, Work and Ambience. Pick the latter and you'll be treated to the tranquil sounds of forests and the sea.
Opera Air also now has built-in breathing exercises, which you can schedule to pop up at your chosen intervals, as well as neck stretches you can follow along to.
The Air browser is purposefully streamlined, so you have to manually add any apps you want to the sidebar. Opera has added new wallpapers that it says incorporate "open spaces, perspective and natural textures" to make your browsing experience as serene as possible. It also now has an automatic dark mode.
Given its resistance to the many distractions of the web, Air naturally has a built-in ad blocker, and you even get a free VPN. It does interface with ChatGPT but that sidebar option is unchecked by default. The resigned user experience builds on the first version of Air that Opera introduced in early 2025 as a mindful antidote to the chaos of the internet.
Opera Air remains free to download on Windows and macOS.

Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.
The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky.
The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.

Riot will sunset League of Legends Classic in January 2027
The throwback mode may reappear as a limited-time event in the future.
Riot Games introduced League Classic in July, offering players a way to re-experience the League of Legends as it was in past years. However, the attempt to recapture the spark of nostalgia from its long-running MOBA appears to have quickly fizzled. League Classic will be ending at the close of Season 3, which will be in early January 2027. In the interim, the studio said it would introduce windowed queues for League Classic in regions where a lack of players has created long wait times for matches. Riot will also continue to add more champions to the Classic pool in the remaining patches planned for 2026.
In a blog post, the dev team said interest waned quickly after Classic launched, noting that many players "have gone back to other parts of League." Rather than completely axe all the work that went into recreating bygone eras of LoL, Riot said that it aims to bring back Classic in the future, "likely as an event mode with adjustments and additions" based on feedback from this inaugural run.
Riot Games had been hyping up League Classic since the throwback mode was announced, including a live show match with ten retired pro players at this summer's Mid-Season Invitational tournament. It's not the only game studio to try and appeal to both new and long-time players by offering a version that turns back the clock on an ever-adapting live game; Blizzard Entertainment has seen success with its World of Warcraft Classic option. But it seems Riot hasn't quite nailed the balance in a way that connected with its audience for long-term success.

Bee unveils two AI note-taking devices, its first new products since being acquired by Amazon
The Eclipse and Frontier are cheap and colorful, but you'll need a Pro subscription to make the most of them.
Just over a year after being acquired by Amazon, wearable AI startup Bee has quite a few products to unveil. It's introducing two new AI devices today, alongside a Pro subscription offering and some software updates.
First up is the Bee Frontier, which is essentially a follow-up to and replacement of the previous Pioneer. Like it, the Frontier is basically a Fitbit-like module that you can slot into a bracelet or a clip so you can attach it to your clothes or bags. It has an onboard button, like the Pioneer, to initiate a note-taking session or invoke the app's Buzz AI assistant, as well as an LED indicator to convey when it's listening or charging, for instance.
But the Frontier has evolved from its first-gen predecessor, which cost $50 and seemed like a product that would appeal most to early adopters. This new version is not only smaller and lighter, but also comes in more colors. The original was only available in one version, and in the box with it came a black band and a yellow band, along with a clip attachment. That selection might fit the bee (insect) vibes, but certainly isn't the most sartorially versatile. I'm a fan of the Lavender and Sage color options for the Bee Frontier, and those who want something more generic can opt for the black (Onyx) version.
Additionally, the Frontier is rated IP67 for dust and water resistance, according to Amazon, whereas the Pioneer was not even water-resistant. Both models have dual microphones with noise filtering to tune out background chatter, though the effectiveness of the Frontier's attempts at this will require in-depth testing to determine.
Those are the main physical differences between the Frontier and the Pioneer. The two share the same 7-day battery life estimate, USB-C charging port and similar functionality. One press of the button can initiate a recording session, where Bee listens to your surroundings and delivers transcripts and summaries of conversations. Pressing and holding the button allows you to ask a question of the AI assistant or leave yourself a voice note.
The Bee Frontier is available now for $75 at Amazon, and you may want to wait till full reviews are out to decide if the water resistance, new colors and smaller size are worth the money. The Pioneer is no longer available to purchase.
The Bee Eclipse is a magnetic AI note taker for your phone
The other piece of hardware that Bee is announcing today is the Eclipse — a magnetic, rectangular puck you can snap onto your phone. It's like a thicker credit card with three onboard microphones, a button on the top left corner and an LED indicator light next to it. The Eclipse is a lot bigger than the Frontier, which also means it can last a lot longer. In fact, it offers three times the battery life, with Bee promising it will last "more than 21 days."
This is a new type of device for Bee, since it's not really a wearable for people and more like a wearable for phones. But at its core the Eclipse basically performs the same functions as a Frontier (or Pioneer). You can push a button to start a session, the indicator light turns on and the AI gets to work, summarizing your discussions and attempting to identify who is speaking or what is being said.
The company said that "like all Bee devices, audio is never stored, cannot be accessed or shared, and users are prompted to gain permission from call participants each time a recording is started." It added that the Eclipse, like the Frontier, "is designed with privacy at its core, with one button to turn it on or off and a visible indicator light on when it's summarizing a conversation."
While the rationale behind a little light signaling to people nearby that a device might be recording is sound, it's worth noting that the shape, size and magnetic attachment of the Eclipse means it closely resembles a portable battery charger. Those things have indicator lights as well, and it can be easy to see how someone might assume an indicator LED means something is charging, rather than listening.
Still, Bee is far from the only company making AI note-taking devices that snap onto your phone. There's Pocket, Plaud, Comu, Innaio, Ruune, Raycon and undoubtedly countless more littering the venture capital-fueled grounds of Silicon Valley. And the issues that Bee's Eclipse will run into relating to its form factor will likely be faced by the entire category as well.
If Bee's offering is of interest and you have $100 to spare, you can get the Eclipse in one of four admittedly attractive colors — Silver, Midnight, Honey and Blush. Amazon says it will be "available soon," and nothing more specific on time frame has been shared.
Bee Pro subscription, plus Amazon and Alexa+ integrations
The company is also unveiling the Bee Pro subscription plan today. For $11.99 a month, it offers some additional features like unlimited recent conversation summaries, suggested to-dos, daily memories, conversation templates, daily memories and a few new integrations that were also announced today.
Before I get into those, though, a quick note for existing Bee users. If you're feeling nervous as these sound like features you've been enjoying and you're concerned they might suddenly be wrested away and put behind a paywall, you might not be affected. Bee's founder Maria Zollo told me in a briefing that for the customers that have been with the company since its early days, "as a sign of gratitude, we're giving to them the Bee they have today." Zollo added that for them, the "entire featureset is free forever." (All new Bee customers also get 30 days of free Bee Pro use.)
If you want the features I'm about to mention, then you'll need a Pro subscription. First, the company is expanding its in-app integrations, which previously included Google Calendar, Gmail and Apple's HealthKit. It's introducing "the ability to connect to Alexa+ and Amazon.com." If you connect it to your Amazon account, your Bee can suggest items you might have mentioned in conversations that you wanted to purchase. These product recommendations will show up on Amazon's homepage, as well as in the Bee apps. You'll also be able to create custom shopping lists including things that came up in your conversations.
If you connect Bee to Alexa+, you can ask your Echo or other Alexa-enabled device for information that your Bee might know. This could be anything from conversation summaries, to-dos or book recommendations from friends. With this enabled, you won't have to hunt for and open the Bee app on your phone and ask for what you want — you can just ask your speaker or TV to do so. Amazon said that the Alexa devices would use voice identification to ascertain that it's you and not, say, a random interloper or nosy partner, before sharing the information.
Amazon stressed that both these features are opt-in, so the user has to give permission before information is shared.
Finally, Bee is launching a desktop app for Mac or Windows, which you can access with a Pro plan. This doesn't just give you access to your recaps and chats on your computer, but also allows you to do additional transcribing from the desktop. It's as full-featured as the mobile app.
A refresher on Bee Private Compute
Given the recent controversy around Apple's Audio Intelligence features — specifically Siri Recap and Live Rewind — it's worth bringing up Bee's "Private Compute." It's what the company described in a blog post on September 24 (about two weeks after the Apple launch) as a "secure and isolated processing environment that no one, including Amazon and Bee, can access." That's not to say this did not exist prior to the Apple event — the post does not make that very clear, other than saying that "Amazon and Bee developed Private Compute from the ground up, and the technology builds on the foundation of the AWS Nitro System and its AWS Nitro Trusted Platform Module."
In today's announcement, Amazon reiterated the tenets of Bee Private Compute, including reminders that no audio is ever stored. "Audio is processed into insights in real time and deleted after processing," the company said in a press release. It also said that no one can access your data unless you choose to share it, transcripts are encrypted using keys that can only be created and controlled by your device and that you can delete your transcripts and summaries whenever you want.

Pope Leo said on Sunday (October 12, 2026) that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
“Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained.”
“The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for the next few days.”
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.
Leo, elected pope by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press office said Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health.
Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake.”

It's finally here.
Tesla unveiled its next-generation Roadster at a livestreamed event Thursday night, giving customers who have waited years their first fresh look at the EV maker's new halo car.
In a dramatic demonstration, the Roadster traveled up a huge curved ramp until it was upside down. The car then flew off the ramp, flipped, and landed safely on the ground, thanks to what appeared to be thrusters attached to the bottom of the vehicle.
"Well, it worked," Tesla CEO Elon Musk said after it successfully landed. 
"Flying cars are real," Lars Moravy, Tesla's VP of vehicle engineering, added.
Musk called the latest Roadster a result of a collaboration with Tesla and SpaceX engineers.
The Tesla CEO said the car uses an "advanced ultra-high pressure air tank" to lift itself.
"The car has obviously altitude control thrusters and main thrusters in the rear, so it can basically fly like a rocket, and it could do rolls," he said.
In a separate recorded demonstration shown on screen, Tesla also showed the Roadster hitting 60 mph in under one second, marking .81 seconds.
Musk said the Roadster will be the only Tesla vehicle meant to be driven manually and that it's not "necessarily a safety-optimized car."
An observant audience member at the event also asked a glaring question: Is it street legal?
"Depends on your street," Musk said. "It'll be a viable car."
The long road behind
The revived nameplate has been a long time coming.
The original Roadster was Tesla's first production vehicle, launching in California in 2008. It used a chassis derived from British sports-car maker Lotus's Elise, but replaced its gasoline engine with an all-electric powertrain. That model ended production in 2012.
Musk surprised audiences in November 2017 at an event for Tesla's Semi truck by unveiling a second-generation Roadster. At the time, Tesla said the two-door sports car would have a 1.9-second zero-to-60-mph time, a top speed above 250 mph, more than 600 miles of range, and a gargantuan 200-kilowatt-hour battery pack.
That month, customers could put down a $50,000 deposit to reserve a Roadster, or pay $250,000 upfront for a Founders Series model.
Musk also floated a SpaceX package for the supercar with cold-gas thrusters that he said might "allow a Tesla to fly."
With the wait time creeping toward a decade, Musk apologized to "long-suffering" deposit holders in an earnings call, adding that Tesla was focusing heavily on its robotics and autonomy programs.
"Roadster is not just icing on the cake; it's the cherry on the icing on the cake," he said at the time. "We are working on it, but it has to come behind the things that have a more serious impact on the world."
Tesla began ramping up the Roadster's design cycle in the summer of 2025, Business Insider previously reported.
Musk had been hyping Thursday's livestreamed event on X. He claimed that event would be "a candidate for greatest product demo of all time" and that "the whole world will watch this."

A gunman is dead after opening fire at an Oregon elementary school on October 15.
Police rushed to Silver Rail Elementary School around 1 p.m. after receiving reports of an “active shooter.”
Law enforcement arrived within two minutes, officials said. The shooter was dead shortly after police got to the Bend, Oregon, school. A department spokeswoman said a bystander may have shot the suspect - but that detail still needed to be confirmed.
Four people were killed in the shooting, and the gunman was shot at the scene. Police have said that children are among the victims.
As police continue to investigate the shooting, here is everything we know about the suspected gunman:
Who was the suspected gunman?
Police have not released any details about the shooter, including the person’s name. The shooter was killed at the scene soon after the gunfire began.
What was the motive?
Authorities have not detailed a motive and say the shooting remains under investigation.
How many victims were there?
Four people were killed in addition to the gunman, according to reports. Police have said that children are among the victims.
How have elected officials responded to the shooting?
Several officials have spoken out after the shooting.
“We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy,” Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook. “We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence. No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders.”
FBI Director Kash Patel stated: “FBI Portland is on the scene and assisting our local partners in the investigation regarding an earlier shooting at a local school. We will make every resource they need available.”

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.
Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.
At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.
Farther south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.
By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.
In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.
The impacts are just a taste of what’s to come across southern California as a historic El Niño unfolds in the Pacific, threatening to unleash severe storms across the region this winter.
Already, the last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.
“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” Phil Klotzbach, a Colorado State University researcher who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press, adding that the last month has been “berserk”.
The El Niño climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the potential to supercharge extreme weather around the world. While it’s expected to strengthen through the end of this year and into next, the excess warmth already measured is climbing off the charts. Forecasters have warned its effects could become exceptionally destructive.
In California – especially in the southern part of the state – El Niños typically carry higher risks of severe storms, and with them elevated threats from landslides, debris flows and flash floods. These dangers become more pronounced around recent burn scars, adding hazards to several areas, including in the neighborhoods still recovering from the 2025 Los Angeles firestorm and swaths of Big Sur above Highway 1.
“This year’s tilt in the odds toward wet and stormy conditions in California will be profoundly unsubtle,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a recent analysis, adding that its unlike anything he’s observed before.
Throughout the winter months, El Niño could also add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist.
Already, El Niño has elevated sea levels up and down the California coast, from the Mexico border up to the San Francisco Bay Area. Warm waters expanding from an extreme marine heatwave combined with a coastally trapped Kelvin wave – a large underwater band of warm water – have already inundated parts of the North American shoreline. More Kelvin waves are likely and California is already bracing for unusually high king tides to hit during holiday weekends this year, arriving near Thanksgiving and Christmas.
While the impacts from heavy rains and high surf are each destructive in their own right, when they align and overlap they can cause even more calamity.
“Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” Swain said. “Even a moderate storm could bring water levels higher still, and a strong storm would likely produce widespread damaging, and probably historic, coastal flooding.”
Meanwhile, as cities across California begin preparations for intense winter weather, there are still months left before the risks from fire begin to subside. The National Weather Service issued fire weather watches for parts of southern California, including in Los Angeles, as seasonal strong, dry winds align with high temperatures. Forecasters warned that there would be “high risk for extreme fire behavior with any new fire starts Thursday through Friday”.
With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, – but all hazards.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the licences of three blood banks in Mumbai for three to five days after an investigation found that Titan watches were distributed as gifts to donors at a blood donation camp held in April this year, in violation of National Blood Transfusion Council (NBTC) guidelines.
The three blood banks are the Indian Red Cross Society Blood Centre, Mumbai; Dean Grant Medical College and Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals Blood Centre, Byculla; and B.Y.L. Nair Charitable Hospital Blood Centre, Mumbai Central. Their licences were suspended for five days, three days, and three days, respectively, under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
However, the blood centres at Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals and Nair Hospital have appealed against the suspension orders before the State Government and secured temporary stays on the orders.
According to the FDA, the blood donation camp was organised by the Young Star Committee, Altamount Road, towards the end of April 2026. Advertisements for the camp stated that donors would receive Titan watches as gifts. However, the NBTC’s Guidelines for Voluntary Blood Donation prohibit offering gifts to donors at voluntary blood donation camps.
During the initial inquiry, the organisers and participating blood banks denied knowledge of the distribution of gifts. However, FDA officials subsequently contacted several blood donors, who confirmed that they had received watches.
Following these findings, the FDA inspected the three blood banks on August 22 and issued show-cause notices on September 2 over the violations detected. Personal hearings were conducted on September 22, during which the blood banks submitted their explanations.
The FDA found their explanations unsatisfactory and subsequently ordered the suspension of their licences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe said blood donation was an important act of social responsibility and service to humanity, and that gifts or inducements should not be used to encourage donations.
“The FDA is committed to ensuring that no gifts or inducements are used to encourage blood donation and that the relevant guidelines are followed. Blood banks must strictly comply with the applicable legal provisions and guidelines,” Mundhe said.
