Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Variety has confirmed.
“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in, with the full support of DC Studios, to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2,'” a studio rep said in a statement. “Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film.”
Soderbergh said in his own statement, “I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.”
Popular on Variety
Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced “The Batman Part II” production pause in early October, stating that Reeves temporarily stepped away from the project to handle a “family matter.”
“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement at the time. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”
Soderbergh is the Oscar-winning director best known for films “Traffic,” “Erin Brockovich,” “Sex, Lies, and Videotape and “Ocean’s Eleven.” His most recent releases include “The Christophers,” “Black Bag,” “Presence” and “John Lennon: The Last Interview.”
The highly anticipated “Batman” sequel has experienced several delays since it was announced at CinemaCon 2022. The original release date was set for Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it to Oct. 1, 2027. In June, the film was pushed again to February 2028. Reeves’ first “Batman” was released in March 2022.
Robert Pattinson returns as the Caped Crusader in “The Batman Part II.” Other cast members include Scarlett Johansson, Colin Farrell, Sebastian Stan, Andy Serkis and Jeffrey Wright.

The Liberty Bell, with its famous crack, hasn’t been rung in 180 years, but that hasn’t stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation’s 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell’s replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today.
Historians aren’t sure when exactly the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn’t work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that “the old Independence Bell… now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb.” Nobody has heard it ring since.
This wasn’t the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the very first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together.
The second recast’s sound was deemed acceptable, and the bell was typically used to summon the Assembly, among other purposes, until it fell into disuse after the American Revolutionary War. As for why the bell was so prone to cracking, a 1975 study of the bell’s chemical composition revealed that the metals used formed “an extremely brittle alloy” that also made it easier for souvenir collectors to chip off pieces from the rim.

Mona Singh has explored a range of roles and storytelling formats throughout her career, moving between emotionally driven dramas and characters that allow her to experiment with different aspects of her acting. With Munjya, the actor stepped into the horror-comedy genre for the first time, taking on a project that offered her an opportunity to move beyond her familiar territory. The film went on to perform well at the box office, bringing together horror, humour and storytelling as part of Maddock Films’ growing slate of genre-based films.
Mona Singh opens up on exploring horror-comedy with Munjya; says, “I really wanted to experience this”
Speaking about what attracted her to horror-comedy and how her perception of the genre changed over time, Mona said she was keen to take up a role that would allow her to explore something different from the intense dramas she had frequently been part of.
She said, “As an actor, I really wanted to experience this because it was a completely different genre for me. More often than not, I end up doing intense dramas, so I wanted to try comedy, and comedy with a dose of horror was something really exciting for me. After Stree, the way I looked at the horror-comedy genre changed a lot because I was used to watching horror content that would give me sleepless nights. I clearly remember being scared out of my wits after watching Manjulika in the original Bhool Bhulaiyaa. So, when I got a call from Maddock Films and they said it was a great script and a horror film, I said, ‘I don’t watch horror films myself.’ Then they said, ‘Ma’am, it’s a horror-comedy.’ I said, ‘Great! I’ve watched Stree. I’m coming!’”
Mona’s account highlights how the success of films such as Stree influenced her outlook on horror-comedy, making the genre more approachable for someone who was otherwise reluctant to watch conventional horror films. Her decision to be part of Munjya also reflected her interest in taking on projects that challenge her to explore unfamiliar creative spaces.
The actor has had a varied year, delivering six different performances across projects and getting the opportunity to portray characters with distinct shades. Her choices reflect an effort to move between genres and formats instead of being associated with a particular kind of role.
Mona is currently shooting for filmmaker Vikas Bahl’s upcoming film. As she continues to take on varied projects, the actor is exploring different storytelling styles and expanding the range of characters she brings to the screen.

Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
- Published
Barack Obama has told an audience in Glasgow that hope is worth fighting for despite big challenges facing the modern world.
The 44th president of the United States said online platforms had shifted in recent years to focus on content that stoked anger and fear, but he believes a drift to extremism is "not inevitable".
The comments came as he addressed an OVO Hydro crowd of 12,150 people while in conversation with British journalist and author Sathnam Sanghera, part of three speaking dates in the UK.
He reflected on his time in the White House and examined the political and social challenges facing the US and the wider world.
Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope
But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.
He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill".
"It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said.
"So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."
But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".
He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler.
"We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'."
"We have not chosen to do that."
Obama, who was president until 2016, said there was a "critical balance" that must be struck between free speech and regulation.
But the 65-year-old said that the world and its leaders are going to need to find mechanisms and new institutions to allow rigorous debate and disagreement while helping people sort out basic facts.
He said: "If I had a blame pie for why politics is so polarised and why we're seeing a rise of populism in many places, it's because of that information that is going into our brains every day."
Obama said this resulted in young people feeling discouraged, and that "it's not a healthy diet that our brains are on at the moment".
He added that he feared this could become even worse with AI making it hard to distinguish between what is true and what is not, something he believes will make democracy hard to function.
Obama says people forget lessons from the past
Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.
The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.
He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet."
He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible.
"I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.
Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted.
"We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."
He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.
Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.

Have you ever taken months off training – maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.
Use it or lose it? Maybe not
For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.
When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasise consistency above all else.
Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.
In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
More than muscle
We areexercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.
To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining – a period of no exercise – and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.
Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.
Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand – meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.
My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
A record that outlives you
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.
In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.
Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.
Every cell remembers
Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.
Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.
Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet – the so-called yo-yo effect.
We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.
To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.
Diego Hernandez-Saavedra, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Yi-Heng (Hank) Huang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

Connecticut orchard outraged after hot air balloon swiped an apple from the sky
The hot air balloon company has claimed that it did not damage the farm’s trees

The owners of a Connecticut orchard were left outraged when a hot air balloon allegedly descended from the sky and swiped at least one apple.
Woodstock Orchards LLC, a family-run farm located in Connecticut’s so-called “Quiet Corner,” said that the incident on Saturday was the second time that the balloon took an apple from their grounds.
An image accompanying the farm’s statement on social media shows a huge balloon hovering amid the trees. Several people can be seen in the vessel’s basket, which sits below a balloon sporting bright yellow, green, purple, blue and pink stripes.
The image also shows that the balloon is clearly stamped with its company name: CT Voyager Balloons.
“For the second time, this hot air balloon has come down into our orchard, with someone reaching out and taking apples from our trees,” a farm spokesperson claimed on Facebook. “In the process, our apple trees have been struck and damaged.”
The spokesperson went on to say that the trees are more than just scenery; they are also the farm’s livelihood.
“They are something we work on and care for all year long,” the spokesperson said. “Through unpredictable weather, drought, pests, rising costs, and countless hours of labor, we do everything we can to grow a quality crop for our customers.”
However, speaking to Boston.com, a representative for CT Voyager Balloons offered a different version of the events on Saturday and detailed more about the firm’s history with the orchard.
The representative said that the balloon passed over the farm several years ago, encountering a “nice young lady” who tossed apples to passengers. The balloon left with no complaint from the farm and without damaging the trees.
Woodstock Orchards LLC did reference the first visit on social media, although it did not share a similar sentiment to the balloon company.
“To have this happen once is upsetting,” the spokesperson wrote. “To have it happen twice makes it even more disappointing.”
During the second incident, the balloon encountered strong winds after taking off at around 4 p.m. When it reached the farm, it remained above the treeline and did not damage the trees, the company representative told Boston.com.
When a 12-year-old reached toward an apple, the pilot lowered the balloon by about three feet to pick the apple for the youngster.
However, the passengers were soon met with a “very angry man” who warned them never to take an apple again and ordered them to leave, despite the pilot returning the apple and offering to pay for it, the representative stated.
The farm said in its statement that its owners were not asked for permission for the balloon company to take apples from the site.
“We do not want anything in return except for this to never happen again,” they wrote.
The balloon company representative apologized to the orchard in the statement given to Boston.com, acknowledging that they should have sought permission from the family-run farm.
“We acknowledge that seeking permission to pick even one apple is justified, although (sic) was not required on our last flyover several years ago,” the representative wrote. “For this, we do apologize for not seeking permission to pick one apple, and our pilot is now well aware of this (new) policy going forward.”
The Independent has contacted Woodstock Orchards LLC and CT Voyager Balloons for comment.

SA chief pledges review over 'disappointing' Test crowds
- Published
A senior South African cricket official has pledged to order a review into the low crowd which attended the first Test against Australia in Durban.
Despite South Africa being the reigning world Test champions and Australia the number one-ranked side in the world, fewer than 20,000 fans attended across the five days.
Australia, who are touring South Africa for the first time since the 2018 sandpaper scandal, won by 214 runs and can wrap up the three-match series when the second Test gets under way in Gqeberha on Sunday.
"It is impossible to overlook our disappointment that just under 20,000 fans attended across the five days," said KwaZulu-Natal Cricket Union chief executive Heinrich Strydom.
"A Test match of this quality deserved greater support in the stands. This is something we will reflect on through a thorough internal review.
"We need to listen to our supporters, reconnect with our communities and continue to find ways to make Test cricket more accessible, engaging and appealing.
"Test cricket is part of our sporting heritage and its future depends on all of us."
Attendances for Test cricket have been declining in many places around the world, most notably in South Africa and the West Indies.
However, live sport does remain a big draw in South Africa.
While the Test against Australia was ongoing, a football cup final between Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns was being held across town in Durban which attracted more than 50,000 fans.
"While we recognise supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience," added Strydom.

Winning a Nobel Prize is a matter of great prestige. Winning a Nobel Prize also means the award going to a small number of people while a large number are left out, even if they really deserved to win.
This is partly because of the prizes’ rules. Alfred Nobel’s will said nothing about the number of people that can be awarded at one time but the Nobel Foundation’s statutes limit each prize to at most three people at a time, and no one that has died by the time a prize is announced. Also, scientists need to have been nominated by nominators who have their own eligibility criteria.
A big-picture view of the science Nobel Prizes through history brings another pattern into view: a preference for singular breakthroughs rather than lifetime achievements.
Boyden, Bamberg, and beyond
Start with the Nobel Prize this year for physiology/medicine, to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, for their work on optogenetics. In 2002, Austrian scientist Gero Miessenböck & co. had first sensitised to light some neurons that were not naturally light-sensitive. Miessenböck is now at the University of Oxford, where his profile page describes him as an ‘inventor’ of optogenetics.
Hegemann and Nagel have been feted for identifying and characterising the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). The next step was to show that it could control neurons. The first author of the paper that did was Edward Boyden, who helped pioneer the application of ChR2 to neuroscience. Boyden is now a professor of neurotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the Broad Institute.
Another author of this paper, Ernst Bamberg, had supervised Nagel’s PhD and was part of the team that established the importance of ChR2. A page on the website of the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Germany, where Bamberg is now an emeritus professor, says he was instrumental in translating the ChR2 finding into practical applications.
Yet another author, Feng Zhang, is also at MIT now, and in 2007, he was a member of one of two teams that adapted another protein, called halorhodopsin, to silence neurons with light instead of activating them. The other team, consisting of Xue Han and Boyden, had demonstrated the same capability.
These contributions together — rather than only those that the laureates led — turned the ability to control neurons with light into a tool of neuroscience with real-world applications, including in medicine.
No lone wolf
Next, the physics prize — which this year demonstrated the brokenness of the Nobel Prizes on a whole other level. Francis Halzen won the prize all by himself “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. But IceCube is an international collaboration involving around 450 experts from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Crucially, the prize-giving committee was not constrained to give the prize to one person here. The Nobel Foundation statutes allow the committee to decide whether its prizes can be awarded to associations or organisations. But the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry, and economics prizes, does not seem to have adopted this option. If it had, the physics prize could have recognised the IceCube collaboration as a whole.
But even if this rule did not exist, it is hard to say why the committee picked Halzen alone. In 1988, Halzen and (today) University of Hawai’i physics and astronomy professor John G. Learned reported the idea of using Antarctica’s ice mass as the target in which neutrinos from outer space could interact with atoms together. Learned then focused on an underwater neutrino experiment called DUMAND while Halzen pursued a project that eventually became IceCube.
Also, in 2012, while searching IceCube data for neutrinos coming from outer space with very high energies, scientists found two candidate events. The data quickly snowballed into evidence proving that neutrinos could be energised significantly by natural phenomena in space — and the prize citation credits this feat to Halzen alone.
But in real-life (as opposed to Nobel-life), the IceCube collaboration had credited Japanese physicist Aya Ishihara with finding those two candidate events, and for which she received an International Union of Pure and Applied Physics award in 2013. This particular oversight is oddly reminiscent of the infamous Jocelyn Bell Burnell story. Ishihara is currently a professor at Chiba University, where she continues to study high-energy neutrinos and develop the next generation of neutrino detectors.
Furthermore, the 2013 Science paper that reported the high-energy neutrinos also named three scientists named Claudio Kopper, Naoko Kurahashi, and Nathan Whitehorn as its corresponding authors.
The physics prize for Halzen is not misplaced. Halzen was very good — but the point is so were very many others. Aside from the scientists named here, it also required engineers and technicians who could build it in one of the most hostile locations on our planet. And all these people had to work together to make the project and its subsequent achievements possible. Halzen alone could never have done it.
Drawing difficult lines
Finally, the chemistry Nobel Prize this year illustrates the problem with the rule that it cannot be given to people who have died by the time the prize is announced. In 1953, the British physicist Frederick Charles Frank came up with a mathematical way to explain how a small chemical imbalance in a specific kind of reaction could force the reaction to make that imbalance the norm. This way required the reaction to have three properties, called autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis, and mutual inhibition.
Between 1986 and 1995, Henri Kagan in France and Kenso Soai in Japan had reported evidence of all the conditions of Frank’s model, providing experimental evidence that it could work in the real world. However, Frank died in 1998, aged 87.
That said, the 1995 paper by Soai et al. included Takanori Shibata, who made essential contributions to this branch of chemistry (and was second author on the paper). And whereas Kagan and Soai had demonstrated different aspects of Frank’s model, Shibata was the first author of a 1999 paper that extended the work of Soai et al. to demonstrate the reaction Frank had tried to model. Shibata is currently at Waseda University. And again, it is not easy to rationalise the prize-giving committee’s decision to not include him among this year’s chemistry laureates.
On the other hand, the committee’s decision to exclude U.S. chemical engineer Donna Blackmond throws light on one possible line of reasoning. A technical statement accompanying the chemistry prize credited her with extending Kagan’s attempts to use mathematics to understand non-linear effects in chemical reactions. Blackmond and her team later also took big strides in making sense of the mechanism of the so-called Soai reaction.
And yet, the committee elected to reward the discovery of the validity of Frank’s model rather than work that explained and further extended it.
The S.N. Bose example
In the final analysis, the citations for the Nobel Prizes should not be mistaken for the history of science. Scientists build on the work of others and science advances in these slow but steady increments. When Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 2013 for predicting the Higgs boson, there was some clamour in India for not recognising the work of Satyendra Nath Bose. The objection was fair to the extent that you can’t have a fruit without the whole tree and yet petty because it is not reasonable to expect one prize to laud the entire history of a field.
This is why each Nobel Prize award can be a chance to reflect on its limitations, and remember that it is not an ultimate recognition. No prize is.
In that vein, we should also not confuse the number of winners every year with the number of people it takes to do excellent science — from grad students who perform simple experiments to senior colleagues to discuss complicated ideas with. In fact, depending on where in the world you are and your socio-economic standing, your ability to be a good scientist may turn on something as deceptively simple as having someone to help with household chores.
Perhaps most of all, while the Nobel Prizes recognise good science, not all good science wins Nobel Prizes.

The scene is familiar. Five days after a caesarean section, a woman in one of our cities is at home with a newborn, a painful surgical wound, and a folder of papers. The papers list the baby’s feeding schedule, immunisation dates, and the paediatrician’s phone number. There is one line about her own care, a follow-up visit in six weeks. She is bleeding more than she expected. She has not slept longer than ninety minutes at a stretch. Her mother tells her this is normal. Her mother-in-law tells her this is normal. It is extremely common. But “common” does not mean harmless.
What’s happening in India
India has done something remarkable in maternal health. The maternal mortality ratio has fallen from 254 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2004–2006 to 87 in 2022–2024, a reduction of nearly two-thirds. The National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6) records institutional births at 90.6%.
But these numbers leave an important question unanswered: What happens to new mothers after birth?
The NFHS-6 reports that 82.8% of mothers received postnatal care within two days of delivery. The postnatal care recorded within 48 hours of an institutional delivery may well be a check that occurs before the mother leaves the hospital. A check before discharge and continuity after it are not the same thing, and the indicator cannot tell them apart.
Why this is important
The World Health Organization’s postnatal care guidance sets a minimum of four contacts. Each is meant to assess the mother as well as the baby. India’s headline statistic largely overlaps with the first of those four contacts. But no headline national indicator shows whether women received the complete schedule, or what those contacts assessed.
This is not merely a question of comfort. A systematic review of 26 studies involving 8.7 million women globally identified 6,142 maternal deaths. Nearly one-quarter of those deaths occurred between postpartum days 8 and 42. That is precisely when an Indian mother is at home, and precisely when what is happening to her is least visible to the system.
Additionally, the caesarean section rate increased from 21.5% at NFHS-5 to 27.2% at NFHS-6. More Indian women are therefore recovering from major abdominal surgery in flats and small houses, with a newborn, some of them without the extended household support that older arrangements assumed.
What is missing
A qualitative systematic review of 51 studies of traditional postpartum practices across more than 20 countries found the same elements recurring: organised support for the mother, a prescribed period of rest, particular foods, and additional help with the baby. Read as medicine rather than ritual, it is a structured plan for recovery. It feeds her at a time when she is depleted and breastfeeding. And it does the thing our health system finds hardest to implement—treating the weeks after birth as a distinct state requiring care, rather than a return to ‘normal’ life.
Home-Based Newborn Care in India schedules an ASHA to visit the house on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42. National guidance is explicit that the visits on days 3, 7 and 42 are for the mother as well as the baby. The ASHA’s job is to look for excessive bleeding, high temperature, foul-smelling discharge, cracked nipples, and engorged breasts. The mother, in other words, is written into the design.
What is missing is the rest of her well-being. The maternal component focuses on danger signs, feeding, and breast problems rather than on recovery. The ASHA’s checklist does not include blood-pressure measurement, a systematic mental health screening, or a follow-up glucose test. And the arithmetic of the schedule tells its own story: six visits for the baby, three of which are hers as well.
Across many Indian communities, the period after childbirth, in some up to 42 days, is marked out and protected. Families understand that a woman who has just given birth needs feeding, rest, and helping hands. The routine postnatal care schedule also centres on the first 42 days.
Yet in both settings, attention can still gravitate toward the baby.
Among 403 women in Gujarat, those with low social support had about two-and-a-half times the odds of postnatal depression compared with women who had strong support. The findings suggest that support may be an important factor, and our households have supplied it for generations. What the customs cannot do is examine the mother. They cannot detect persistently high blood pressure or determine whether anaemia is contributing to the exhaustion everyone is calling normal. Some customs and practices are not actual care; indeed, they may actively prevent a woman from being taken to a doctor when she is bleeding heavily or running a fever. A good postnatal system would add an examination to the help that supportive households give.
What is needed
What would it take to consider the mother’s condition as well as the baby’s? The schedule already exists and so do the workers. What is missing is scope, ownership, and measurement. Visits to the mother and baby after discharge should assess the mother’s recovery as well as her danger signs. Responsibility for the mother’s follow-up should rest with a designated healthcare provider or service, which should document her care after the delivery record is closed.
A structured review can begin in minutes. It should ask about bleeding, pain, and her surgical wound. It should include measuring her blood pressure, particularly if she was hypertensive in pregnancy. It should test for anaemia when her tiredness, or her pregnancy, points that way. It should ask if she is experiencing changes in mood or sleep and whether she’s been having frightening or intrusive thoughts. It should ask about feeding difficulty, urinary leakage, prolapse, and whether she’s experiencing pain during sex. It should arrange a follow-up glucose test for the woman who had gestational diabetes and now carries a substantial lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes.
The point is not the panel. The point is that somebody asks.
Making it part of the system
Primary care also belongs here, not in place of the obstetrician or the ASHA but as part of the system that holds on to what the pregnancy revealed. It is often during pregnancy that high blood pressure or high blood sugar first appears. When the delivery record closes, that knowledge should not close with it.
We measure delivery and newborn outcomes in detail. We should give equal attention to maternal recovery after discharge. Until maternal recovery is counted, too much of it will continue to unfold privately at home, with symptoms described as ‘normal’ by everyone, including the mother herself, until enough time passes that she stops mentioning them and lives with ill health instead.
(Dr. Sowmya Josyula is an internist and public health specialist. She writes on women’s health and on traditional practice examined against evidence. sowmya.josyula@kushalahealth.com)

After public school teacher Gary Keblish was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019, a surgeon cut out the tumor. But he wasn’t out of the woods. In some patients, melanoma aggressively recurs after surgery, so his doctors referred him to a new trial: for Merck and Moderna’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine.
Speaking by video at the STAT Summit on Thursday, Keblish compared the journey — in all its physical and emotional turbulence — to a trip on Ms. Frizzle’s Magic School Bus. “Seatbelts, everyone!” he said, quoting the iconic line.
He’s glad he went. Today, he is still teaching, and Merck and Moderna are preparing to file the vaccine for approval, after announcing in August that it significantly delayed both cancer recurrence and the development of metastatic disease in melanoma patients like Keblish, in a large Phase 3 trial.
It’s a landmark moment for a cancer vaccine field that has long struggled to live up to its hype. But the two companies’ work is far from complete. They are now looking to prove the vaccine isn’t just a powerful tool for certain melanoma patients but that it can also transform a sea of other tumors, as an early generation of immunotherapies did.
It is careful and costly work.
“We have a lot of exploring to do and need to prioritize where we explore,” Moderna President Stephen Hoge said on stage at the summit.
Beside Hoge, Merck R&D chief Dean Li outlined an exploration strategy. The vaccine, known chemically as intismeran autogene, works in combination with Merck’s blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which has been tested in thousands of trials over the last 15 years. Keytruda works better in some tumors — so-called hot tumors, which often have lots of mutations — than other so-called cold tumors.
“We know exactly where I-O [immuno-oncology] works, where a checkpoint inhibitor works, where it doesn’t, where it almost worked and didn’t make it,” said Li.
The pair has largely focused to date on settings where Keytruda has worked best, such as an adjuvant — add-on — therapy for melanoma patients whose visible tumors have already been removed by a surgeon. They are already running trials in adjuvant lung, kidney, and bladder cancer.
Li and Hoge suggested other settings they may explore or where trials are just beginning, including in tumors where Keytruda failed but another kind of immunotherapy worked, or as a standalone therapy in very early-stage tumors. “There’s an incredible opportunity to think about how we bring immunotherapy into earlier interventions and really intercept cancer so that we don’t present with stage 3, stage 4 disease later,” said Hoge.
Li contrasted their approach with “other people” who “may not have the advantage” of their expertise and have chosen to go after cold or metastatic tumors — an apparent nod at Moderna’s mRNA rival BioNTech, which has some early promising early data but also notable failures.
“We have chosen not to do this,” Li said. “But I can tell you: Anyone has positive data and it’s out there, you will never see Moderna and Merck pivot [so] fast.”
Small tests in adjuvant pancreatic and gastric cancer are underway, to test the possibility. Li also floated the possibility of using the vaccine in patients whose metastatic tumors have already been shrunk by other treatments.
In the meantime, they continue to try to improve the technology. The vaccine is made by looking at individual tumors and using an algorithm to select up to 34 mutant proteins, in hope that you can then flash those as a “wanted sign” to the immune system.
The algorithm is imperfect. But by closely analyzing the immune systems of patients in their trials, Moderna and Merck could in theory build even better software.
“It’s a real privilege to have all that information across the now several thousand people in our Phase 3 program,” Hoge said. “I’m looking forward to digging into it.”

Defence tech startup Tonbo Imaging’s IPO was fully subscribed within hours of opening for bidding, with demand led by non-institutional investors (NIIs). The public issue received bids for 1.26 Cr shares against 85.26 Lakh shares on offer, translating into an overall subscription of 1.47X as of 13:06 IST. The NII portion was subscribed 2.73X, receiving bids for 49.82 Lakh shares against an allocation of 18.24 Lakh shares. Within this category, the portion for applications above ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 1.92X, while that for applications above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 4.36X. Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) bid for just 7,707 shares against the 24.32 Lakh shares reserved for them. Meanwhile, retail investors bid for 75.07 Lakh shares against their allocation of 42.56 Lakh shares, subscribing to their portion 1.76X. The employee portion was booked 3.93X, attracting bids for 55,083 shares against 14,000 shares on offer. The opening-day demand follows Tonbo’s ₹255.4 Cr anchor allocation ahead of the public issue. The startup allotted 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 anchor investors at ₹700 apiece. Domestic mutual funds accounted for 57.7% of the anchor allocation, with 12 funds participating through 25 schemes. Other anchor investors included Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, WhiteOak Capital, Aranda Investments, and Allianz. Tonbo has set a price band of ₹665–₹700 per share for its ₹852.1 Cr IPO, which will close on October 19. The issue comprises an OFS of up to 1.2 Cr shares, meaning the startup will receive no proceeds. Selling shareholders include cofounders Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza, alongside CEAQ Technologies and Artiman Partners. Inside Tonbo’s Defence Tech Business Tonbo develops imaging and sensor systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and other military applications. Its products include thermal weapon sights, driver-vision systems, fire-control systems, and missile seekers. The startup outsources manufacturing to partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology, while handling prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house. The IPO comes after a decline in Tonbo’s annual revenue and profit. Operating revenue fell 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25, while net profit dropped 30.2% to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr. In Q1 FY27, Tonbo reported an operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr.

As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.
Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.
“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman, was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”
Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.
For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.
The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.
On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.
“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.
Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of occur in peatland areas, which can burn for weeks underground and are difficult to extinguish.
“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

Thieves targeted the mid-day meal storage room at a government school in Dhurkada here on two separate occasions, making off with four gas cylinders, food supplies and utensils, police said on Thursday.
The unidentified accused broke the lock and stole four gas cylinders, 50 steel tumblers used by the children for drinking milk, various food supplies, and cooking utensils.
The complaint filed with the police states that on October 12, after school hours, the staff locked the mid-day meal room before heading home.

On a complaint by the school in-charge, Pratibha Gupta, the Ambala City Sadar police station has registered a case against unknown persons and initiated an investigation.

The 'leap second' could disappear. How a minor time adjustment became a major problem
International time-keeping body may vote to ditch the decades-long tradition Thursday
For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth.
On Thursday, an international timekeeping body in France is expected to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour, which could take centuries or even millennia.
The precise atomic time we use to track our days — developed in the 1950s and measured by tracking the natural vibrations of atoms — is slightly out of sync with solar time, which is based on the position of the sun in the sky relative to a specific location on Earth, because the planet's rotation has been gradually slowing.
The leap second was introduced in 1972 as a way to correct the discrepancy. Ten seconds were added immediately, says Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre.
Since then, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, which tracks the difference between the solar day and atomic time, has monitored the discrepancy to determine when an extra second is needed.
When that threshold is reached, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures adds a second at either the end of December or the end of June. Leap seconds have been added 27 times, most recently in 2016.
Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, says leap seconds are becoming increasingly difficult to manage as more systems rely on precise timekeeping. (National Research Council Canada)
If we didn't make those tiny adjustments, nothing would perceptibly change in our lifetimes. But eventually, Beattie says, "you might get the brightest part of the day at midnight and the darkest part of day at noon."
The concept is similar to leap years, whereby a day is added to the end of February every four years to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons because the Earth's orbit around the sun takes about 365¼ days.
Without leap years, our hottest months would eventually fall during what is now winter, and the colder months during summer, Beattie says.
What's the problem?
But the time has come when leap seconds seem to be causing more trouble than they're worth.
"The basic global agreement is that we want to do away with these abrupt leap seconds," Beattie said.
That's because the small adjustment can be a headache for tech and telecommunications companies and infrastructure that relies on precise timekeeping.
Companies also have different ways of implementing leap seconds, such as changing their clock rates to stretch the extra second over several hours or an entire day.
Beattie says that variation among networks creates a risk of system failures.
The leap second was blamed for Reddit and LinkedIn crashes in 2012, for example, and brief outages at Cloudflare in 2016.
"The problem is that the needs for timing and network synchronicity are just going up and up, they're ever increasing," Beattie said. "And so the risks are just increasing along with them, because all you need is for some system to not implement it properly and then you could have a cascade effect that could cause quite significant problems."
Negative seconds?
There's another complicating twist.
Over the last six years or so, the Earth's rotation has actually sped up, raising the possibility that a "negative leap second" — in which a second would be taken away — could be needed in the future.
Tech giant Meta said in 2022 that a negative leap second could have a "devastating effect" on software, adding, "In any case, every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures."

The proposed fix, which would take effect in May 2027, is instead to let those extra seconds add up to 3,600 — a full hour — before adjusting the clocks, pushing the issue many generations down the road.
Not everyone is impressed by this approach.
Paul Delaney, a York University physics and astronomy professor emeritus, says he was "surprised" to hear the proposal.
"It is a problem for an increasingly computerized, AI-oriented economy, and that's obviously what we have," he said. "But that said, gosh, don't we still hire computer programmers to sort these sorts of things out? Some part of me says that we're throwing in the towel and saying, 'Oh, it's too difficult to do, and what the heck, it is just a second.'"
'Not a perfect system'
Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, says many factors affect the Earth's rotation speed, but it has tended to slow over time, in part because of the moon's effect on Earth's tides.
But complex variables, including climate change and glacial melting, can cause changes in that trend.

She says there is no perfect system for our clocks to account for these shifts and "we'll be fine" without leap seconds.
"This is a real human problem that we've been struggling with forever, as long as we've been watching the stars move across the sky and tracking when the sun rises and sets, and trying to get the patterns right," Lawler said.
"It's always going to be a little bit wrong, and I think we just have to accept that."

Food, from the moment it’s in the mouth until it’s excreted as poop, goes through digestion—and this process is a wild journey. Food containing carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids is chewed into a mush in the mouth, where some degree of starch and lipid digestion occurs before it is swallowed. In the stomach, the swallowed ‘ball’ of chewed food is continuously ground and churned until the food particles are small enough to enter the small intestine. Simultaneously, hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsin (an enzyme) in the stomach break down complex proteins in the food.
The food, now in a semi-liquid form, reaches the digestive enzyme-rich small intestine, where its fate is sealed for major chemical digestion before being converted into absorbable nutrients. Enzymes in the small intestine break down the partially digested macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids—into smaller molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, along with vitamins and minerals.
What remains is indigestible food, along with leftover digestive fluids and cellular waste, which enters the colon (large intestine), where digestive enzymes are lacking. However, the gut microbiota—the body’s dynamic ‘organ’—in the colon compensates for this dearth by fermenting indigestible food, including dietary fibres and indigestible proteins. Enzymes produced by the gut microbiota break this indigestible food into useful metabolites and gases before the remainder is expelled as poop.
What are intestinal gases?
In humans, intestinal gases include nitrogen (N2), oxygen (O2), carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), and trace amounts of hydrogen sulphide (H2S)—the gas with the rotten egg smell. While N2 and O2 mostly reflect swallowed air, H2 and CH4 are odourless gases produced by gut microbiota. It is H2S that is primarily responsible for the smell of gas.
The colon—which hosts the highest microbial densities—harbours microbes that prefer indigestible carbohydrates as food, or as an energy source. These indigestible-carbohydrate-loving microbes (carbohydrate-fermenting) flourish in the colon region close to the small intestine (proximal colon), where their energy source availability is higher. Microbes including Bacteroides scavenge (ferment) human-indigestible carbohydrates such as dietary fibres and resistant starch, producing substantial quantities of hydrogenas a major by-product.
Also thriving in this oxygen-poor, hydrogen-rich ecosystem are microbes that compete for, and convert hydrogento methane, like methanogenic archaea. Likewise, sulphate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in these regions of the colon convert hydrogeninto hydrogen sulphide in small amounts. As the food passes through the colon, the availability of indigestible carbohydrates decreases over time. Microbes like SRB in regions of the colon close to the rectum (distal colon) also ferment human-indigestible proteins for energy, producing hydrogen sulphide in the process.
Studies so far suggest that host cells (through distinct mechanisms) and microbial cells utilise intestinal gases. Excess gases are eliminated as exhaled gas (from the lungs) and flatulence.
What do intestinal gases do?
Recent studies suggest intestinal gases are more than just gas. They can, in fact, serve as markers of gastrointestinal (GI) health, and can regulate gut motility and transit time. Gut motility refers to the muscle contractions in the digestive tract that move the food, and gut transit time is the time it takes for food to move through the gastrointestinal tract before being excreted.
Advancing research reveals that hydrogencan influence gut motility and, in experimental models, shorten transit time. Methane, by contrast, has been shown to slow gut motility and increase transit time. However, findings on the effect of hydrogen sulphide on gut motility and transit time have been mixed.
Microbiota research has also pointed to links between imbalances in gut microbiota and intestinal gas levels and gastrointestinal(GI) diseases/symptoms.
A real-world study measured hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulphide levels using breath testing in 3,004 participants with GI symptoms, especially excessive bloating and flatulence, from the United States. The study found associations between intestinal gas levels and GI symptoms: higher hydrogen levels (≥20 ppm above baseline) with diarrhoea; higher methane levels (≥10 ppm) with constipation; and higher hydrogen sulphide levels (≥2 ppm) with severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain. The study also suggested dysregulated hydrogen sulphide production was associated with greater diarrhoea, urgency, bloating, and symptom severity.
Animal models and clinical studies have reported similar associations between intestinal gases and GI symptoms. However, these studies lack identical methodologies and comparison with healthy participants as controls.
Monitoring gases for diagnosis
The most commonly adopted method for measuring intestinal gases is breath testing—measuring gases in exhaled breath. Microbial fermentation activity and gut motility are also assessed indirectly with this method.
However, new techniques are being devised for non-invasive, real-time continuous monitoring of intestinal gases. To capture eliminated intestinal gases (exhaled gas and flatus), researchers have designed respiration/fermentation chambers (airtight rooms with gas sensors and continuous air supply) to explore microbial fermentation activity, track intestinal gases, and monitor the effects of therapeutic interventions.
Alternatively, as flatus has relatively higher concentrations of intestinal gases, researchers at the University of Maryland have developed a device that can be attached to underwear. The device, designed to objectively measure hydrogenin flatus, monitors real-time gas profiles and gas-release patterns, providing insights into gut microbial activity and digestive health.
Why this is important
Measuring and monitoring real-time gas profiles could enable researchers to expand gut microbiota research: define ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ levels in intestinal gases, establish mechanisms behind gas effects, and study diverse populations, involving both healthy people and people with GI diseases, over long periods. Doctors could also potentially tailor a treatment plan—diet or gas-targeted medication—to rebalance the gut microbial ecosystem and modulate gas production and track GI health progress.
Therefore, the next time someone lets one rip, remember that intestinal gases have uses beyond popular humour or emptying out a room. These gases are part of a dynamic system that shapes the gut microbiota and influences digestive health, including how one poops, and can serve as markers of GI health.
(Smruthi Prabhu is an independent science writer from Mangalore. smruthigp@gmail.com)

For patients with advanced cancer and other life-limiting illnesses, palliative care often needs to extend beyond hospital wards to their homes, where families grapple with pain, emotional distress, and the demands of long-term caregiving.
At the State-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO), the Department of Palliative Medicine has made home-based care a key part of its services, reporting more than 750 home-care visits, over 12,000 km travelled and more than 3,000 beneficiaries, including patients and caregivers.
These services were highlighted while observing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day on October 10, which this year carried the theme ‘Pain management: An essential part of palliative care’.
“With the help of volunteers and NGOs, we also extend financial support for children’s education. We provide waterbed and airbed, ration kits, and nebuliser machines for use at home. It is not just about treating the patient,” M.K. Yadhuraj Gowda, Head of the Department of Palliative Medicine at KMIO, told The Hindu.
The home-care service is intended for patients who find it difficult to travel to the hospital because of advanced illness, reduced mobility, or other challenges. Multidisciplinary teams provide medical assessment, symptom management, nursing care, and support in familiar surroundings, helping reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
The department’s approach also recognises that serious illness affects entire families. Caregivers may need help managing the practical demands of looking after a patient, as well as support in coping with emotional and financial pressures, Dr. Gowda said.
Beyond death
Palliative care also includes bereavement support for families after the death of a loved one. KMIO’s department provides guidance to help family members cope with grief, manage emotional distress and access support during the grieving process.
The service reflects the broader role of palliative care, which addresses not only physical pain and other symptoms but also the psychological, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patients and their families. Volunteer services add another layer of support for families navigating serious illness and loss.
Pain relief and care for children
Institute director R. Krishnappa said the department provides inpatient palliative care for patients who require specialised management of pain and other distressing symptoms, with capacity for more than 30 patients. Its services include medication and interventional procedures such as nerve blocks and neurolysis for selected patients with severe cancer-related pain that remains inadequately controlled with conventional treatment.
It also provides paediatric palliative care, with age-appropriate pain and symptom management, emotional support and guidance for families caring for children with cancer and other serious illnesses, he said.
Music and sound therapy sessions are conducted for inpatients on Wednesdays, while yoga therapy sessions are held on Thursdays to promote relaxation and emotional well-being alongside medical treatment.
Teleconsultations extend specialist support
The department has relaunched its ‘Call for Care - Neravina Kare’ service to connect patients living outside Bengaluru and in distant locations with specialist palliative care. Through telephone and video consultations, a team comprising a palliative care physician, nurse and clinical psycho-oncologist offers guidance on symptom management and emotional support. Patients and caregivers can contact the service on 9008441708.

Bhima Jewellers has appointed actor Janhvi Kapoor as its brand ambassador as the jewellery retailer looks to strengthen its presence across markets and connect with consumers across different regions. The association is part of the brand’s efforts to expand its audience while continuing to focus on craftsmanship, trust and cultural relevance.
Janhvi Kapoor appointed brand ambassador of Bhima Jewellers as brand eyes wider reach
With a legacy spanning 100 years, Bhima Jewellers has built its presence in the jewellery retail sector by catering to customers across generations. The appointment of Janhvi Kapoor aligns with the brand’s plans to reach a wider consumer base while maintaining its established relationships with existing customers.
Janhvi’s visibility across India is expected to support the brand’s efforts to connect with consumers across regions and demographics. The collaboration also reflects Bhima Jewellers’ approach to engaging with a new generation of buyers whose preferences combine cultural traditions with contemporary relevance. Through the association, the brand aims to strengthen its consumer engagement while adapting to changing purchasing patterns.
The partnership also draws a connection between Janhvi’s association with South India and Bhima Jewellers’ regional roots. The brand intends to use this alignment to introduce its South Indian heritage to a wider national audience while continuing to build on its existing market presence.
Sharing her thoughts on the association, Janhvi Kapoor said, “Some of my fondest memories are of seeing jewellery become a part of our family’s celebrations and milestones. It holds stories that are passed down through generations. That’s what makes my association with Bhima Jewellers so special. With a legacy spanning 100 years, Bhima Jewellers beautifully reflects trust, tradition, and timeless craftsmanship, and I’m delighted to join its legacy.”
Commenting on the appointment, a Bhima Jewellers spokesperson stated, “At Bhima Jewellers, we have always believed that jewellery is much more than an ornament. It is a part of life’s most treasured moments, carrying memories, emotions, and traditions across generations. Janhvi Kapoor’s warmth, elegance, and deep appreciation for her roots make her a natural fit for our brand. There is an authenticity about her that resonates with the values we hold close, and we are delighted to welcome her to the Bhima Jewellers family. We look forward to celebrating timeless stories, meaningful connections, and special milestones together.”
Founded in 1925 by Shri K. Lakshminarayana Bhattar, Bhima has established itself as a jewellery brand associated with craftsmanship in South India. The company currently operates 21 stores across Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, alongside an e-commerce platform.
With Janhvi joining as its brand ambassador, Bhima Jewellers aims to build on its regional foundation and expand its reach across India. The collaboration forms part of the brand’s broader strategy to increase visibility, engage with a wider consumer base and support its long-term growth across markets.

In late September, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna of California introduced the Free Child Care for America Act, an $80 billion-a-year proposal to make childcare free for nearly every family with kids under six. The bill would let families choose between sending their child to a daycare center, having a relative, friend, or neighbor paid a living wage to care for them, or taking a $1,000 monthly stipend to keep the child home for the first three years. It comes from a lawmaker who openly says he’s considering a run for president. “I want 2028 to be a big-ideas primary,” Khanna told ABC. “A contest on who’s going to have ideas of the future that meet the moment.”
Universal childcare is set to be a 2028 presidential test
Democrats are already rolling out big plans.
