"Back home when we play in front of our own fans, just to see the fans, the crowd get behind us, singing the national anthem... it makes me cry every time."
Edwin Ipape gets emotional when travelling with his Papua New Guinea team-mates to the national stadium.
Children, so mad about rugby league that they will fashion a ball out of anything they can find, run alongside the team bus, eager to catch a glimpse of their heroes. Players are mobbed wherever they go.
The buzz around rugby league in Papua New Guinea can sometimes be daunting for visiting teams. In the past, passion has boiled over to the point where police have fired tear gas into the crowds.
But the national game – and in particular its men's national team, the Kumuls – is also a powerful symbol of unity in a land that can be torn apart by tribal fighting and where more than 800 different languages and dialects are spoken.
When the PNG fans are at their best and noisiest, a 15,000 crowd can sound like twice that number and is so loud that the players on the field cannot hear each other.
They will be at full volume this month when the island's capital Port Moresby is the venue for four Rugby League World Cup matches, as PNG co-hosts the tournament with Australia and New Zealand.
"People in Papua New Guinea probably don't know who the prime minister is, but they know all the NRL [National Rugby League] players," joked Elsie Albert, a prop who plays for PNG's women's side – the Orchids – and for Parramatta Eels in Australia's NRL Women's Premiership.
So, how has an island perched off Australia's northern tip become so obsessed with the sport?
Rugby League World Cup
15 October - 15 November
Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand
Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app
The seeds were sown by Australian miners in the 1930s, who introduced the game, one with deep roots in New South Wales and Queensland, to the local population.
It took hold as the devotion spread. The ferocious physicality of rugby league sat easily with the Papuans, who had long fought battles without a ball on their soil.
These days, the people of PNG are among the most knowledgeable and passionate. Only the Cook Islands can lay similar claims to an all-out obsession with the game in terms of national importance.
Sometimes that fervour spills over, with violence souring matches in their domestic league,, external something the authorities are keen to stamp out. In the past, tear gas was needed to quell over-excited crowds, such as when Great Britain came to tour in the early 1990s.
Generally though, rugby league is more of a peacekeeper. Villages will settle around a television set to watch rugby league, whether it is the NRL or Super League.
Participation levels are high. There are thousands of would-be Edwin Ipapes across the island, running about on bits of grass, on gravel, on the scrawniest patch of clear land somewhere, anywhere they can get the ball out and play.
The games can be rough, bordering on brutal. They are the perfect breeding ground for talent. But kit can be basic.
"If you're lucky enough, you play with a rugby league ball," Ipape recalled of his childhood, growing up in Mount Hagen, in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea.
"Otherwise, you play with containers, you put stuff in it, fill it up and then make it like a ball and whatever... whatever we can get our hands on, we may pretend that it was our rugby ball.
"I remember saving up my lunch money to buy myself one of those American footballs and using it as a rugby ball so we could play."
The Highlands of Papua New Guinea were a testing place to grow up - there is a long history of brutal tribal rivalries. Today, violence in those parts of the country has escalated - as access to increasingly sophisticated weaponry has brought deadly consequences.
Ipape, though, only ever had eyes for rugby league. Larsen Marape and Menzie Yere were the heroes of his youth: the faces on the posters adorning his walls in Mount Hagen.
The sport not only brings unity to the country - for those who make it to the top, it also offers a chance to cross the globe.
Ipape, 27, has played for his country, and travelled worldwide. The hooker now plays in Super League for Leigh Leopards.
The 'Birds of Paradise' - as Kumuls translates - have been life-transforming.
"Rugby league has given me pretty much everything," he said. "It's instilled discipline and it's taught me a lot of lessons about life.
"I've welled up with tears a few times on our way to the stadium in Papua New Guinea, just looking at the young kids running alongside the bus.
"I'm so blessed and privileged to be in the position to represent my country. It's a dream I'm living right now."
For any young hopeful looking to become the next Ipape, the first goal is to play for a village, then a province. Then it is the PNG Hunters, who play in Australia's Queensland Cup.
That can be the ticket to the big leagues, whether that be the NRL - as it was for former Melbourne Storm centre Justin Olam - or Super League, as it has been for Ipape.
From 2028 onwards, there will be an NRL team based on the island, the PNG Chiefs.
While much of their initial recruitment has been high-profile, such as Samoa half-back Jarome Luai, compatriot Brian To'o, and New Zealand international Joey Manu, Papuan players have also been sought to bolster the ranks.
Visiting teams can sometimes find the excitement around rugby league in Papua New Guinea unsettling. Any familiar face from the sport draws attention - but the fans only want to show affection and respect.
"We went to a little market and people were recognising us," Leigh Leopards' Papuan hooker Liam Horne told BBC Sport. "We actually needed a lift to go to one of these shopping centres, so we just hitchhiked.
"We got this random guy to pick us up and he couldn't believe it. He had two Kumuls in his back seat and he was freaking out.
"The people over there, they love it. They're welcoming."
Some of the Kumuls of today are second-generation Papuans born and raised in Australia, such as Leigh back-rower Jacob Alick-Weincke.
Being a PNG international is a chance to connect with the culture, understand more about their heritage, upbringing, and the people.
"People there just want to be around you in your presence," Alick-Weincke added.
"We always go to the shops or go to local villages. We went to one of the markets last time we were over there. That was a really cool experience. Just people everywhere."
The rise of the women's team - chronicled in the 2019 documentary Power Meri,, external which followed the Orchids to their debut World Cup in 2017 - has been helped by Elsie Albert's star power.
Albert is PNG's first female superstar - but that meant challenging some old values back home.
"Women were supposed to stay at home and do household chores, so when this great game came over [for women], it was seen as a threat to the culture," Albert said in 2023 as part of an NRL storytelling campaign.
"The pioneering girls had men throwing bottles at them into the stadium, but in 2019 everything changed for us when we played England."
In that two-Test series, England won the first match 24-10 in Goroka. But the second, in Port Moresby, brought a memorable - and defining - 20-16 victory for the hosts.
"You could feel the atmosphere," Albert recalled. "The crowd was there and to get a win in front of everyone, especially the men... for them to see that women could do what men can do, was a great feeling.
"You could feel it was going to change. Rugby league is a great way for us to to advocate for change."
Even well-known rugby league family names of the past are growing new branches, with Fleur Ginn Wagambie following in the footsteps of elders John and Richard when she made her PNG debut in 2025 - and now hopes to make a World Cup debut.
"I've always wanted to represent the Orchids and I was really lucky last year to make my debut in the Pacific Cup," Wagambie, a Parramatta team-mate of Albert, told ABC Pacific.
"Being lucky enough to play in a World Cup, in Port Moresby, in front of my family is really exciting."
Papua New Guinea's rugby league influence can be felt at Championship club London Broncos.
Jason Demetriou, the Kumuls head coach, is in charge at Plough Lane, and his influence persuaded a host of Papuan players to come over.
Championship player of the year Gairo Voro, full-back Morea Morea, prop Epil Kapinias, centres Alex Max and Robert Mathias, hooker Finley Glare and back-rower Jeremiah Simbiken were all recruited by the Super League aspirant Broncos.
Together, they steered the club to a treble - the Championship League Leaders' Shield, the 1895 Cup and the divisional Grand Final title.
Their progress alerted the PNG Chiefs, who have signed Voro, Glare and Morea for the 2028 season onwards.
"There's going to be eyeballs on every player in the World Cup," Demetriou added.
"We're playing against Lebanon, which will be stacked full of NRL players, playing against England that are full of Super League and NRL players, and Samoa, which is one of the top international sides in the world at the moment.
"We know what's in front of us, but on the flip side of that, they're going to play against PNG as well. We have to make sure that when they go out on the field, they understand that there's some elite level players out there.
"If we want opportunities, we want to be respected, then we need to start with beating teams on the world stage."
Santos National Football Stadium - where the co-hosts will play the four Rugby League World Cup matches they are staging - has a capacity of just under 15,000. It will seem a lot more than that on Saturday, though, when the Orchids face France and the Kumuls take on Lebanon. And that will be thanks to the atmosphere.
"Loud" was how Horne put it. "It sounds like 30,000." Kumuls stalwart Lachlan Lam - forced to miss this World Cup because he needs wrist surgery - likened the atmosphere to "a proper scream".
Team-mate Alick-Wiencke said: "I've not experienced anything like it. You can't hear yourself talking to other team-mates and things like that.
"And, just the heat - you can't believe the whole stadium is packed out. It's like 40C and they're up there singing and dancing and carrying on. So the atmosphere is unbelievable."
Whatever happens at this World Cup, rugby league shows no signs of losing its appeal in Papua New Guinea. And the passion of those supporters might yet give Ipape reason to shed a few more tears.

Anthropic's revenue growth slowed in the third quarter, disappointing some investors as the AI startup prepares to go public.
There's an intriguing explanation for at least part of the slowdown: The company may be getting better at stopping rivals from stealing its AI secrets.
Anthropic generated $16.8 billion in revenue during the third quarter, my colleague Stephen Council reported on Wednesday. While that's impressive growth by almost any standard, but it's a slowdown from earlier in the year.
Here's where things get interesting.
Anthropic told prospective investors this week that 5% to 7% of its revenue comes from something called distillation, The Information reported.
This is when rival AI developers use Anthropic's Claude models to help train their own competing systems.
One way to do this is to create thousands of Anthropic accounts and bombard Claude with carefully chosen questions. The rivals collect the answers and use them to teach their own AI models how to perform similar tasks.
All these "distillation" accounts and questions generate revenue for Anthropic, even though the customers are effectively trying to copy its technology.
Anthropic has repeatedly accused Chinese AI companies of doing this and has been cracking down on the practice. And lately, the company has said this effort has been successful.
That creates an unusual problem: Anthropic's success in protecting its technology could be hurting its reported revenue growth.
It also raises questions about whether some of the company's spectacular growth earlier this year was artificially boosted by rivals paying to copy its models. It's unclear how much of the recent slowdown can be attributed to the crackdown.
Indeed, the company told investors this week that revenue from distillation is expected to decline further, according to The Information.
There's a precedent for this in the tech industry.
When Twitter went public, investors closely watched its user growth. Some accounts were bots rather than actual people, complicating the numbers investors used to judge the company's health.
Twitter disclosed estimates of fake and automated accounts in its regulatory filings, giving investors more information to assess its growth. The result was that user growth numbers came down.
Anthropic could face a similar challenge as it prepares for an IPO that could value the company at $1.5 trillion or more.
The important distinction is that a decline in distillation-related revenue doesn't necessarily mean Anthropic's underlying business is weakening. It could simply mean fewer rivals are paying to exploit its technology.
Of course, competition and other factors could also be slowing growth.
But investors will need to separate genuine customer demand from revenue generated by companies trying to copy Anthropic's AI.
Sometimes losing customers isn't such a bad thing.
I asked Anthropic about this on Wednesday and didn't hear back by Thursday morning.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Match report as Sunderland earn second Europa League win of league phase by beating Torreense; hosts took shock lead through Volnei's wondergoal; Regis Le Bris had to bring on regular first-teamers after making seven changes; Jules Ahoka headed in equaliser; Noah Sadiki netted late winner

Sunderland survived a huge scare as they came from behind to clinch back-to-back Europa League victories with a 2-1 win over Torreense following Noah Sadiki’s 93rd-minute winner.
Regis Le Bris' side made hard work of their first European away fixture in 53 years, trailing at half-time to the Portuguese second division club, who took a shock lead through centre-back Volnei Feltes' outstanding strike from 25 yards that nestled in the top right corner.

Manufacturing company Zetwerk has raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors ahead of the opening of its initial public offering (IPO) for public subscription on October 15. The company allotted 14.91 Cr equity shares to anchor investors at ₹151 apiece, the upper end of its IPO price band. Domestic mutual funds accounted for around 46% of the anchor book, picking up 6.80 Cr shares through 61 schemes across 22 fund houses. Notably, 40% of the anchor investor portion was reserved for domestic mutual funds, life insurance companies and pension funds. SBI Mutual Fund emerged as the largest among these investors, acquiring 1.02 Cr shares through two schemes. ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund also accounted for around 7% of the anchor allocation. Other participating fund houses included Bajaj Finserv, Abakkus, Baroda BNP Paribas, Motilal Oswal and Edelweiss. Global institutional investors accounted for a significant part of Zetwerk's anchor book. Capital Group's Smallcap World Fund Inc received the largest individual allocation, worth ₹288 Cr, accounting for 12.79% of the total anchor portion. Government Pension Fund Global and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's Monsoon fund were each allocated shares worth about ₹75 Cr, while Nomura India Investment Mother Fund received an allocation worth ₹50 Cr. Among international investors, the anchor book featured the likes of Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, First Sentier Investors and Societe Generale. Zetwerk’s ₹5,012 Cr IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 17. At the upper end of the price band of ₹143-₹151 per share, the offering values the company at a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr, or approximately $2.7 Bn. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 14.45 Cr shares, amounting to ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end of the price band. The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP). The OFS component has also expanded by 49.2% from approximately 9.7 Cr shares. Zetwerk’s promoters and cofounders, Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other shareholders offloading their stakes include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Kae Capital. The company plans to deploy ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue towards repaying or prepaying borrowings of Zetwerk and certain subsidiaries. The remaining proceeds will be used for acquisitions and general corporate purposes. On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue rose to ₹15,739.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in FY25. However, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25 due to discontinued operations over the past fiscal. The FY26 loss included an exceptional charge of ₹796.4 Cr linked to changes in share conversion ratios and an impairment charge of ₹453 Cr related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue grew 55.4% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr was attributable to discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included exceptional charges of ₹803.2 Cr from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

Dead fish in Yamuna near Burari raise alarm over Delhi river’s water quality
Several dead fish spotted along Yamuna near Burari in north Delhi since Wednesday night, raising concerns over the river’s water quality
Several dead fish have been spotted along the Yamuna near Burari in north Delhi since Wednesday night, raising concerns over the river’s water quality and possible industrial pollution. Wildlife experts and activists have flagged the incident, citing the possibility of untreated industrial effluents and low dissolved oxygen levels.
Wildlife enthusiast and conservationist Hemant Garg, who spotted the dead fish on Wednesday, said, “We regularly go in Yamuna to wildlife conservation, bird census and tracking wildlife. The fish were observed last night and thousands of dead fish have been seen way upstream up to shank number 10, 11 and 12. The water usually clean here. We should be wary as drinking water is also sourced from this part of river.”
Ranjan Mukhia, a boatman in Burari, said that the water has a strong stench and the fish deaths are not restricted to this stretch alone. “We have our fellow boatmen upstream who have reported that dead fish have been seen upstream in Haryana as well. We have to remove dead fish to ensure water doesn’t get even more polluted with carcasses,” he said.
Bhim Singh Rawat, a Yamuna activist and member of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People (SANDRP), said that such mass fish mortality incidents are usually reported in summer months when high temperatures lead to lower levels of dissolved oxygen.
“We cant recall the last such episode in winter months. The possibility in this case could be untreated industrial effluents. There is drain number 2 from Panipat, drain number 8 and one drain in Burari which may have discharged large amounts of untreated industrial effluents,” Rawat said. “The flow in the river has been restricted despite monsoonal flow,” he added.
Yamuna activist Pankaj Kumar wrote to the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, seeking urgent intervention.
“Fish mortality is critical bio indicator of severe ecological stress the primary causes are low dissolved oxygen, high biochemical oxygen demand and presence of toxic industrial effluents. If toxic substances are present in river in sufficient quantity to kill fish, the same water being abstracted downstream at Wazirabad for drinking purposes poses direct health risk to public health,” he said.
The New Delhi Nature Society, in a post on X, said, “Hundreds, maybe thousands, of fish found dead on 14th October in the Yamuna river near Burari, Delhi. Specific cause not established. Locals allege chemical waste discharged from Haryana through canals. Could it be related to the acid rain on Oct 12th?”
In May 2026, hundreds of fish died at Sanjay Lake in east Delhi amid a heatwave and receding water levels. Experts pointed to a combination of high temperatures, concentrated pollutants and declining dissolved oxygen, which can make aquatic conditions lethal for fish. Earlier, in April 2026, thousands of dead fish surfaced in Delhi’s Najafgarh drain, with locals reporting that industrial effluents from Haryana were a likely cause.
In May 2025 and, before that, in July 2024, hundreds of dead fish were recorded along the Yamuna banks near Burari in north Delhi.
The monthly Yamuna water quality report for September shows that, despite the monsoon season, the river stretch in Delhi failed to show significant improvement or dilution of pollutants. A comparison of the water quality reports for September 2025 and September 2026 shows that the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and faecal coliform levels were much higher at several locations along the river.
At Palla, the faecal coliform level this year was 1,100 units (MPN/200 ml), compared with 790 units last year. At the ISBT Bridge, it was recorded at 35,000 units, compared with 2,800 units last year. At Okhla barrage, faecal coliform levels of 21,000 units were recorded —six times higher than the 3,500 units recorded in September last year. Faecal coliform is an indicator of untreated sewage in the water. The level should ideally be below 500 units, with a maximum limit of 2,500 units.
At ISBT Bridge, BOD was 30 mg/l this year, compared with 8 mg/l on September 3 last year. Chemical oxygen demand (COD) rose from 44 mg/l to 92 mg/l over the same period. A BOD level of 3 mg/l or less and dissolved oxygen of at least 5 mg/l are specified for bathing. At ITO Bridge, BOD climbed from 4 mg/l to 18 mg/l, while COD rose from 20 mg/l to 60 mg/l. Faecal coliform levels increased from 1,800 to 17,000 MPN/100 ml.

NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
Windows PCs may finally catch up to Apple Silicon.
Last week, I spent two days hearing how Microsoft and NVIDIA are "reinventing the PC" with RTX Spark, the new system-on-a-chip powering the Surface Laptop Ultra and several other Windows PCs this fall. It's the first time we've seen powerful Arm CPUs joined together with NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU technology and up to 128GB of ultra-fast unified memory on a single chip. Theoretically, RTX Spark should allow for thin-yet-powerful laptops (and a few small desktops) that can handle AI tasks locally, as well as tackling content creation and gaming. So sure, I suppose NVIDIA and Microsoft have a reason to gloat a bit.
But, just like the launch of Snapdragon-powered Copilot+ systems two years ago, it was hard to ignore the elephant in the room: RTX Spark is clearly a response to Apple Silicon and the transformational changes it brought to Macs six years ago. Apple's chips are also made up of a powerful Arm CPU, capable GPU and fast unified memory, and they span the company's lineup from the tiny Mac mini to the super-powerful Mac Studio and 16-inch MacBook Pro. With RTX Spark, Windows users finally have a way to see the benefits of an efficient Arm-based SoC on high-end PCs, while the recent batch of Qualcomm chips covers the low-end and mid-range.
There weren't many surprises at Microsoft's AI launch event (featuring the Surface Laptop Ultra), or at NVIDIA's RTX Spark Editor's Day, which I attended alongside other media and analysts. Both companies want to sell us a future where we can run AI models and agents right from an RTX Spark-powered Windows laptop, something that seemed clear since the chip was announced at Computex. But even if that future doesn't come to pass, RTX Spark could still lead to some intriguing changes in the PC world.
Under the hood with RTX Spark
The RTX Spark SoC is powered by up to 20 NVIDIA Grace Arm CPU cores (10 performance cores and 10 efficiency cores), a Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5x memory running at 9,400 Mbps. There's also a slightly less powerful configuration with 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores. RTX Spark also includes much of what you'd find on NVIDIA's latest GPUs, including fifth-gen tensor cores, fourth-gen ray tracing cores, and a Blackwell video engine (with support of AV1 UHQ and 4:2:2 encoding and decoding).
By shoving all of this hardware onto a single chip, NVIDIA claims the RTX Spark is twice as efficient as a laptop powered by an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H and RTX 5070 dedicated GPU, while gaming at 60 watts. NVIDIA has previously said RTX Spark systems should be similarly powerful to RTX 5070 laptops, though as you can tell from the chart below, those dedicated GPU systems can also draw a lot more energy for better performance.
If you plan to be connected to power most of the time and don't need to travel with your laptop, you may see little benefit from choosing an RTX Spark system. But if you need to do serious creative work on the go, RTX Spark's improved efficiency allows PCs to work as fast on battery as they are while plugged in, according to NVIDIA. From my brief time with the Surface Laptop Ultra, I didn't notice any performance drops while playing Gears of War: E-Day on battery power. The game still looked silky smooth in 1440p with high graphics settings.
RTX Spark is built for AI, but also helps content creation and gaming
With its support for tons of unified RAM, RTX Spark systems should appeal to AI developers and researchers who need as much memory as they can to run large AI models locally, like the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. An RTX Spark system could significantly reduce the amount of money spent on cloud AI tokens, or replace that demand entirely. One researcher I spoke with was jealous that his colleagues were able to easily run AI models on modern Mac laptops, and he was excited about the possibility of doing the same on a Windows notebook. RTX Spark is also coming along as Microsoft is adding more support in Windows 11 for on-device AI tools like Perplexity, as well as simplified ways to set up AI agents like OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot.
Not surprisingly, NVIDIA is also touting RTX Spark's gaming capabilities. Since it features a Blackwell GPU front and center, it'll deliver all of the features you'd expect from RTX 50-series cards, including support for DLSS 5. As I mentioned before, you can expect performance similar to an RTX 5070 — NVIDIA is specifically touting 1440p as the intended resolution for RTX Spark systems, though I'd be interested to see how they perform in 4K with DLSS. A new performance mode for DLSS Frame Generation can push Cyberpunk 2077 up to 280fps with 6x frame gen, compared 213fps without performance mode. (It's unclear what you lose to achieve that frame bump, though.)
Since RTX Spark is Arm-based, it won't natively run every game on Windows, but NVIDIA claims recent titles like Control Resonant and the aforementioned Gears of War: E-Day will be supported at launch thanks to Microsoft's Prism emulator for x86 software. NBA 2K27, the main DLSS 5 launch game, will also be supported, alongside World of Warcraft: Forever. NVIDIA says it's also working with major anti-cheat providers to support their products, something that's prevented multiplayer games from working on Arm Windows systems in the past.
I'll have to spend more time with RTX Spark systems to see how well they actually handle gaming, beyond my minutes with Gears of War: E-Day. But if playing games is a priority, you'd still be better off with an Intel or AMD system with a dedicated GPU. At least then you wouldn't have to worry about potential emulation issues.
RTX Spark systems will also be useful content creation — again, as you'd expect from PCs with RTX Blackwell GPUs. You can lean on hardware acceleration in tools like Blender, and notably, Adobe is re-architecting Photoshop and Premiere specifically for NVIDIA's platform. That's a major sign of faith from one of the biggest software companies around, though I suppose Adobe is also reading the tea leaves and seeing a bright future for Arm-based Windows systems in general.
RTX Spark isn't for everyone, but that's okay
NVIDIA isn't targeting casual consumers with RTX Spark, not with a starting price of $2,600 for 18-core systems, or an eye-bleeding $3,700 for the full-powered 20-core models. Both NVIDIA and Microsoft are targeting AI developers and researchers who have the money to spend on insane amounts of RAM. And they should be prepared to open their wallets — a Surface Laptop Ultra with 128GB of RAM will cost a smooth $5.900. Still, that's a good deal cheaper than a fully-equipped M5 Max 16-inch MacBook Pro with 128GB of RAM, which costs $7,000.
Simply by existing, the RTX Spark platform will likely push Intel and AMD in creative new directions. AMD is trying to accomplish something similar with its Ryzen AI Max 400 chips, which can also house a ton of unified memory, but can also run existing x86 software without any emulation. And Intel has been eager to prove itself against AMD for the last few years, which has resulted in its powerful Core Ultra Series 3 chips. As always, competition is great for consumers.

'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
Aiden Pleterski read his victim impact statement in sentencing of kidnapper Thursday
Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski blamed his kidnapping for the fact he's currently representing himself at his own trial in a victim impact statement he read at the sentencing submissions hearing for his kidnapper on Thursday.
"I have had to forego any normal routines, like having a steady job, as a safety precaution, which has spiralled into significant financial difficulties which have had far reaching consequences," said Pleterski in Superior Court in Toronto.
"The most significant is my inability to pay for a lawyer to defend me against the false allegations that this individual and others have made against me."
Pleterski's jury trial is currently underway in the same courthouse. He's pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. So far Pleterski has only cross-examined the first of a dozen witnesses called by the Crown.

Deren Akyeam-Pong pleaded guilty to nine charges related to Pleterski's 2022 kidnapping in October of last year. Those charges include kidnapping, assault and various gun charges.
This photo of Pleterski during his December 2022 kidnapping was entered as an exhibit during the guilty plea of his kidnapper Deren Akyeam-Pong. (Ontario Superior Court)
Pleterski, now 27, thought he was meeting with a potential investor on Dec. 5, 2022, when a gun was pressed into his ribs in the backseat of a pickup truck in Toronto. The abduction was the beginning of a three-day-long kidnapping during which Pleterski was threatened and tortured.
The torture included waterboarding, cigarette burns and getting beaten with golf clubs as his captors drove him between several locations in southern Ontario, according to the agreed statement of facts from Akyeam-Pong's guilty plea.
Three other men have also been charged in Pleterski's kidnapping. Their trial is expected to start later this year.
'Cannot sleep at night': Pleterski
"The thought that I may soon end up sharing a jail cell with my kidnappers has completely debilitated my ability to think clearly through this," read Pleterski in court Thursday.
"I cannot sleep at night. I come to court alone and am being asked to represent myself, but all I think about is being locked in a prison for an extended period of time with the same people who kidnapped, beat and threatened me."
Pleterski also spoke about the "emotional consequences" of his kidnapping, which he said are "difficult to explain to those who have not lived through it."
"Fear, stress, uncertainty and the continuing effort to process what happened consumes my thoughts and affects my well-being on a continuous basis."
The Crown in Pleterski's fraud and money laundering trial is alleging he spent investor money on himself, including on flights on private jets. (aiden_pletersik/Instagram)
The Crown in Pleterski's trial is alleging he guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.
"Whatever opinions people may have of me, my financial affairs or the circumstances that preceded these events, no financial dispute justifies kidnapping, violence or intimidation," Pleterski said in his victim impact statement.
"Ultimately, I want to be able to move forward with my life without being defined by these events. I just hope that the time will come that I don't have to look over my shoulder or worry about the safety of my family."
Tracey Vogel, the Crown prosecutor in the kidnapping sentencing, is asking for a 23-year sentence for Akyeam-Pong related to the kidnapping conviction and a separate conviction for eight gun and drug-related offences.
Craig Zeeh, Akyeam-Pong's lawyer, is asking for a 12-year sentence. Sentencing submissions are expected to continue Thursday and Friday.
Pleterski's fraud trial is expected to continue Friday.

FTC subpoenas OpenAI and Anthropic following safety failures
The department is investigating possible consumer harms at the major AI companies.
The US Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for information about recent safety incidents with both businesses' AI models. Axios first reported that agency had sent civil subpoenas to the companies, and a spokesperson from the FTC confirmed the action to CBS News.
Axios' source said that the FTC is exploring possible consumer protection violations at Anthropic and OpenAI. The subpoenas are looking for documents regarding security incidents and safeguards, as well as some of the companies' marketing materials and content about their privacy policies. The individual also claimed the FTC plans to seek testimony from the top executives at both businesses. The department will allegedly send investigative demands to third-party AI companies at a later time.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson is also part of the White House's recently-assembled task force for artificial intelligence, although that group seems more aimed at furthering US industry leadership than at AI regulation.
There have been several calls among tech and AI executives and employees for government intervention, particularly around frontier model development, which has come under increased scrutiny following a string of safety failures. OpenAI has seen its AI agents escape testing safeguards multiple times in recent months, including instances where the models hacked government websites and the business Hugging Face. This month, Anthropic's models have been caught attempting to access various levels of government sites and one sent a false homicide tip to Philadelphia law enforcement.
Today's move from the FTC echoes several lawsuits that are also underway regarding AI safety concerns. Most recently, eight state Attorneys General filed a suit against OpenAI yesterday on claims that the company violated consumer protection laws.

The livestream execution of the Fort Hood attacker will not be livestreamed, President Donald Trump announced Thursday.
The controversial execution of Nidal Malik Hasan will still continue, the president said.
“Nidal Malik Hasan, a former U.S. Army Major turned traitor, is a very bad and evil man, who killed 13 people, including a pregnant soldier, who died, along with her unborn son, and injured, very seriously, 32 more innocent people. Barack Hussein Obama’s Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) intercepted electronic communications between Hasan and the radical Yemeni-American cleric, Anwar al-Awlaki,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

E Ink's new Kaleido 4 could inch us closer to the perfect color e-reader
The new display tech offers improved color reproduction and refresh rates.
E Ink has announced the latest version of its Kaleido color e-paper technology, introducing improvements that could be the selling point of future e-readers and writing tablets. The company's new Kaleido 4 display is supposed to be able to produce a wider range of colors, while improving things like refresh rate, a common problem with e-paper screens.
Kaleido 4 "doubles the color gamut volume" so it can produce over 40,000 colors, according to E Ink, while increasing "white reflectance" and contrast. The company also claims that the refresh rate improvements introduced with Kaleido 4 mean it can display video content at 18 fps. That sounds ridiculous when compared to the 120Hz OLED screen you might already have in your smartphone, but for the typically slow refresh rates of e-paper, it's meaningful.
Because E Ink's screens are used by some of the biggest names in e-readers, like Amazon, Kobo and Boox, the improvements offered by Kaleido 4 could mean your next e-reader will have more accurate color images, without compromising as much on the clarity of black and white text. The relative fuzziness of text on older Kaleido 3 displays is one of their drawbacks, and why some companies use Gallery 3, one of E Ink's other color e-paper technologies. Kaleido displays apply a color filter to the black and white pigments that move around to form text and images on a traditional e-paper panel. E Ink's Gallery displays use colored pigments, which produce richer images and text, but take longer to refresh.
E Ink says the addition of an oxide backplate to its display stack improves refresh rates on the Kaleido 4, a similar modification Amazon said it made to the Kaleido screens used in the original Kindle Colorsoft. We'll have to compare the new tech alongside older Kaleido displays to see how big of a difference E Ink's improvements have made, but for now, Kaleido 4 is only officially being used in one device: Hanvon Technology's M10 C II. The e-paper tablet is only available in China and ships with a Kaleido 4 screen, a redesigned front light and micro-etched glass that offers a more paper-like feel when you write on it.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.

Enterprise AI startup Shamrock AI has raised $5 Mn (about ₹47.4 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Endiya Partners, with participation from Capria Ventures. The Shillong-headquartered startup said it will use its first institutional funding round to accelerate product development, expand its team across India and the US, scale go-to-market efforts, and expand its presence in the Middle East. Founded in 2026 by Sarat Addanki, Anuraag Nallapati, and Michael Gallagher, Shamrock AI is building an agentic assurance platform that helps large enterprises deploy AI agents across critical business processes, ensuring they operate reliably in complex environments. Its platform uses an Enterprise Business Knowledge Graph to connect business processes, systems, data, and configurations, giving AI agents context about how an enterprise operates. The startup is initially focusing on using AI agents to automate testing across large enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformations, including SAP S/4HANA migrations. Shamrock AI said continuously testing and validating business processes helps its platform build an increasingly accurate representation of an enterprise’s operations. It plans to use this foundation to extend into data observability and autonomous business process automation. The startup said it already serves multiple Fortune 500 customers, including a Fortune 100 AI hardware manufacturer and a Fortune 100 healthcare company. Shamrock AI expects 70%-80% of its workforce to be based in India and plans to build a client-facing team in the US. Besides its Shillong headquarters, it has offices in Hyderabad and San Francisco. The fundraise comes amid a rise in funding for India’s AI startups. In Q3 2026, Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn across 35 deals, up 265% YoY. President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is defending her self-description as a lawyer, while acknowledging that she took the bar exam and considered the results "inconsequential."
Zacharia's legal qualifications have faced growing scrutiny since her debut White House media briefing earlier this week, when shortly afterward she was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied: "When I moved to China."
In an interview Thursday with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice, she did not deny reports that she'd failed to pass the bar.
Zacharia, who moved to China after earning her law degree in 2011, told Posobiec she had already preregistered for the bar exam before moving to Beijing, where her husband was working at an American private equity firm.
"I didn't want to withdraw from that," Zacharia said of the bar exam. "And we knew we would be moving out to China, and I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I had been long-distance from for at least a year."
Zacharia said she thought she'd take the bar and "see what happens."
"The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," said Zacharia.
The Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that Zacharia failed California's bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University in 2011.
A Business Insider review of records for all 50 states and the District of Columbia found no evidence that Zacharia had been admitted to practice law in the US.
In China, Zacharia said she took a job in the international practice division of the Zhong Lun law firm, where she said she worked on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements and cross-border transactions. She said she was one of four associates under a senior partner.
"After moving to China, I didn't really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on," Zacharia told Posobiec, adding, "There's no Chinese bar. I had enough credentials, which was my law degree, to be able to do this practice."
"I had all the necessary requirements to do that, and I was able to do it effectively and well," she said.
She also said that she never retook the bar exam after returning to the US and having the first of four children with her husband within six years.
Zacharia said she consulted with people within the legal field "for a very long time" and was told it would be acceptable to call herself a lawyer "and provide legal analysis, not legal advice."
"They said absolutely, absolutely across the board — you can call yourself a lawyer, you have a JD, and to buffer that, you have international legal experience in transactional law," Zacharia said.
"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy," she said. "The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law."
Zacharia's LinkedIn page says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a political advocacy group, between January 2024 and March 2025. In California, it is a misdemeanor to practice law or to advertise yourself as an attorney without a license.
At least two watchdog groups have filed a complaint about Zacharia with the State Bar of California this week.

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

Delhi: Customs officials seize 148 kg of suspected cannabis hidden in plastic spools
The consignment had been declared as PU tubes and packed in 19 cartons. It was placed on hold after officers suspected a misdeclaration.
Customs officers at the Air Cargo Complex in Delhi foiled a major smuggling attempt after intercepting a consignment from Bangkok containing 148.67 kg of suspected cannabis concealed inside plastic spools, a release said on Thursday.
The operation was conducted by officers of the Special Intelligence and Investigation Branch (SIIB) following locally developed intelligence, according to a press release issued by the Office of the Principal Commissioner of Customs.
The consignment had been declared as PU tubes and packed in 19 cartons. It was placed on hold after officers suspected a misdeclaration. During an examination conducted in the presence of the importer's representative, officers discovered plastic spools containing the consignment. When the spools were opened, hidden cavities revealed packets of compacted green substance wrapped in polythene. Such packets were found in 15 cartons.
Preliminary diagnostic tests indicated that the seized material was ganja or marijuana.
120 spools concealed weed
The customs department stated that a total of 120 spools concealed 148.67 kg of suspected hydroponic weed. The seized substance was valued at approximately ₹52 crore, while its estimated street value in India was put at ₹150 crore.
The suspected narcotics, along with the concealment and packaging materials, were seized under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.
The operation lasted more than 72 hours and culminated in the arrest of one person on Thursday, October 15. The individual was produced before a magistrate on the same day.
Follow-up searches at five premises across three states have provided further leads for the ongoing investigation, the press release stated. The operation was monitored by senior customs officers at the levels of the Chief Commissioner and Principal Commissioner, ACC Imports, and supervised by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, ACC Imports.
The department said that further investigation was in progress, adding that customs officers remained vigilant and committed to protecting society from the threat of narcotics.

- Activision CMO Tyler Bahl says GTA 6 and Modern Warfare 4 are the "two biggest games of the year".
- He doesn't consider The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake in the same category, adding, "No offense to Zelda."
- Modern Warfare 4 launches on October 23, 2026, two weeks before the Zelda remake and four weeks before GTA 6.
While developers are busy moving their games out of the way of GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, Activision is taking a different approach. The Call of Duty publisher thinks GTA 6 and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 are 2026’s biggest games, not the Zelda remake.
Speaking to The Game Business, Activision’s Chief Marketing Officer Tyler Bahl acknowledged the intense competition in releasing a game close to both GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake. However, he’s incredibly optimistic, saying, “Well, no offense to Zelda, but [GTA and COD] are the two biggest games of the year.”
More people coming in to the dashboards, more people taking the dust off their Xbox or PlayStation and playing again, is going to be more eyeballs for us overall.
It’s a pretty bold claim, since Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 releases on October 23, 2026, two weeks before the Zelda remake arrives on November 5, and four weeks before GTA 6 debuts on November 19. However, Bahl says, “If more people are talking about games, if there’s more press around it, that’s going to be good for everybody, not just us.”
Modern Warfare 4 has one big advantage over GTA 6 and the Zelda Remake despite both being among the year’s biggest games: a PC launch. With GTA 6 not expected on PC until 2027, and Nintendo never porting games to PC, Activision could win over players on both platforms eager for a new blockbuster.
But Modern Warfare 4’s nearly 120GB install size, even without Warzone, could put some players off. That’s not to say the new Call of Duty won’t succeed, but whether it can hold its ground against GTA 6 and the Zelda remake remains to be seen.
That said, do you think GTA 6 and Call of Duty are the two biggest games of the year, ahead of the Zelda remake? Or is Activision too overconfident? Tell us in the comments section below.

Ahead of the 2026 mideterm elections, people shared a purported "breaking" rumor alleging that Maricopa County Elections in Arizona issued an apology to President Donald Trump after officials made a striking discovery regarding the 2020 election results. The final tally showed Trump losing Arizona to former President Joe Biden by just under 11,000 votes.
According to the rumor, officials presented evidence that Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat who in 2020 was Arizona's secretary of state, and former Arizona House Speaker Rusty Bowers, a Republican, ordered the destruction of tens of thousands of Trump voters' ballots and also to count of tens of thousands of votes that immigrants lacking permanent legal status illegally cast to help elect Biden.
Snopes readers asked about this matter via email and searches.
This rumor was false. Searches for proof failed to find any credible sources reporting about Maricopa County Elections issuing an apology to Trump about large-scale voter fraud in the 2020 election. Instead, those queries indicated the original post came from a user who has shared similar misinformation before, including a false rumor about Georgia's 2020 election results.
People sharing this story copied and pasted the same text, which touched on Trump's false, oft-repeated claim that officials engaged in massive election fraud in 2020 — supposedly resulting in a "stolen election." The Associated Press extensively investigated Trump's claims involving battleground states and found no evidence of any large-scale fraud.
We emailed Maricopa County Elections to ask if the office could confirm that it did not issue an apology to Trump. We also emailed the White House to ask about this rumor and will update this article if we receive any further information.
Researching the rumor
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo for keywords related to the rumor failed to locate any news media outlets credibly reporting about Maricopa County Elections issuing an apology to Trump — including from conservative publications and outlets supporting the Trump administration.
Instead, the searches found numerous social media users reposting the claim, for example on Facebook (archived), Gettr (archived) and X (archived). That "breaking" rumor read as follows:
🚨#BREAKING: The Maricopa County Board of Elections has issued an apology to President Trump, claiming that local officials presented evidence that then Secretary of State (now Governor) Katie Hobbs and then Speaker of the Arizona House Rusty Bowers personally ordered them to destroy tens of thousands of mail-in ballots for President Trump and to count tens of thousands cast by illegal aliens for Joe Biden in Arizona's largest county during the 2020 election.
This is described as outcome-determinative fraud by those entrusted to conduct, oversee, and certify the vote; Hobbs and Bowers are alleged to have been paid by at least three hostile foreign governments, the George Soros Open Society Foundation, and the DNC in exchange for rigging the 2020 election in Arizona.
Simply put, there is now irrefutable and indisputable proof that President Trump won the state in that stolen election, spoken by the very people who counted the ballots.
LOCK THESE TREASONOUS CROOKS UP NOW! 💪🏻🔥🇺🇸
The posts improperly labeled the county's elections body, officially named Maricopa County Elections, as the "Maricopa County Board of Elections." The body's website displays a footer reading, "Elections in Maricopa County are overseen by both the County Board of Supervisors and the County Recorder."
Apparent origins of rumor
Searches of X for the above posts' copied-and-pasted text indicated a user named Joshua Hall (@JoshHall2024) first posted the rumor (archived) on March 19. Hall's post also began with the word "breaking." We found the claim was neither breaking nor true, whether in March or this month.
(@JoshHall2024 via X)
According to Hall's own posts, he appeared to be the same Joshua Hall that a judge sentenced to 20 months in prison for, as the Justice Department announced, "making threats to kill a member of the United States Congress" — fomer Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. — and "impersonating family members of the then-President of the United States on social media to fraudulently raise funds for a fictitious political organization."
Trump has at least once shared a screenshot on Truth Social (archived) of one of Hall's X posts from December (archived) promoting a false claim about Georgia twice tallying hundreds of thousands of votes. That post said the state owed Trump an apology.
In March, Hall posted a newer iteration of the Georgia rumor (archived) similar to the one about Arizona, falsely claiming the Fulton County Board of Elections said it owed Trump an apology.
We privately messaged Hall to ask for evidence to support the rumor and have not received a response. He has not made any new X posts since July; he reportedly faces charges including stalking and witness intimidation, and jail records in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, show a man with the same name in custody.
'Unsupported by factual evidence'
In early March — just days before Hall's X post about Maricopa County — the FBI reportedly subpoenaed 2020 elections records to continue investigating Trump's unfounded claims of fraud.
Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, issued a statement in response, repeating details of elections officials' exhaustive investigations and calling the claims "unsupported by factual evidence":
The 2020 General Election in Arizona has been exhaustively reviewed. Multiple audits, court proceedings, and independent investigations — including those pursued by members of the same political party of the President — found no evidence of fraud sufficient to alter the outcome. These findings are not in dispute by any credible authority. The election results were certified, litigated, and affirmed.
In fact, under the direction of my predecessor, Attorney General Mark Brnovich, agents and support staff of the Arizona Attorney General's Office spent over 10,000 hours investigating voting irregularities and alleged instances of illegal voting by high-profile election deniers. Complaints and allegations submitted to the Arizona Attorney General's Office by members of the public were also unsupported by factual evidence.
On Oct. 5, Trump criticized Maricopa County elections officials for sending out more than 3,000 ballots six days early. The Maricopa County Recorder's Office issued a statement saying that an election services company mistakenly mailed the ballots early, that the error "affected only the timing of the mailing" and that "the correct ballots were mailed to the correct voters."
For further reading, we previously reported about a rumor claiming officials found 712,152 new votes for Trump in Arizona for the 2020 election.

Petite, lightweight, and kind of kicky for a cargo bike. Can fit in a car’s back seat. Fat tires provide stability. Cushy bike seat is comfortable for long rides. So many accessories. Surprising 500-pound payload.
TIRED
Fast braking requires a firm hand. Range is middling. Battery indicator sneaks up on you. Not as petite as other JackRabbits. Technically a scooter, not an ebike.
I am not an obvious target customer for a cargo ebike, as I neither have kids to tote nor a large space for bike parking. But the new JackRabbit MG Cargo is so tiny, it doesn't conjure the dully utilitarian, heedlessly bulky nature that's common to other cargo ebike models. In fact, when I tested the wee, plucky ebike, I found its fat tires and tiny wheelbase make it feel more like a speedy urban dirt bike than anything else.
But despite being a relative lightweight (55 pounds) and petite enough to fit in the back seat of my old Montero, the MG sports a 750-watt motor that can haul nine times the bike's weight uphill. I even threw a grill onto a bike trailer to test this claim, which held up.
Note that likeall JackRabbits WIRED testers have reviewed, the MG is less an ebike than a scooter that looks and acts like an ebike: Instead of pedals, you get pedal-like footrests, plus a throttle. This means when the battery runs out, the bike stops moving. Also, the listed 48-mile range drops considerably when you ride at top speed or haul a large load. Nonetheless, the MG may have converted me to the pannier class.
After testing this MG for a couple of months, I no longer use my car when I need groceries, even when I'm taking a longer trek to the Grocery Outlet for discount steaks or salmon. The same is true when I want to haul a slushie machine across Portland’s steep mid-city ridge to a friend's house for cheeky weekday margaritas. By not acting like a cargo bike, the MG has convinced me to haul cargo on a bike.
Zippy Little Devil
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
“How exactly is this a cargo bike?” my editor asked when I showed her a photo of the MG Cargo after it arrived. She wasn't asking out of wonderment. As mentioned, the MG flat-out looks less like a bike you'd use to haul stuff and more like a dirt bike.
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.
Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a 200-pound man with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.
Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.
The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
While I can't quite stow the MG as easily as other JackRabbit models, it's still small enough that I can slide it into my back seat—as long as I uncork the front handlebars and turn its front wheel backward. (Some sources refer to the MG as “foldable,” but this isn't strictly true: it just has a quick-release wheel and an easily removed handlebar.)
Which is to say, even without the cargo component, I could like the MG just as a fun little commuter, especially with the welcome addition of a cushy Kinekt active-suspension seat post that provides some added give for longer rides.
The Little Cargo Ebike That Could
Despite its petite size, the MG performs well as a true cargo hauler that you could use to move trailers full of groceries or the more precious cargo of your own children. I didn't borrow any kids to test rear child trailers or JackRabbit's mini-me rear seat and handlebar set ($175). But I did use the MG's preinstalled Burley trailer hitch to haul a box containing a 150-pound grill up a hill with a 7 percent grade. While the MG didn't get to full speed on the ascent, it pulled the grill and my 200-plus-pound self surprisingly well.
The MG's stability and cornering capabilities also fared better than I expected, given its short base. Cargo bikes tend to lengthen their frame to add stability and make room for riders to pedal comfortably while carrying loads on the front or the back. The MG Cargo's stability mostly comes from its cushy fat tires, largely thanks to the clever design of the larger front tire, which both adds stability up front on rugged terrain and lowers the center of gravity where cargo hangs. The lack of pedaling also naturally removes some wobble.
You will make compromises, though: Cornering while hauling a large load can yield a jumpy ride, leading to the occasional overcorrection. The range also drops considerably with heavy carries, given that you can't add your own pedal power. Braking is fast but does require a good grip, especially with larger loads downhill.
For the Occasional Hauler
The MG Cargo lives in an interesting middle ground between commuter and cargo ebike. If I were primarily using it to transport children or work gear, I'd probably opt for a bulkier hauler or the Specialized Global Haul ST, WIRED's top-pick electric cargo bike that offers a more reliable long range.
The best use cases for the MG Cargo are as a fun recreational ebike that stows easily into your back seat or as a multipurpose commuter with built-in storage that saves its rider from needing to wear a backpack. In either case, the cargo capabilities function as bonus features as opposed to being the main draw.
It's less a workhorse than a hobby pony: I've slipped books and a blanket into a pannier so I can read at the park, and I've spontaneously brought home six-packs from the brewery a couple of miles down the road. When I grocery shop using the MG Cargo, I'm spared the bother of tightly packed parking lots that make me angry before I reach the aisles. I zip in, I unlock the panniers, pop in my groceries, and zip right back out. In this way, the MG Cargo also doubles as the cheapest therapist I know.
Matthew Korfhage was a staff writer on WIRED’s Reviews team, where he focused on coffee, home, and home office technology. Pope Leo XIV's surgeon confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday (October 13, 2026).
The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli Hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localised nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct 20.
But the decision to have the operation clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
