IT advisory firm Infotech has acquired Bengaluru-based SaaS startup Zluri to add the latter’s application discovery, identity governance and administration capabilities to its offerings stack. The terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Following the acquisition, Zluri will operate as a standalone division within Infotech, retaining its product development and core engineering teams in Bengaluru. It will also contribute to Infotech’s newly launched CIO Analytics platform, an API-driven advisory model that combines operational IT data with AI-assisted services and analyst expertise. For Zluri, the acquisition would open a pathway to expand its reach among enterprise customers by tapping into Infotech’s global community of more than 30,000 IT leaders. Founded in 2020 by Ritish Reddy, Chaithanya Yambari and Sethu Meenakshisundaram, Zluri offers businesses a software that helps them track and manage all the digital tools their employees use. These include work apps (Asana, Slack, etc), cloud software as well as AI tools. Its platform also helps companies control who can access what tools, identify unused subscriptions, reduce software costs and protect sensitive company data by removing unnecessary or unauthorised access. Zluri caters to over 250 enterprise clients globally, including Monday.com, Tipalti, Whoop, Catapult Sports, Razorpay, Smartnews, Amagi, Daxko, and Traveloka, and earns over 60% of its total revenue from Europe and North America. It will continue serving existing customers post acquisition. “We started Zluri to give IT and security teams visibility and control over every application and identity in their organisation. Joining Infotech lets us put that data at the heart of how IT leaders make decisions, and we’re excited to build together,” said Zluri’s cofounder and CEO Ritish Reddy. The startup has raised over $32 Mn in funding from marquee backers like Lightspeed, MassMutual Ventures, Endiya Partners, and Kalaari Capital – most recently bagging a $20 Mn Series B fundraise in 2023. Meanwhile, Infotech (erstwhile Info-Tech Research Group) is an Ontario-based IT research and advisory firm that helps organisations improve their tech operations by developing IT strategies with key focus areas like cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, data and AI. As of now, the firm is seeking to expand beyond its traditional research and advisory business. It claims to have grown by more than 340% over the past seven years and crossed $300 Mn in annual revenue. The deal is in line with an emerging trend of global companies acquiring Indian SaaS startups to expand their capabilities. Most recently, Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks recently acquired US-based Torii to expand its AI and software spend governance capabilities as well. Besides, software giant Adobe also acquired Peak XV Partners-backed Rilo back in September to build broader marketing workflows for its customers and integrate Rilo’s agentic capabilities into its enterprise suite.

Martinez apologises for outburst and fined by Man Utd
- Published
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has issued an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.
After United's Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday Martinez said that the club had left head coach Michael Carrick with an under-equipped squad.
Following talks with United on Thursday, the Argentina international released a statement saying "I want to apologise".
It is also understood he has been formally punished for his outburst with a fine.
"Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager," Martinez said in a social media post.
"It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday's game.
"Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity.
"The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise."
Carrick will hold a news conference on Friday, prior to the game against Leeds United on Sunday.
He takes his side to Elland Road on the back of just two wins from nine games this season, placed 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games.
Following the loss to Atletico, Martinez said he expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".
He later said he "spoke out of anger and frustration" in making those comments and that he had "belief in my team-mates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward".
Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane, speaking on The Overlap podcast,, external described the situation at his former club as "a bit of a circus".
"Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not help with that," added Martinez on Thursday.
"I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition: bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve.
"With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together."
It remains to be seen whether Carrick selects Martinez for the trip to Leeds.
Nevertheless, there is understood to be significant doubt over Martinez's long-term future at Old Trafford.
His current deal expires at the end of the season but the club have the option of extending the contract by 12 months.
While the issue over his recent comments is now considered closed, the club are still to decide whether they want to trigger the contract option.

The death of actor Nana Patekar, 75, has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, a condition in which a blood clot forms in an artery supplying the heart. What causes these clots, who is at risk, and how is the condition diagnosed and treated?
The story so far:
According to published accounts of the autopsy report, actor Nana Patekar died after a blood clot blocked the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a large part of the heart muscle. A blockage in this artery can severely restrict blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack. The reported finding has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, the formation of a blood clot within a coronary artery.
What is coronary thrombosis?
Coronary thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored.
This form of thrombosis is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years.
When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture, the material beneath the plaque’s surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery.
What are the warning signs?
A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur.
The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed.
Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention.
Who is at risk?
People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease.
In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel.
Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.
How is this condition diagnosed?
Doctors assess symptoms and medical history and use tests to determine whether a coronary artery is blocked and whether the heart muscle has been damaged. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle.
Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition.
How is it treated?
Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition.
Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open.
Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option.
Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines.

The Supreme Court’s Order
In a special hearing on Sunday morning, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro chief D Thara on a contempt petition alleging a prima facie violation of the court’s October 9 order against a complete shutdown of Metro and train services on Saturday. The bench said the petitioners had made out a prima facie case, and it asked for responses by October 13.
The court also asked for internet connectivity to be normalised and said there must be no illegal detentions, particularly of peaceful, unarmed gatherings beyond areas where Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders are in force. It directed free movement in the city subject to law and order and traffic requirements, ordered the installation of barricades to be reviewed at once, and ordered prohibitory orders around the Supreme Court and other courts withdrawn. It also said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be hindered in discharging their professional duties.
Lawyers led by senior advocate Kapil Sibal told the court that police had continued detentions even in areas where prohibitory orders were not in force. Senior sdvocate Shadan Farasat, who was detained outside the Supreme Court on Saturday, said he was manhandled and bundled into a police vehicle. Senior advocate and Trinamool Congress MP Menaka Guruswamy called the episode an “undeclared emergency.”
CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka condemned the detention of journalists and remarked, “We are in a state of emergency.”
Contempt Plea Filed
A contempt petition was filed in the Supreme Court on October 12 by Free Speech Collective over the alleged detention and forcible removal of journalists. The plea alleged wilful disobedience of the Court’s October 11, 2026 order directing that lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in discharging their professional duties. It sought contempt action, identification of the police officers and supervising officials responsible, and disclosure of how the order was communicated to personnel on the ground.
According to the plea, journalists continued to be detained and removed from reporting locations, including R K Ashram Marg and Connaught Place, despite identifying themselves as members of the press.

Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.
French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.
The hacks that didn’t have to happen
Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.
A raft of critical vulnerabilities fixed in the past few months in Copeland/Dixel controllers also give similar remote access.

My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

Whoop has never been known for marketing to an older population. Performance athletes headline ads for the wearable company, which aims to turn continuous streams of physiological data into useful insights for behavior change — mostly, for a young, fit customer base.
But this year, Whoop became one of the first consumer wearable companies to be accepted into Medicare’s ACCESS program, making it available at no cost to many traditional Medicare patients ages 65 and up. On Wednesday, at the STAT Summit in Boston, Whoop’s newly appointed chief medical officer Ami Bhatt spoke about how the company is moving to build experiences — and demonstrate outcomes — for a very different population.
“Number one on our roadmap — and I think I’m allowed to say this, if I’m not, I’m saying it — is simplification of the app,” said Bhatt, who previously chaired the Food and Drug Administration’s digital health advisory committee and served as the American College of Cardiology’s chief innovation officer. Surveys suggest, said Bhatt, that even members of the Silent Generation, who are older than 80 today, trust their clinicians with their data. “It’s not that they’re averse to giving data,” she said. “It’s how easy can we make it for that population to be able to share their data.”
Bhatt said that Whoop, which recently raised $575 million from investors including Mayo Clinic and the sovereign wealth fund of Qatar, is working with the National Council on Aging and AARP to think about how to personalize the product to older adults’ individual priorities. “For each of us, how we feel, how we perform, how we age, we have our own goals,” said Bhatt. “The thing is, we don’t want to decide for you what that is.”
The goals are less diffuse for the 10-year pilot ACCESS program, which published a directory of initial participants last month. Through those 55 companies, Medicare patients can access chronic condition management for little or no cost — Whoop serves patients with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, and prediabetes — and Medicare will pay the companies based on their health outcomes. Whoop will provide patients with a wearable, a 12-month subscription to its app, and access to clinicians who can help them make sense of their data and offer advice.
“The goal is, how do we bring technology closer to the patient, but not put the cost on the patient — rather, put the demand on the company,” said Bhatt. “Whoop takes responsibility for, in 12 months, I am going to make these people better. I’m going to show you outcomes in the Medicare population who have these risk factors to demonstrate that my technology can help them engage in their own health.” To receive full payment under the ACCESS model, Whoop will be required to show that it improved or controlled measures tied to its patients’ chronic conditions, including blood pressure, hemoglobin A1C, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
Bhatt said it was her role to help the company — which until recently focused on selling a product intentionally binned in the wellness category — develop and demonstrate those kinds of outcomes that bring them closer to clinical practice. The company just this year announced the ability for users to discuss their wearable data with clinicians, shortly before the FDA closed its warning letter that had initially said Whoop’s blood pressure-estimating feature qualified as a medical device — not a wellness feature.
While Whoop demonstrates good patient engagement, said Bhatt — users check the app eight times a day, on average — research into the original “wearable” for diabetes, continuous glucose monitors, suggests that engagement doesn’t necessarily translate to better health outcomes.
“In order to actually create personalized health at a population level, you need to start thinking about outcomes,” said Bhatt. “Can we show that we decrease blood pressure by five millimeters of mercury in individuals on Whoop — which, by the way, we have shown — so that we can say, hey, the outcome of cardiovascular disease and stroke, we know that outcome is better.”
At the same time, Bhatt said, the utility of continuous data is limited within the traditional health care system. As a practicing physician, “I had some really great patients who would print out binders of their wearable data,” she said. “This is me: I love this data. And I’d be like, ‘Oh, God.’” Despite her interest and the patient’s engagement, it was impossible to handle in a 20-minute visit.
Ultimately, Bhatt imagines Whoop could help solve that problem, perhaps by delivering contextualized reports to clinicians that summarize a patient’s continuous data along with key points from their own journaling entries and interactions with their Whoop app coach. “When you put that together and you actually have a comprehensive report you can give to a clinician, now your clinician says, ‘Oh, that’s what I needed.’”

Financial service giant Goldman Sachs has sold 53.4 Lakh shares of foodtech giant Eternal in a major block deal worth ₹168.7 Cr. According to NSE data, the investment bank, via its entity Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE, sold the shares at ₹316 apiece to rake in the amount. The investor offloaded the stake at a discount of more than 2.6% to the stock’s last closing price on Thursday. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Bank of America, via its affiliate BofA Securities Europe, for ₹168.7 Cr. This is the second block witnessed by Eternal in the past two months. In early September, French financial services giant BNP Paribas and US-based hedge fund Millennium Management together sold over 9.9 Cr shares of the listed foodtech giant for a sum of ₹3,264.8 Cr. This latest block deal comes as investors continue to be bullish on Eternal. Shares of the foodtech giant have surged nearly 10% in the past three months, and are up 16.2% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. The uptick in Eternal’s shares has come on the back of strong financial performance by the startup despite intensifying competition in the quick commerce space and the entry of new players like Rapido’s Ownly, Flipkart and Swish. What has been powering the stock’s rise is Eternal’s quick commerce arm Blinkit, which continues to dominate the instant delivery market. On the financial front, Eternal reported a consolidated net profit of ₹92 Cr in Q1 FY27, up nearly 3.7X from ₹25 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 182% YoY and 17% QoQ to ₹20,211 Cr during the quarter under review. Shares of Eternal closed Thursday’s trading session 2.77% higher at ₹324.35 on the BSE.

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

The international trailer of Ramayana: Part 1, directed by Nitesh Tiwari, was unveiled in Bengaluru on October 15, marking the beginning of Sony Pictures’ global campaign to take Namit Malhotra’s ambitious adaptation of the Indian epic to audiences across international markets. The launch was attended by Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi, Yash, Ravi Dubey, composer A. R. Rahman and director Nitesh Tiwari, among other members of the cast and crew.
Ramayana International trailer shares a glimpse of Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama having an epic face off with Yash as Ravana
Hosted by Prime Focus Studios and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations, the event offered audiences a fresh look at the film ahead of its worldwide theatrical release. The international trailer presents the story on an expansive fantasy scale, centring on the cosmic conflict between light and darkness and the battle against tyranny.
The nearly two-and-a-half-minute preview opens in a mythic era of celestial order, when men and gods are depicted as coexisting, with Kunal Kapoor appearing as Lord Indra. The narrative then shifts to the rise of Yash as Ravana, who declares, “Before me, every head will bow”, establishing the central conflict that drives the epic.

Sai Pallavi as Sita also features in glimpses that hint at the emotional dimension of the story, while the preview places considerable emphasis on large-scale battles, ancient architecture, atmospheric landscapes and visual effects by DNEG.
The film’s score, composed by Hans Zimmer and A. R. Rahman, further shapes the trailer’s expansive presentation of the epic. The preview offers a glimpse of the scale on which the makers have envisioned the story for the big screen, combining its mythological setting with large-scale fantasy elements.
Ramayana stars Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana, Sunny Deol as Hanuman and Ravi Dubey as Lakshman. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the two-part saga is produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios in collaboration with DNEG and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations.

These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs
KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica. It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.
It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.
Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."
Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."
Seeking "egocentric data"
India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.
"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P., a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."
Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.
What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole, economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."
The power question
But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."
That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.
The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."
He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.
Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.
There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.
Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.
"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."
The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000.
Working in a fake kitchen
Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.
Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.
For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.
And to amass recordings of humans doing work with their hands for clients who request ecocentric data, Ramaswamy says, they pay hundreds of people across India to undertake domestic jobs, like Sneha Jegadish, a 24-year-old who lives on the edge of town.
Jegadish clipped her smart phone to a headset and began chopping a carrot, her phone recording her every hand movement.
She records herself doing housework for a few hours a day, for about $2.60 an hour, and makes around $120 a month. Jegadish folds clothes, wipes the floor, does the dishes — jobs she was never expected to do growing up, because her mother wanted her to focus on her studies. So when she got this gig a few months ago, "my mother had to show me how to do those jobs," she smiles.
Money or not, it's still drudgery, says Jegadish. One day, she hopes, she'll have a robot to do her housework. "The work we are doing now is going to be done by robots in the future," she says.
That's the same conclusion that 42-year-old textile worker Kannagi Periyasaamy has come to.
At the textile factory, Periyasaamy was folding and packing aprons with a GoPro fastened to her head.
She's one of the few workers who is paid about $2.60 an hour to record herself, and she's been told why. She explains: "We are training them [the robots] on how to package the aprons, how to do a quality check, how to fold the aprons."
Periyasaamy says she's been doing this for the past three months, enough for her to be convinced that someday, a robot will take over her job. When that day comes, she says, "I'm thinking about taking up farming" — the family owns a scrap of land where she could raise cattle. Meanwhile, Periyasaamy thinks of AI robots as her students and says, "I'm proud I can teach it to do a good job."

The first day of the STAT Summit did not disappoint. We had biotech’s biggest stars, the perils and promise of AI, and moving anecdotes from patients. Here are a few snippets of the day’s action.
- FDA heads sound off: In this extremely juicy panel, former Food and Drug Administration commissioners offered sharp criticisms of the current health regime and candid reflections about their own time at the helm. No agency was spared. As Rob Califf opined, “DOGE will go down as one of the biggest disasters in American history.” Read more from STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.
- Whoop! (There it is): Whoop built its reputation as a wearable company mainly used by young, fit consumers. That may soon change. Whoop’s newly appointed Chief Medical Officer Ami Bhatt spoke about the company’s recent acceptance into Medicare’s ACCESS program, which would make their wearables available at no cost to many traditional Medicare patients ages 65 and up. What else did Bhatt say about AI and wearables? Read more from STAT’s Katie Palmer.
Ovaries don’t go gentle into that postmenopausal night
Ovaries stop having a clear function relatively early on in life. For decades, women carry around an obsolescing organ — but is nothing truly all ovaries do after menopause? New research from Northwestern University suggests the answer is no. In a study of healthy ovaries from 28 women aged 50 to close to 80, published on Wednesday in Aging Cell, researchers found that there were hundreds of proteins in the ovaries evolving in the decades after menopause.
“It wasn’t that there was just a cluster of proteins that are being turned on and they’re staying constant; we actually saw quite dynamic changes that were happening across this period of time,” said Francesca Duncan, a professor in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the study’s corresponding author. As they age, the ovaries’ tissue changes, showing increased inflammation as well as higher concentration of proteins associated with ovarian cancer. This doesn’t mean all aging ovaries will develop ovarian cancer, though it does raise the potential question “of whether or not at a certain point it actually could be beneficial to take your ovaries out,” said Duncan.
40%
Forty percent of high school students in the United States reported binge eating in the last month, according to a new government survey.
It’s the first time the biennial survey, conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has asked about binge eating, and the first data on disordered eating collected by the Youth Risk Behavior Survey in a decade. The high rates were striking, especially among young people of color.
Digging into the crosstabs, the survey found that binge eating was more prevalent among female than male students (19% versus 16%). It was also more common among Black (19%), Hispanic (20%), and multiracial (20%) students compared to white (15%) and Middle Eastern or North African students (10%).
Read more from STAT’s Sarah Todd about this striking survey.
The maddening journey to not to share patient data with Epic
Alex Rosenblat had a goal: stop her Ohio hospital from sharing her health data with Epic’s gigantic health network.
But when she logged into her MyChart account, there was no button to easily opt out. The simple-seeming request turned into an arduous task that would require scores of emails, multiple phone calls with Epic employees, a flight to Las Vegas, and a software update.
That was just one of three months-long journeys Rosenblat embarked on last year to keep her hospital from sharing her personal health data with outside vendors. Read on to find out why the researcher and reporter had to call a notary.
Kenya reports second Ebola case
Another person has fallen ill with Ebola in Kenya. The 39-year-old man is a relative of the country’s first case and had already been in quarantine when symptoms appeared, according to Kenya’s Ministry of Health.
A World Health Organization official said Wednesday that despite the two cases, there was no evidence of an Ebola outbreak in Kenya. The initial patient — a Kenyan citizen — caught the deadly virus while living in Congo and died earlier this month. The Kenyan Ministry of Health identified 128 people who had been in contact with this patient; 108 are in quarantine, 5 have left Kenya, and 15 have not been tracked down. Tracing the second patient’s contacts has now begun.
The situation in Congo is still quite dire. Authorities have confirmed more than 4,000 deaths and 9,000 cases as officials have struggled to contain one the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.

Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
- Published
An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison.
Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea.
But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it.
The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November.
Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept.
After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.
Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death.
"We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network.

Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
- Published
Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.
The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.
Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.
Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.
The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.
Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers want to see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."
The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.
Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.
"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.
Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.
But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.
The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.
The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.
Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.
The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.
"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.
"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

Tip-off foiled US teen's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
- Published
A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say.
Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon.
Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said.
Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people.
Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis.
"These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief.
According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis.
Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime.
The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother.
According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast".
Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago.
He is thought to have acted alone.
The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour.
Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack.
In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS.
Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative.
The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures.
India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US".
US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident.
In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday.
The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US.

For almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.
On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.
In doing so, the LNP risks placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire.
The proposals would give the increasingly influential deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, the power to break strikes by public sector workers in certain circumstances, including if it is deemed “in the public interest”.
The government will also make it more difficult for public servants, including emergency services workers, to claim compensation for psychological injuries. Under the proposed laws, workers with such claims will only be entitled to support if they can show their workplace was the primary cause.
Law firm Slater and Gordon said the changes would make it harder for Queenslanders to access support for psychological injuries. The United Workers Union, which represents paramedics and some healthcare workers, said the changes were “an underhanded attack on Queensland ambulance officers and other hospital staff”.
Several business groups welcomed the changes.
The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday morning the proposals were a “Newman-era attack on workers”, and the only thing surprising about that statement was that it took so long (roughly 14 hours) for the spectre of Campbell Newman’s government to, once again, loom over Queensland politics.
The collapse of the Newman government explains almost everything about the current one. The premier, David Crisafulli, and Bleijie had front-row seats for the “crash through” tactics that quickly turned voters off Newman, including proposals to sack public sector workers, and led to mass protests.
The lessons since have been that most suburban voters are uncomfortable with the LNP putting ideology on show. And so it went to the 2024 election – and won comfortably – talking mainly about crime and keeping all those vote-losing positions on things like abortion and budget cuts off the table.
Approaching the midway point of the term, the LNP has finally decided to show its teeth.
There are readers who will, understandably, take issue with the idea that the Crisafulli government has been “tentative” or has been, up to this point, unthreatening.
It has been unapologetic in attacking Indigenous representation within government, trans healthcare, and suppressing pro-Palestine protests.
These moves have been underpinned by a simple calculation: that the issues are marginal for most suburban and regional voters, whose concerns are mostly the cost of living and crime.
Those who care about evidence-based policy, human rights and civil liberties have every right to be furious. The polls suggest that fury hasn’t gone mainstream, and that suburban voters are OK with the government punching down, so long as it doesn’t affect them.
Workplace reforms affect them. If nothing else, those survivors of the Newman government who still sit in the cabinet room will have learned a lesson that in Queensland, the public sector (which employs more than 320,000 people) is a powerful political bloc in its own right.
The morning after announcing the changes, Bleijie seemed only too aware of the scale of the coming fight.
“You’re going to see a mammoth campaign by the Labor party,” he told reporters at a press conference at Newstead.
“It’s going to be a lot of mistruths and misinformation, and I think everything they will be able to say … we will be able to debunk with facts.”
The Crisafulli government remains comfortably ahead in the relatively few public polls, a recent snapshot in Brisbane Times seemed to show Labor in Queensland had taken the biggest hit from the rise in support for One Nation.
But the bright orange cloud is still looming. And a simple look around the country reveals that in modern times, whether policy is decided by ideology or focus group, there’s no guarantee political capital will last.
Better use that capital while you can. Even if it means, as it will for the Queensland LNP, picking a fight with many of the suburban middle-class voters who put the party into office.
- Ben Smee is Queensland state correspondent

The Delhi government has made Aadhaar authentication or proof of Aadhaar possession compulsory for consumers seeking benefits under its electricity subsidy scheme, according to a notification issued by the power department, Hindustan Times reported.
The notification, dated September 30 and published in the Delhi Gazette, requires eligible consumers to submit proof of their Aadhaar number through an online portal or any other method specified by the government.
The rule will cover beneficiaries served by power distribution companies, including BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd (BRPL), BSES Yamuna Power Ltd (BYPL) and Tata Power Delhi Distribution Ltd (TPDDL). Consumers in areas served by the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) and Military Engineer Services (MES) will also be covered.
According to official figures cited by PTI in a report, by February 2026, the Delhi government's allocation for power subsidy reached ₹4,037.63 crore. The government's budget for the current financial year stands at ₹3,500 crore.
Power consumers in Delhi stands at 73 lakh, rising by nearly 40% in the last decade.
Around 84 per cent (52.3 lakh) of 73 lakh domestic consumers in 2024-25 availed power subsidy in Delhi. It rose to 87 per cent (55 lakh) in 2025-26.
Under the Delhi government's scheme, consumers get up to 200 units of electricity free every month. Those using between 201 and 400 units receive a 50% subsidy, capped at ₹800 per month.
According to the Power Department's notification, the electricity subsidy scheme is implemented through power distribution companies BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd (BRPL), BSES Yamuna Power Ltd (BYPL) and Tata Power Delhi Distribution Ltd (TPDDL), along with the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) and Military Engineer Services (MES) in their respective areas.
Issued under Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016, the notification says the requirement is intended to establish beneficiaries' identities and ensure that subsidies reach the intended recipients. The scheme's expenditure is funded through the Consolidated Fund of Delhi.
Consumers who do not yet have an Aadhaar number will not be excluded from applying for the subsidy. They can submit an Aadhaar enrolment application and provide their details along with the 14-digit enrolment ID to claim the benefit.
The power department and agencies implementing the scheme have been instructed to publicise the new requirement through the media to inform consumers about the change.
Officials cited by Hindustan Times said a dedicated online portal will be introduced to simplify the process. Beneficiaries will also have to renew their choice annually to continue receiving the electricity subsidy.

- The claim that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease is unproven.
- On Oct. 12, after the Russian technology giant Yandex reported that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had seen "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after the strikes.
- However, Snopes found no credible evidence that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline. Social media posts that attributed changes in online activity on certain topics such as MAGA, the far-right German political party Alternative für Deutschland or various health-related topics failed to directly connect those changes to Russian bots.
- Zelenskyy's office reportedly told the BBC on Oct. 13 that he was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity when he made the remarks about the effect of Ukrainian strikes.
- Darren Linvill, an expert on the effects of foreign information manipulation and interference, told Snopes that Ukraine's strikes had likely mainly affected legitimate, automated Yandex traffic rather than propaganda operations, which Russia often runs from overseas.
In early October, a claim (archived) circulated that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease.
Yandex, a Russian technology giant that provides search engine, email and cloud services and facilitates payments, ride hailing and food deliveries, confirmed on Telegram and to local media that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga (archived) and Vladimir from Oct. 7 to 11. Work to restore services affected by the strikes continued on Oct. 13.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had struck "Yandex data centers" and that "a lot of people" had seen fewer Russian bots on social media platforms as a result.
The Facebook page Occupy Democrats, which spread the claim about the consequences of Ukrainian strikes against Russian bots, wrote:
Zelenskyy might just have saved our democracy. The genius is brilliantly bombing Russian data centers linked to FAKE NEWS pro-MAGA bot farms in Moscow. Without them, Putin's midterm influence will accidentally fall from a 30th floor window.
MAGA, an acronym for Make America Great Again, is a political movement supportive of U.S. President Donald Trump. The U.S. has previously accused Russia of using "bot farms" to create false social media accounts that spread disinformation in the U.S.
On Oct. 11, Tomáš Zdechovský, a member of the European Parliament, shared data (archived) he claimed showed a drastic decrease in online activity around Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland political party in the days following the strikes. Other social media users claimed searches for various health-related topics (archived) and the number of social media accounts advocating for Alberta to seek independence from Canada (archived) also fell after Ukraine's strikes.
Whether Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers had indeed taken Russian bots that spread propaganda or misinformation offline was unproven at the time of this writing. As we will lay out below, social media users claiming a direct connection between Ukraine's strikes and falling web traffic generated by Russian propaganda bots tended to identify correlation rather than causation.
Darren Linvill, who studies the tactics, strategies, and impacts of foreign information manipulations and interference at Clemson University, told Snopes via email on Oct. 13 that the Russian propaganda campaigns he studies do not use physical infrastructure within Russia for their efforts, meaning they would be unaffected by Ukraine's strikes. Linvill, along with U.S. and international media, also said that a lot of the traffic that was affected by the strikes was likely legitimate, automated traffic, such as web crawlers that index Yandex's search engine.
Data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare shared by some accounts (archived, archived) as proof of Russian "bot traffic" decreasing after Ukraine's strikes showed graphs accounting for all automated traffic, not propaganda bot accounts specifically. Linvill described measuring a drop only in Russian propaganda bot accounts as "exceedingly difficult."
Lacking credible proof that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline, we leave this claim unrated.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy's office appeared to redefine his statement from the previous day that there was "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after Ukraine's strikes. The office reportedly told the BBC that Zelenskyy was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity.
Snopes has contacted Zelenskyy's office to verify this statement to the BBC.
Parsing the 'evidence' of falling Russian bot activity
Some social media users shared data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare that they suggested showed that Russian bot traffic "dropped to nearly zero" after Ukraine's strikes.
The data in question, called "Bot vs. Human Traffic," tracked HTTP requests, which are messages that a client (this could be a browser or a mobile app) sends to a server. Cloudflare assesses HTTP requests a given client sends and scores them according to whether it thinks a human or a bot sent the request.
Cloudflare's data showed that HTTP requests from Yandex bots dropped on Oct. 8 and again on Oct. 10, dipping to 0.3% of maximum levels. Bot requests had been at 88.2% of maximum levels the week before. Cloudflare's data also showed that almost all (99.6%) of the HTTP requests sent by Yandex clients were automated, which Cloudflare described as being from bots.
It is important to note that "bot" in Cloudflare's terminology is not just propaganda bots but any requests that the company classifies as automated. The technology publication Mashable and Euronews reported that Yandex's automated traffic likely included web crawlers, which are tools that search engines use to keep their database of websites up to date. Mashable reported that damage to a Yandex's data centers or servers would bring traffic such as web crawlers to a halt.
Linvill also credited the fall in "bot" traffic from Yandex to legitimate, automated traffic such as web crawlers not operating from damaged servers. He wrote that Cloudflare's data did not suggest there was "a particular reason to believe the strikes would have a significant impact on social bot activity from Russia."
Other claims about a decrease in Russian bot traffic failed to directly connect Russian bots to any perceived changes in online activity. For example, Zdechovský's post presented a graph with no source that did not specify what it measured. Another post that claimed a decrease in Google searches for various health-related topics compared data across only two weekends, which was unlikely to be enough to establish and analyze a trend.
An account that claimed accounts calling for Alberta to seek independence from Canada "fell off the face of the earth" after Ukraine's strikes provided no supporting evidence for the claim that linked it to Russian propaganda bots.
We contacted Zdechovský to ask for the source of his graph and await a reply.
Russian propaganda campaigns hard to track
According to Linvill, actually documenting a fall in Russian propaganda bot activity would not be straightforward. He wrote:
It would be exceedingly difficult to measure. You would first have to figure out what it was, exactly, you were measuring? There is no one path to influence and no one way malign propaganda is conducted. These efforts are run on global systems across a multitude of platforms and emanating from multiple actors even within the same country. They make it hard on purpose.
Linvill added that the Russian campaigns he followed did not use bots they ran themselves, instead paying for services run from outside Russia. He wrote: "It has clearly become important for Russia to outsource these services than to run them in house. It's likely cheaper and easier, but also more secure and decentralized."
In sum, readers should be cautious of blanket claims that Ukraine's strikes on Yandex's servers heavily affected Russia's propaganda operation. While that may be the case, there was no credible evidence at the time of this writing directly linking strikes on servers to a fall in Russian propaganda activity online. Linvall suggested that Russian propaganda campaigns could come from overseas, meaning domestic strikes would not be effective against them, a point that Mashable's reporting also made.

10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర సవరణ (SIR)లో జరిగిన అవకతవకల కారణంగా, ఇష్టానుసారంగా ఓటర్లను తొలగించారని ఆరోపిస్తూ, ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసనను నిర్వహించింది. ఈ ప్రదర్శనలకు ప్రతిస్పందనగా, అధికారులు రాజధాని అంతటా భద్రతా చర్యలు చేపట్టారు. డజన్ల కొద్దీ మెట్రో స్టేషన్లను మూసివేశారు, రైళ్లను రద్దు చేసి నిషేధాజ్ఞలను అమలు చేశారు. పోలీసులు అరవింద్ కేజ్రీవాల్, పినరయి విజయన్, మమతా బెనర్జీ వంటి రాజకీయ ప్రముఖులతో పాటు, CJP వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేతో సహా వేలాది మందిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు, అయితే వారిని తరువాత విడుదల చేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పోలీసు నిర్బంధాల మధ్య ఢిల్లీకి పెద్ద ఎత్తున నిరసనకారులు చేరుకున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో బాగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) చేపట్టిన నిరసనను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో అస్సాంలోని తిన్సుకియా నగరంలో జరిగిన మహాలయ సంబరాలకు సంబంధించినది. దీనితో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, అవే దృశ్యాలతో ఉన్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) లభించాయి. వాటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో అస్సాంలోని టిన్సుకియా నగరంలో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న జరిగిన మహాలయ ఉత్సవాలకు సంబంధించినదని తెలిసింది. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే దృశ్యాలను, ఈ ఉత్సవానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియోలతో పోల్చి చూడగా, ఇది టిన్సుకియాలో జరిగిన మహాలయ ఉత్సవానిదేనని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
అలాగే, గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, ఈ వీడియోను అస్సాంలోని టిన్సుకియా నగరంలో ఉన్న ఠాణా చరియాలి ప్రాంతంలో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు నిర్ధారించవచ్చు. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోకు ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలతో ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదని చెప్పవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, అక్టోబర్ 10న జరిగిన CJP నిరసన దృశ్యాలంటూ అస్సాంకి చెందిన వీడియోను తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Flipkart Group reported an 18.2% jump in consolidated revenue from operations to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up from ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally by 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹8,646 Cr in FY25. The numbers reflect the performance of the Flipkart Group as a whole, rather than the standalone financials of the Flipkart ecommerce marketplace. The financial results come after the Walmart-backed ecommerce giant completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026. The restructuring brought the group’s holding structure back to India, ahead of a potential domestic public listing. The consolidated entity includes businesses such as Myntra and Cleartrip, alongside logistics, platform services and other specialised operations. “As part of its re-domiciliation to India, (the) Flipkart Group is publishing consolidated financial results under Flipkart Internet Private Limited. The results reflect the group’s performance over the reporting period for the year ended March 2026 and provide a historical view of the business rather than a current trading update,” said the ecommerce giant in a blog post. On the operational front, the company said that its gross margins rose 23% YoY in FY26, while adjusted EBITDA improved by around ₹1,500 Cr during the fiscal. “Adjusted operating margin improved by 230 basis points, from -7.7% to -5.4%, supported by higher gross margins and lower overheads,” added the ecommerce major. Flipkart also noted its adjusted operating business losses, before finance costs, tax, other income and exceptional items, narrowed by 17%, or around ₹1,600 Cr, during the fiscal under review. However, this improvement in operating losses translated into only a marginal reduction in net losses. Flipkart attributed the higher net losses to higher finance costs, the derecognition of deferred tax assets recognised in earlier periods and certain exceptional items. How Did Flipkart’s B2C Arm Perform? Meanwhile, the ecommerce major’s B2C arm, Flipkart Internet Private Limited, reported a 19.3% YoY decline in revenue from operations to ₹16,295 Cr in FY26 compared with ₹20,202 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Including other income of ₹744 Cr (down from ₹947 Cr in FY25), the B2C vertical’s total income stood at ₹17,039 Cr in FY26, 19.4% lower than ₹21,149 Cr in the previous fiscal. On the expenses front, Flipkart Internet Pvt Ltd’s total expenses fell 3.6% to ₹22,522 Cr from ₹23,361 Cr in FY25. Overall, the B2C business’ net loss rose to ₹5,498 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,694 Cr a year earlier. Notably, the FY25 figures were restated to account for the business combination. Where Did Flipkart Group Spend In FY26? Despite the growing top line and narrowing losses, Flipkart Group’s total expenses rose 16% to ₹1.54 Lakh Cr in FY26 as against ₹1.33 Lakh Cr in the year-ago period. Purchase Of Traded Goods: This was the biggest cost-centre for the company. Expenses under this head climbed 17.4% YoY to ₹1.17 Lakh Cr in the fiscal under review. Employee Benefit Expenses: The group’s employee benefit costs remained relatively flat at ₹8,376 Cr compared with ₹8,268 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Expenditure under this bucket nearly doubled to ₹1,209 Cr from ₹649 Cr in FY25. Logistics & Storage Service Charges: Expenses under this header stood at ₹15,154 Cr in FY26, up 28.9% from ₹11,759 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. The expense accounted for nearly 54% of the group’s total other expenses of ₹28,277 Cr in FY26, highlighting the cost of running its logistics, warehousing and delivery operations.

Trump’s staff rushed to add new renovations to the White House - so they’d be in place for his 80th birthday
In early June, the White House contracting documents detailed “urgent” work to install the chandeliers

Donald Trump’s unknown birthday president has been revealed - with the White House getting some new chandeliers through another no-bid contract.
Four new light fixtures were installed in the West Wing just ahead of the president’s June birthday. The Washington Sun was the first outlet to report the renovations.
In early June, the White House contracting documents detailed “urgent” work to install the chandeliers. The paperwork set a specific deadline for the work.
“This must happen over the weekend as these must be in place before the June anniversary events,” the document read, according to the Sun.
That weekend was the same as Trump’s 80th birthday and featured a UFC fight on the White House lawn. The weekend included several activities tied to the celebration of America’s 250th - but also Trump hitting the milestone.
The work was done through a no-bid contract with Agile1Tech, a Virginia-based company, according to the Sun. It was the same company that created the viewing/gaming room for the UFC fight.
The White House argued in the documents that the contract couldn’t be competitively bid because of the timing and the uniqueness of the ceilings.
“Agile1Tech is familiar with how to brace these chandeliers in a structure that may not support such weight,” the documents noted. “Based on the results of market research, the government determined that a limited number of vendors were available, but none possessed the capability to properly install a complex chandelier in a historic environment.”
That led to the installation of the four chandeliers in the West Wing.
The White House did not respond to the Sun’s request for comment. The Independent has also reached out to Trump officials about the chandeliers.
The chandeliers are the latest in Trump’s effort to remake the White House in his gold-filtered preference. The Oval Office has been decked out in gold decorations and picture frames that fill nearly every wall.
The president also added the letters in gold, “The Oval Office,” to the exterior of the famed room.
Trump’s renovations to the White House don’t stop there. He has torn down the East Wing to make room for his $330 million ballroom. Private donors covered most of the cost, and the work continues on the facility that dwarfs the rest of the White House.
Other renovations for the president have included paving over the Rose Garden to make it a patio in the style of his Florida Mar-a-Lago home, adding a helipad to the grounds, and installing a wall of presidents at the White House - that mocks his Democratic rivals.
