These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices
📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App
Some key voters say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.
NPR observed two online focus groups Tuesday night with 12 Georgians who voted for President Biden in 2020 and then supported Trump in 2024.
Almost every voter — 11 out of 12 — said they were disappointed with the overall job Trump has been doing. And 10 said they regret voting for him.
"I've been disappointed," said Charles P., 43, who identified as a Democrat. (The voters participated under the condition their last names would not be used.)
"I just don't feel like there's any positive to this administration at all," he continued. "Inflation has only gotten worse, there've been more wars. The tariffs haven't done anything. It seems like we have more enemies now than ever. I just don't see anything positive with his tenure."
Richard A., a 56-year-old Republican, said he's been out of work for 10 months and there is a long list of problems he sees with the direction of the country under Trump.
"Food crisis, starting the war with Iran, inflation," he said. "ICE immigration has just torn families apart, has caused deaths. ... It just seems like everything has gone downhill."
The comments align with Trump's faltering approval rating and a darkening midterm outlook for Republicans. Trump has picked up his campaign travel in recent days, touting his record and arguing for the GOP to retain control in Washington.
These focus groups with swing voters are conducted every month in battleground states across the country. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project.
Focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, but they do provide insight into what voters are thinking. And in this case, they provide some insight into how voters are deciding who they are supporting this fall.
Swinging to Democrats
Rich Thau, president of Engagious, moderates these focus groups. He said for the first time this year, a majority of swing voters said Trump was going to influence their midterm decisions.
"In previous months, when we asked people whether President Trump would influence how they vote, they would say things like, 'Well, I'm looking mainly at the candidates themselves,' or 'I'm looking at the overall sort of environment in the country,'" Thau said.
"This month, seven out of 12 said that he would influence them to vote for Democrats. And that was new."
Karla S., a 49-year-old Democrat, was one of those seven.
"I did vote Republican for 2024," she said. "I made up my mind. I've been so disappointed that I'm just going to go straight and just do Democrat, Democrat, Democrat. Because I'm so disappointed with how this administration has been doing."
Cedric, a 41-year-old independent, said he won't be voting for any politicians that are closely aligned with Trump.
"I think we're not going in the right direction, so I don't want to vote for a candidate that's not going to stand up to him or they're going to go along with his policies," he said. "I'm looking for something different."
Ten out of the 12 participants said they plan on voting for Georgia incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Some voters said they wanted to keep him in office specifically because he wouldn't be aligned with Trump.
Restoring order
Thau said some voters felt that if Democrats take control of Congress, it could provide some needed stability to the country — and the economy, in particular.
"There was some sense that Democrats could restore some semblance of order, and that they'd be able to control a bit of what the president is trying to do or has been doing, to the point where that might restore some of their confidence in the economy," he said.
That's what Thomas M., a 65-year-old independent voter, said is his expectation of a Democratic-run Congress.
"I think there would be more controls placed on Trump with people who are not afraid to stand up to him," he said.
In contrast, if Republicans retain power, Thau said "some respondents told us they thought that the president would have even more control over what goes on because Republicans are afraid to stand up to him."
Jennifer W., a 43-year-old Republican, said she worries "Trump would have free rein."

A Republican super PAC, not the Republican National Committee, paid for the ad. A spokesperson for the super PAC, Defending Main Street Superpac, said media vendor Cross Screen Media had made the mistake. We await confirmation from the vendor and its parent company.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that Republicans had inadvertently paid for a campaign ad targeting Troy Jackson, Maine's Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate and incumbent Susan Collins' opponent, to air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.
Posts multiplied on social media making the claim, including on Facebook and X. One X post by the betting platform Polymarket said "Anti-Troy Jackson ads intended for Maine voters are reportedly appearing in Oregon, sparking speculation that advertisers confused Portland, Maine, with Portland, Oregon" (archived):
The post included maps of the states of Oregon, on the West Coast, and Maine, on the East Coast.
The claim is true, although some social media users were imprecise about who paid for the ads, saying it was "the GOP" or "Republicans" as a whole. A review of Google's Ads Transparency Center revealed the anti-Jackson ad, paid for by Republican super PAC Defending Main Street Superpac Inc, aired not only in Portland, Oregon, but also Washington state, between Oct. 8 and Oct. 12.
A spokesperson for Defending Main Street Superpac acknowledged the mistake in an email to Snopes, saying it had originated with the super PAC's media vendor, Cross Screen Media, whose parent company is 1903 Group.
"During a recent independent expenditure, our media vendor mistakenly placed approximately $25,000 in digital advertising in the Portland, Oregon, media market instead of Portland, Maine," the email read. The spokesperson added Cross Screen Media was refunding the ad buy.
We reached out both to Cross Screen Media and to 1903 Group to confirm and we will update this report should we receive a response.
Ad buys and social media chatter
The ad in question attacked Jackson for seeking to raise taxes in Maine:
The super PAC is an independent political advocacy group that supports Collins, who is seeking her sixth term in the Senate (she was first elected in 1996). Collins' campaign had no say in the ad's content, nor where it aired. Polls revealed that Collins and Jackson were in a tight race.
Data from Google's Ads Transparency Center showed that the ad ran in Oregon for four days and was seen between 1 million and 1.25 million times there. The buyer spent between $15,000 ad $20,000. The ad also ran in the state of Washington during that time, and cost between $5,000 and $6,000, for 350,000 and 400,000 views.
"The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend. No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor's error," the super PAC's spokesperson told Snopes in the email.
Meanwhile, internet chatter indicated that people in Oregon had seen the anti-Jackson ad. On Oct. 11, an account on X named Lillian Belle, whose bio reads "Obsessed with Oregon Politics. Ask me about Oregon and the Judiciary," said (archived) "I've gotten 5 anti-Troy Jackson ads in the last 24 hours. I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands."
Someone responded to this post, saying (archived) "Ive gotten so many this week," to which Belle responded "Interesting that it's not just me."
Asked if the ads were "digital or cable," Belle said (archived) "Digital which isn't that precise but still a lol [laugh out loud]"
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about the 2026 U.S. elections, including a false claim that voting ballots are disqualified with poll workers mark them.

Bus hits train near Channel Tunnel in France, injuring 19
The bus was carrying truck drivers heading to travel on a LeShuttle train, which carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel
A minibus collided with a stationary train in a Channel Tunnel vehicle boarding area in France on Thursday evening, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, authorities said.
Five people were severely injured, though no one’s life appeared to be in danger, the local prefect said in a statement.
The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities who were heading to travel on a LeShuttle train, which carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.
The area around the tunnel entrance was sealed off on Thursday evening, journalists at the scene reported, with a helicopter and several emergency vehicles present.

Three children and a teacher killed by 16-year-old at Oregon primary school
- Published
A 16-year-old fatally shot three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander.
The unnamed attacker forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the US city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, police said.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the teen was shot dead by "a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him".
The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, police said. It is unclear if the assailant had any links to the school.
"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in a statement.
"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."
Local law enforcement responded to reports of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, at 12:59 local time, Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.
The first call indicated that an unknown suspect had shot into a car, she said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.
Minutes later, the local county dispatch received a flood of 911 calls and law enforcement were sent to the scene.
The suspected shooter was shot dead at around 13:02pm, Miller said.
While police said the shooter was a local 16-year-old boy, they declined to add further details pending the ongoing investigation.

The F1 pit stop that helped save lives
- Published
When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.
But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.
The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.
At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.
Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.
Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.
As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.
Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.
"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.
"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."
The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.
From trackside to bedside
Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.
Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.
Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.
Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.
Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.
The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.
The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.
Every second counts
F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.
At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.
This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.
David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."
Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.
Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

The Union Health Ministry has asked all States and Union Territories to ensure the prominent display of rates charged for services and facilities offered by clinical establishments.
In a move aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and patient-centric healthcare delivery, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava, in a letter to the Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, called for compliance with regulatory provisions, and ensuring information on service charges was clearly visible to patients and their attendants.
“Display of rates would help patients and their families understand the likely cost of treatment, make informed healthcare decisions, and plan their medical expenditure,’’ Ms. Srivastava said, adding that greater transparency would also help minimise avoidable confusion and billing-related disputes.
The letter refers to the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.
Under the Rules, clinical establishments in States and Union Territories where the Act is applicable are required to display the rates charged for each type of service provided, along with facilities available, at a conspicuous place, in the local language as well as in English.
Since health is a State subject, in States and Union Territories where clinical establishments are regulated by their own respective frameworks, several of which also contain provisions relating to the display of rates, the Health Secretary has called upon Chief Secretaries to ensure effective compliance.
The letter also places particular emphasis on transparency in healthcare pricing for international patients.
States and UTs have been requested to encourage the prominent display, wherever applicable, of package rates offered to foreign patients travelling to India on medical or Ayush visas.
“This would enable international patients to make informed choices, help minimise pricing and billing-related grievances and further strengthen India’s position as a trusted destination for medical and Ayush care,’’ the Ministry said.

Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell.
Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
A $6,000 media player slathered is gold is the perfect gift for the millionaire audiophile in your life.
All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD (Direct Stream Digital) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise.
The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference.
What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated.
This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

In a city where couples can stay connected over their phones all day but struggle to find a few uninterrupted minutes together, even a simple kiss can turn into an adventure. Exploring this idea is Kiss Ka Kissa, an upcoming romantic Hindi short film starring real-life couple Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Joshi. Landmarc Entertainment, led by filmmaker-producer Vidhi Kasliwal, has announced that the film will be released on October 22, 2026.
Kiss Ka Kissa: Vidhi Kasliwal announces romantic short film starring Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Josh
Set in Mumbai, Kiss Ka Kissa explores the romantic dreams people carry from their younger days and the little moments that sometimes remain unfulfilled. Combining humour, affection and everyday situations, the film looks at modern relationships and the ways romance can be found in seemingly ordinary experiences.
The pairing of Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Joshi, who are also a couple in real life, brings an element of familiarity to the story. Rather than relying on grand romantic gestures, the film focuses on the emotions that emerge from everyday interactions. At its core, it celebrates spontaneity in love and the small moments that bring two people closer.
For Vidhi Kasliwal, the project continues her interest in stories centred on human emotions. Her filmmaking journey includes working with Rajshri Productions alongside Sooraj R. Barjatya before making her writing and directorial debut with Isi Life Mein.
"What drew me to Kiss Ka Kissa was its simplicity. We often associate romance with grand gestures, but sometimes the smallest moments carry the deepest emotions. There is something wonderfully relatable about two people trying to find a little space for themselves in a city that never slows down. At Landmarc, we have always believed that stories don't need to be larger than life to touch lives. They simply need to feel real," says Vidhi Kasliwal.
Written and directed by Ashish Sharma, Kiss Ka Kissa marks his fiction debut following more than a decade of work in advertising films, music videos and branded storytelling. The film is presented by Landmarc Entertainment and produced under its Landmarc Films banner. Vidhi Kasliwal has handled the production and creative direction, while Aarti Bagdi serves as the creative producer.
Speaking about the film, Ashish Sharma shares, "I wanted to make Kiss Ka Kissa for two reasons: the little romantic dreams we carry from our younger days, and the joy of telling a simple, feel-good story. A first kiss, a stolen moment, a romantic adventure—sometimes life moves on, leaving these little dreams unfinished. Set against the chaos of Mumbai, the film explores how even the simplest romantic gesture can become an adventure when privacy is a luxury. I wanted the humour to emerge naturally from everyday situations. At its heart, the film celebrates love, youthful innocence and life's delightful unpredictability. I hope it leaves audiences smiling and perhaps remembering a little unfinished romantic story of their own."
Over the past 15 years, Landmarc has developed a filmography that includes Sanngto Aika, Vazandar, Ringan, Gachchi, Redu, Pipsi, Nashibvaan and Medium Spicy. As the company transitions into Landmarc Entertainment, it is expanding its operations through three initial verticals: Landmarc Films, Landmarc Melodies and Landmarc Digital. The company aims to explore new storytelling formats and support new voices while continuing to focus on emotionally driven narratives.
The film's creative team includes Vidhi Kasliwal as producer and creative visionary, Ashish Sharma as director, Aarti Bagdi as creative producer, Vikrant Thakur as director of photography and Puloma Pal as editor. Sarthak Karkare has composed the music, written the lyrics and created the background score. Prince Kumar of Casting Cubicle is responsible for casting, while K. R. Mahadevan [Mohan] serves as executive producer.
With its title reflecting the story's central idea, Kiss Ka Kissa looks beyond the kiss itself to explore the circumstances surrounding it. Against the pace of Mumbai, the film highlights how finding time for romance can be challenging, and how a single moment can become meaningful when two people make the most of it.

School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
- Published
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.

  - Published23 September
- Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump 
  - Published9 August 2025
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.
Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.
President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".
Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.
That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

Minus 17 to European dreams as Bournemouth fairytale continues
- Published
It was a night soundtracked by the Impossible Dream.
And it was no coincidence that was the song chosen at the Vitality Stadium before Bournemouth's first European home game in the club's 127-year history.
As supporters lucky enough to bag a ticket for the historic occasion waved flags to the Andy Williams classic, a giant tifo rose from behind one of the stands, bearing the words 'Minus 17 to European dreams. AFC Bournemouth, established 1899'.
As recently as 2008, a night like this would have been unthinkable for Cherries supporters.
Just 18 years ago, Bournemouth were facing the prospect of no longer existing.
After entering administration, the club were relegated from League One after being handed a 10-point deduction.
But that was not the end of their troubles. To be allowed to compete in the 2008-09 season, Bournemouth, then managed by Eddie Howe, had to accept a further 17-point deduction in League Two.
It left them at the bottom of the Football League and seemingly destined for life as a non-league side.
By the end of the season, the Cherries had not only completed one of the greatest escapes in English football history to secure a 21st-place finish and survival, but had also laid the foundations for a decade of success, which culminated in a first promotion to the Premier League in 2015.
Fast-forward to the present day and Bournemouth are making history for all the right reasons in the Europa League. Thursday's 3-0 win over Sturm Graz meant they became only the second English side to win their first two matches in a major European competition since Bolton achieved the feat in the Uefa Cup 21 years ago.
"It's a moment that will live long in their memories," former defender Joel Ward told TNT Sports. "The club should relish this night.
"The owner [Bill Foley] manifested this moment when he first came into the club. He set the standards for this club, he has invested a lot into it and he wanted to see this club in Europe.
"He got his wish, and they have certainly started incredibly well so far."
Smith embodies Bournemouth's fairytale
It was a night that always seemed destined to produce a fairytale storyline, such has been the nature of Bournemouth's rise since 2008.
At Wednesday's pre-match press conference, defender Adam Smith - the club's longest-serving player after initially joining on loan from Tottenham in 2011 - admitted he would never have imagined captaining the Cherries in Europe.
But there was more to come for Smith. The right-back earned his own piece of history by providing the assist for Bournemouth's first European goal on home soil, with Evanilson heading his cross home late in the first half.
"It's been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it, so we are very happy," Smith told TNT Sports.
"We had a chat with each other and we got a reaction today. That's an AFC [Bournemouth] performance right there."
Since making his move from Tottenham permanent in 2014, Smith has made more than 430 appearances for the Cherries.
In that time, the 35-year-old has helped Bournemouth secure three promotions, two of which have taken them to the Premier League.
When he was replaced by James Hill midway through the second half, the home supporters rose to their feet and chanted Smith's name as he departed the field.
"He's an example to everyone of what hard work looks like and the rewards that you get, even towards the latter stages of your career," added Ward.
"He's extremely professional, and he fully deserves the success he's getting now. Nights like this are what you live for. To walk out captaining that side is emotional and makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck."
'If we stick together and play like this... then we are hard to play against'
It was no surprise to see Bournemouth supporters remain in their seats long after the final whistle as they attempted to soak up as much as they could of a landmark night on the south coast.
For Marco Rose and his players, though, the focus will quickly shift to Sunday's Premier League clash with Sunderland.
Despite soaring to new heights in the Europa League during the opening weeks of the season, their Premier League campaign is yet to get going.
The Cherries sit 18th in the table and are one of only three teams, alongside Fulham and Tottenham, yet to win a match this season.
"If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans, then we are hard to play against and it's hard to beat us," said Rose, who succeeded Andoni Iraola in June.
"That's what we should take into the next game."
Bournemouth's remarkable story will enter arguably its most glamorous chapter yet when AC Milan visit the Vitality Stadium next week.

Time and time again as we celebrate achievements in health care, a measurable pinnacle of which could be the Nobel for Physiology/ Medicine, a sobering dose indicating the power of pathogen is delivered to us. This time, with the reported case of all things, the plague, in Russia. This week we discovered that the entire issue is mired in mystery, with not much information being shared by the nation. What was clear during the COVI-19 pandemic was the absolute criticality of sharing information globally, but with every squeak about the break out of infectious disease. In fact the Pandemic Agreement includes an aspect of Pathogen Sharing and Benefits among member nations. However, practically, sometimes nations find it difficult to easily share information with the global community.
Initially, the WHO cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. A WHOOfficial said the global organisation doesn’t know exactly how lab worker in Russia died in plague case. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the agency doesn’t know the “causative agent” behind the woman’s October 2 death, and urged Russia to share more information. The EU also urged Russia to be ‘transparent’ on plague reports - The Hindu
On its part, in tersely-worded statements, Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the case to pneumonic plague, maintaining that “extensive” testing found no evidence the lab worker’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Russia earlier said she died of pneumonia — a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection — and its health authorities have found no cases of plague recently. Moscow also denied sanitary measures over plague reports.
For an idea of what we actually know for sure now, do read this explainer: Pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia?
In addition, there was a fresh scare from Ebola-affected Africa: Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after patient dies in Nairobi. Why is this significant? I explain here: Ebola death recorded in Kenya after victim travelled from DRC. The victim had been living in DRC for years, and was reportedly already ill before he took a road trip, and then, a flight back home to Nigeria. He was admitted to a hospital in Nigeria by a relative, but succumbed to his illness. This is the first case of an Ebola death that has occurred in a country, outside of the DRC and Uganda, during the outbreak raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities. Kenyan authorities have called for stricter controls at the airports and also undertaken efforts to spread awareness and urge citizens to test if they notice symptoms. While the WHO has not issued a travel ban to the affected countries, self declaration by travellers has become mandatory at all international ports.
The past week also saw some hectic health-related activity in India. The most significant among them was easily the Supreme Court calling for a cap on trade margin for all essential medicines and medical products, as Aaratrika Bhaumik reported. As the government declared that it had proposed a 30% trade-margin cap on patented and non-patented cancer medicines, but top court asks why a margin cap cannot be extended to all medicines and medical products; the court says the government has to ensure that DPCO-approved medicines, whose price is legally regulated, reach patients. That is jumping the gun though, first read Bindu Shajan Perappadan’s article: Centre to cap trade margins on non-scheduled cancer drugs to 30% of MRP.

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine is expected to begin in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of October, World Health Organization experts said Tuesday.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,000.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will go through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
"We have got strong reassurances that... it should be starting before the end of this month," said Anthony Scott, chair of the WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunisation (SAGE).
The group said insights that Ervebo might offer cross-protection against Bundibugyo were no match for evidence from standardised vaccine trials.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC -- a single trial framework that can test the efficiency of multiple vaccines -- should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Need for data
The Tumaini trial "will generate urgently-needed data on the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease, and will help formulate the policy decisions we need", Scott told a press conference.
"In addition, we welcome the accelerated development of vaccines that are specifically targeting Bundibugyo.
"They're both progressing rapidly through early clinical development."
SAGE said it was deeply concerned about the ongoing challenges in controlling the Ebola outbreak.
"The key elements here are insecurity and population displacement, and they're hindering access to care, disrupting surveillance, and delaying critical research, including, from our perspective, research on vaccine trials," said Scott.
Kate O'Brien, director of the WHO's immunisation department, said a WHO technical advisory group would be meeting to review evidence from the small-scale trials of the Oxford and Moderna candidate vaccines.
She suggested the Oxford jab could drop into the broader Tumaini trial fairly swiftly -- as doses are ready to roll -- if the safety and the immunogenicity data from the first trial is "positive and reassuring".
Therefore "everything is lined up for at least two products to be moving quickly", she said.
The medical charity Doctors Without Borders is conducting a data-gathering study -- not a full clinical trial -- of Ervebo's effectiveness in frontline health workers in DRC provinces hard-hit by the Bundibugyo outbreak, with the jab being offered to volunteers as an interim measure.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

At least four people died in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, police said. The deceased included three children ages 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher.
Another child and teacher were taken to the hospital, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz was quoted by The Associated Press as saying.
The shooter, 16, was found dead inside the school when police arrived, Krantz said. A community member had pursed him into the school and shot him, he added.
Authorities believe that at least five people were dead following a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, according to two law enforcement officials with knowledge of the case.
The officials told The Associated Press the death toll was preliminary and could change.
The suspected shooter was 15 or 16 years old, one of the sources said. Any other detail about the shooter is awaited.
Bend police spokesperson Sheila Miller earlier confirmed the suspect is dead. It wasn’t clear if the suspect was included among the five.
Miller also said multiple victims were children.
“We don’t have a number at this point. We know children are among the victims,” Miller said during a media briefing.
Authorities received a call about a shot fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 p.m. and arrived on scene within minutes. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, she said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school soon after police arrived, Miller said.
It was not immediately clear if it was by police, a bystander or self-inflicted.
Miller said two people were transported to St. Charles Bend hospital following the shooting, and their conditions were not immediately known. A spokesperson for the hospital did not immediately return a request for comment from the AP.
Silver Rail Elementary was under lockdown, the Bend-La Pine school district wrote on Facebook.
“We’re in the process at this time of going room by room and evacuating each of the people who are in that school. ... This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It’s devastating,” Miller said, pausing to control her emotions.
The school in Bend, Oregon, which is more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.

When markets turn unsettled, daily price movements can dominate the economic conversation. Foreign selling becomes a verdict on the country, a weaker currency feeds doubts, and individual disappointments become evidence of a wider problem. These signals deserve attention. But judging India’s prospects also requires examining what businesses, borrowers and investors with longer horizons are doing.
Two recent developments provide that perspective. The government has approved a Fairfax subsidiary as strategic buyer for the proposed sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for approximately ₹52,878 crore. Separately, Blackstone’s Jon Gray has outlined an ambition to increase the firm's India investments from about $50 billion to $100 billion over five years. These represent substantial confidence in India’s future.
Having worked closely with Prem Watsa and Fairfax, I have seen their willingness to support businesses through difficult periods. Their experience also teaches caution. Transforming a smaller private-sector bank in southern India has required years of investment in technology, diversification and scale. An investment in a leading PVC producer has faced setbacks too. Patient capital needs sound execution, realistic expectations, and a willingness to correct course.
Quick answers to key questions
The proposed ₹52,878 crore purchase of a 60.72% stake signals that a major foreign investor is willing to take a long-term position in India’s banking sector. It also reflects the government’s willingness to give private capital a larger role.
The article points to India’s growth prospects, favourable demographics, rising household investment and stronger corporate and banking balance sheets. These factors may create opportunities when market prices fall more than business fundamentals justify.
Monthly SIP contributions reached a record ₹32,490 crore in September, showing continued participation by domestic savers despite market weakness. These recurring investments deepen markets and broaden the domestic investor base.
Investors should consider valuation, earnings and currency risks, as well as global interest rates. The article also highlights challenges from a deficient monsoon, inflation, expensive oil and India’s need for capital inflows to help finance its current account deficit.
The article argues that removing LTCG tax on genuinely long-term equity investment could attract patient capital, and that extending relief to domestic investors could support household wealth creation. It presents this as a policy view, not a confirmed change.
Portfolio investors deserve a fair hearing. Their selling can reflect concerns about valuations, earnings, currency risk and global interest rates. The extraordinary investment in AI infrastructure is also competing for global capital. This helps explain the environment in which allocations are changing, although it cannot explain every outflow from India. When reallocations depress prices beyond what business fundamentals justify, they create opportunities for discerning long-term investors. Experienced investors are recognizing that possibility.
India offers a compelling foundation. Its growth is faster than that of the other large economies: real GDP expanded 7.8% in April–June, and the IMF projects 7% growth for FY27. Its favourable demographics add depth to the opportunity. A large working-age population can sustain production, consumption and savings for years, provided education, skills and employment keep pace.
Indian households are demonstrating their own confidence. Monthly mutual fund SIP contributions reached a record ₹32,490 crore in September, despite market weakness. These recurring savings reflect a growing willingness to participate in the country’s corporate future. They also deepen markets and provide a broader domestic investor base.
That matters to overseas investors. Confidence to enter a market depends partly on confidence that an orderly exit will be possible. Blackstone's Gray has highlighted the strength of India’s public markets and listing opportunities. Alongside liquidity, India offers a vibrant democracy, an independent judiciary and established legal protections. Faster dispute resolution and more consistent enforcement would make those institutional advantages stronger still.
The financial foundation has improved too. Crisil estimates that median corporate gearing roughly halved over the past decade to around 0.5 times by March 2026. Banks’ gross NPAs stood at 1.68% in June, with a robust capital adequacy of 17.78%. Healthier borrowers and lenders give expansion a firmer foundation. Icra also reports healthy repayment performance in rated secured retail securitization pools, although unsecured segments require scrutiny.
Public investment reinforces this strength. Central government capital expenditure reached approximately ₹5.10 lakh crore during April-August. Better transport, power and digital connectivity generate demand while improving productivity and widening markets for businesses.
There are a few significant challenges. A deficient monsoon threatens farm incomes and food prices. September retail inflation reached 5.54%, while expensive oil affects household budgets and business costs. The Reserve Bank of India’s October rate increase demonstrates vigilance. Policy must provide calibrated support to growth without losing sight of inflation.
Oil dependence also creates a recurring external financing challenge. Services exports and remittances offset much of the merchandise trade deficit, but India generally runs a current account deficit. The gap requires net capital inflows or a drawdown of reserves.
Special FCNR deposit schemes can mobilize foreign currency quickly, while limits on banks’ open forex positions can help manage instability. These measures have their place, but deposits mature and restrictions cannot create a lasting supply of foreign exchange. Sustained equity and debt investment must help finance greater productive capacity and more jobs.
India should, therefore, offer investors a dependable welcome through predictable taxation, timely approvals and straightforward entry and exit. Foreign capital complements domestic savings by expanding financing and sharing risk. Our competition for internationally mobile capital comes from other investment destinations. Attracting it on sensible terms can improve prosperity for Indians.
Tax exemptions for eligible foreign investors in government securities are an encouraging first step. The larger opportunity lies in equities. The finance minister’s openness to hearing investor views on LTCG taxation is welcome.
Removing LTCG tax on genuinely long-term equity investment could attract patient capital. Extending relief to domestic investors would avoid apparent discrimination and support household wealth creation. In my view, the resulting expansion in investment, businesses and taxable economic activity could more than offset the initial revenue loss over time.
Domestic savers and experienced global investors are expressing confidence through their actions. India should build on that confidence with policies that attract durable capital and turn it into productive businesses, better jobs and higher living standards.
Nirmal Jain is founder of the IIFL Group

Turkey and Azerbaijan have long called themselves "one nation, two states". Now, a row over the hijab (headscarf) is testing that bond. Experts have pointed out that while the headscarf controversy is the immediate trigger, Azerbaijan’s ties with Israel could be a deeper source of tension. The controversy has also brought to the fore a deeper geopolitical fault line in the relationship between Ankara and Baku. Videos purportedly showing girls wearing headscarves being denied entry to educational institutions have been widely shared on social media. Mint could not independently verify the authenticity of these videos. The two countries have long described their relationship as "one nation, two states". However, Azerbaijan's restrictions on religious dress in public schools have drawn criticism from Turkish political figures and prompted a sharp response from Azerbaijan's ruling party, which has defended the country's right to determine its domestic policies. While the controversy centres on religious dress and secular education, analysts say the implications extend beyond the immediate dispute. Azerbaijan's strategic relationship with Israel, at a time when Turkey's ties with Israel have deteriorated, could present a more significant challenge to Ankara-Baku relations. In an analysis published on September 29 by the Turan Research Center, titled "The Hijab and the Secular State in the Turkic World", Joseph Epstein argued that Azerbaijan's headscarf restrictions raise broader questions about sovereignty over religious life, national identity and the role of the secular state. Epstein noted that Azerbaijan's approach reflects a wider pattern among several post-Soviet states, where governments have sought to keep religious dress out of public schools while presenting secular education as central to a shared national identity. He argued that the dispute also highlights the limits of Turkey's influence over Azerbaijan. Although the countries share close cultural and strategic ties, Baku has maintained a distinct approach to secularism and has resisted external pressure over its domestic policies. Epstein also pointed to the criticism Azerbaijan's ties with Israel have attracted in Turkish media since the Gaza war, adding another dimension to the tensions between the two countries. Professor Muddassir Quamar, Associate Professor, Jawaharlal Nehru University and an expert on West Asian affairs, while talking to Mint said the hijab controversy was primarily a cultural and religious issue concerning the imposition of dress codes on women. Despite protests and statements in Turkey, he said, the dispute was unlikely to have a serious impact on bilateral strategic relations. The differences over Israel, however, could pose a bigger challenge. Azerbaijan has developed close defence and strategic ties with both Israel and Turkey, while Turkey's relations with Israel have deteriorated, Quamar said. This divergence could become a more difficult issue for Ankara and Baku to manage as their regional priorities evolve. The distinction is important: the hijab dispute may have brought the tensions into public view, but it does not necessarily explain the deeper strategic differences between the two countries. The challenges extend beyond Israel. Quamar identified the US-Israel war on Iran and its implications for the South Caucasus as another factor that could complicate bilateral relations. "There are several regional and geopolitical factors that might pose challenge including the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran and how it impacts the situation in the South Caucuses, as well as Turkish ambitions in Central Asia and the South Caucuses region, and its attempted outreach to Armenia to improve relations and access in the neighbourhood. However primarily, the differences in approach to Israel might pose the most difficult challenge for Turkey-Azerbaijan relations today," Quamar said. The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.
The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.
The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.
The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.
The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.
A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.
The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.
Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

People with longCOVID, where symptoms persist after recovery from an acute Covid-19 infection, may have distinct differences in the mix of bacteria living in their mouths and lungs, research has shown.
The differences in the lung microbiome are linked to respiratory symptoms, as well as the cognitive and digestive problems known to occur in longCOVID, researchers said.
The findings, published in the European Respiratory Journal, may contribute towards understanding why some people develop long COVID and point to new ways to treat the condition, they said.
"Prior studies have shown some changes in the gut microbiome with long COVID, but Covid is a lung disease and so it makes sense to look to see if the lung microbiome is changed in long COVID," lead author Daniela Alferes de Lima Headley from the University of Dundee, UK, said.
"We know that millions of people worldwide are still affected by long COVID and its cause is still unknown. Long Covid affects multiple organs. The microbiome is important to maintain health throughout the body, so it is a strong candidate for something that may contribute to long COVID," she said.
The study examined 771 people treated for Covid-19 at one of 38 UK hospitals between February 2020 and March 2021.
The participants were divided into four groups based on how bad their symptoms were five months after being discharged from hospital, ranging from 'very severe' with serious physical, mental, and cognitive impairments to 'mild', with few symptoms and good recovery.
Six months after hospital discharge, samples were collected from patients' mouths through saliva and from their lungs through sputum. DNA sequencing was used to identify the microbes present.
By analysing the variety and quantities of microbes and comparing them with patients' symptoms, researchers found that people with very severe long COVID had marked differences in their oral and lung microbiomes compared with those who did not have severe long COVID.
The results also revealed differences linked to specific symptoms, including reduced lung function, in which the lungs cannot hold as much air as normal or air cannot flow in and out as easily.
The researchers also found differences in the mouth and lungs microbiome between people with varying neurocognitive symptoms -- including 'brain fog', difficulties with memory, attention and concentration -- and gut symptoms, including pain, nausea, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.
Among the changes associated with long-COVID symptoms, was an over-abundance of bacteria that produce lactic acid, which was also linked to signs of inflammation found in samples of patients' blood.
Lead researcher James Chalmers, chair of respiratory research at the University of Dundee, UK, said, "People who had the worst symptoms five to six months after COVID infection had big changes in the microbiome in their mouth and lungs."
"We also found that changes in the airway microbiome were linked not just to lung problems, but also to symptoms like brain fog and gut symptoms, suggesting the lung microbiome could have effects on health more broadly," he said.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has proposed sweeping changes to the rules governing initial public offerings (IPOs) of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). In a consultation paper floated on October 14, the markets regulator has proposed changes to SME IPO norms, including regulations pertaining to valuation thresholds, profitability and shareholder exits. The regulator has invited public feedback on the paper till November 4. Citing its rationale, the regulator said that the paper has been formulated by its working group due to rapid increase in the funds raised through SME IPOs and the number of investors participating in such issues. Since launch in 2012, about 1,500 companies have opted to list on the SME platform and have raised ₹40,222 Cr. Startups like Zappfresh, DroneAcharya, TAC Infosec, Yudiz, are a few startups that have also taken this route to go public. In view of this, the regulator has proposed multiple changes, including lowering the minimum application threshold and removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements. Here’s a look at some of the key changes that have been proposed: The Market Cap-Based Listing Criteria Under the proposed framework, companies with a post-issue market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less can now list on the SME platform. Those valued in the range of ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr can also choose to list either on the SME platform or the main board. Companies valued over ₹4,000 Cr will have to list on the main board. SEBI has also proposed replacing the existing paid-up share capital criterion with post-issue market capitalisation to determine whether a company can list on the SME platform or the main board. Currently, companies with post-issue paid-up share capital of up to ₹25 Cr can opt for the SME platform, subject to other eligibility conditions. In addition, companies in the ₹1,000 Cr to ₹4,000 Cr band choosing the SME platform would also have to submit restated consolidated financial statements under Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) for the preceding three financial years, if they have not already adopted Ind AS. If an IPO applicant’s estimated market capitalisation crosses the applicable threshold during the IPO process, it would have to refile under the relevant listing framework. Minimum Profitability Requirements Raised SEBI has proposed mandating SME IPO applicants to report an average operating profit of at least ₹3 Cr annually over the preceding three financial years, based on restated consolidated financial statements. In contrast, the existing framework requires operating profit of at least ₹1 Cr in at least two of the preceding three fiscal years. However, the consultation paper refers to EBIT in its narrative, while existing provision mentioned EBITDA. This requires clarification. Companies that fail the proposed profitability test could still list on the SME platform through an alternative route. They would have to use the book-building process and allocate at least 75% of the net offer to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). If the required allocation is not achieved, the entire subscription amount would have to be refunded. New Rules For Converted And Reorganised Businesses SEBI has proposed changing the eligibility rules for SMEs seeking an IPO after converting from a proprietorship, partnership or limited liability partnership (LLP). These draft rules also cover companies undergoing qualifying business reorganisations. Currently, such companies generally need to complete at least one full financial year before filing their draft IPO papers. Under the new proposal, they would need to complete four consecutive financial quarters from the date of conversion or qualifying reorganisation and submit at least one annual audited financial statement prepared after the change. The proposal also covers acquisitions, succession and schemes of arrangement, where more than 50% of the revenue comes from businesses that previously operated as proprietorships, partnerships or LLPs. In such cases, the earlier business' operating track record could be considered when assessing IPO eligibility. The ₹10 Cr Cap On GCP Allocation May Go SEBI has proposed removing the ₹10 Cr cap on the amount that the companies can allocate, from their IPO proceeds, towards general corporate purposes (GCP). Currently, GCP allocation cannot exceed 15% of the amount raised or ₹10 Cr, whichever is lower. Under the proposal, the 15% limit would remain, but the fixed ₹10 Cr ceiling would be removed, allowing companies raising larger amounts to allocate more funds to general business needs. SEBI Looks To Reshuffle OFS Rules SEBI has also proposed a dedicated offer-for-sale (OFS) framework with a one-year holding requirement, subject to specified exemptions. The draft framework also seeks to remove the existing 20% ceiling on the OFS component for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). The Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) went a step further and suggested removing the 50% cap on a QIB’s pre-issue holding as well. These exemptions, however, would not apply to companies using the alternative listing route after failing the proposed profitability test. Lock-In Periods To Be Revised SEBI has proposed revising the lock-in periods for promoters and other shareholders after an SME IPO. The draft changes include: Minimum promoters' contribution: The three-year lock-in on minimum promoter contribution would begin from the IPO allotment date. In contrast, the lock-in date is currently linked to the commencement of commercial production. Promoter holdings above the minimum contribution: The existing staggered lock-in would be replaced with a uniform one-year lock-in. Non-promoter pre-issue capital: The lock-in will reduce from the current one year to six months. Promoter group holdings: A separate one-year lock-in would apply from the IPO allotment date. Depositories could also mark shares that cannot be locked in electronically as non-transferable for the applicable period. SEBI to Further Trim Minimum IPO Application Threshold The markets regulator has proposed lowering the minimum application amount for SME IPOs to ₹1 Lakh from the existing requirement of more than ₹2 Lakh. Investors would have to apply for at least four lots worth a minimum of ₹25,000 each. The ₹2 Lakh minimum was introduced in March 2025 to limit participation by smaller retail investors. The consultation paper also proposes aligning investor categories and allocation rules more closely with the mainboard framework, including the introduction of the ‘Retail Individual Investor’ category. Under the regime, Issuers can also allocate up to 60% of the QIB portion to anchor investors in book-built issues. SEBI has also proposed increasing the minimum number of allottees from 200 to 500. Under the alternative route for companies failing the profitability test, up to 10% of the net offer would go to retail investors, up to 15% to NIIs and at least 75% to QIBs. SME Shares Could Be Traded In Lots Of One SEBI has proposed allowing investors to trade SME-listed shares in lots of one share, replacing the existing price-linked lot sizes. The consultation paper notes that around 5% of unique PAN-based shareholders held odd-lot shares, on average. The proposed change could make it easier for investors to sell their entire holdings, but it will not change the minimum IPO application amount. End For Mandatory Underwriting And Market-Making? SEBI has proposed removing mandatory underwriting and market-making requirements for SME IPOs to reduce listing costs. Currently, SME IPOs must be fully underwritten, with lead managers required to underwrite at least 15% of the issue themselves. Under the proposal, these requirements would be removed. The 75% QIB portion under the alternative listing route would not need to be underwritten. Underwriting fees accounted for 49.52% and 38.41% of total SME IPO issue expenses on the NSE in FY25 and FY26, respectively. The corresponding figures for the BSE were 32.20% and 33.99%, according to SEBI. The minimum subscription requirement would remain at 90% of the offer, excluding OFS. If the threshold is not met, application money would have to be refunded within four days of the issue closing. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to maintain market-makers for three years after listing. Market-making fees accounted for 1.25%-4.20% of total issue expenses across the NSE and BSE in FY25 and FY26. The change could reduce costs but may affect liquidity in SME stocks with limited trading activity. Changes To Mainboard Migration Rules SEBI has proposed revising the rules that govern SME-listed companies, when they move to the mainboard. Under the proposed framework, companies with a market capitalisation of ₹1,000 Cr or less would not have to migrate solely because of their valuation. Those valued above ₹1,000 Cr but below ₹4,000 Cr could voluntarily migrate, subject to the main board's eligibility criteria. Companies valued at ₹4,000 Cr or more would have to mandatorily migrate. Board approval would be sufficient for migration, without a shareholder vote. SEBI has also proposed removing the requirement to migrate when paid-up capital is likely to exceed ₹25 Cr and scrapping migration from the main board to the SME platform. Companies already listed on the SME platform, when the new rules are notified, would continue to follow the existing migration framework.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
- Published
Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.
If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.
Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.
The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.
And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.
City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses.
Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.
BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.
How the figures are worked out
When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.
Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.
The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.
City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.
Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?
This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.
Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.
It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.
It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.
Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.
This is purely about domestic impact:
- Lost prize money by league placing
- Missed potential Champions League earnings
- Europa League payments
- Loss of Premier League status
- Impact of cup final defeats
