How City gained £1.17bn, and others may have lost £844m
The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m.
- £188.2m in Premier League placing money
- £349.7m in relegation costs
- £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money
- £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League
We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.
For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.
For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.
For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.
But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.
Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn:
- £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues
- £363.4m via the Champions League
- £900,000 from the FA Cup victory
- £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories
The most impacted: How Spurs could have missed out on £120m
"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.
"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."
You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.
BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.
Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League.
The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m.
Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m.
The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.
Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.
Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m.
Did City's EFL Cup win cost Liverpool £37.8m?
The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.
Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.
Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.
Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.
Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of £37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was £26.6m.
While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.
The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.
Together with Premier League place money of £10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was £52.3m.
As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was £900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.
Everton were denied Europe five times
Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.
The Champions League place is calculated to be worth £32.6m - the £39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' £6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.
The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is £23.2m.
Add on the £10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is £66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.
Did two relegations cost Hull City £99m?
While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.
Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?
There are a couple of ways of looking at this.
Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.
Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?
Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.
BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.
Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.
Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers £93.78m.
The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding £5.2m in place money to the sum.
It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on £99m.
Swansea are fourth in the table with £63.1m. Of that total, £54m is from relegation and £9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.
Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected £60.4m, of which £7.9m was place money.
Norwich (£43.8m), Wigan (£39.6m), Burnley (£31.1m), Bolton (£26.4m) and Birmingham (£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.
The loss of Champions League money
Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.
The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.
City earned £79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting £39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of £39.8m.
Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, £32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, £22.1m deficit).
The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.
City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning £42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving £37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of £4.8m.
The cumulative cost of league places
In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.
Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.
It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.
It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.
Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?
The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.
In 2010-11 it was £755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to £1.94m.
If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of £10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.
West Brom and West Ham's total is £9.9m, with Swansea on £9.1m.
At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (£756,756), Portsmouth (£800,424) and Huddersfield (£1.93m).

US President Donald Trump has cancelled plans to livestream the execution of former US Army major Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting in Texas.
Trump said on Thursday (October 15) that Hasan would still be executed by firing squad as scheduled on December 3, but the event would not be broadcast. He added that the victims’ immediate family members could watch the execution in person if they wished.
The decision reverses an earlier announcement by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that the execution would be made public, drawing criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers, religious leaders and other observers.
Trump said he had considered whether broadcasting the execution could deter future attacks but decided against livestreaming it after hearing objections from people who did not want to watch a person die.
In a social media post, Trump described Hasan as responsible for the deaths of 13 people, including a pregnant soldier and her unborn child, and said 32 others were seriously injured.
He argued that a public broadcast could have demonstrated the consequences of terrorism but acknowledged that many people opposed showing the execution.
“ He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump wrote, adding that the victims’ immediate families would be allowed to attend if they chose.
Trump had indicated previously that he would make the final decision, saying there were arguments both for and against broadcasting the execution.
Earlier this month, Hegseth announced that Hasan would be executed by firing squad on December 3 at Fort Hood, the Texas military installation where the attack occurred.
Hegseth had said the broadcast would ensure that people understood there were serious consequences for such acts. The Pentagon subsequently confirmed that the execution would be livestreamed, prompting a backlash.
The proposal was particularly controversial because no other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions.
Critics also raised concerns that images of the execution could be used for propaganda or contribute to radicalisation rather than serve as a deterrent.
Vice President JD Vance expressed reservations about the proposed broadcast, saying he did not intend to watch it if it went ahead.
“I’m not going to be watching it,” Vance said, while stressing that the controversy over the method of execution should not overshadow the killings for which Hasan was convicted.
Several Republican and Democratic lawmakers also criticised the plan. Religious leaders raised objections, while Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, voiced concerns. Pope Leo has condemned capital punishment in all its forms.
Public opinion also appeared to weigh against the proposal, with recent polls indicating that a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming the execution.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, was convicted in a military trial in 2013 for the November 5, 2009, shooting at Fort Hood.
He entered a medical building where soldiers were waiting for immunisations and medical clearance before deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar”, meaning “God is great” in Arabic, before opening fire with a handgun.
Hasan said he wanted to prevent soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan and killing fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that argument as a defence during his trial.
Hasan was shot in the back by law enforcement officers during the attack and was left paralysed from the waist down. He now uses a wheelchair.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Bolt comparisons a 'privilege' - Dambile
- Published
Commonwealth 200m champion Sinesipho Dambile says it is a "privilege" to be compared with Jamaican great Usain Bolt as he looks to establish himself among the world's leading sprinters.
The South African has enjoyed a breakthrough season, producing a string of impressive performances and underlining his credentials as one of Africa's emerging track stars.
Speaking to the Warm Up Track podcast, the 24-year-old revealed that he "enjoys the pressure" that comes with being mentioned alongside the fastest man in history.
"Pressure is a privilege," he said. "I love it because that's where I excel."
Dambile recalls meeting the eight-time Olympic champion at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, where the Jamaican offered him some advice.
"For Bolt, charisma naturally goes to him. Being able to meet him in person last year in Tokyo, he said: 'Please make sure you enjoy this thing'.
"That, until this day, still stuck with me."
Victory at last year's South African national championships secured Dambile's place in Tokyo, where he finished eighth in the 200m final, having set a new personal best of 19.97 seconds in the semi-finals.
That time was broken this season as Dambile accelerated his development.
June's Diamond League meeting in Doha saw him clock 19.74 seconds - the fourth-fastest time recorded by any athlete in 2026.
He went on to finish second behind the USA's Kenny Bednarek, but ahead of Botswana's 2024 Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, in last month's Diamond League final in Brussels, while he was fourth in the inaugural Ultimate Championships.
However, the year's high point was undoubtedly the Commonwealth gold medal won in Birmingham in July, a result which made him the first South African to win the event.
While it is clear the 200m remains Dambile's principal event, he is "mentally willing to put in the work" to mimic Bolt, who likewise began his career specialising in the longer distance before going on to also dominate the 100m.
"He (Bolt) paved the way," Dambile said.
"I spoke to my team a couple of times and I was like, 'I want you guys to count me in on the 100m'.
"I want to do both. I know I'm going to be successful."
Akani Simbine's mentor role
A relaxed character, Dambile insists he will follow Bolt's advice to enjoy his time on the track, promising that fans will "get more of my personality" in future.
"I've never been a loud person, trying to bring attention to me," he said, contrasting his approach to the brash showmanship of Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles.
"I'm always smiling out there, I'm always looking at the crowd, looking at the kids, and that's just me.
"I just want to go out there and do my thing, to make sure that everybody enjoys the show."
Dambile's success has coincided with a growing sense of belief within South African sprinting.
He was part of the quartet that won 4x100m gold at the World Relays in Guangzhou last year, running alongside team-mates Bayanda Walaza, Bradley Nkoana and Akani Simbine.
"We go as a squad, so we have that little bit of energy," Dambile said when explaining how the group's camaraderie has played an important role in their success.
"We pump each other up because we're going for the one thing - doing it for our country.
"The biggest sport in our country is rugby, so you get the Springboks going there winning the World Cup and we wanted to have the same feeling."
The influence of the experienced Simbine has been crucial.
The 2018 Commonwealth 100m champion finally landed an Olympic medal at Paris 2024, picking up silver in the 4x100m relay, having agonisingly finished fourth in the individual 100m finals in both the French capital and at the 2020 Games in Tokyo.
"He's made all the finals. He's been there. He's been the guy. He's been one of the best sprinters in the world," said Dambile.
"So when someone like that from home can do it, we also start to believe that it's actually possible to do it."

Just like Simbine, Dambile is a product of the TuksSport team at the University of Pretoria, a breeding ground for South Africa's top talent, including fellow sprinter Gift Leotlela, who finished fourth in the 100m final at this year's Commonwealth Games, and 2025 world indoor 800m champion Prudence Sekgodiso.
"We all were scouted through different processes and we all ended up at the same school," said Dambile.
"Best place to train in as a sprinter."
All four Pretoria alumni competed in Birmingham this year, but only Dambile came away with a Commonwealth medal.
"It was so much relief because what I did was not just a small thing," he explained.
"It was huge, especially for myself [and] the country of South Africa. My emotions were all over the place.
"I just pushed through everything and when I was in that moment, I knew I deserved it because of the amount of work I've put in."
A double medallist at the 2021 Under-20 World Championships in Nairobi, Dambile's progression from promising junior to established senior athlete has not, however, been straightforward, with injury curtailing much of his 2024 season.
This year's success has changed things.
"It's easier to recognise me in the country now with me winning the Commonwealth," he explained.
"A bit of fame now - you can see people when they talk about you. It's like I've been experiencing beautiful things happening."
Things could get even better with plans already being made for next year's World Championships in Beijing and the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
"We've already set up a map towards that," he said.
"We definitely know how important it's going to be over the next two years.
"I want to be the best 200m athlete the sport has ever seen.
"I need to make sure that I have the World Championship [and] Olympic title. I want to do things that have never been done in my country."

Author Steven Galloway finishes testifying at defamation trial
Galloway alleges defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault
Author and former University of British Columbia (UBC) creative writing chair Steven Galloway has concluded testifying in his defamation lawsuit trial in Vancouver.
Galloway, who alleges the defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault, took questions from Glynnis Kirchmeier, a defendant in the case who is representing herself and attending the trial remotely.
The former UBC student pressed Galloway about whether he believed she had been involved with an advocacy group for victims of sexual violence and harassment, and had also contacted other defendants, including A.B., another former student who made the allegations against Galloway.
Galloway says he found it "unlikely" Kirchmeier wasn't involved with the group because she was on one of its fundraising pages, and he recalled becoming nauseated about one of her tweets, and wondering "why is this person I’ve never met calling me a rapist?"

The court heard during the brief hearing in B.C. Supreme Court on Thursday that the next witness is expected to be Ronna Syed, a producer for the CBC program the fifth estate.

Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software.

Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
“The [Federal Aviation Administration] has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard drivers license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

Minibus driver fined after dragging motorcyclist for several metres in crash
The victim had lacerations on his leg that were deep enough to expose bone.
SINGAPORE: A minibus driver was fined S$5,000 (US$3,900) on Friday (Oct 16) over an accident where a motorcyclist was dragged for several metres on the road.
Muhammad Zulhadzly Sulaiman, 32, pleaded guilty to a charge of driving without reasonable consideration that caused grievous hurt to the victim.
The father of seven was also banned from driving for five years. He elected to serve five days' jail in default of the fine.
The court heard that at about 10.43pm on Mar 9, the victim, who was not named in open court, was driving his motorcycle on Woodlands Avenue 6 towards Woodlands Industrial Park E4.
The motorcyclist stopped for pedestrians at a red traffic light signal, and another vehicle stopped behind him.
As Zulhadzly's minibus approached the two stationary vehicles, he failed to keep a lookout and did not slow down. He collided into the rear of the vehicle behind the victim's motorcycle.
This propelled the vehicle forward with enough force for it to travel beyond the pedestrian crossing. The vehicle struck the motorcycle in front before coming to rest in the adjacent lane.
Zulhadzly's minibus continued forward and struck the rear of the motorcycle, causing the victim to be thrown off it.
The victim became trapped under the side of the minibus, where he was dragged along the road for several metres.
He was later taken to hospital by ambulance, where he was found to have deep cuts on his leg that exposed the bone. He underwent a procedure to clean the wounds and remove damaged tissue.
He was discharged on Mar 11 and received 58 days of hospitalisation leave.
The police prosecutor said it was fortuitous that Zulhadzly's actions did not cause harm to the driver of the other stationary vehicle, nor any of the 14 passengers in the minibus at the time.
Calling for the fine and driving ban, he said that as Zulhadzly was driving a minibus, he should have been exercising more care, but did not slow down even though there was a red light ahead.
Zulhadzly was emotional as he addressed the court, saying he took responsibility for his actions. He also asked for leniency.
The punishment for driving without reasonable consideration and causing grievous hurt is a jail term of up to two years, a fine of up to S$5,000, or both penalties.

Firm accused of cost-cutting, false declarations over fire-safety parts in 48 lifts

Hong Kong authorities have uncovered alleged corner-cutting and false declarations involving fire-safety components in a contractor’s replacement of 48 lifts at two public housing estates.
The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said on Thursday that surprise inspections had found serious deficiencies in projects carried out by Taizoom Elevator (Hong Kong) at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin.
It said 39 lifts replaced between May 2025 and July this year were affected at Pok Hong Estate. Nine lifts replaced between February and July at Tsui Ping (North) Estate were also affected.
The department said that although Taizoom had submitted fire-resistance test reports, inspectors found that it had only installed fire-resisting doors and not the corresponding door-frame components required before reporting the works as completed.

Ukraine's access to military-grade Starlink services appears to have been at least partially restored on Thursday, a day after Kyiv was stunned by sudden speed limits that it said hamstrung some drone operations.
Ukrainian defense ministry sources told Business Insider that Starshield services remained functional while in motion as of roughly 11:45 a.m. local time on Thursday, according to reports that they had received from military units.
The sources said the defense ministry is working to understand how and why there was a disruption to the operation of Starshield, SpaceX's dedicated satellite network for military services.
Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider that Starshield services had been restored to their pre-disruption capacity.
Ukrainian officials and service members were caught off guard on Wednesday by the unexpected Starshield disruption, which they said restricted speeds above 100 miles per hour. Some units experienced a loss of connection at speeds as low as 45 miles per hour.
The full extent of the service limitation remains unclear.
Yuriy, an officer with Ukraine's National Guard, told Business Insider that his units use Starshield to support drone operations and that speeds were back above 100 miles per hour as of Thursday morning. He asked to be identified only by his first name for security purposes.
However, Yuriy said that several operations were disrupted during the earlier restrictions.
Defense ministry sources said the disruption complicated mid-range strikes, air defense intercepts, and front-line logistics. Starlink does not work inside Russia, so the issue was limited to missions in Ukrainian territory or Russian-occupied territory.
The sudden Starlink disruption caused widespread confusion and raised questions about the source of the decision and whether it was connected to tensions between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy facilities.
Ukrainian forces use Starlink, the commercial satellite internet service run by SpaceX, and Starshield, a secure network for military and government work built by the company but operated by the US government. Some Ukrainian officials initially blamed SpaceX for the disruption.
In an X post on Wednesday responding to Ukraine's former defense minister, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk put the issue on the Trump administration, saying that Starshield was "owned and controlled by the American government." He said "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
A senior US official told Business Insider Thursday afternoon that "no such request was ever made by the President."
The Pentagon has not responded to requests for comment.
Sprawling influence
The outage and impact on front-line operations have called attention to Ukraine's deep dependence on Starlink, which has become critical for battlefield communications and drone warfare.
As Business Insider recently reported, Starlink's rapid expansion has given Musk and SpaceX an enormous source of influence and soft power, and the world's richest man has not been shy about using that power in Ukraine to influence the course of the war.
Musk said in 2023 that he refused a request from Ukraine's military to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on the occupied Crimean peninsula. Earlier this year, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' use of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, handing Ukraine a key battlefield advantage.
While support for Ukraine has varied, Musk has consistently been a prominent critic of the Ukrainian president. In an X post late on Wednesday, hours after responding to Ukraine's defense minister, he wrote that it was "time for Zelenskyy to go."
The sudden Starlink disruptions came as Ukraine faces growing pressure from the US, with Trump pushing Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian energy facilities. The US president said on Tuesday that Washington had not cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine, another concern for the country.
Cherniev, the Ukrainian lawmaker, confirmed on Thursday that the US continues to share intelligence with Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Russia has intensified its ballistic missile attacks against Ukraine, firing dozens overnight. Recent attacks have targeted Kyiv and Ukrainian energy facilities.

China opens joint airfield in Laos with eyes on its military role
China’s newly opened joint military airfield in Laos is Beijing’s first overseas facility focused on air power
BANGKOK -- China's new airfield in Laos is a work in progress, with satellite imagery showing many areas where construction appeared to be ongoing even as it was officially opened at a September ceremony.
The airport jointly run with Laos is China's first military facility abroad focused on air power and the latest project in Beijing's efforts to project force beyond its borders, which includes a base in Djibouti, the Ream naval facility in Cambodia, the rapid militarization and expansion of islands in the South China sea and a growing carrier fleet.
Neighbors of Laos, a poor and landlocked Southeast Asian nation of about 8 million people, and defense experts are now keeping a close eye on the airport, less for what it currently is, but what it might become.
Like the Ream navy base in Cambodia, the Ban Keun airport, which is about 50 kilometers (31 miles) north of the Laotian capital Vientiane and the Thai border, doesn't “radically alter any balance of power or give China much ability to project force toward the Strait of Malacca that it doesn't already have,” said Greg Poling, director of the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
But the airport, with a potential for expansion, is certain to be a concern for neighboring Vietnam, which has competing territorial claims with Beijing in the South China Sea, said Poling, who suggested the Laos project was a “target of opportunity” for China, like the Ream naval base in Cambodia, which was renovated with Chinese money and now hosts a joint China-Cambodia training center.
“China's overseas basing strategy at the moment seems a lot more like playing roulette than poker,” he said. “Small bets over the board that occasionally pay off.”
The Ban Keun airport currently has a runway of about 2,000 meters (6,560 feet), a parallel taxiway and an apron with spots for two dozen aircraft to park, according to an Associated Press analysis of satellite images from two weeks ago.
The runway is already long enough to accommodate fighter aircraft, and the satellite images indicate there is enough room to extend it at least another 1,000 meters (3,280 feet), which could allow use by bigger aircraft, including bombers.
In announcing the opening of the facility last month, China's Ministry of Defense said the “China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy” at Ban Keun are intended to “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and “are not directed against any third party.”
China has not said whether it plans to permanently station aircraft and crews at the facility and did not immediately respond to questions. The state-run Global Times newspaper cited an expert saying there would be no independent Chinese garrison or exclusive use rights.
Laos' government did not respond to multiple requests for comment on how the airport would be jointly run or plans for its use.
For now, Laos' neighbors seem willing to take China's statement at face value, but also are watching closely to see how the facility takes further shape.
“Vietnam considers the Chinese military program as a training center primarily focused on training and humanitarian relief,” a Vietnamese official with knowledge of the internal discussions said.
“However, Vietnam also believes that China’s decision to establish a military program at this point is intended to strengthen its influence in Laos,” said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk with the press.
“China’s deployment of military forces in Laos would naturally place a certain degree of additional military pressure on Vietnam as well,” the official said.
Vietnam’s Foreign Ministry and Cambodia’s Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The military-run government of Myanmar, which neighbors Laos to the northwest and is embroiled in a bloody civil war, has not issued any statement.
The Institute for the Study of War said that while the Ban Keun facility is not yet equipped to provide the Chinese People's Liberation Army Air Force the ability to execute major combat operations like U.S. military bases overseas, its location alone already makes it a significant addition.
“The base would give the PLA alternate routes to access disputed areas of the South China Sea and strategic air routes around Vietnam,” the think tank said in a written analysis.
Thailand, which is a treaty ally of the United States but also regularly conducts joint military exercises with China, does not see the establishment of the facility close to the border as a threat to Thai security, but will continue to watch the situation, Defense Ministry spokesperson Rear Adm. Surasant Kongsiri told the AP.
Laos has the “legitimate freedom to choose and consent to agreements with a partnering country under their own sovereign rights, and within the international law and norm,” he said. “However, Thailand will continue to monitor on the development concerned as part of our routine security assessment. This same response also goes for the Ream Naval Base.”
On a broader level, the airfield could complicate U.S. strategy for the defense of Taiwan, should China ever decide to take the democratically self-governed island by force, which President Xi Jinping has not ruled out for the territory that China claims as its own, said Evan Laksmana, a Singapore-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The Laos airfield is much farther from Taiwan than considerably larger air bases in mainland China, but could provide an alternate landing strip for damaged aircraft and a place for repairs. The facility could conveniently be supplied by a new high-speed rail line connecting China's Yunnan province to the Laotian capital that was a signature project of Xi's Belt and Road initiative, Laksmana said.
“This complicates how the U.S. may have to think,” he said. “Does this mean the U.S. would have to attack a joint facility in Southeast Asia?”
Laos is one of Southeast Asia's poorest nations and deeply in debt to China for the new railway and many other infrastructure projects. While the airfield does improve Laos' strategic balance with its more powerful neighbors, Laksmana said, it may have also been an opportunity for China to use its leverage to build a facility where it can hone its abilities to operate an air base on foreign soil.
“For me, the opportunity is less about the war-fighting part but the familiarity with overseas engagements and activities,” he said.
Even though it is billed as a facility to train Laotian pilots, the Laos air force currently only has seven combat capable aircraft, according to the annual Military Balance report from the International Institute of Strategic Studies.
If the country plans to expand the air force, however, the joint agreement with China could help lead to a better deal for Chinese combat aircraft in the future, Poling said.
“But I suspect it's as much a target of opportunity for Laos as it is for China; not some major strategic vision driving the decision,” he said.

The company has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners. On the financial front, Zetwerk posted a consolidated net loss of ₹733 Cr in Q1 FY27 against operating revenue of ₹4,117.9 Cr.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.
ALSO READ: Bengal bypolls: Facebook restricts local news pages covering Opposition campaign in Rejinagar
On the same day, prominent local news outlet NBTV Bangla’s (@nbtvbngla) Facebook page was also restricted in India for seven days following the same notification. With over five lakh followers, the outlet reported critically on issues of the government or law enforcement in the context of the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls.
Alt News learnt that the two videos uploaded by the Facebook page of NBTV which were restricted in India directly addressed allegations of voting malpractices in the Rejinagar by-election.
The first of the two videos — both of which are still accessible on Instagram — shows a woman claiming that voters in Rejinagar were being intimidated away from the polling booths. A man also appears in this video, alleging that not even 10 voters had been able to cast their votes.
View this post on Instagram
Another video shows allegations being levelled by voters of the Mirzapur Gram Panchayat area in Rejinagar. “Who I choose to vote for is entirely my own decision. They marked our fingers with ink and sent us home, even though we had not yet cast our votes,” a man appearing in the video claims.
View this post on Instagram
“It is not the first time this has happened. Several of our social media posts have been restricted in the past,” Zeba Noshin, a reporter at NBTV, told Alt News.
Notably, the notices received by Congress’ Murshidabad district page and NBTV Bangla state that the account had been restricted pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or official complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being flagged by Meta’s own content-moderation process.

A video uploaded on Facebook by Bengali digital media outlet Inscript.me was restricted in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 on the day of the polls, October 6. A representative of the platform told Alt News that the banned video was regarding allegations of rigging in Rejinagar.
The title of the video visible on the notice sent by Meta reads, “People of Rejinagar allege rigging in byelection”.
On October 9, another Facebook post by Inscript.me, a report on Rahul Gandhi’s detainment by Delhi Police during the protests demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, was also restricted.
A Facebook user named Diya Maity also alleged that her page with close to 2.5 lakh followers had been restricted for seven days. She was also posting content on the alleged election rigging in the Rejinagar constituency.

The October 6 bypolls were necessitated in Murshidabad’s Rejinagar and East Medinipur’s Nandigram, after AJUP chief Humayun Kabir and Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari chose to vacate these two seats respectively, having secured victory in two constituencies apiece.
Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency, Nandigram has a Muslim population of around 27 per cent. He vacated this seat, and retained Bhabanipur, where he defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee.

Opposition leaders repeatedly alleged that the BJP was manipulating votes and applying pressure tactics in the lead up to the polls. On the day of polling, the AJUP chief was taken into custody by the police after a heated altercation. He was released from the Rejinagar police station after spending 12 hours in custody.

Massive brawl at 8-year-old’s football game sparks investigation into whether adults were sports betting on the kids
Police have yet to make any arrests over of the brawl

A football game between 8-year-olds descended into a brawl, and now police are investigating whether adults were betting on the kids, sparking the brawl
Over the weekend in Winter Haven, Florida, two teams of 8-year-olds met for a football game. However, a massive brawl broke out when one of the adults attacked an opposing coach, according to Fox 13.
Video released by the Polk County Sheriff’s Office showed kids and adults running around in the middle of the field during the brawl. One person was on the ground as the crowd formed, and some threw punches.
Kids in football gear walked around as parents either joined in or tried to separate groups fighting.
Now, sheriff’s officials are investigating whether betting played a role.
The fight eventually stopped when police showed up, but one person told authorities that parents were gambling on the game before the scrum.
"If you're at these youth sporting events, and you're gambling on these teams, we're going to go undercover and look for that conduct, and we'll arrest you quick. That's totally inappropriate on every level," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said.
The sheriff seemed at a loss for words over the allegation, telling WFLA: “Who would think that we would have to have undercover investigations at children’s sporting events because they’re gambling? Are you kidding me?”
Investigators admitted they have no video evidence to prove the claim.
So far, no one has been arrested in the case, and police have not determined who started the fight.
Police will try to identify the people involved, according to Fox 13. The suspects could face misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct or affray.
There could also be additional charges if police determine betting was part of the game.
Sheriff’s deputies will also be at future football games to make sure there is no more violence.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met India’s Asian Games medal-winners here on Thursday and said the country is not just becoming a stronger force in terms of performance but also evolving into a “credible host” for major international events.
The PM posed for pictures with the medal-winners and was presented with memorabilia ranging from signed jerseys to a bow from 17-year-old recurve archery sensation Kumkum Mohod, who won two gold medals (individual and women’s team) and a silver (mixed team) at the recently-concluded Games.
The contingent was accompanied by top officials of their respective governing bodies, including International Cricket Council (ICC) Chairman Jay Shah and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) President P T Usha among others. Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya was also present during the interaction that took place at the Major Dhyan Chand Stadium.
“You have made 140 crore Indians proud. The biggest success is to make the tri-colour fly high. That’s why your success is not just yours but it belongs to crores of our countrymen. I congratulate you on behalf of the entire country,” the PM said in his address to the medal winners.
“India is emerging in establishing itself as a credible and hospitable country for international sports events. We are bidding for the 2036 Olympics and it is our resolve that we will host the games,” he asserted.
India won 85 medals at the Asian Games, including 21 gold. The count was lower than the 106 medals achieved in the previous edition in Hangzhou but the performance of India’s Games debutants was heartening as they claimed 41 medals for the country.
“I especially want to congratulate our women athletes, they contributed 38 medals to our tally and 11 of those medals were gold,” Modi said, lauding the cricket teams, the hockey teams and the performance of archers, who won five gold medals.
ALSO READ: Sports Ministry reviews India’s Asian Games performance, questions raised over injured athletes
“The women’s hockey team ended a 44-year wait with its gold medal, it is highly appreciable,” he added.
The entire men’s T20 team led by Shreyas Iyer, which has a match against the West Indies in Bengaluru on Saturday, was in attendance, along with the women’s team, which is due to take on Zimbabwe in a T20I in Raipur on Friday.
Harmanpreet Kaur, who captained the side to the Asiad gold before stepping down from her role a few days ago, was also present and gave a jersey signed by the medal-winning team to the PM. Her successor Smriti Mandhana also posed alongside her.
Golfer Pranavi Urs gave Modi her glove and a golf ball in a frame.
“ Sankalp aur sapne ek din mein poore nahi hote (Dreams are not achieved in a day). It takes years of hard work and dedication. In the last 12 years, India has shown patience and worked hard to create a sports ecosystem,” he said.
“There was a time when India would win very few medals at big event. The country did not know so many sports. We resolved to end this pessimism and the result is our increasing representation on the global stage.
“Today India is winning medals even in those sports in which we had never won a medal in the history of the Asian Games before,” said Modi, referring to first-time Asiad medals in Mixed Martial Arts, Soft Tennis and some sailing competitions.
“A transparent system is in place for sports now,” he added.
He also highlighted the direct financial support to athletes, including a Rs. 50,000 allowance under TOPS and funding for international coaching stints.
“If there is a need to go outside the country for coaching in any sport, the government is facilitating that too and providing financial assistance for it,” said Modi.
Looking ahead to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, India’s hosting of the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, and the aspiration to host the 2036 Olympics, he recalled his Red Fort announcement of a nationwide village-level talent hunt.
“These identified players will bring medals for India in the times to come,” he said.
Urging the medallists to shoulder the responsibility of mentoring the next generation, the Prime Minister asked them to visit schools and engage with children in their home towns.
“Perhaps, a word from you might give a child the courage to move ahead in sports,” he said.
